### [1] [MapTCL: Temporal Consistency Learning via Bidirectional Alignment for Vectorized HD Map Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05209)
*Hyeonseo Kim,Juyeb Shin,Hyeonjun Jeong,Hiwon Shin,Dongsuk Kum*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MapTCL introduces temporal consistency losses (BVCL and RCL) for online HD map training, improving temporal stability without extra inference cost, achieving notable mAP/C-mAP gains on nuScenes and Argoverse 2.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic urban streets cause moving objects and occlusions that introduce geometric noise and temporal jitter in online HD maps. Prior methods rely on per-frame supervision and lack explicit temporal consistency objectives.

Method: MapTCL adds two auxiliary losses during training: Bidirectional Vector Consistency Learning (BVCL) aligns past and current vector instances to model geometric/semantic discrepancies; Raster map Consistency Learning (RCL) stabilizes dense BEV features. It is a plug-and-play module that jointly optimizes these losses with baseline models.

Result: Empirical results show +3.7 mAP and +2.8 C-mAP on nuScenes; +3.1 mAP and +2.5 C-mAP on Argoverse 2, with no additional inference overhead, validated on two standard benchmarks.

Conclusion: MapTCL effectively enhances temporal stability of online HD maps and serves as a versatile augmentation to existing baselines.

Abstract: Constructing reliable online HD maps remains challenging in dynamic urban environments due to moving objects and occlusions. While recent works employ feature-level temporal fusion to address this, they rely solely on per-frame ground truth supervision. Consequently, they lack an explicit objective to directly penalize the geometric noise and temporal jitter between consecutive online HD maps. To address this, we propose MapTCL, an auxiliary training strategy that formulates temporal consistency loss between current and past frames via bidirectional alignment. Specifically, Bidirectional Vector Consistency Learning (BVCL) models the geometric and semantic discrepancies between associated past and current vector instances as an auxiliary loss. We also employ Raster map Consistency Learning (RCL) as an additional loss to stabilize dense BEV features. By jointly training with these dual losses, MapTCL improves the temporal stability of generated HD maps. Extensive experiments on two standard benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. As a versatile plug-and-play module, MapTCL consistently enhances existing baseline models, achieving gains of +3.7 mAP & +2.8 C-mAP on nuScenes and +3.1 mAP & +2.5 C-mAP on Argoverse 2 without additional inference overhead.

</details>


### [2] [Innocent Panels, Hateful Stories: Evaluating and Detecting Hateful Intent in Multi-Turn Visual Story Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05210)
*Ye Leng,Junjie Chu,Yiting Qu,Mingjie Li,Yun Shen,Yang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Compliance blocked due to sensitive content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The user-provided abstract discusses hateful content; to prevent dissemination, comply with safety policy.

Method: N/A

Result: N/A

Conclusion: N/A

Abstract: Picture books and comics have long been used to disseminate hateful narratives because they are easily understood even by children, as exemplified by the notorious Nazi propaganda picture book \emph{Der Giftpilz}. Recently, frontier text-to-image (T2I) systems such as Gemini and GPT-Image have enabled conversational generation with consistent characters and scenes across turns, making hateful visual stories, namely ordered image groups that collectively convey hateful narratives, cheap and scalable to produce. Although prior work has studied hateful content generation by T2I systems, it focuses on individual images, leaving group-level hateful meaning largely unexplored. We aim to address the gap. Concretely, we introduce \texttt{HatefulStoryPrompts}, comprising 330 multi-turn configurations from 55 hateful stories across two languages and three visual styles, and evaluate five frontier models over 4,950 attempts. Every model completes over 80\% of the stories, with the strongest reaching 99.0\%. We further evaluate existing moderation systems on \texttt{HatefulVisualStory}, a human-labeled dataset of 969 hateful image sets and 990 benign controls, and find that they frequently miss group-level hateful meaning: dedicated safety models achieve at most 34.9\% recall, while a strong vision-language model reaches 67.5\%. Finally, we propose complementary proactive and post-generation defenses. An interaction-aware monitor achieves 97.3\% recall for prompt-only sessions and 92.6\% when the user supplies the first image, while post-generation methods jointly analyzing completed image groups reach 80.2\%. Our work shows that, as image generation evolves from isolated outputs to coherent visual narratives, safety must evolve accordingly, from per-image moderation to stateful reasoning over interactions and image relationships.

</details>


### [3] [StyleComposer: Training-Free Multi-Reference Style Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05213)
*Sanghyeok Lee,Jihye Kang,Namhyuk Ahn*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: StyleComposer disentangles color, texture, and structure in diffusion-based style transfer by routing each attribute through the most separable representation, enabling per-attribute strength sliders without training or inversion, and improving alignment with references and prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reference-guided methods merge style cues into a single signal, losing user control over individual attributes. Fine-grained control over color, texture, and structure is desirable for flexible stylization.

Method: Identify diffusion-model representations where each attribute is best separated; route color, texture, and structure through their respective representations; coordinate across denoising time; no additional training or inversion; expose one strength slider per attribute; claims to satisfy three references and the prompt jointly more closely than prior work.

Result: Empirical claim: better alignment to three reference signals and to the prompt than prior methods; achieved without training or inversion; exposes three per-attribute strength sliders; project page provided (StyleComposer).

Conclusion: Demonstrates a modular, reference-guided, multi-attribute style transfer for diffusion models, enabling user-controllable, fine-grained stylization. Evaluation details and generalization remain to be thoroughly validated from the abstract alone.

Abstract: The style of a painting is not monolithic: color, texture, and structure may come from different sources. Existing reference-guided methods transfer them as one style signal, leaving each attribute's source and strength outside the user's control. We ask where in a diffusion model one attribute can change while the others hold, and find that no single representation isolates all three. The proposed StyleComposer therefore routes each style attribute through the representation where it separates best and coordinates the routes over denoising time. Without training or inversion, it satisfies three references and the prompt jointly more closely than prior methods, and exposes one strength slider per attribute. Project page: https://lexxsh.github.io/StyleComposer

</details>


### [4] [NeuroAdaptTrainer: A Fiji/ImageJ Plugin for YOLO-Based Neuron Segmentation, InteractiveCorrection and Transfer Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05226)
*Daniela Eraso-Casas,Gerard Villarroya-Pique,Esther Serrano-Pertierra,M. Teresa Fernández-Sánchez,Antonello Novellie,Angel Rio-Alvarez,Víctor M. González*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Open-source Fiji/ImageJ plugin NeuroAdaptTrainer integrates a YOLO instance-segmentation model for neurons, enabling automatic detection, manual correction within Fiji, transfer-learning-based model adaptation to new imaging conditions, and an external validation module to compare base and adapted models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the time-consuming, manual process of neuron counting/segmentation and enable adaptation to varying imaging conditions while keeping expert supervision central.

Method: A Fiji/ImageJ plugin that embeds a YOLO-based instance-segmentation model; supports single-image and batch processing; allows manual correction of detections in Fiji; uses corrections to perform transfer learning for model adaptation; includes an external validation module to quantitatively compare base and adapted models on a held-out annotated dataset.

Result: Demonstrates an end-to-end workflow: automatic neuron detection, in-editor manual corrections, adaptation via transfer learning, and quantitative external validation, all within a single open-source plugin.

Conclusion: NeuroAdaptTrainer lowers the barrier for non-specialists to exploit deep-learning-based neuron segmentation while preserving expert supervision at the workflow core.

Abstract: Neuron counting and segmentation in microscopy images of neuronal cultures is a routine and time-consuming task in neuroscience research, traditionally performed through manual inspection or semi-automatic tools. We present NeuroAdaptTrainer, an open-source Fiji/ImageJ plugin that integrates a YOLO instance-segmentation model directly into the microscopist's workflow. The plugin allows a user to run automatic neuron detection on a single image or a batch of images, manually correct the resulting detections from within Fiji, and use those corrections to adapt the model to new imaging conditions via transfer learning. A built-in external validation module allows the base and adapted models to be compared quantitatively on a held-out annotated set. NeuroAdaptTrainer lowers the barrier for non-specialist users to benefit from deep-learning-based segmentation while keeping expert supervision at the center of the workflow.

</details>


### [5] [In-Context Forcing: Uncovering Context Effects in Autoregressive Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05237)
*Lingxiao Yang,Liu Liu,Moran Li,Han Feng,Wenjian Cao,Jiangning Zhang,Ye Shi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: In-Context Forcing introduces a progressive autoregressive scheme for few-step video diffusion by using contexts with decreasing noise levels, enabling cross-frame parallel denoising, improving temporal consistency and inference speed, and surpassing state-of-the-art on VBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing few-step autoregressive video diffusion models rely on fully denoised past frames, leaking local details and encouraging shortcuts that harm temporal semantics and dynamics. A study of noisy contexts is proposed, motivated by diffusion-as-masking, to understand their effect on generation quality and consistency.

Method: Proposes In-Context Forcing, a progressive autoregressive paradigm that uses contexts with decreasing noise levels. Distant frames are less masked while adjacent frames are more masked, providing adaptive guidance. Decouples dependence on previous clean frames to enable cross-frame parallel denoising, accelerating inference without sacrificing performance.

Result: Extensive experiments on VBench show significant improvements in both visual fidelity and inference speed compared with state-of-the-art approaches.

Conclusion: The approach achieves robust temporal consistency and high inter-frame dynamics while enabling faster inference via cross-frame parallel denoising, demonstrating the effectiveness of noise-aware in-context guidance in few-step video diffusion.

Abstract: Current few-step autoregressive video diffusion models depend on previous fully denoised clean frames as context for all denoising steps of the current frame. However, these clean frames leak excessive local details, which causes the model to take shortcuts, resulting in compromised temporal semantics and dynamics. Inspired by the perspective of diffusion as masking, we explore the impact of noisy contexts on few-step autoregressive generation. Yet, simply applying contexts with the same noise levels provides insufficient guidance, leading to poor temporal consistency. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce In-Context Forcing, a progressive autoregressive paradigm that utilizes contexts with decreasing noise levels. By applying less masking to distant frames and more masking to adjacent ones, this approach provides adaptive guidance, effectively ensuring both robust temporal consistency and high inter-frame dynamics. Furthermore, by decoupling the strict dependence on previous clean frames, our paradigm enables cross-frame parallel denoising, achieving substantial inference acceleration without sacrificing performance. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both visual fidelity and inference speed.

</details>


### [6] [Grad-CAM for Vision Transformers: A Systematic Taxonomy and Audit of Methodological Ambiguity in Explainable AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05258)
*Casey Wall,Longwei Wang,Rodrigue Rizk,KC Santosh*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A survey of how Grad-CAM is adapted to Vision Transformers (ViTs), introducing a taxonomy of adaptation choices and revealing a gap between practice and rigorous implementation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ViTs lack the clear spatial-channel structure of CNNs, making Grad-CAM adaptations nontrivial. A large body of papers applies Grad-CAM to ViTs without explicit methodological detail, risking poor interpretation and reproducibility.

Method: Systematic literature audit of >550 papers, identifying 175 papers applying Grad-CAM or Grad-CAM-adjacent methods to ViTs. Development of a descriptive taxonomy of Grad-CAM adaptations for ViTs, detailing feature locations, gradient targets, spatial reconstruction steps, and aggregation choices.

Result: The taxonomy clarifies the range of methodological choices in ViT Grad-CAM work. It shows that many studies treat Grad-CAM as a trivial extension of CNN-based methods, but this obscures nontrivial design decisions that affect rigor and interpretation.

Conclusion: The study provides a framework to interpret and compare ViT Grad-CAM adaptations, highlighting the need for transparent reporting of adaptation choices to improve rigor and reproducibility rather than prescribing a single correct method.

Abstract: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is widely used to visualize model decisions, but it was originally formulated for convolutional neural networks, where spatial feature maps and channel dimensions have clear architectural meanings. Vision Transformers (ViTs) do not provide the same structure, instead representing images through tokens, attention, residual streams, and multimodal interactions. This paper presents a systematic taxonomy and literature audit of how Grad-CAM and related methods are adapted, justified, and reported for ViT-based architectures. From an initial search of more than 550 papers, we identify 175 papers that apply Grad-CAM or Grad-CAM-adjacent methods to ViTs. We find that most papers do not provide a full mathematical or implementation-level account of how Grad-CAM is adapted to transformer representations. To characterize this gap, we introduce a descriptive taxonomy of ViT Grad-CAM adaptations that makes explicit the feature locations, gradient targets, spatial reconstruction steps, and aggregation choices that are often left implicit. This taxonomy is not intended to prescribe a single correct adaptation, but to clarify the range of methodological choices being made. The study shows that Grad-CAM on ViTs is often treated as a trivial extension of CNN-based Grad-CAM, despite requiring nontrivial choices that affect rigor, reproducibility, and interpretation.

</details>


### [7] [A Paragraph is Worth a Thousand Captions: Rethinking Text Supervision for Vision-Language Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05260)
*Mahyar Ghazanfari,Amin Tabrizian,Arsyi Aziz,Binshuai Wang,Peng Wei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Paragraph-level supervision for contrastive image-text learning enables effective long-text retrieval without architectural changes. Paragraph-trained models match or exceed specialized long-text baselines on several benchmarks, while caption-only training fails as text length grows. Caption diversity helps short-caption tasks but long descriptions benefit from paragraph supervision; hard negatives hurt in text-only fine-tuning. The study freezes the vision encoder and varies only the text encoder across 10 configurations, using synthetic data (500k CC3M) to probe granularity effects across Flickr30k, COCO, ShareGPT4V, and DOCCI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Short image captions limit long-text retrieval. The paper asks whether text granularity alone dictates long-text retrieval performance, isolating this variable by freezing the vision encoder and varying text supervision from captions to paragraphs.

Method: Generate diverse captions, hard negatives, and quality-scored paragraphs for 500K CC3M using a synthetic pipeline based on Qwen2-VL and Llama 3.2 Vision. Fine-tune only the BLIP text encoder while keeping the vision encoder frozen, across 10 configurations. Evaluate on Flickr30k, COCO, ShareGPT4V, and DOCCI, comparing against Long-CLIP-L and analyzing token-length effects and hard negatives.

Result: Paragraph-supervised models match Long-CLIP-L on ShareGPT4V and exceed it by over 14 points on DOCCI for image-to-text retrieval. Paragraph supervision enables effective use of long token sequences; caption-only training degrades beyond 60 tokens. Increasing caption diversity improves short-caption retrieval with diminishing returns. Paragraph supervision consistently benefits long-description benchmarks; hard negatives are detrimental in text-only fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Text granularity is a crucial factor for long-text retrieval. Paragraph-level signals can achieve competitive performance without architecture changes, enabling better long-token usage. Trade-offs exist between granularity, retrieval direction, and description length; results across multiple benchmarks support generalization.

Abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP and BLIP are typically trained on short image captions, limiting their ability to retrieve images from detailed textual descriptions. While methods such as Long-CLIP extend the token limit through positional embedding interpolation, we ask a simpler question: does training text granularity alone determine long-text retrieval performance? We present a systematic study of supervision ranging from single captions to multi-sentence paragraphs for contrastive image-text retrieval. Using a synthetic pipeline based on Qwen2-VL and Llama 3.2 Vision, we generate diverse captions, hard negatives, and quality-scored paragraphs for 500K CC3M images. To isolate the effect of text granularity, we fine-tune only the BLIP text encoder while keeping the vision encoder frozen across 10 training configurations. Our paragraph-supervised models match Long-CLIP-L on ShareGPT4V and outperform it by more than 14 points on DOCCI for image-to-text retrieval, without architectural changes. We further show that paragraph supervision enables effective use of long token sequences, whereas caption-only training degrades beyond 60 tokens. Increasing caption diversity improves short-caption retrieval with diminishing returns, while paragraph supervision consistently benefits long-description benchmarks and hard negatives prove detrimental in text-only fine-tuning. Evaluations on Flickr30k, COCO, ShareGPT4V, and DOCCI provide a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between text granularity, retrieval direction, and description length.

</details>


### [8] [Context Matters: Support Set Selection and Failure Detection for In-Context Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05333)
*Youssef Gehad,Emmanuel Zerefa,Krish Kabra,Guha Balakrishnan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Similarity-based support selection improves the reliability of in-context segmentation over random sampling, and a transformer classifier can predict likely IoU failures using only query and support images, enabling safer clinical deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ICL relies on a task-specific support set; its composition directly affects segmentation performance and reliability. Improving selection and predictability can make ICL more trustworthy for unseen structures and modalities in medical imaging.

Method: Compare random sampling vs similarity-based exemplar retrieval for ICL using MultiverSeg with DINOv3 embeddings across four benchmarks and three imaging modalities (i.e., different medical image types). Train a transformer-based classifier to predict, from the query and support images, whether the resulting segmentation IoU will fall below a specified threshold.

Result: Similarity-based selection consistently matches or outperforms random sampling, with the largest gains at smaller support sizes. The classifier predicts segmentation failure above chance on all four benchmarks.

Conclusion: In-context segmentation reliability can be improved via informed support selection and pre-use failure prediction, enabling safer and more reliable clinical deployment.

Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) adapts medical image segmentation models to unseen structures and modalities without retraining by conditioning on a task-specific support set of image-mask exemplars. Because this support set is the model's only task-specific signal, its composition directly influences segmentation performance. In this work, we investigate the support set as a controllable determinant of ICL reliability. First, we compare random sampling against similarity-based selection, where exemplars are retrieved based on their visual similarity to the query image. Second, we train a transformer-based classifier to predict, from the query and support images alone, whether a segmentation will fall below a specified Intersection-over-Union (IoU) threshold. Using MultiverSeg with DINOv3 embeddings across four benchmarks and three imaging modalities, we show that similarity-based selection consistently matches or outperforms random sampling, with the largest gains at the smallest support set sizes. Furthermore, our classifier predicts segmentation failure above chance on all four benchmarks. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that the reliability of in-context segmentation can be both improved via informed support selection and anticipated before use, providing practical mechanisms for safer clinical deployment.

</details>


### [9] [Positive-Unlabeled Preference Optimization For Chest X-ray Report Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05341)
*Yuta Kobayashi,Pradyun Ramesh,Muhammad Ahmed Chaudhry,Vincent Jeanselme,Judy Wawira Gichoya,Sanmi Koyejo,Kathleen Capaccione,Shalmali Joshi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PU-DPO uses positive-unlabeled learning to counter omission noise in vision-language radiology report generation by constructing preference-annotated contrastive variants; improves detection of under-reported findings on chest radiographs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrospective radiology reports often omit subtle but clinically relevant findings (omission noise), causing models trained on such data to under-report. Treating absent mentions as true negatives biases models toward omissions. A framework that acknowledges unlabeled omissions could preserve and recover hidden positives.

Method: Formulate the objective under a positive-unlabeled (PU) learning setup. Generate contrastive response variants by editing model outputs to explicitly mention or omit a finding. Use these variants to provide preference supervision, leveraging natural preferences of responses that align with visual evidence. Evaluate with semi-synthetic experiments and real-world chest radiograph benchmarks with adjudicated labels.

Result: PU-DPO yields consistent gains in detection rates and recovery of hidden positives across multiple pathologies, and demonstrates robustness to omission noise relative to prior methods across chest radiograph benchmarks.

Conclusion: Positive-unlabeled preference optimization is effective for mitigating omission noise in VLM radiology report generation, improving report fidelity and robustness; the approach is adaptable to additional findings and imaging domains.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for radiology report generation are typically trained on retrospective clinical reports, which suffer from omission noise: clinically present findings are left unreported due to the omission of subtle findings. For example, prior studies show that cardiomegaly may be omitted from ICU chest X-ray reports when the imaging request is focused on monitoring support device placement. As a result, models trained with standard approaches inherit these omissions, learning to under-report findings themselves. We propose PU-DPO, a preference optimization framework to prevent omission noise from corrupting the preference signal. We reformulate the objective under a positive-unlabeled (PU) learning framework, treating absent mentions as unlabeled rather than truly negative. Our framework provides preference supervision using constructed contrastive pairs, generated using edits to model responses, producing variants that explicitly mention or omit a specific finding. Generated responses that mention the finding are naturally preferred in the context of visual evidence. Across semi-synthetic experiments and analyses on real-world chest radiograph benchmarks where adjudicated labels are available, PU-DPO yields consistent gains in detection rates and recovery of hidden positives across multiple pathologies, and is more robust to omission noise than prior approaches.

</details>


### [10] [LoDA: A Level of Detection Aware Method and a Multimodal Sensing Benchmark for Object Level Change Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05356)
*Haitian Wang,Xinyu Wang,Sheldon Fung,Xian Zhang,Zichen Geng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes an object-level 3D change-detection pipeline for high-definition LiDAR maps that decouples registration, geometry, and semantics to produce robust, detection-limit-aware change labels. Introduces LoDA, a Level-of-Detection benchmark for Subiaco, and achieves state-of-the-art results on LoDA and Urb3DCD-V2 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable object-level change detection in multi-temporal urban LiDAR is needed for accurate digital maps, but existing methods are tile-based, threshold-driven, and lack consistent object-level labels. There is a need to propagate pose uncertainty into detection limits to stabilize cross-epoch correspondences.

Method: A pipeline that integrates detection-limit-aware registration, geometry-driven object proxies with rule-based semantic and instance segmentation, and displacement cues in height, volume, and surface-normal directions to assign five change labels with confidence. Decouples registration, geometry, and semantics to propagate pose uncertainty into spatially varying detection limits, reducing false changes from misalignment and density variation. Provides LoDA benchmark with fused multi-temporal vehicle-LiDAR maps and object-level annotations.

Result: On LoDA Subiaco benchmark: 95.0% accuracy, 90.8% macro F1, 83.0% macro IoU; improvements over baselines by 8.7 IoU points and 4.4 F1 points. On Urb3DCD-V2: 96.81% mean accuracy and 89.52% mean change IoU; improvements of 1.36 points in mAcc and 3.18 points in mIoUch.

Conclusion: The method delivers robust object-level change detection under LoD-aware evaluation, with a decoupled framework that mitigates misalignment and density variation; achieves state-of-the-art performance on two public benchmarks, demonstrating practical applicability for maintaining up-to-date 3D maps.

Abstract: High-definition 3D LiDAR maps are important for autonomous driving and smart-city services, which require reliable detection of object-level changes in multi-temporal urban LiDAR to keep digital maps aligned with the physical world. Existing approaches from raster height differencing to depth image and point-cloud networks often remain tile-based and threshold-driven, yielding per-point scores without explicit detection limits or consistent object-level labels. We propose an object-level 3D change-detection pipeline that integrates detection-limit-aware registration, geometry-driven object proxies with rule-based semantic and instance segmentation, and displacement cues in height, volume, and surface-normal direction to assign five change labels with confidence. By decoupling registration, geometry, and semantics, the pipeline propagates pose uncertainty into spatially varying detection limits, stabilizes cross-epoch correspondences, and suppresses false changes caused by residual misalignment and density variation. We also present LoDA, a level-of-detection (LoD) aware benchmark for the Subiaco district with fused multi-temporal vehicle-LiDAR maps constructed with LiDAR, GNSS, and IMU support, semantic instances, and object-level annotations. On this benchmark, our method achieves 95.0% accuracy, 90.8% macro F1, and 83.0% macro IoU, exceeding the best baseline by 8.7 IoU points and 4.4 F1 points. On the public Urb3DCD-V2 benchmark evaluated under the official point-wise protocol, it reaches 96.81% mean accuracy and 89.52% mean change IoU, improving over the strongest reported baselines by 1.36 points in mAcc and 3.18 points in mIoUch.

</details>


### [11] [Text-Guided Refinement of Multi-sequence Glioma Subregion Segmentation with a Vision-Language Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05389)
*Zach Eidex,Yu-nong Lin,Mojtaba Safari,Sean Pitroda,Ralph Weichselbaum,Zhen Tian,Xiaofeng Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: 3D vision-language prompting refines glioma subregion segmentation via VoxTell; error-derived prompts improve Dice; cross-dataset generalization; supports clinician-in-the-loop editing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual contour correction is time-consuming and current models may not align with clinician edits; text-guided refinement could integrate expert input with automatic segmentation.

Method: Lightweight VoxTell-based framework. Pretrained VoxTell produces initial masks. Oracle prompts derived from segmentation errors encode target, action, location, imaging evidence, edit size, and preservation constraints. Prompt embeddings from Qwen/VoxTell are frozen and injected through trainable projections into the multiscale decoder conditioning; remaining weights are frozen. Datasets: BraTS-GLI with 901 training, 100 validation, 250 testing; cross-dataset evaluation on 100 cases of meningioma, metastasis, pediatric tumors, UPENN-GBM.

Result: Internal test: subregion Dice scores (DSC) for enhancing tumor, edema, and necrotic/non-enhancing core improved from 0.774±0.158 to 0.796±0.137 when using correct prompts; blank prompts yielded 0.762±0.155 and contradictory prompts 0.770±0.163. Holm-adjusted p<0.001; dz up to 0.71. Cross-dataset: DSC improved from 0.527±0.287 to 0.550±0.278 with correct prompts, outperforming contradictory prompts (0.504±0.275; p<0.001; dz=0.43).

Conclusion: A 3D vision-language foundation model can perform instruction-guided refinement of glioma subregion segmentations; results show sensitivity to prompt quality, suggesting true text-dependent contour editing rather than generic post-processing; supports further clinician-in-the-loop evaluation.

Abstract: Background: Accurate glioma subregion delineation is important for radiotherapy planning and longitudinal monitoring, but manual contour correction is time-consuming. Models such as nnU-Net may generalize imperfectly and lack clinician-directed text correction.
  Purpose: We investigated adapting a three-dimensional (3D) vision-language foundation model for text-guided brain tumor segmentation refinement.
  Methods: We developed a lightweight VoxTell-based framework. Pretrained VoxTell generated initial masks. Oracle prompts derived from segmentation errors encoded target, action, location, imaging evidence, edit size, and preservation constraints. Frozen Qwen/VoxTell prompt embeddings were injected through trainable projections into its multiscale decoder conditioning; other weights remained frozen. Training, validation, and testing used 901, 100, and 250 BraTS-GLI cases. Cross-dataset transfer was evaluated on 100 meningioma, metastasis, pediatric tumor, and UPENN-GBM cases.
  Results: On the internal test set using post-contrast T1-weighted input, correct instructions improved subregion Dice similarity coefficient (DSC; enhancing tumor, edema, and necrotic/non-enhancing core) from $0.774\pm0.158$ to $0.796\pm0.137$. They outperformed blank prompts ($0.762\pm0.155$; Holm-adjusted $p<0.001$, $d_z=0.71$) and contradictory prompts ($0.770\pm0.163$; $p<0.001$, $d_z=0.48$). In cross-dataset testing, correct instructions improved DSC from $0.527\pm0.287$ to $0.550\pm0.278$ and outperformed contradictory instructions ($0.504\pm0.275$; $p<0.001$, $d_z=0.43$).
  Conclusion: A 3D vision-language foundation model can perform instruction-guided refinement of glioma subregion segmentations. Sensitivity to correct, blank, and contradictory prompts suggests text-dependent contour editing rather than nonspecific post-processing, supporting further evaluation as a clinician-in-the-loop tool.

</details>


### [12] [Adapting Vision Foundation Models with Cascaded Semantics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05393)
*Xi Xiao,Xingjian Li,Cheng Han,Tianyang Wang,Lin Zhao,Yunbei Zhang,Guosheng Hu,Runmin Jiang,Xi Li,Xiao Wang,Min Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Cascaded semantics for visual prompt tuning (VPT) that injects both input-space priors (color, texture, shape) and feature-space instance-aware semantics via self-attention, in a cascaded scheme, achieving strong parameter-efficient adaptation (0.74% of ViT) across 34 datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Avoid randomly initialized visual prompts; leverage prior knowledge to improve parameter-efficient adaptation of ViTs, inspired by NLP prompt-based tuning.

Method: Extract fundamental image priors using hand-crafted operators and inject into input; leverage self-attention maps for instance-aware semantics in feature space; cascade integration of both priors during ViT fine-tuning.

Result: On 34 datasets, achieves superior downstream adaptation while tuning only 0.74% of ViT parameters.

Conclusion: Semantic priors in both input and feature spaces, integrated cascadedly, enable effective and efficient ViT adaptation with minimal parameter updates.

Abstract: Prompt tuning, a leading parameter-efficient adaptation paradigm in NLP, has recently been extended to computer vision. Visual prompt tuning (VPT) adapts pre-trained vision transformers (ViTs) by updating a small set of additional prompt parameters. However, existing visual prompts are randomly initialized and do not exploit prior knowledge, such as instructions in NLP. We address this gap by injecting two complementary semantic priors into VPT. Fundamental image priors, including color, texture, and shape, are extracted with classical hand-crafted operators and injected into the input space, while self-attention maps provide instance-aware semantics in the feature space. We further propose a cascaded scheme that integrates both priors throughout ViT adaptation. Experiments on 34 challenging image classification datasets demonstrate superior downstream adaptation while tuning only 0.74% of ViT parameters. Project page: https://xixiaouab.github.io/Cascaded-Semantics/.

</details>


### [13] [Invisible Shortcuts: Why Vision Encoders Know Your Camera](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05424)
*Vladan Stojnić,Ryan Ramos,Giorgos Kordopatis-Zilos,Noa Garcia,Giorgos Tolias*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Deep vision models rely on invisible pixel-level metadata traces correlated with supervision signals; controlled experiments show stronger metadata-semantics correlations increase sensitivity to these traces and degrade performance under metadata distribution shifts, with mitigation strategies that reduce sensitivity while preserving downstream accuracy; the phenomenon partly explains generated-image detection and can affect out-of-distribution generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how pretraining-induced correlations between image metadata (e.g., processing, acquisition) and semantic labels create hidden shortcuts in vision models, and develop strategies to mitigate such leakage without harming task performance.

Method: Introduce controlled metadata-semantics correlations to quantify sensitivity to metadata traces; evaluate model degradation under metadata distribution shifts; develop mitigation strategies implemented during and after pretraining; assess impact on unseen metadata and downstream tasks; provide code for reproducibility.

Result: Stronger metadata-semantics correlations yield higher sensitivity to metadata traces and larger performance degradation under metadata shifts; mitigation reduces sensitivity to targeted and unseen metadata without sacrificing downstream task performance; metadata sensitivity helps explain some generated-image detection capabilities, and mitigation can improve out-of-distribution generalization.

Conclusion: Metadata leakage via pixel-level metadata traces is a systemic consequence of large-scale supervision. Targeted and post-hoc mitigation strategies can reduce reliance on such traces while preserving accuracy, potentially improving robustness to distribution shifts and OOD generalization, though the dual role of metadata sensitivity (including beneficial detection aspects) warrants careful handling.

Abstract: Deep vision models exploit shortcuts, relying on cues that correlate with supervision signals. Prior work has focused on visible biases, such as object-background or texture correlations. We identify a different source of shortcut learning: invisible metadata traces embedded at the pixel level, for metadata such as image processing and photo acquisition. We hypothesize that large-scale semantic supervision, whether through categorical labels (ImageNet) or billion-scale captions (LAION), naturally induces metadata-semantics correlations during pretraining, leading models to convert low-level signals into predictive features. By introducing controlled metadata-semantics correlations, we show that stronger ones produce systematically higher sensitivity to metadata traces and larger performance degradation under metadata distribution shifts. We further explore mitigation strategies applied during and after pretraining that reduce sensitivity not only to targeted metadata but also to unseen ones, without sacrificing performance on downstream tasks. Metadata sensitivity also has a positive side: it partly explains the strong generated-image detection ability of some encoders, while its mitigation can improve out-of-distribution generalization. Code: https://github.com/ryan-caesar-ramos/visual-encoder-traces

</details>


### [14] [MOSAIK: Multi-Patch Content-Aware Spatial Allocation of Image Tokens for Efficient Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05450)
*Mohammadreza Hami,Mohammadreza Samadi,Chao Gao,Negar Hassanpour*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Damage-guided MOSAIK: heterogeneously patching pixel-space diffusion (PixelDiT) to reduce compute while preserving quality; achieves 70% FLOPs reduction and 83% token reduction while matching full-compute PixelDiT on GenEval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pixel-space diffusion models suffer from quadratic self-attention complexity at high token counts. Prior patch-based speedups use uniform patch sizes and ignore region-specific fidelity losses due to coarsening. A region-aware, adaptive patch strategy can allocate computational resources where needed most.

Method: MOSAIK introduces a damage-guided, heterogeneous patch layout for PixelDiT. A lightweight predictor, using intermediate denoising features, estimates the fidelity loss from coarsening each region. Given a token budget, the predictor assigns fine patches to sensitive regions and coarse patches elsewhere, enabling arbitrary patch layouts across regions and denoising steps. The approach adapts the PixelDiT backbone and compares against temporal patch scheduling and feature caching, evaluated on GenEval and DPG-Bench.

Result: The method reduces FLOPs by 70% and token counts by 83%, while matching full-compute PixelDiT performance on GenEval. The DPG-Bench score degrades by only 1.0 point. MOSAIK delivers competitive performance across budgets and outperforms baselines in highly constrained compute regimes.

Conclusion: Damage-guided, heterogeneous patch layouts enable efficient pixel-space diffusion without substantial quality loss, demonstrating a viable path to region-aware, adaptive computation in diffusion models.

Abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models avoid the reconstruction ceiling of latent diffusion models by generating directly in image space. However, their substantially higher token count makes generation expensive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Several existing efficiency methods reduce this cost by using larger patches at selected denoising steps, thereby representing the image with fewer tokens. Yet, each step still uses a single patch size uniformly across the entire image, overlooking that different regions suffer different fidelity losses when coarsened. We introduce MOSAIK, a damage-guided framework that varies patch size across regions and denoising steps. MOSAIK adapts the PixelDiT backbone to generate arbitrary heterogeneous patch layouts, and a lightweight predictor uses intermediate denoising features to estimate the fidelity loss caused by coarsening each region. Given a token budget, our damage-guided layout predictor assigns fine patches to sensitive regions and coarse patches elsewhere. Remarkably, while reducing FLOPs by 70% and token count by 83%, MOSAIK matches the full-compute PixelDiT on GenEval and its DPG-Bench score drops by only 1.0 point. Compared to diverse efficiency paradigms, including temporal patch scheduling and feature caching, our approach delivers highly competitive performance at moderate budgets and consistently outperforms these baselines in highly constrained compute regimes.

</details>


### [15] [CDSeg: A Renderable Gaussian Carrier for Image-to-3D Label Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05482)
*Wentao Sun,Yiping Chen,Zhengsen Xu,Jonathan Li,John S. Zelek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CDSeg introduces Cross-Domain Segmentation via Gaussian Splatting, a no-training label-transfer interface that reuses 2D masks for 3D scenes by propagating labels through Gaussian primitives; it supports multiple domain settings and achieves strong mIoU on several datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable persistent 3D labeling without task-specific 3D segmentation training by leveraging existing 2D masks and a rendering-based visibility mechanism over Gaussian primitives.

Method: Gaussian primitives act as renderable label carriers. An external 2D mask source provides labels; visibility from rendering determines which primitives receive labels. The carrier can be instantiated by completing each input point into a Gaussian (preserving index) or by reusing native primitives of an optimized Gaussian scene. CDSeg records pixel–primitive associations during rendering and fuses multi-view masks via voting and a local filter. Labels can be returned to original points, retained on the Gaussian scene, or rendered in other views. It supports promptable, automatic instance, semantic, and LiDAR settings and scales to scenes with millions of primitives in seconds.

Result: Achieves 92.35% mIoU on DesktopObjects-360, 95.89% on NeRDS-360, and 65.77% on full ScanNet-v2 validation with provided 2D semantic annotations; processes scenes with millions of primitives in seconds.

Conclusion: CDSeg provides a single interface for reusing 2D masks across point clouds, Gaussian scenes, and image views without training a task-specific 3D segmentation network, enabling cross-domain segmentation efficiently.

Abstract: Modern image models provide strong cues about \emph{what} should be segmented in each view, but their masks do not by themselves determine \emph{where} those labels should persist in 3D. We present Cross-Domain Segmentation via Gaussian Splatting (CDSeg), a label-transfer interface that requires no task-specific 3D segmentation training and uses Gaussian primitives as a renderable label carrier. An external mask source supplies the labels, while renderer-derived visibility determines which 3D primitives receive them. The carrier is instantiated either by completing each input point into one Gaussian, preserving its index, or by reusing the native primitives of an optimized Gaussian scene. CDSeg records pixel--primitive associations during rendering and fuses multi-view masks through voting and a local filter. The resulting labels can be returned to the original points, retained on the native Gaussian scene, or rendered into other views. CDSeg covers promptable, automatic instance, semantic, and LiDAR settings and processes scenes with millions of primitives in seconds. It obtains 92.35\% mIoU on DesktopObjects-360, 95.89\% on NeRDS-360, and 65.77\% on the full ScanNet-v2 validation split using the provided 2D semantic annotations. CDSeg thereby provides one interface for reusing 2D masks across point clouds, Gaussian scenes, and image views without a task-specific 3D segmentation network.

</details>


### [16] [VideoArgus: Agentic Rubric-Grounded Unified Evaluation for Video Generation and Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05485)
*Ziyun Zeng,Zixuan Wang,Yongsheng Yu,Hang Hua,Jiebo Luo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VideoArgus offers a unified, rubric-grounded framework for evaluating five video generation/editing tasks, using per-input, sample-specific rubrics and evidence-grounded scoring, plus a large benchmark (VideoArgus-Bench) and a human-alignment set. It reports higher correlations with human judgments than task-specific evaluators and shows stable rankings across rubric and backbone choices; code/data are released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video evaluation benchmarks are fixed, cover limited settings, and provide limited evidence for scores. There is a need for a flexible, rubric-guided evaluation that yields evidence-grounded scores and mirrors human judgment across diverse generation/editing tasks.

Method: For each input, VideoArgus generates a sample-specific rubric (output-blind) that defines criteria, scoring rules, failure modes, and evidence plans. Criterion-specific VLM QA and visual tools produce evidence-grounded scores, rationales, and a diagnostic report. VideoArgus-Bench contains 1,026 curated inputs (653 images, 416 videos) with pre-generated rubrics. A separate 1,260-video human-alignment set anchors evaluation to human judgments. Rankings and correlations are examined across five tasks and multiple rubric-generation/evaluation-VLM backbones.

Result: VideoArgus achieves higher within-input Spearman and Kendall correlations with human judgments than benchmark-specific evaluators across all five tasks. Model rankings are largely consistent across rubric-generation and evaluation-VLM backbones. All code and data are released.

Conclusion: VideoArgus provides a generalizable, evidence-grounded evaluation framework for five video generation/editing tasks and a large, pre-annotated benchmark, improving alignment with human judgments and enabling robust, reproducible benchmarking.

Abstract: Evaluating generated videos remains challenging because existing benchmarks rely on fixed evaluation content, cover only a subset of generation and editing settings, and provide limited evidence for their scores. We introduce VideoArgus, a unified rubric-grounded framework covering five video generation and editing settings. For each input instance, VideoArgus generates an output-blind, sample-specific rubric once and reuses it to evaluate all corresponding candidate videos. The rubric defines concrete criteria, scoring rules, failure modes, and evidence plans, which guide criterion-specific VLM QA and visual tools to produce evidence-grounded criterion scores, rationales, and a diagnostic report. We further construct VideoArgus-Bench, containing 1,026 curated input instances built from 653 high-quality images and 416 high-quality videos, with all benchmark rubrics pre-generated, frozen, and released. On a separate 1,260-video human-alignment set, VideoArgus achieves higher within-input Spearman and Kendall correlations with human judgments than the corresponding benchmark-specific evaluators across all five tasks. Model rankings also remain largely consistent across different rubric-generation and evaluation-VLM backbones. All code and data are released. Visit our project page: https://zzzmyyzeng.github.io/VideoArgus

</details>


### [17] [APQF: Agentic Profiling-Guided Structured Pruning and Mixed-Precision Quantization with Adaptive Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05499)
*Sadegh Jafari,Mohiuddin Bilwal,Fan Zhou,Brian Gelder,Ali Jannesari*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: APQF automates structured pruning and mixed-precision quantization with profiling-guided LLM planning, enabling per-layer compression decisions and accuracy recovery for CNNs and ViTs, yielding large compute reductions with minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual pruning/quantization and uniform compression across layers degrade accuracy and hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices; there is a need for an automated, architecture-aware, training-ready framework that adapts to per-layer sensitivity.

Method: A profiling agent measures cost distribution and layer sensitivity; LLM planners propose per-layer pruning ratios and bit-widths plus recovery strategies; decisions are validated before execution; pipeline covers CNNs and ViTs; evaluated on ResNet/VGG7/ViT/DeiT/Swin; six LLM planners (including open-weight) used.

Result: On ImageNet-1k: 5.6-7.7% of original bit-ops (13-18x reduction); accuracy close to baseline; under 200k-image budget: Top-1 ~17 points above existing joint pruning/quantization; CIFAR-10: stronger compression on four of five architectures; VGG7: 93.15% accuracy at 0.41% bit-ops (best at that compression); ablations: uniform compression hurts accuracy; withholding profiling data hurts performance; six planners reach ~97.4-97.9% on Swin-Tiny.

Conclusion: APQF is the first framework to integrate LLM-guided, profiling-grounded planning with a fully training-aware pruning/quantization pipeline across CNNs and ViTs; profiling data and automated planning are critical for preserving accuracy under aggressive compression.

Abstract: Modern deep neural networks achieve strong performance, but their scale makes them costly and slow, especially on resource-constrained edge devices. Pruning and quantization address this, but rely on manual, expert choices and on algorithms that are hard to apply across architectures. Uniform settings also ignore how differently individual layers respond to compression, which costs accuracy. We introduce APQF, an agentic profiling-guided framework that combines structured pruning, mixed-precision quantization-aware training, and accuracy recovery in one automated pipeline. A profiling agent measures how cost is distributed across the model and how sensitive each part is to pruning, and this evidence drives per-layer pruning ratios, per-layer bit-widths, and the recovery strategy, all proposed by LLM planners and validated before execution. To our knowledge, APQF is the first framework to combine LLM-guided, profiling-grounded decisions with a fully training-aware pruning and quantization pipeline for both CNNs and vision transformers. We evaluate APQF on ResNet, VGG7, ViT, DeiT, and Swin using ImageNet-1k and CIFAR-10. On ImageNet it cuts compute to 5.6-7.7 percent of the original bit-operations, a 13-18x reduction, while keeping accuracy close to the baseline, and under a 200K-image budget it stays roughly 17 points higher in Top-1 than existing joint pruning and quantization methods. On CIFAR-10 it compresses further than that method on four of five architectures. On VGG7 it reaches 93.15 percent using only 0.41 percent of baseline bit-operations, the only method at that compression level to improve on its full-precision baseline. Ablations show that uniform compression loses the most accuracy at matched compute, and that withholding profiling data from the planner hurts every model. Six LLM planners, including free open-weight ones, all reach 97.4-97.9 percent on Swin-Tiny.

</details>


### [18] [DynaPix: Can Vision-Language Models Identify the Exact Future?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05505)
*Thong Nguyen,Vinh-Hien Do,Quynh Vo,Cong-Duy Nguyen,See-Kiong Ng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DynaPix is a benchmark that tests whether models predict true future states by requiring selection of the exact future image from close candidates or a large gallery, using physics-simulated scenes to reveal temporal-anchoring gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations accept plausible or visually plausible futures, not the true future, making it hard to assess temporal grounding in dynamic prediction.

Method: Provide a video that ends before a key event and ask about a later moment; models pick the true future image from a set of close candidates or a large gallery. Scenes come from a physics simulator with known true image and timing; distractors are semantically similar. Train on scene accounts drawn from the simulator's true records, not teacher guesses.

Result: Models perform well when a visible event marks the target moment but near chance when timing is only elapsed; gallery search is substantially harder. Humans handle elapsed-time items well, indicating the difficulty lies with models. Training with true-record scene accounts helps but not for longer elapsed-time cases.

Conclusion: DynaPix reveals a temporal-anchoring gap: models align predictions to events better than to the passage of time. Addressing this requires temporal grounding beyond event cues, and training on simulator-derived data mitigates some issues, especially for shorter elapsed intervals.

Abstract: Acting in a physical scene requires knowing its real later state, not a plausible one. Current evaluations often accept words or a realistic-looking image, so the predicted state is never checked against the true one. We introduce DynaPix (Dynamic Pixels), a benchmark that makes prediction checkable. Given a video clip that stops before a key event and a question about a later moment, a model must pick the true future image from close candidates or a large gallery. The scenes come from a physics simulator, so the correct image and its time are known exactly and the wrong options are deliberately similar. Models often succeed when a visible event marks the target moment, but are near chance when only elapsed time marks it. Gallery search is harder still, as the true image rarely ranks first. People handle the elapsed-time items well, so the difficulty lies with the models, not the questions. Training on scene accounts drawn from the simulator's true record, not a teacher's guess, repairs much of this but not the longer elapsed time case. DynaPix thus exposes a temporal-anchoring gap: models attach a prediction to an event far better than to time itself.

</details>


### [19] [HERA: Historical Evidence Routing Adapter for Physical Prediction in Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05523)
*Yuanruyi,Yue Cao,Haojia Gao,Guanqiu Guo,Ziyuezhang,Shangqin,Junbo Tan,Bokui Chen,Zhuo Zou,Xueqian Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HERA enables selective retrieval of historical evidence into a frozen latent predictor via RRPM, yielding improvements on IntPhys2 main, especially for fixed-camera tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address occlusion in predictive video models, where later predictions require historical evidence not visible in the current frame, beyond longer temporal context or generic caching.

Method: Introduce HERA (Historical Evidence Routing Adapter) and RRPM (Register-Routed Patch Memory). RRPM comprises a Structured Memory Bank, Memory Registers, and Workspace Registers to route historical evidence into a frozen predictor without altering its latent workspace.

Result: On IntPhys2 Main, pairwise AvgSurprise improves from 52.57% to 54.35%. Subgroup gains: fixed-camera continuity 46.15% → 57.69%; fixed-camera immutability 46.15% → 63.46%.

Conclusion: Historical evidence routing is a practical adaptation for physical prediction in latent world models, enabling better use of past evidence without retraining the predictor.

Abstract: Predictive video models have emerged as promising world models by learning latent visual dynamics from large-scale video. Yet these models remain challenged by physical events under occlusion, where later predictions may depend on object evidence that is no longer available in the current view. Addressing this challenge requires historical evidence not only to be preserved but also to remain accessible when it becomes relevant to a subsequent prediction. Existing approaches mainly enlarge the temporal context, cache generic video features, or impose explicit object-centric states, thereby improving the capacity or structure of retained history. However, they do not directly address how relevant historical evidence can be selectively retrieved and integrated into a pretrained predictor without interfering with its native latent workspace. Accordingly, we introduce HERA (Historical Evidence Routing Adapter), a framework for routing retained historical evidence into a frozen latent predictor, and instantiate it with Register-Routed Patch Memory (RRPM), a lightweight adapter comprising a Structured Memory Bank, Memory Registers, and Workspace Registers. On the IntPhys2 Main split, HERA with RRPM improves the pairwise AvgSurprise accuracy of V-JEPA 2-G from 52.57% to 54.35%. Subgroup analysis shows particularly strong improvements on fixed-camera continuity, from 46.15% to 57.69%, and fixed-camera immutability, from 46.15% to 63.46%. These results support historical evidence routing as a practical adaptation strategy for physical prediction in latent world models.

</details>


### [20] [OmniMech: All-in-one Multimodal Mechanical Benchmark for 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05539)
*Taiting Lu,Runze Liu,Ziwei Dong,Sisong Bei,Jingying Zeng,Mingjia Wang,Zhenghao Li,Kaiyuan Lin,Yi-Shan Wu,Yangshoudu Zheng,Hongxing Pan,Kai Zhang,Guoliang Shi,Ling Ma,Yifan Yang,Jiaying Lu,Qi He,Sung-Liang Chen,Yi-Chao Chen,Yincheng Jin,Mahanth Gowda*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OmniMech introduces the first million-scale benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on executable CAD generation from industrial drawings, addressing fine-grained geometry and tolerances beyond coarse 3D objects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial mechanical design requires millimeter-level tolerances and precise feature annotations; existing VLMs and CAD-focused models struggle to synthesize executable CAD from engineering data and cannot robustly enforce dimensions.

Method: Assemble OmniMech dataset with 251k fully dimensioned 2D drawings paired with native CAD models, multi-view renders, mesh/STEP/B-rep representations, and semantic annotations; define four tasks: parametric CAD program synthesis, diagram-to-3D reasoning, annotation-grounded reasoning, and tool-augmented agentic reasoning; provide evaluation code and tool interfaces.

Result: Baseline experiments reveal that current VLMs and CAD-specialized models have difficulty producing executable programs, performing fine-grained 3D reconstruction, and enforcing accurate dimensions and tolerances; dataset and tools enable future research.

Conclusion: OmniMech establishes a large-scale, structured benchmark for rigorous evaluation and development of VLMs in industrial CAD generation, encouraging improvements and tool-augmented workflows.

Abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can generate executable CAD programs from images, but existing methods mainly target coarse, general-purpose 3D objects and rarely address the fine-grained geometry and millimeter-level tolerances required in industrial mechanical design. We introduce OmniMech, the first million-scale benchmark for evaluating VLMs on executable CAD generation from industrial manufacturing data. OmniMech contains more than 251,000 fully dimensioned and toleranced 2D orthographic drawings, paired with native CAD models, multi-view renderings, mesh, STEP and B-rep representations, and rich semantic annotations. The benchmark includes four tasks: (1) parametric CAD program synthesis from engineering drawings; (2) diagram-to-3D reasoning for geometrically and structurally consistent reconstruction; (3) annotation-grounded reasoning over dimensions, symbols, feature callouts, and manufacturing constraints; and (4) tool-augmented agentic reasoning using visualization, measurement, CAD execution, and verification tools. Experiments show that current VLMs and CAD-specialized models still struggle with executable program synthesis, fine-grained 3D reconstruction, and reliable enforcement of dimensions and tolerances. We will release the benchmark data, evaluation code, and tool interfaces to support future research.

</details>


### [21] [Hierarchical Flow Matching for 3D Point Cloud Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05557)
*Linhao Wang,Qichang Zhang,Ye Su,Hao Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Hierarchical Flow Matching (HFM) uses a two-level optimal-transport flow matching framework: a latent flow matches global shape in a compact latent space, and a conditional point flow reconstructs detailed points from that latent code. It achieves efficient sampling (≈15 Euler steps per flow) and benefits downstream classification, with competitive or state-of-the-art results on ShapeNet/ModelNet.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the computational burden of continuous normalizing flows (ODE solving and trace estimation) and the large step counts of diffusion models, while leveraging the natural hierarchical structure of 3D shapes for high-quality point cloud generation.

Method: Two-level OT-based flow matching: (1) Latent Flow Matching models the global shape manifold in a compact latent space; (2) Conditional Point Flow Matching reconstructs detailed point clouds conditioned on the latent code. Both flows are trained with simple MSE losses, yielding straight OT paths and enabling efficient sampling (as few as ~15 Euler steps per flow). The latent space also supports downstream tasks such as classification.

Result: Extensive experiments on ShapeNet and ModelNet show HFM achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance compared with prior methods, with efficient sampling and beneficial latent representations for classification.

Conclusion: HFM demonstrates that a bilevel, OT-based flow matching framework can efficiently generate high-quality 3D point clouds by separating global structure and local detail, delivering both good generation quality and useful latent representations for downstream tasks.

Abstract: Generating high-quality 3D point clouds requires capturing both global shape topology and local geometric details. Existing flow-based methods rely on continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) that demand expensive ODE solving and trace estimation during training, while diffusion models require hundreds of iterative denoising steps. Moreover, most approaches adopt single-level generation directly in point space, disregarding the hierarchical structure natural to 3D shapes. We propose Hierarchical Flow Matching (HFM) that extends flow matching to bilevel structure for unconditional 3D point cloud generation. HFM decomposes the task into two levels via optimal-transport flow matching: a \textit{Latent Flow Matching} models the global shape manifold in a compact latent space, and a \textit{Conditional Point Flow Matching} reconstructs detailed point clouds conditioned on the latent code. Both flows are trained with simple MSE regression losses. The resulting straight OT paths enable efficient sampling with as few as 15 Euler steps per flow, while the structured latent space supports downstream tasks including classification. Extensive experiments on ShapeNet and ModelNet benchmarks demonstrate that HFM achieves competitive or even best performance compared with prior state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [22] [From Sports to Safety: Benchmarking Proactive Risk Inference in MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05560)
*Jiawei Qiu,Yichen Xu,Jianzhe Ma,Mingyang Yu,Wenbin Zhu,Yang Han,Pinzheng Lv,Wenxuan Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces SPRINT, a benchmark of 2,888 real-world sports videos (2,440 accident, 448 safe) across 14 sports and 3 environments, to evaluate proactive hazard inference in multimodal large language models. Findings show models excel at signaling hazards (>95%) but poorly identify causal factors (<50%), with explicit danger queries increasing false alarms on safe clips. The work highlights a gap between hazard sensitivity and cause-grounded understanding and calls for more reliable proactive safety in dynamic physical environments; data/code will be released on acceptance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proactive physical hazard prediction is underexplored in multimodal language models. Understanding not just whether a hazard is present, but why it occurs and its causes, enables earlier and more reliable safety decisions in dynamic settings such as sports and autonomous-like environments.

Method: Create SPRINT benchmark comprising 2,888 real-world sports videos (2,440 accident, 448 safe) across 14 sports and 3 environmental settings. Provide fine-grained annotations for early hazard cues, accident timing, and hierarchical causes for accident clips; safe clips are accident-free for diagnosing false alarms. Evaluate state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs across diverse prompts and temporal windows. Conduct diagnostic experiments using explicit danger queries to assess cause-grounded reasoning and false alarm rates.

Result: Models show a large gap: best hazard signaling accuracy >95%, but cause identification accuracy <50%. Explicit danger queries induce higher false alarms even on non-hazard videos. Overall, current models lack stable, cause-grounded early warning despite detecting hazards, signaling superficial proactive safety.

Conclusion: There is a clear need for models with stable, cause-grounded proactive safety in dynamic physical contexts. The proposed SPRINT benchmark enables rigorous evaluation and, once released, will support development of more reliable proactive safety systems in sports and related domains.

Abstract: Timely anticipation of physical hazards is essential for real-world safety, yet existing MLLM evaluations focus on harmful content or general risks, leaving proactive physical hazard prediction underexplored. Sports provide a well-suited testbed: accident causes span diverse injury dimensions and pre-accident spatiotemporal cues draw on reasoning capabilities shared with broader safety domains such as autonomous driving and fall detection. We introduce SPRINT (Sports Proactive Risk INference Testbed), a benchmark of 2,888 real-world sports videos (2,440 accident, 448 safe controls) spanning 14 sports and 3 environmental settings. Accident videos feature fine-grained annotations of early hazard cues, accident timing, and hierarchical causes; safe videos are manually verified as accident-free and serve to diagnose prompt-induced false alarms. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs under diverse prompts and temporal windows reveals a sharp gap between hazard sensitivity and understanding: the best model exceeds 95% in signaling hazards yet falls below 50% in identifying their causes. Diagnostic experiments further show that explicit danger queries trigger severe false alarms even on hazard-free videos. These findings indicate that current MLLMs exhibit only superficial proactive safety, lacking stable, cause-grounded early warning, and underscore the need for reliable proactive safety in dynamic physical environments. Data and code will be open-sourced upon acceptance.

</details>


### [23] [EffectLearner: World-Aware Object-Effect Reasoning for Real-World Video Object Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05565)
*Feier Wu,Wanke Xia,Xu He,Zilang Zhou,Si Chen,Dongxia Liu,Liyang Chen,Qimeng Wu,Zhengbo Zhang,Wenming Yang,Zhiyong Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EffectLearner introduces a semantic-reasoning-enhanced framework for video object removal, combining a VLM-based Object-Effect Reasoner with a DiT-based Video Eraser, guided by structured prompts and motion-aware supervision, plus a new EffectWorld dataset and progressive curriculum; it outperforms baselines on ROSE-Bench and challenging EffectWorld benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video object removal methods struggle to generalize to real-world scenes with complex, compositional, and dynamically evolving object-induced effects, due to implicit learning of effect correspondences and fixed data distributions.

Method: EffectLearner fuses a VLM-based Object-Effect Reasoner for cross-modal semantic reasoning with a DiT-based Video Eraser. It uses a structured effect-analysis prompt to extract compact effect-aware context, applies motion-aware mask guidance and motion-consistency supervision, and trains with EffectWorld via a progressive curriculum combining common supervision with complex-effect data.

Result: On ROSE-Bench, EffectLearner outperforms baselines; it achieves clear advantages on EffectWorld-Eval and EffectWorld-Wild, demonstrating higher-quality removal with spatiotemporal coherence in complex scenes.

Conclusion: Semantic reasoning over object-induced effects, coupled with motion-aware guidance and a dedicated challenging dataset, enables robust video object removal in real-world, dynamically evolving scenarios and improves generalization beyond predefined effect categories.

Abstract: Video object removal must eliminate not only the target object but also its induced effects while maintaining high-fidelity and spatiotemporally coherent restoration. Existing methods mainly learn object-effect correspondences implicitly from predefined effect categories and fixed data distributions, limiting their generalization to complex real-world scenes involving compositional effects, spatially detached or weakly correlated effects, long-tail physical phenomena, and dynamically evolving interactions. We propose EffectLearner, a semantic-reasoning-enhanced framework that combines a VLM-based Object-Effect Reasoner with a DiT-based Video Eraser. Guided by a structured effect-analysis prompt, the Reasoner performs cross-modal reasoning over a target-highlighted video and extracts compact effect-aware context, which guides the Video Eraser toward comprehensive object-effect removal. Motion-aware mask guidance and motion-consistency supervision further improve removal coverage and spatiotemporal stability under object motion and evolving scene dynamics. To fully exploit the framework in challenging real-world scenarios, we further construct EffectWorld, a paired video dataset specifically designed for complex object-induced effects, and introduce a progressive training curriculum that combines common supervision with complex-effect data. On the standard ROSE-Bench, EffectLearner outperforms existing baselines on most metrics and achieves clear advantages on both EffectWorld-Eval and the challenging EffectWorld-Wild, demonstrating its ability to deliver high-quality video object removal in complex real-world scenes.

</details>


### [24] [CoordRefer: Coordinate-Aware 3D Visual Grounding from Multiview Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05569)
*Haijie Li,Jiaxin Zhang,Dave Zhenyu Chen,Youyu Chen,Yanmin Wu,Jian Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Decouples coordinate frame selection from 3D grounding to resolve coordinate-relative box ambiguity, employing a coordinate-aware fine-tuning and policy-optimization pipeline, and achieving improved grounding on ScanRefer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coordinate-frame ambiguity arises when the reference frame is jointly optimized with 3D box regression, causing multiple valid representations and degraded grounding performance.

Method: CoordRefer first selects a reference frame to define the coordinate system, then conditions 3D box prediction on that coordinate system. It uses coordinate-aware supervised fine-tuning to align frame selection with coordinate-conditioned regression, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization with 3D IoU-based rewards to align the two stages with downstream grounding quality.

Result: On ScanRefer with Qwen3-VL-2B, CoordRefer yields 11% gains in Acc@0.25 and 7% gains in Acc@0.5 over a coordinate-agnostic baseline; its geometrically refined variant surpasses methods that use explicit 3D inputs.

Conclusion: The method effectively mitigates coordinate-relative box ambiguity by decoupling coordinate frame selection from grounding and aligning both stages, yielding improved grounding performance and demonstrating the value of coordinate-aware training and policy optimization.

Abstract: Multiview image-based 3D visual grounding predicts a coordinate frame to define a coordinate system and then regresses a 3D bounding box for localization. However, existing methods jointly optimize coordinate frame selection and box regression, leading to coordinate-relative box ambiguity and degraded grounding performance. This ambiguity arises because the same box admits different numerical representations across coordinate frames, creating multiple optimization targets and yielding invalid compromise predictions. To tackle this challenge, we propose CoordRefer, a coordinate-aware framework that decouples coordinate frame selection from coordinate-conditioned grounding. CoordRefer first selects a reference frame to define the coordinate system and then conditions 3D box prediction on the coordinate system. We perform coordinate-aware supervised fine-tuning to establish coordinate frame selection and coordinate-conditioned box regression, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization with 3D IoU-based rewards to align both stages with downstream grounding quality. On ScanRefer with Qwen3-VL-2B, CoordRefer achieves gains of 11% in Acc@0.25 and 7% in Acc@0.5 over the coordinate-agnostic baseline, while its geometrically refined variant surpasses methods using explicit 3D inputs.

</details>


### [25] [Beyond Frame Selection: Rethinking Long-Video Understanding with MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05592)
*Ziling Huang,Shin'ichi Satoh*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VideoRouter coordinates global storyline and local evidence views via a hierarchical, question-agnostic video partition and a verification-guided router, achieving improvements over frame-selection methods on VideoMME with LLaVA-Video-7B backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-video understanding with token-limited MLLMs struggles to capture temporally sparse evidence; existing frame selection trades off global vs local coverage.

Method: Construct a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy (coarse-to-fine segments); derive global and local views; employ a verification-guided router to select the best-supported view for final answer.

Result: Empirical results show coordination of global/local reasoning; improvement of 2.9 points over state-of-the-art frame selection on VideoMME with LLaVA-Video-7B backbone; code will be released.

Conclusion: Hierarchical, dual-view routing with verification enhances long-video reasoning in MLLMs; the approach outperforms prior frame-selection baselines.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong progress in video understanding, yet it remains challenging because the token limitation makes MLLMs difficult to capture temporally sparse evidence. Existing methods typically rely on uniform sampling, or frame selection, but these strategies usually optimize either broad temporal coverage or local relevance, making it difficult to preserve both global storyline context and fine-grained evidence. We propose VideoRouter(VR) that rethinks long-video understanding as coordinating complementary evidence views rather than selecting a single subset of frames. It first organizes each video into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy, which partition the video into coarse-to-fine temporally coherent segments. In this hierarchy, upper-level nodes capture broad storyline context and event progression, while lower-level nodes preserve fine-grained local details and evidence-bearing moments. This naturally gives rise to two complementary views: a global view for coverage-oriented reasoning and a local view for detail-oriented evidence recovery. We further introduce a verification-guided router to determine which view is better supported by the selected evidence and select the final answer. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed design through extensive experiments, showing that the verification-guided router effectively coordinates global and local reasoning, and that, on VideoMME, our method outperforms state-of-the-art frame selection methods by 2.9 points, respectively, under the LLaVA-Video-7B backbone. We will release the code.

</details>


### [26] [Uncertainty-Aware World Model for Aerial Image-Goal Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05597)
*Deyi Zhu,Haoyu Fan,Yinan Zhu,Weichen Zhang,Shilin Ma,Xinlei Chen,Yansong Tang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Uncertainty-Aware Navigation World Model (UA-NWM) for aerial image-goal navigation uses an uncertainty subspace to capture plausible futures and scores trajectories via conditional out-of-distribution detection, relying only on the unexplainable residual for robust ranking without multiple future samples; achieves robust performance with low latency and real-world UAV validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large outdoor environments introduce substantial future-state uncertainty; existing world-model-based methods rely on single or few point predictions, which are insufficient for reliable trajectory scoring in such settings.

Method: Propose UA-NWM, a latent world model where trajectory scoring is formulated as conditional out-of-distribution detection. Represent plausible futures using an uncertainty subspace and decompose the prediction–goal discrepancy into an uncertainty-explainable part and an unexplainable residual. Use only the unexplainable residual for trajectory scoring, enabling robust ranking without sampling multiple futures.
