Result: From a held-out scan, the model recovers a recognisable likeness of the patient (identity-region MAE = 0.163); the model also synthesises a scan from the non-medical image; demonstrates that de-identified scans retain identifying information and function like photographs of the patient.

Conclusion: Imaging data should be treated as biometric data rather than anonymisable records, and privacy protections must address pixel-level identity leakage in addition to metadata de-identification.

Abstract: Medical images are routinely de-identified---names, dates, and other metadata removed---and then shared for research, teaching, and public benchmarks under the assumption that this renders them anonymous. Such de-identification protects the metadata but not the pixels, and---apart from scans that directly contain facial structures---whether the image content itself identifies the patient has received little scrutiny. We investigate this question by learning a cycle-consistent correspondence between a cross-sectional medical image and a non-medical, patient-identifying image, using a pair of coupled, cycle-consistent variational autoencoders. From a held-out scan, the model recovers a recognisable likeness of the patient (identity-region MAE = 0.163); conversely, it synthesises a scan from such an image. These results indicate that a de-identified medical scan remains identifying---it is, in effect, a photograph of the patient---and that imaging data should be governed as biometric data rather than as anonymisable records. To support reproducibility, the code and trained models are shared at https://github.com/attilasimko/public-repository.

</details>


### [76] [Respect Your Zero-Shot Uncertainty: Conservative Calibration for Test-Time-Adapted Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05945)
*Jingyan Jiang,Yaru Sun,Xiao Chen,Jiazhen Huang,Caiting Li,Zhijian He,Yin Chen,Pingting Hao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ZAEC is a label-free post-hoc calibration method for vision-language models under test-time adaptation (TTA). It uses zero-shot entropy as a reference to restore entropy on predictions that became sharper due to TTA, via minimal temperature scaling, without labels or learned parameters, preserving accuracy and rankings. It yields lower post-hoc macro ECE across multiple TTA methods and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TTA improves recognition under distribution shift but often worsens calibration. Existing label-free calibrations are tied to prompts or logit statistics and may not capture the predictive distribution well. There is a need for a simple, data-free, post-hoc calibration method that preserves accuracy while improving calibration.

Method: Propose Zero-Shot-Anchored Entropy Calibration (ZAEC). ZAEC identifies sharpened predictions after TTA and applies minimal, selective temperature scaling to restore the entropy to the zero-shot reference, using zero-shot entropy as a sample-specific uncertainty anchor. No labeled calibration data or learned parameters are required, and class rankings are preserved.

Result: ZAEC achieves the lowest post-hoc macro-average ECE among five TTA methods across 15 datasets on ViT-B/16, with consistent gains on RN50. It preserves accuracy and ranking while improving calibration, demonstrating that entropy-based anchoring can effectively calibrate TTA predictions without labels.

Conclusion: ZAEC offers a simple, parameter-free, label-free post-hoc calibration approach for TTA that improves calibration (lower macro ECE) without sacrificing accuracy or rankings. It reveals that leveraging zero-shot entropy as a stable reference can guide minimal temperature adjustments to restore reliable confidence estimates under distribution shift.

Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) can improve the recognition accuracy of vision-language models under distribution shift, but often degrades calibration, making predictive confidence unreliable for downstream decision-making. Many existing label-free calibration approaches are either coupled to prompt optimization or rely on logit-range statistics that provide only a coarse characterization of the predictive distribution. We show that TTA can increase confidence and reduce entropy even when the top-1 prediction and its correctness remain unchanged, a failure mode we term prediction-preserving sharpening. Across diverse TTA methods and benchmarks, larger entropy reductions relative to paired zero-shot predictions are associated with greater increases in Expected Calibration Error (ECE). On entropy-reduced samples, confidence gains also tend to exceed accuracy gains. Based on these findings, we propose Zero-Shot-Anchored Entropy Calibration (ZAEC), a label-free post-hoc method that uses zero-shot entropy as a sample-specific uncertainty reference. ZAEC selectively restores the zero-shot entropy of sharpened predictions through minimal temperature scaling while leaving all other predictions unchanged. It requires no labeled calibration data or learned parameters and preserves class rankings and classification accuracy. Across five TTA methods and 15 datasets, ZAEC achieves the lowest post-hoc macro-average ECE on ViT-B/16, with consistent gains on RN50.

</details>


### [77] [Big, Bright, or Invisible: A Frozen-Feature Benchmark of 3D CT Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05960)
*Maulik Chevli,Johannes Brandt,Rickmer Braren,Daniel Rueckert,Philip Müller*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: No universal state-of-the-art among 10 frozen 3D-CT encoders for thoracic CT; performance varies by context; small, low-contrast lesions remain hard; region-/lesion-level pretraining may be needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess the diagnostic breadth of 3D CT foundation models by benchmarking multiple frozen encoders across cohorts and evaluation setups to identify what governs detection performance.

Method: Benchmark ten frozen CT encoders on three thoracic CT cohorts (including an unseen internal dataset) using k-nearest neighbors, zero-shot prompting, and linear probing; perform controlled within-organ comparisons to assess how contrast and spatial extent affect detectability.

Result: No universal SOTA; rankings fluctuate with evaluation context. Models with fine-grained tokenization plus vision–language alignment tend to perform best, but a lightweight supervised encoder is highly competitive. The primary determinant of performance is the physical detectability of findings, scaling with contrast and size. High-contrast, widespread abnormalities (devices, effusions) are reliably recovered; small, low-contrast focal lesions remain challenging across encoders. Global embeddings’ limitations suggest region- or lesion-level pretraining is needed for accurate small-structure representation.

Conclusion: Architecture alone does not guarantee high performance; to improve detection of small, low-contrast findings, adopt region-/lesion-level pretraining or hybrid approaches combining global representations with region-focused signals; evaluation context strongly influences reported performance and should be incorporated into model development and benchmarking.

Abstract: Routine CT interpretation is inherently comprehensive, capturing incidental findings across the entire scan volume. 3D CT foundation models could assist this process by providing generalizable representations of anatomy and pathology. To evaluate their diagnostic breadth, we benchmark ten frozen CT encoders across three cohorts of thoracic CT scans, including an unseen internal clinical dataset, using $k$-nearest neighbors, zero-shot prompting, and linear probing. We find no universal state-of-the-art, with rankings fluctuating significantly depending on the evaluation context. While models combining fine-grained image tokenization with vision-language alignment generally perform best, a lightweight supervised encoder remains highly competitive, demonstrating that explicit labels can effectively substitute for scale. Crucially, rather than model architecture, we observe that the primary determinant of performance is a physical bottleneck: a finding's detectability scales with its contrast against surrounding tissue and its spatial extent. Through controlled within-organ comparisons, we empirically demonstrate that widespread or high-contrast abnormalities, such as devices and effusions, are reliably recovered. Conversely, small, low-contrast focal lesions remain a persistent challenge across all evaluated encoders. We attribute this to the inherent limitations of globally pooled embeddings, suggesting that accurately representing small, low-contrast structures will require region- or lesion-level pretraining.

</details>


### [78] [Topology-Aware Neighborhood Learning for Source-Free Cross-Scene Hyperspectral Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05964)
*Qingmei Li,Juepeng Zheng,Jiarui Zhang,Jianxi Huang,Haohuan Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A source-free domain adaptation framework for cross-scene hyperspectral image classification that uses topology-aware learning: entropy momentum pseudo-labeling (EMP) to refine pseudo-labels, and a contextual neighborhood topology (CNT) to capture global and local target space structure, resulting in state-of-the-art performance with ablations confirming each component.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Privacy/storage limits prevent accessing source-domain data, making conventional DA infeasible. Hyperspectral data are high-dimensional and domain shifts across scenes are common; leveraging target geometry without source data is essential for practical remote sensing adaptation.

Method: Entropy Momentum Pseudo-Labeling (EMP) refines k-means assignments using entropy-aware confidence and temporal momentum of predictions. Contextual Neighborhood Topology (CNT) exploits intrinsic geometry of the target feature space by combining global structure via collaborative representation with local structure via nearest-neighbor relations. The learning objective combines cross-entropy on refined pseudo-labels, log inner product-based topology consistency, and an information-maximization term to encourage balanced class predictions in a source-free setting.

Result: Empirical evaluation across three cross-scenarios shows the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies demonstrate the contribution of EMP and CNT and their synergy in improving robustness and accuracy without access to source data.

Conclusion: Topology-aware modeling is crucial for effective, robust hyperspectral image classification in source-free domain adaptation, enabling practical deployment under data privacy/storage constraints.

Abstract: Domain adaptation has advanced cross-scene hyperspectral image classification, significantly improving discriminative capability in complex scenarios. However, privacy rules or storage limits often block access to data from the source domain. Conventional domain adaptation methods become impractical, severely restricting their utility in realistic remote sensing scenarios. To tackle this challenge, we propose a topology-aware source-free learning framework. We first introduce the entropy momentum pseudo-labeling (EMP) to refine k-means assignments by leveraging entropy-aware confidence and temporal prediction momentum. Under the guidance of the refined pseudo-labels, we further utilize the contextual neighborhood topology (CNT) to exploit the intrinsic geometric structure of the target feature space. Combining the global structural information extracted by collaborative representation with the local similarity information modeled by nearest neighbor search, the CNT accomplishes the comprehensive encoding of manifold-level geometric properties in the target domain feature space. The overall objective integrates cross-entropy on refined pseudo-labels, log inner product-based topology consistency, and an information-maximization term for balanced classification, ensuring stable adaptation in the source-free setting. Extensive experiments on three typical cross-scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method exceeds state-of-the-art performance, and ablation studies further validate the contribution of each module. The results highlight the critical role of topology-aware modeling in achieving robust and accurate classification without source data.

</details>


### [79] [Diff-VF: Training-free High-quality Long Video Generation via Diffusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05976)
*Haoning Yang,Xinyuan Chen,Yaohui Wang,Guo Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Diff-VF provides a training-free, plug-and-play framework to extend short-video diffusion models to long videos, using Hybrid Noise Initialization, Weighted Window Sampling, and Temporal Extended Sampling, with an optional Skip Residual Guidance enhancement; it outperforms training-free baselines on temporal coherence and motion diversity while preserving frame quality across two base models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-quality long-video generation is challenging for diffusion models trained on short clips: maintaining long-range temporal coherence and diverse motions without fine-tuning the base model requires a training-free, model-agnostic solution.

Method: Introduce three complementary strategies—Hybrid Noise Initialization (HNI) to constrain global semantics, Weighted Window Sampling (WWS) to reduce inter-window discontinuities, and Temporal Extended Sampling (TES) to enable long-range dependencies via timestep-varying fusion. Diff-VF is training-free and model-agnostic. It can be extended to long-video enhancement via Skip Residual Guidance with timestep-dependent guidance.

Result: VBend-Long evaluation shows Diff-VF achieves a better balance between temporal coherence and motion diversity than the base models and recent training-free baselines (FreeNoise, FreeLong, RIFLEx), while maintaining competitive frame-wise quality. Experiments on two base models demonstrate applicability across different spatial-temporal modeling strategies. Extensive ablations validate the contribution of each component and hyperparameters.

Conclusion: Diff-VF offers a universal, training-free approach to converting short-video diffusion backbones into long-video generators with improved long-range coherence and motion diversity, and provides a pathway for enhancement through Skip Residual Guidance; the method is validated across multiple base models and baselines with thorough ablations.

Abstract: Recently, diffusion models have made great progress in video generation. However, most existing video diffusion models are trained with short videos, and degrade when extrapolated to long videos, struggling to maintain long-range temporal coherence while retaining diverse motions. To generate consistent, high-quality and dynamic long videos, we propose Diff-VF, a training-free, plug-and-play and model-agnostic framework that converts existing short-video diffusion backbones into long-video generators without modifying or fine-tuning the base model. Diff-VF couples three complementary strategies: Hybrid Noise Initialization (HNI) to constrain global semantics, Weighted Window Sampling (WWS) to remove inter-window discontinuities, and Temporal Extended Sampling (TES) to establish long-range dependencies with a timestep-varying fusion. We further extend Diff-VF to long-video enhancement via Skip Residual Guidance that balances fidelity and realism through timestep-dependent guidance. VBench-Long evaluation results show that Diff-VF achieves a more favorable balance between temporal coherence and motion diversity than base models and recent training-free long video generation baselines, including FreeNoise, FreeLong, and RIFLEx, while maintaining competitive frame-wise quality. Experiments on two base models demonstrate the applicability to video diffusion models with different spatial-temporal modeling strategies. Extensive ablations validate the contribution of each component and hyperparameters.

</details>


### [80] [Multi-Year Geospatial Reasoning using Interannually-Consistent Historical Predictions as a Free Input Modality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05979)
*Syed Roshaan Ali Shah,Kasper Bonte,David Bekaert,Kristof Van Tricht,Dieter Wens*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Incorporate historical model predictions and external layers into single-year crop-type mapping to enable cross-year reasoning; a Crop Type embedding encoder and consistent BVL representation yield modest but meaningful gains in F1 and reduce recall bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve consistency and accuracy of annual land-cover and crop-type maps by leveraging the model’s own past predictions and ancillary layers that are typically ignored or used post hoc.

Method: Introduce a Crop Type (CTY) embedding encoder that encodes past predictions as confidence-scaled, time-ordered tokens and attends over the year axis. Evaluate how to represent the Base Vegetation Layer (BVL) mask within inputs/outputs. Compare designs on a 18-crop-class subset, using a pan-European dataset (~5.4M labeled pixels).

Result: Adding prediction history increases crop-only F1 by 1.6 percentage points and improves recall across underrepresented classes (notably olives, fruits, nuts). Consistent BVL representation adds about 2.5 percentage points to crop-class performance. The approach yields a low-cost, scalable improvement for recurring geospatial class-mapping models.

Conclusion: Embedding historical model outputs and consistent ancillary masks enables cross-year reasoning in single-task pixel classifiers and serves as a practical, low-cost enhancement for operational, year-on-year EO mapping pipelines.

Abstract: Machine learning, and deep networks in particular, are increasingly used to derive higher-level Earth observation (EO) products such as annual land-cover and crop-type maps. Many are generated operationally: each year a new acquisition is processed, typically with the same model, extending a multi-year archive. In the process these systems accumulate two kinds of useful signal that are almost never fed back into the model: the system's own archive of past predictions, and ancillary layers produced by other partners in a processing consortium. Both are normally used outside the network, as rule-based post-processing or a fixed input mask. Using the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service High Resolution Layer (HRL) Croplands crop-type product as a testbed, we show that bringing both signals inside the model turns a single-year, single-task pixel classifier into one that reasons across years. We introduce a Crop Type (CTY) embedding encoder that represents each past prediction as a confidence-scaled, time-ordered categorical token and attends over the year axis, and we study how the externally provided Base Vegetation Layer (BVL) mask should be represented in the model's inputs and outputs. To compare designs fairly when they relabel non-crop pixels, we evaluate on the 18 crop classes only and report precision and recall separately. On a pan-European dataset of about 5.4M labelled pixels, adding the prediction history raises crop-only F1 by 1.6 percentage points (pp) and, more importantly, corrects a recall-skewed error profile, with the largest gains on perennial and tree crops (olives +4.6, fruits +3.7, nuts +3.2 pp). Representing the BVL mask consistently in both the history and the target year adds about 2.5 pp on the crop classes. The approach is a low-cost recipe for any recurring geospatial or foundation model that emits class maps.

</details>


### [81] [Universal Concept Disruption for SAM3 Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05983)
*Hao Wang,Yuxuan Zhang,Wei Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces Universal Concept Disruption (UCD), a universal cross-concept adversarial attack on SAM3 for open-vocabulary segmentation. Learns a single bounded perturbation from image-noun-phrase pairs to disrupt the integrated concept-grounding system, lowering mask quality and cgF1 across multiple datasets; the attack transfers to SAM3.1 and video inference with limited recovery from simple defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess robustness of promptable segmentation (SAM3) to universal cross-concept adversarial attacks and understand vulnerabilities across text-conditioned localization and mask generation pipelines.

Method: Train a single bounded perturbation using (image, noun-phrase) pairs to attack SAM3 end-to-end. The perturbation targets (i) text-conditioned input path, (ii) shared visual features, (iii) presence-gated scores, and (iv) spatial validity of masks via area collapse and clean-mask Dice disruption. The attack is universal (one perturbation works across concepts) and transfers to related models (SAM3.1) and video inference without re-optimization.

Result: UCD consistently outperforms baselines on SACo-Gold, LVIS, RefCOCO, PhraseCut, and OpenImages, reducing average mask AP from 59.43 to 18.73 and cgF1 from 50.32 to 20.49. Perturbation transfers to SAM3.1 and SAM3 video inference without re-optimization; prompt ensembling, lightweight head fine-tuning, and temporal filtering offer limited recovery.

Conclusion: UCD reveals a critical vulnerability in SAM3’s open-vocabulary segmentation pipeline and establishes a baseline for universal cross-concept adversarial attacks, motivating the development of robust defenses and future research on securing promptable segmentation systems.

Abstract: SAM3 extends promptable segmentation from geometry-driven mask prediction to open-vocabulary concept segmentation, where a text-conditioned grounding model decides whether a concept is present and segments all matching instances. While this presence-gated design improves concept-level prediction, its adversarial robustness remains unexplored. In this paper, we introduce Universal Concept Disruption (UCD), the first universal cross-concept adversarial attack tailored to SAM3 image segmentation. UCD learns a single bounded image perturbation from (image, noun-phrase) pairs and attacks SAM3 as an integrated concept-grounding system. It jointly disrupts the text-conditioned input path, maximizes divergence in prompt-shared visual features, suppresses the final presence-gated concept scores, and corrupts the spatial validity of retained masks through area collapse and clean-mask Dice disruption. Across SACo-Gold, LVIS, RefCOCO, PhraseCut, and OpenImages datasets, UCD consistently outperforms all baselines under a matched evaluation protocol, reducing average mask AP from 59.43 to 18.73 and average cgF1 from 50.32 to 20.49. The learned perturbation also transfers to SAM3.1 and to SAM3 video inference without re-optimization, while prompt ensembling, lightweight head fine-tuning, and temporal filtering provide limited recovery.

</details>


### [82] [Wan-Animate-2: Pushing the Application Boundaries of Character Animation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06009)
*Guangyuan Wang,Li Hu,Dechao Meng,Zhongyi Zhang,Peng Zhang,Mingyang Huang,Ruoshi Zhang,Ke Sun,Zhe Zhang,Xingjun Wang,Gang Cheng,Bang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Wan-Animate-2 is an end-to-end diffusion-transformer framework for real-time character animation that consumes driving video directly, with Wan-Animate-2-Lite enabling streaming at real-time latency via a three-stage training strategy; introduces text-driven viewpoint control and will release base weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of existing pipelines: explicit motion representations cause extraction errors and identity drift; implicit motion features lose fine-grained dynamics; in-context learning is computation-heavy; all methods are offline. The aim is an end-to-end, real-time, interactive character animation solution.

Method: Replace intermediate motion extraction with a redesigned Diffusion Transformer that directly ingests driving video; incorporate text-driven viewpoint control to decouple camera from driving input; propose Wan-Animate-2-Lite with a three-stage training: teacher forcing pretraining with error buffer, and Self-Forcing distillation with chunk-wise backpropagation.

Result: Qualitative evaluations and user studies report high-fidelity animation across diverse characters and motion patterns; Wan-Animate-2 achieves superior motion fidelity and identity preservation.

Conclusion: Wan-Animate-2 enables streaming, interactive character animation; Wan-Animate-2-Lite achieves real-time latency; releasing Wan-Animate-2-Base weights to the public to accelerate research and adoption.

Abstract: Character image animation remains a foundational yet challenging task in computer vision. Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into three paradigms: methods based on explicit motion representations suffer from extraction errors and identity drift; methods based on implicit motion features lose fine-grained dynamics through compression; and in-context learning approaches avoid intermediate representations but incur prohibitive computational costs. Furthermore, all current systems are designed for offline synthesis, unable to meet the real-time requirements of interactive applications such as digital avatars and live-streaming hosts. To address these limitations, we present Wan-Animate-2, an end-to-end character animation framework that directly consumes the driving video within a redesigned Diffusion Transformer. Our architecture achieves superior motion fidelity and identity preservation by eliminating intermediate motion extractors entirely. We further introduce text driven viewpoint control that decouples the output camera perspective from the driving video--a capability rarely supported by prior character animation methods that rely on explicit motion representations. Beyond generation quality, we present Wan-Animate-2-Lite, an efficient variant that reduces inference latency to real-time thresholds through a three-stage training paradigm: teacher forcing pretraining with error buffer mechanism, and Self-Forcing distillation with chunk-wise backpropagation. This enables streaming character animation for interactive applications, opening new deployment scenarios that were previously infeasible. Qualitative evaluations and user studies demonstrate that Wan-Animate-2 achieves high-fidelity animation results across diverse characters and motion patterns. To foster further research and community development, we will release the Wan-Animate-2-Base model weights to the public.

</details>


### [83] [Iterate or Widen? When Test-Time Refinement Helps LiDAR Scene Completion: A Controlled Study of Evidence Geometry, Training Coverage, and Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06014)
*Shijie Hao,Weining Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: One-shot vs wider predictor vs iterative multigrid refiner in LiDAR semantic scene completion; iterative gives modest gains in some conditions but incurs higher compute; results indicate geometry-conditioned boundary and that robustness strategies vary by perturbation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate when test-time compute via iterative refinement is preferable to simply widening a predictor, controlling for denoising curricula, corruption augmentation, capacity, and unpaired evaluation; use a controlled protocol in LiDAR scene completion.

Method: Compare a one-shot predictor, a parameter-matched wider predictor, and a weight-tied multigrid refiner initialized from the same frozen predictor across five seeds and SemanticKITTI sequence-08; protocol decouples coherent region removal, independent thinning, range-dependent attenuation, and additive clutter while preserving scene-condition pairing; evaluate with mIoU under various perturbations and report bootstrap CIs.

Result: Iterative system improves mIoU by 0.911 over the wide control under contiguous angular removal with 95% bootstrap CI [0.804, 1.040], surpassing a predeclared 0.5-point margin. Under independent 75% thinning, iteration adds 0.300 points [0.166, 0.436]. Observation-family augmentation adds 5.975 points [5.662, 6.140]. Additive clutter is not repaired. Iteration costs 10.74 ms and 0.75 GiB/frame, vs 6.25 ms and 0.23 GiB for the wide control.

Conclusion: There is no universal advantage to iteration; geometry-conditioned scenarios can justify fixed-depth refinement, broad thinning is better addressed by training coverage, and spurious evidence requires a different robustness mechanism.

Abstract: Should a completion model spend extra test-time compute by iterating, or spend a similar parameter budget on a wider one-shot predictor? The answer is easily confounded by denoising curricula, corruption augmentation, capacity, and unpaired evaluation. We study this question in LiDAR semantic scene completion by comparing a one-shot predictor, a parameter-matched wider predictor, and a weight-tied multigrid refiner initialized from the same frozen predictor. The protocol separates coherent region removal, independent thinning, range-dependent attenuation, and additive clutter while preserving exact scene-condition pairing. Across five training seeds and 815 SemanticKITTI sequence-08 frames, the full iterative system improves mIoU over the wide control by 0.911 points under contiguous angular removal, with a 95% moving-block bootstrap interval of [0.804, 1.040] that clears a predeclared 0.5-point practical margin. Under independent 75% thinning, iteration adds only 0.300 points [0.166, 0.436], whereas observation-family augmentation adds 5.975 points [5.662, 6.140]. Neither intervention repairs additive clutter. The iterative system also costs 10.74 ms and 0.75 GiB per frame, versus 6.25 ms and 0.23 GiB for the wide control. These results establish a geometry-conditioned empirical boundary rather than a universal advantage: coherent gaps can justify fixed-depth refinement, broadly thinned evidence is addressed more effectively by training coverage, and spurious evidence requires a different robustness mechanism.

</details>


### [84] [PaCoNet: Deep Data Extraction for Parallel Coordinates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06030)
*Poonam Poonam,Hannah Kniesel,Pere-Pau Vázquez,Timo Ropinski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PaCoNet is the first deep learning method for extracting data from parallel coordinate plots, enabling extraction of line coordinates and individual data samples, supported by a large-scale dataset; it significantly outperforms unadapted baselines and enables automated analysis and redesign of parallel coordinate plots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data extraction from visualizations is challenging in computer vision, especially for high-dimensional parallel coordinate plots that can become cluttered; automated extraction can aid analysis and redesign of such visualizations.

Method: Introduction of PaCoNet, a deep learning model tailored for parallel coordinate analysis that extracts line coordinates and individual data samples. Development of a large-scale parallel coordinate dataset for training and testing. Public release of code, models, and data generation scripts after acceptance.

Result: PaCoNet outperforms unadapted baselines by a significant margin, demonstrating strong extraction capabilities for parallel coordinate data and sample-level data.

Conclusion: PaCoNet establishes the first deep learning approach for parallel coordinates, enabling automated analysis and redesign of parallel coordinate plots and advancing the intersection of computer vision and data visualization; it enables future complex visualization analysis.

Abstract: Extracting data from visualizations has long challenged computer vision, with current research focused on bar, line, and pie charts, among other low-dimensional visualizations. However, parallel coordinates as a widely used high-dimensional data visualization approach, remain largely unexplored in this context. As parallel coordinate plots can quickly become cluttered and difficult to interpret when poorly designed or densely populated, automated data extraction from such visualizations is of particular interest. In this paper, we propose PaCoNet, the first approach for parallel coordinate data extraction. PaCoNet not only extracts line coordinates, but also enables the extraction of individual data samples for further analysis. Towards this end, we make the following contributions. We present the first deep learning approach tailored for parallel coordinate analysis, and demonstrate that it outperforms unadapted baselines by a significant margin. We further introduce a large-scale parallel coordinate dataset for training and testing. Together, these key contributions enable for the first time the automated analysis and redesign of parallel coordinate plots. PaCoNet thus lays the groundwork for complex visualization analysis, and further advances the intersection of computer vision and data visualization. All code, trained models, and data generation scripts will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.

</details>


### [85] [DARAD: Dual Adapters and Ranking-Aware Distillation for Continual Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06059)
*Xi Chen,Xu Chen,Xiangyang Jia,Wei Wang,Xu Zhang,Zhenyuan Sun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DARAD is a continual RS-ITR framework using a dual-adapter architecture (spatial fusion for visuals; multi-expert textual routing) and bidirectional ranking distillation against a frozen teacher to preserve historical cross-modal ranking while learning from evolving data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address cross-modal alignment space distortion in continual RS-ITR caused by scale variation and distribution shifts; safeguard historical retrieval performance while integrating new visual/textual concepts.

Method: Visual branch with a spatial fusion adapter combining coarse regional cues and fine-grained patch cues; textual branch with multi-expert semantic routing separating shared semantics from specialized residuals; bidirectional ranking distillation using a frozen teacher and historical anchors to maintain historical cross-modal ranking structure across stages.

Result: Empirical results under a multi-stage continual retrieval protocol show DARAD outperforms existing continual learning methods, achieving better adaptation to new data while retaining effectiveness on historical data.

Conclusion: DARAD effectively preserves historical cross-modal ranking structure and mitigates alignment space distortion in continual RS-ITR, enabling robust continual retrieval across evolving remote-sensing archives.

Abstract: With the rapid growth of Earth observation technologies, remote sensing archives are rapidly expanding, making remote sensing image-text retrieval (RS-ITR) increasingly important. However, continual RS-ITR remains challenging because scale variation and distribution shifts in RS aggravate cross-modal alignment space distortion, making it difficult for existing continual learning (CL) methods to support reliable continual retrieval. To address this challenge, we propose DARAD, a dual-adapter and ranking-aware distillation framework that preserves the historical cross-modal ranking structure while learning new visual and textual concepts from evolving archives. Specifically, the visual branch introduces a spatial fusion adapter, which integrates coarse regional cues and fine-grained patch cues to accommodate RS scale variation while anchoring visual updates to the pretrained alignment space. The textual branch employs multi-expert semantic routing, which separates shared textual semantics from semantically specialized residuals to absorb newly emerging descriptions while constraining global text embedding drift. Furthermore, bidirectional ranking distillation uses a frozen teacher model and historical anchors to preserve the historical cross-modal ranking structure, thereby mitigating alignment space distortion across continual stages. Experiments under a multi-stage continual retrieval protocol show that DARAD achieves superior performance over existing CL methods, improving adaptation to newly arrived data while maintaining effectiveness on historical data.

</details>


### [86] [Learning from Failures: Retrieval-Centric CoT via Hard Negatives for Unified Multimodal Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06060)
*Zelong Sun,Jun Wang,Kaicheng Yang,Tiancheng Gu,Ziyong Feng,Zhiwu Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Retrieval-centric chain-of-thought (RC-CoT) via an adviser improves multimodal retrieval by reasoning over initial retrieval results, enabling reranking or full-corpus re-retrieval when needed; trained with hard negatives and reinforcement learning to align reasoning with retrieval outcomes, showing consistent gains on MMEB-V2 and other benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LVLM-based retrievers often miss fine-grained cues and misinterpret top candidates. Traditional CoT explains the query, not retrieval misunderstandings. Conditioning reasoning on retrieval feedback can reduce confusion among semantically similar items and improve ranking accuracy.

Method: An embedder-adviser framework (UniME-R1). The embedder performs initial retrieval. The adviser analyzes candidates to identify discriminative cues that cause confusion. If the target is in top-k, it re-ranks directly. Otherwise, it generates RC-CoT to refine the direction and executes a full-corpus re-retrieval using a dual-mode embedder. Training uses hard negatives, joint optimization of direct and RC-CoT-enabled retrieval, and alignment of the adviser with outcomes via supervised learning and retrieval-focused reinforcement learning.

Result: Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and other multimodal retrieval benchmarks show consistent retrieval performance gains over strong baselines.

Conclusion: Leveraging retrieval-conditioned RC-CoT guided by an adviser effectively addresses misranking due to coarse initial embeddings and demonstrates the value of feedback-driven reasoning in multimodal retrieval pipelines.

Abstract: Unified multimodal retrieval aims to identify candidates that satisfy complex user intent expressed through heterogeneous inputs. Although Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM)-based retrievers are efficient and scalable, directly encoding raw multimodal inputs often misses fine-grained discriminative cues, leading to confusion among semantically similar candidates. Recent methods mitigate this limitation by generating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales to enrich the query representation. However, such reasoning is typically derived from the query alone: it explains what the query describes, but not what the retriever misunderstands. We argue that effective retrieval reasoning should instead be conditioned on retrieval feedback. Based on this insight, we introduce UniME-R1, an embedder-adviser framework that learns to reason over initially retrieved candidates and generate Retrieval-Centric Chain-of-Thought (RC-CoT). The adviser analyzes candidates individually to identify the discriminative cues confused by the embedder. If the target appears in the initial top-k set, UniME-R1 directly reranks the candidates; otherwise, it generates RC-CoT to refine the retrieval direction and performs full-corpus re-retrieval with a dual-mode embedder. To train the framework, we mine hard negatives to simulate realistic retrieval failures, jointly optimize direct retrieval and RC-CoT-augmented retrieval, and align the adviser with retrieval outcomes through supervised learning and retrieval-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and a diverse set of general multimodal retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that UniME-R1 consistently improves retrieval performance over strong baselines.

</details>


### [87] [Bar-JEPA: Extracting Values from Bar Chart with Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06062)
*Poonam Poonam,Alexander Epple,Timo Ropinski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A self-supervised JEPA-based pipeline for per-bar numeric value recovery in bar charts, using a JEPA encoder to produce semantically rich latent features; a simple decoder outputs tick and bar coordinates to recover values; outperforms supervised baselines; code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeling real-world bar chart data for de-rendering is data- and time-intensive. Semantic, high-quality features learned via self-supervision (JEPA) can improve data extraction when labeled data are scarce.

Method: Train a JEPA encoder to learn semantically rich latent features from bar chart images. Use a lightweight decoder to predict coordinates of axis ticks and bar boundaries, enabling per-bar value recovery. Fine-tune self-supervisedly and compare to end-to-end supervised baselines.

Result: Self-supervised fine-tuning yields features that enable a simple, fast-to-train decoder to recover per-bar values, outperforming end-to-end supervised baselines in the reported experiments.

Conclusion: JEPA-based self-supervised feature learning is effective for bar-chart data extraction, offering strong data-efficiency and transferability. The approach reduces labeling needs and provides a modular pipeline; code and data are available on GitHub.

Abstract: Bar charts are commonly used in data visualization, and while they are easily understood by humans, it is non-trivial to extract the underlying data computationally. For a machine-learning-based approach, training chart de-rendering models usually requires labeled, real-world data. Labeling data is a time consuming task, which is why annotated data is scarce. Models can learn more efficiently when provided with features of high semantic quality, which a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) is designed to learn in a self-supervised manner. We present a per-bar, numerical value recovery pipeline for bar charts, where a JEPA encoder is used to produce semantically rich latent features. The decoder model consuming these features is simple and quick to train and outputs the coordinates of ticks and bars, which can be used to recover bar values. The effectiveness of self-supervised finetuning and quality of the extracted features is evident when comparing our model to end-to-end supervised baselines. Code, datasets and checkpoints are available on \href{https://github.com/dralois/Bar-JEPA}{GitHub}.

</details>


### [88] [The Next Screenshot Knows: Gated Hindsight Distillation for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06065)
*Weiwei Li,Junzhuo Liu,Tong Chu,Hengfu Yu,Wen Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Gated Hindsight Distillation (GHD) uses the next screenshot as privileged information during training to address lack of rationale in offline GUI agent imitation. A teacher with access to the future observation reprompts or re-scores the student's on-policy actions, with distillation applied only when the student fails and the teacher recovers the demonstrated action. It yields improved task success over GRPO on AndroidWorld/AndroidLab across two vision-language models; code will be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard offline imitation learning discards the evidence visible only in subsequent observations, preventing the agent from learning the correct reasoning behind actions. This is especially problematic for GUI tasks where menu or state changes reveal the correct action.

Method: Train a student model from observable trajectory prefixes. A parameter-sharing teacher also observes the next screenshot as privileged information and re-scores the student’s on-policy actions. Distillation is applied selectively: when the student fails and the teacher can recover the demonstrated action. The approach leverages hindsight from future observations during training.

Result: GHD improves task success over GRPO on AndroidWorld and AndroidLab across two vision-language models.

Conclusion: Incorporating privileged future observations via hindsight distillation can significantly enhance learning of GUI agents from offline trajectories, with results validated on two datasets and two VL models; code and checkpoints will be released.

Abstract: GUI agents are commonly trained offline from successful interaction trajectories. Standard training decomposes each trajectory into prefix-action pairs: the agent predicts an action from the current screen and interaction history, while the subsequent observation is discarded. This removes the rationale of why an action is correct: the evidence often appears only on the subsequent screen. For example, to enable Soft Wrap, the agent should click Edit or View, but nothing reveals this until the menu opens. Without such evidence, standard imitation gives the model little chance of ever sampling and thus learning the correct reasoning. To address this issue, we propose Gated Hindsight Distillation (GHD), which uses the next screenshot as privileged information during training. A student predicts from the observable trajectory prefix, while a parameter-sharing teacher additionally observes the next screenshot and re-scores the student's on-policy responses. We apply distillation only when the student fails and the hindsight-conditioned teacher recovers the demonstrated action. GHD improves task success over GRPO on AndroidWorld and AndroidLab across two vision-language models. The code and checkpoints will be made available.

</details>


### [89] [Domain-Grounded Candidate Selection for Agentic Image Editing: A Shadow Removal Case](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06075)
*Shilin Hu,Jingyi Xu,Dimitris Samaras,Hieu Le*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Commercial vision-language models can aid shadow removal but do not replace physics-informed low-level priors; an agentic, physics-grounded pipeline improves reliability and reduces artifacts, achieving substantial CDD gains on ShadowRemovalRefine.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether modern vision-language editors can supplant traditional low-level priors in a physics-constrained task (shadow removal) and to address failure modes like content hallucination by grounding the process in shadow-formation physics.

Method: Use a commercial generative editor for shadow-free edits; identify failure modes (content regeneration, misinterpretation of shadows). Propose an agentic candidate-selection pipeline: editor generates a guided probe; evaluator screens failures; perform retries; sample multiple candidates; filter and select final result. Grounding the process by treating shadows as illumination effects (not material/geometry). Evaluate on ShadowRemovalRefine with CDD as metric.

Result: Physics-grounded, agentic pipeline yields CDD of 0.0075, improving by at least 47% over the strongest prior method on ShadowRemovalRefine.

Conclusion: Commercial vision-language models augment but do not replace classic low-level priors. Physics-based constraints improve reliability and consistency, guiding underconstrained generation in vision tasks like shadow removal.

Abstract: Commercial vision-language models are reshaping computer vision, with visual priors broad enough to rival task-specific systems. This raises a natural question: do they reduce the need for classic, physics-informed low-level vision? We study this through shadow removal, a problem shaped by scene geometry, illumination, materials, and occluders, where paired shadow and shadow-free data are hard to collect at scale. We find that a commercial generative editor, used directly, can produce clean shadow-free edits that preserve surface texture and local appearance. However, this comes with a new failure mode: the same editor can regenerate scene content, hallucinate objects, or misread a shadow as material or geometry, producing plausible but physically wrong edits. We address this with an agentic candidate-selection pipeline: the editor generates a guided probe, an evaluator screens for major failures, retries when needed, samples multiple candidates, filters them, and selects a final result balancing shadow removal against scene preservation. Grounding this process in shadow-formation physics makes it more reliable: prompting the generator and evaluator to treat shadows as illumination effects caused by light occlusion, not material or object structure, measurably improves quality and consistency. On the ShadowRemovalRefine benchmark, our physics-oriented pipeline achieves a CDD of 0.0075, reducing CDD by at least 47% over the strongest prior method. These results suggest that commercial vision-language models do not replace classic low-level vision priors; instead, such priors remain useful for constraining and steering physically underconstrained generation.

</details>


### [90] [Dense-Cast: A lightweight ensemble of deep learning architectures for precipitation nowcasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06082)
*Gourav Jyoti Kalita,Hidam Kumarjit Singh*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A lightweight deep learning approach for half-hourly precipitation nowcasting in NE India using DenseNet, residual connections, and transformer encoders; predicts the next 2 half-hours from the previous 5 steps; trained on GPM IMERG (30-min cadence); reported MAE 0.235 mm, RMSE 0.735 mm, KLGE 0.816.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Short-term precipitation nowcasting is challenging due to high variability, nonlinearity, and spatiotemporal dependencies; requires efficient models with limited parameters for operational use.

Method: Hybrid architecture combining DenseNet features, residual connections, and transformer encoders to capture spatial and temporal dependencies. Input: five consecutive 30-minute steps; output: predictions for the next two 30-minute steps. Dataset: GPM IMERG with 30-minute cadence; region: North-Eastern India; evaluation at 30-minute interval.

Result: MAE = 0.235 mm, RMSE = 0.735 mm, KGE = 0.816 at 30-minute interval; reported as best performance.

Conclusion: Proposes a parameter-efficient architecture that blends CNN-based feature extraction with transformer-based temporal modeling for precipitation nowcasting in a monsoon-dominated region; shows promising accuracy with reduced model complexity; further validation across other regions and longer horizons recommended.

Abstract: Proper short-term forecasting of precipitation is crucial in disaster management and preparedness. Nonetheless, the variability and nonlinearity of precipitation make short-term forecasting challenging for meteorologists. Moreover, capturing temporal dependencies in spatiotemporal data is a challenge in precipitation nowcasting. In this article, we introduce a lightweight deep learning model for half-hourly precipitation nowcasting. This model has been designed by incorporating the DenseNet architecture, residual connections, and transformer encoders for effective precipitation nowcasting with reduced model parameters. The North-Eastern region of India has been selected as the area of interest for our study. The region receives the highest precipitation during the months of June-September due to the monsoon season. The proposed model takes the previous five time-steps of half-hourly precipitation as inputs and predicts the precipitation in the next two half-hours. The GPM IMERG precipitation dataset with a 30-minute cadence has been used in this study for training and testing the model. The proposed architecture achieves best MAE of 0.235 millimetres, RMSE of 0.735 millimetres, and KGE score of 0.816 at an interval of 30 minutes.

</details>


### [91] [Confidence matters: Leveraging Multi-view Geometric Priors for GS-based Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06117)
*Hongyu Zhou,Zorah Lähner*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a widely-used tool for novel view synthesis, offering real-time rendering in a sparse representation. However, the method's reliance on structure-from-motion initialization and photometric optimization can lead to suboptimal geometric reconstruction, particularly for objects with high specularity. In this work, we investigate the integration of geometric priors, in the form of predicted normal and depth maps, into the 3DGS framework to improve the reconstruction quality. We analyze the effect of incorporating these priors into GS-based methods and our evaluation reveals that multi-view predictions, as they are done by the recent visual geometry grounded transformer (VGGT), outperform single-view alternatives. A major factor is the existence of a confidence map for the estimations, which comes as a by-product of multi-view models and which can significantly improve the effectiveness of priors by weighting each prediction appropriately. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show consistent improvement in reconstruction quality and significant gains in complex scenes including specular objects.

</details>


### [92] [Sample-Adaptive Latent Rewards for Uncertainty-Guided Diffusion Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06125)
*Rui Li,Yuanzhi Liang,Ke Hao,Ziqiao Weng,Haibin Huang,Chi Zhang,XueLong Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified latent-space reward framework (SURE) for diffusion models that jointly models reward values and uncertainty in latent space, enabling uncertainty-guided dense feedback and stable optimization without pixel-space decoding, achieving state-of-the-art results on VBench and related metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent reward models for diffusion models currently output only scalar scores, lacking uncertainty estimates. This makes it hard to assess feedback reliability, risks guiding optimization astray (reward hacking), and reduces training efficiency. Introducing uncertainty-aware latent rewards can improve reliability and stability of alignment with human preferences.

Method: SURE-LRM: a sample-adaptive latent reward model that predicts a Gaussian utility for each noisy latent; mean is the reward score, variance captures prediction uncertainty without extra annotations. SURE-REFL: uncertainty-guided reward feedback learning that uses the detached variance as reliability weights for samples at the same transition, querying SURE-LRM at selected transitions and backpropagating rewards only through local transitions. All computations stay in latent space, with no pixel-space decoding or full denoising graph traversal.

Result: Empirical results claim that SURE-LRM improves preference prediction over strong baselines; SURE-REFL achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and improves optimization stability; it attains the highest VBench quality, semantic, and total scores among evaluated methods.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-aware, dense latent-space reward learning can substantially improve alignment of diffusion models with human preferences while maintaining efficiency by avoiding pixel-space decoding and full denoising graphs, and offering improved stability and performance.

Abstract: Latent reward models can supervise visual diffusion models without decoding intermediate states into pixel space. This makes alignment with human preferences more efficient. However, existing latent reward models output only scalar scores. They do not estimate the uncertainty of each prediction. The generator therefore cannot determine which feedback is reliable. This can drive optimization in the wrong direction and lead to reward hacking. We propose \textsc{SURE}, a unified latent-space framework for image and video diffusion models. It learns reward distributions and directly uses their reliability to guide dense post-training. First, we propose sample-adaptive latent reward model (\textsc{SURE-LRM}). It predicts a Gaussian utility for each noisy latent. Its mean predicts the reward score. Its variance reflect the uncertainty of prediction without human annotation. The learned distribution then guides post-training through uncertainty-guided reward feedback learning (\textsc{SURE-REFL}). This method provides uncertainty-guided dense feedback along the denoising trajectory. At selected transitions, \textsc{SURE-REFL} queries the frozen \textsc{SURE-LRM}. It converts detached variance into reliability weights for samples at the same transition. Each weighted reward is backpropagated only through its local transition. The entire process remains in latent space and requires neither pixel-space decoding nor the full denoising graph. Experiments show that \textsc{SURE-LRM} improves preference prediction over strong baselines. \textsc{SURE-REFL} achieves the sota performance among various metrics and further improves optimization stability. It also achieves the highest VBench quality, semantic, and total scores among the evaluated methods.

</details>


### [93] [Patient Pose Assessment Using a CT-Based Framework for Synthetic Data Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06126)
*Manuel Laufer,Dominik Mairhöfer,Malte Sieren,Hauke Gerdes,Fabio Leal dos Reis,Arpad Bischof,Thomas Käster,Erhardt Barth,Jörg Barkhausen,Thomas Martinetz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Synthetic CT-derived depth data for radiograph pose estimation yields up to 11 pp improvement on real upper-ankle radiographs, addressing data scarcity due to regulatory hurdles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated, reliable pose assessment is crucial for diagnostic radiography; collecting paired depth radiographs is hindered by regulatory constraints; synthetic data offers a feasible alternative.

Method: Create synthetic depth-image pairs from CT scans to train a pose-assessment model; pretrain on 3077 synthetic upper-ankle image pairs; evaluate on real joints.

Result: Pretraining on synthetic data yields up to 11 percentage points improvement in pose assessment on real upper-ankle joints (relative to baseline without synthetic pretraining).

Conclusion: CT-derived synthetic data is a promising approach to bridge the domain gap for radiographic pose estimation, reducing data collection burdens; further work needed on generalization to other joints and domain adaptation.

Abstract: An adequate diagnostic quality of radiographs is essential for reliable diagnoses and treatment planning. The patient's pose during radiography is one of the most important factors determining the diagnostic quality. Since patient positioning is difficult and not standardized, an automated AI-based approach using depth images to automatically assess the patient's pose before the radiograph has been taken would be helpful. Due to regulatory hurdles, however, it is difficult in practice to acquire the required depth images and corresponding radiographs. In this paper, we present a framework that can generate such training data synthetically from Computed Tomography scans. We further show that by pretraining on our generated synthetic dataset consisting of 3077 image pairs of upper ankle joints, the pose assessment of real upper ankle joints can be improved by up to 11 percentage points.

</details>


### [94] [Learning visual representations for compositional analysis of artworks and photographs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06142)
*Fatemeh Behrad,Tinne Tuytelaars,Johan Wagemans*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Two compositional analysis paradigms are compared: a human-inspired perceptual grouping approach and fine-tuned foundation models trained on large compositional datasets. With frozen encoders, the human-inspired method is competitive and interpretable; when data allows, fine-tuned self-supervised models outperform but lose interpretability and cross-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Composition understanding is central to visual meaning and aesthetics but remains underformalized. The study investigates whether human-inspired perceptual grouping can yield meaningful, interpretable representations versus data-hungry foundation models, and how each generalizes across domains.

Method: Two paradigms were evaluated: (1) a human-inspired approach using object-centric region decomposition and a graph attention network to model spatial relationships; (2) large foundation models fine-tuned on expansive compositional datasets. Experiments cover three tasks—composition score/category prediction, compositional image retrieval, and visual saliency detection. Analyses consider frozen encoders versus fine-tuning.

Result: With frozen encoders, the human-inspired method achieves competitive performance and remains interpretable. When sufficient data enables fine-tuning, large self-supervised models outperform significantly, but at the cost of interpretability and cross-domain generalization.

Conclusion: Trade-offs prevail: the human-inspired, interpretable approach offers robustness and domain transfer with limited data, while fine-tuned large models deliver higher accuracy given ample data but sacrifice interpretability and generalization across domains. A hybrid or biased approach may leverage strengths of both.

Abstract: Composition, the deliberate arrangement of visual elements, is central to how meaning, emotion, and aesthetic quality are conveyed in artwork, yet it remains among the least formalized dimensions of visual understanding. Prior work highlights a persistent gap in learning meaningful compositional representations, attributing it to semantic bias and suggesting that human-inspired approaches may be key. We compare two parallel paradigms for composition analysis: a human-inspired method grounded in perceptual grouping, and fine-tuned foundation models enabled by recent large-scale compositional datasets. The human-inspired approach uses object-centric models for region-level decomposition and a graph attention network to capture spatial relationships between elements. Both paradigms are evaluated on composition score/category prediction, compositional image retrieval, and visual saliency detection. With frozen encoders, the human-inspired method achieves competitive performance while remaining interpretable. When sufficient data enables fine-tuning, large self-supervised models outperform significantly, but at the cost of interpretability and cross-domain generalization.

</details>


### [95] [BendTwin: Robust Dense-to-Sparse Physical Reconstruction with Bending-Aware Differentiable Spring-Mass Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06164)
*Yixiong Jing,Qi Wang,Lin Chen,Junwei Jiang,Guangming Wang,Haibing Wu,Olaf Wysocki,Wanli Ma,Brian Sheil*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BendTwin adds bending constraints to a differentiable spring-mass model for video-based reconstruction of deformable objects, improving stability and deformation realism. It outperforms the axial-only PhysTwin baseline and remains robust under different downsampling, enabling mechanically faithful digital twins from sparse RGB-D videos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Axial-spring models become mechanically under-constrained and fail to preserve stable local deformation when the physical graph is coarsened. This limits the mechanical fidelity of video-based reconstruction and future prediction.

Method: Introduce bending stiffness and damping on local surface triplets by penalizing deviations from rest angles and regularizing higher-order deformation, within a differentiable spring-mass framework similar to PhysTwin.

Result: Experiments show BendTwin consistently outperforms the axial-only PhysTwin baseline; ablation studies demonstrate improved stability across downsampling ratios and better performance than the original PhysTwin.

Conclusion: A bending-aware extension of a differentiable spring-mass model yields more mechanically faithful reconstructions and stable future predictions from sparse-view RGB-D videos, while preserving the simplicity of the spring-mass formulation.

Abstract: Reconstructing objects with mechanical properties from video observations enables physically consistent dynamic prediction, benefiting robotics planning and interaction. Existing spring--mass based physical driven reconstruction approaches offer efficient and differentiable physical reconstruction, but they typically rely on axial springs alone. Such formulations oversimplify the underlying structural mechanics and can become mechanically under-constrained when the physical graph is coarsened, limiting their ability to preserve stable local deformation. We present BendTwin, a bending-aware differentiable spring--mass framework for video-based reconstruction and future prediction of deformable objects. BendTwin introduces bending stiffness and damping over local surface triplets, penalizing deviations from rest angles and regularizing higher-order deformation. These bending constraints improve mechanical stability while preserving the simplicity of spring--mass system. Experiments show that BendTwin consistently outperforms the axial-only PhysTwin baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate that the bending constraints maintain system stability across different downsampling ratios and consistently improve upon the original PhysTwin formulation. Overall, BendTwin provides an effective approach for constructing mechanically faithful digital twins from sparse-view RGB-D videos.

</details>


### [96] [Support Operation Factorization: Compositional Readout of Frozen Vision Encoders under Controlled Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06174)
*Zhongyao Wang,Wanli Ouyang,Taoyong Cui,Pheng Ann Heng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes injectively aligned leave-one-cell-out protocol and a factored SO-OPF readout to separate binding formation and recoverability in frozen vision encoders, addressing operation laundering. Shows strong injective assignment accuracy on Shapes3D-Extended and COCO with DINOv3, improved by axis-aware supervision; partial generalization on MuJoCo with slot collapse. Demonstrates substrate-dependent boundary between recoverability from flat labels and renderer failures, but not universal recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the conflation between what changes (bindings) and where they change (grid alignment) in compositional analysis of frozen vision encoders. Combat operation laundering where multiple operations reuse the same slot by enforcing injective, support-aware evaluation and a readout that jointly reasons about support salience and operation posterior.

Method: Introduce an injectively aligned leave-one-cell-out protocol over support x operation grids and a readout (SO-OPF) that factorizes cell energy into support salience and a competitive operation posterior. Evaluate on frozen DINOv3 features across Shapes3D-Extended, COCO, and MuJoCo substrates under varied supervision (matched-axis-aware), comparing against dense carriers and flat-label baselines.

Result: Known factorial assignment accuracy: Shapes3D-Extended 0.874; COCO 0.799. Learning assignment from flat labels: Shapes3D-Extended 0.769; COCO 0.762. With matched-axis-aware supervision on Shapes3D, factored carrier raises learned-assignment accuracy from 0.653 to 0.841 and eliminates laundering gap; SigLIP2 reproduces COCO separation. On a rebuilt MuJoCo substrate, learned-assignment accuracy drops to 0.569 (DINOv3) and 0.484 (SigLIP2) with substantial slot collapse.

Conclusion: Factored readout and injective evaluation enable recovery of held-out bindings on multiple substrates and reveal a renderer-specific failure boundary, but they do not demonstrate universal recoverability from flat labels; performance is substrate-dependent and bound by slot collapse and renderer characteristics.

Abstract: Compositional analysis of frozen vision encoders should determine both what changed and where it changed. Standard factor probes score these axes separately, however, and can reward multiple operations that reuse the same predicted slot. We call this failure operation laundering. We introduce an injectively aligned leave-one-cell-out protocol over support x operation grids and SO-OPF, a readout that factors cell energy into support salience and a competitive operation posterior. This formulation separates two questions that aggregate scores conflate: whether the carrier composes held-out bindings when the grid is known, and whether that grid can be recovered from flat cell labels. With frozen DINOv3 features, known factorial assignment reaches 0.874 injective accuracy on Shapes3D-Extended and 0.799 on globally image-disjoint COCO; learning the assignment from flat labels reaches 0.769 and 0.762, respectively. Under matched-axis-aware supervision on Shapes3D, the factored carrier improves learned-assignment accuracy from 0.653 to 0.841 over a dense carrier and eliminates its laundering gap. SigLIP2 replicates the COCO separation. A rebuilt MuJoCo substrate exposes a boundary: learned-assignment accuracy is 0.569 with DINOv3 and 0.484 with SigLIP2, with substantial slot collapse. Thus factored readout and injective evaluation recover held-out bindings on two substrates while exposing, rather than hiding, a renderer-specific failure boundary; they do not establish universal recovery from flat labels.

</details>


### [97] [EvReflection: Event-Driven Micro-Dynamics for Reflection Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06184)
*Jiaxiao Wang,Dachun Kai,Huyue Zhu,Quanquan Hu,Zhenyang Xu,Xiaoyan Sun*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Event-driven reflection removal (EvReflection) uses event-camera signals to resolve the reconstruction ambiguity between reflection and transmission layers, via a Micro-Dynamics Decoupler and Parallax-Attention Rectifier, aided by a parallax-aware simulation pipeline and the EVR^2 dataset; achieves state-of-the-art results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reflection-removal methods rely on static single-frame priors and struggle with intrinsic ambiguity between layers. Introducing event streams captures micro-dynamics that reveal differential motion between reflection and transmission, enabling better layer separation.

Method: 1) Micro-Dynamics Decoupler extracts layer-specific motion priors from event streams. 2) Parallax-Attention Rectifier uses these priors to remove artifacts from the RGB image. 3) Parallax-aware simulation pipeline generates data; 4) EVR^2 provides real-world benchmarks; code and models are released.

Result: EvReflection achieves state-of-the-art performance on synthetic and real benchmarks, surpassing the best competing method by >1.6 dB and >1.2 dB in PSNR, respectively.

Conclusion: Leveraging event-driven micro-dynamics effectively decouples reflection and transmission layers and facilitates cleaner removal of artifacts; the proposed dataset and pipeline support broader evaluation and replication.

Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in reflection removal, current methods primarily exploit static image priors from a single frame and still suffer from severe residual artifacts due to the inherent ambiguity between the reflection and transmission layers. In this paper, we propose leveraging event signals to break this ambiguity. By employing event cameras to capture micro-dynamics, we reveal the differential motion between these two layers. We thereby present a novel event-driven reflection removal network, EvReflection, that utilizes these dynamic cues for layer separation. Specifically, we design a Micro-Dynamics Decoupler to disentangle layer-specific motions from event streams as priors, which then guide a Parallax-Attention Rectifier to cleanly remove artifacts from the RGB image. Furthermore, to address data scarcity, we develop a parallax-aware simulation pipeline and construct the EVR$^2$ benchmark dataset, the first real-world dataset for this task. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvReflection achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks, surpassing the best competing method by more than 1.6 dB and 1.2 dB in PSNR, respectively. The code, dataset, and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/JiaxiaoWang/EvReflection.

</details>


### [98] [HOPE: Hand-Object Pressure Estimation from Monocular Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06192)
*Subin Jeon,Byungjun Kim,Hanbyul Joo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A vision-based, hand-centric framework HOPE predicts temporally evolving per-vertex pressure and contact on the hand mesh from monocular video, unifying object-agnostic pressure estimation across surface, object, and contact supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating contact pressure is critical for understanding hand-object interactions, but prior vision methods are limited to planar sensors or fixed viewpoints; a dynamic, object-agnostic, video-based approach is needed.

Method: HOPE lifts multiple pressure and contact annotations into a shared hand vertex space and uses a vertex-anchored video transformer where each vertex is a persistent token. It aggregates visual features and hand pose over time and employs a contact-gated pressure head to ensure pressure is zero without contact. Outputs are temporally evolving per-vertex normal pressure and on-hand contact predictions.

Result: HOPE is validated on OpenTouch, PressureVisionDB, and hand-object contact benchmarks, performing across object-pressure, surface-pressure, and contact-supervised HOI settings. It generalizes to bare-hand egocentric and in-the-wild videos and produces joint contact and pressure predictions that surpass purely contact-only or planar-pressure baselines.

Conclusion: HOPE provides a unified, generalizable framework for vision-based pressure estimation from monocular video, leveraging multi-source supervision and a per-vertex token representation to handle diverse objects and surfaces.

Abstract: Estimating physical pressure from vision is essential for understanding contact-rich hand-object interaction. However, prior vision-based pressure estimation methods are largely limited to planar surfaces and single image input, making them difficult to apply to dynamic hand-object interaction with diverse objects. We instead formulate pressure estimation as a hand-centric video prediction problem with monocular video as input. This formulation predicts temporally evolving per-vertex normal pressure and contact directly on the hand mesh, yielding a unified output space independent of object shape and sensor layout. Building on this formulation, we propose \textbf{HOPE}, a framework with two key components. First, we lift tactile-glove pressure, planar-sensor pressure, and distance-based hand-object contact annotations into a shared hand vertex space, allowing bare-hand contact data to regularize pressure learning where metric labels are unavailable. Second, we introduce a vertex-anchored video transformer that treats each vertex as a persistent token, aggregates visual features and hand pose over time, and uses a contact-gated pressure head to enforce that pressure vanishes without contact. Experiments on OpenTouch, PressureVisionDB, and hand-object contact benchmarks validate HOPE across object-pressure, surface-pressure, and contact-supervised HOI settings. Despite using metric pressure supervision primarily from gloved-hand videos, HOPE generalizes to bare-hand egocentric and in-the-wild videos, producing joint contact and pressure predictions beyond the scope of contact-only or planar-pressure baselines.

</details>


### [99] [CFGPNet: Cross-Attention-Based Fused Gradient Programmed Network Framework for Multispectral Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06205)
*Nima Hatami,Karim Faez,Saeed Sharifian,Hamidreza Amindavar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CFGPNet presents an efficient RGB–T object detector that enhances cross-modal interaction via CrossCEA and ASAF, using a RepViT-like backbone with re-parameterized blocks and a programmable-gradient auxiliary branch; it achieves strong accuracy on five benchmarks with favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The abstract targets the bottlenecks in RGB–T detection: weak cross-modal interaction, unstable fusion due to modality gaps, and high computational cost from heavy attention. The work aims to enable robust multispectral perception with efficient fusion.

Method: Introduce CFGPNet with (1) an improved GELAN backbone using RepViT-style re-parameterized blocks; (2) Cross Computation Efficient Attention (CrossCEA) for cross-modal interaction; (3) Attention Selection and Aggregation Fusion (ASAF) for compact fused representations via dense aggregation and selective attention; (4) a programmable-gradient auxiliary branch to improve gradient flow. Evaluated on five datasets with multiple model scales.

Result: On FLIR, M3FD, LLVIP, VEDAI, and MFAD CFGPNet attains notable mAP50/mAP50:95 values (e.g., 80.7/45.0 on FLIR, 89.9/63.4 on M3FD, 97.8/68.9 on LLVIP, 83.3/56.9 on VEDAI, 83.4/61.8 on MFAD), demonstrating strong accuracy and favorable efficiency trades across diverse scenes and scales.

Conclusion: CFGPNet is an effective, practical solution for multispectral object detection, achieving robust cross-modal fusion with improved efficiency, and is accompanied by code and pretrained models.

Abstract: RGB--T object detection exploits the complementary strengths of visible and infrared imagery, supporting robust perception in low-light, adverse-weather, and complex multi-scale environments. However, existing methods still suffer from insufficient cross-modal interaction, unstable fusion from modality distribution gaps, and the high computational cost of heavy attention-based architectures. To address these issues, CFGPNet is proposed, a Cross-Attention-Based Fused Gradient Programmed Network framework for multispectral object detection. CFGPNet uses an improved GELAN backbone with RepViT-style re-parameterized blocks to strengthen feature representation while preserving computational efficiency. A Cross Computation Efficient Attention (CrossCEA) module is introduced to enhance cross-modal feature interaction and reduce redundant information transfer between visible and thermal branches. To generate compact and discriminative fused representations, an Attention Selection and Aggregation Fusion (ASAF) network combines dense feature aggregation with selective attention-based emphasis. Moreover, a programmable-gradient auxiliary branch is integrated into each CFGPNet variant to improve gradient delivery and optimization quality. Experiments on five public multispectral benchmarks, FLIR, M3FD, LLVIP, VEDAI, and MFAD, demonstrate that CFGPNet achieves strong and consistent performance across diverse scenes, object scales, and modality balances. In particular, the framework attains 80.7% mAP50 / 45.0% mAP50:95 on FLIR, 89.9% / 63.4% on M3FD, and 97.8% / 68.9% on LLVIP. It also reaches 83.3% / 56.9% on VEDAI and 83.4% / 61.8% on MFAD. These results show that CFGPNet is an effective, practical solution offering useful accuracy--efficiency trade-offs across three model scales. The code, data, and fine-tuned models are available at https://github.com/NimaHatami99/CFGPNet.

</details>


### [100] [EmoWorld: A Decoupled Affective Field for Controllable Emotional Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06231)
