*Bingyuan Wang,Baistan Zhyldyzbekov,Kunyu Feng,Zeyu Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EmoWorld decouples atmosphere, semantics, and temporal cues in video diffusion, enabling modular control of emotion through Visual Atmosphere Steering (VAS), Semantic Affective Steering (SAS), and Temporal Affective Steering (TAS) with a one-time preparation on neutral and emotion-edited panoramas.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video generators entangle global atmosphere, affect-bearing semantics, and temporal progression within a single text prompt, complicating reliable emotion control and stability; a decoupled framework is sought to independently modulate these factors.

Method: A frozen flow-matching Video Diffusion Transformer (Video DiT) is prepared once to extract layer-specific affect directions and a reusable cue library from neutral and emotion-edited panoramas. Inference injects atmosphere into hidden states via Visual Atmosphere Steering (VAS), uses a separately scalable prompt residual for semantic cues via Semantic Affective Steering (SAS), and interpolates endpoint residual fields for time via Temporal Affective Steering (TAS). Evaluation spans Wan2.2 and 27 emotion categories in text-to-video and image-to-video settings, across multiple Video-DiT backbones, with camera-conditioned composition without updating generator parameters.

Result: Quantitative gains on Wan2.2: VAS improves target-emotion alignment by 19% and reduces a temporal-fluctuation proxy by 48%; SAS improves alignment by 37% and increases detected affect-bearing cues by 36%; TAS improves transition monotonicity by 15% over the strongest baseline. EmoWorld demonstrates portability across backbones and supports camera-conditioned composition without modifying generator parameters.

Conclusion: EmoWorld effectively decouples atmosphere, semantic cues, and temporal progression to enhance emotion-guided video generation, delivering substantial alignment and stability gains across diverse backbones and conditioning scenarios.

Abstract: Emotion shapes how viewers interpret a scene, yet existing video generators entangle global atmosphere, affect-bearing semantic cues, and temporal progression within a single text condition. We present EmoWorld, a framework that decouples these factors within a frozen flow-matching video diffusion transformer (Video DiT). A one-time preparation stage extracts layer-specific affect directions and a reusable cue library from geometry-preserving neutral and emotion-edited panoramas. At inference, Visual Atmosphere Steering (VAS) injects atmosphere directions into hidden states, Semantic Affective Steering (SAS) isolates a separately scalable prompt residual for semantic cues, and Temporal Affective Steering (TAS) interpolates endpoint residual fields across denoising and video time. On Wan2.2, VAS improves target-emotion alignment by 19% while reducing a temporal-fluctuation proxy by 48%; SAS improves target-emotion alignment by 37% and increases detected affect-bearing cues by 36%; and TAS improves transition monotonicity by 15% over the strongest baseline. EmoWorld is evaluated across 27 emotion categories in text-to-video and image-to-video settings, demonstrates portability across multiple Video-DiT backbones, and supports camera-conditioned composition without updating generator parameters.

</details>


### [101] [Depth-Guided Video Object Counting in Crowded Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06236)
*Yuanjing Xu,Xinyan Liu,Weidong Chen,Zixuan Zou,Linhao Zhang,Zhuangzhe Meng,Antoni B. Chan,Weigang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes DG-Det: a depth-guided RGB-D detector for video object counting in crowded scenes, with cross-attention, occlusion prediction, and a de-duplication step, plus a RGB-D counting dataset; achieves ~62% MAE improvement over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RGB-only video object counting struggles in crowded/occluded scenes; depth cues can enhance discrimination and spatial understanding for robust counting.

Method: Introduce Depth-Guided Detector (DG-Det) with multi-scale RGB-D cross-attention, explicit occlusion prediction, and a unified de-duplication pipeline across frames; release a RGB-D Video Object Counting dataset; provide source code.

Result: Significant performance gain: 62.01% MAE reduction vs. baselines; improvements in RMSE; consistent gains across experiments; robust counting in crowded/occluded scenes; dataset and code released.

Conclusion: Depth-guided, RGB-D counting with occlusion handling and cross-frame deduplication yields robust object counting in challenging scenes and offers datasets/code to accelerate future research.

Abstract: Our primary objective is to advance video object counting in crowded scenes, aiming to robustly count all instances of a target category based on given text or visual prompts. Existing methods rely on RGB information, limiting their discriminative ability in crowded and occluded conditions. To address this, we propose a Depth-Guided Detector (DG-Det) along with a general post-processing pipeline. By integrating depth cues with multi-scale RGB-D cross-attention and explicit occlusion prediction, our method enhances spatial understanding and achieves robust detection in crowded and occluded scenes. Furthermore, we introduce a unified de-duplication framework to eliminate cross-frame redundant counting. To facilitate future research, we also release a new RGB-D Video Object Counting dataset featuring depth information and multiple object categories persequence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a 62.01\% reduction in MAE compared to existing baselines, and also produces consistent improvements in RMSE. We provide the source code at https://github.com/streamer-AP/DG-Net and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/aerospace123/RGBD-VideoCount.

</details>


### [102] [PRISM: Distribution-Gated Flow Matching for Controllable Unpaired Image Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06240)
*Elad Yoshai,Natan T. Shaked*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PRISM: a GAN-free flow-matching framework for unpaired image-to-image translation that replaces global guidance with per-feature gates informed by standardized distance to the target distribution, enabling selective preservation and controlled changes. It uses gate-driven initialization and ODE transport with task-matched corruption (AdaIN for structure-preserving, partially anchored for structure-changing) and supports local override at inference without retraining; achieves strong quantitative results across diverse benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unpaired I2I translation must decide per image which content to preserve and what to change. Global noise/guidance values hinder separating content from appearance. A per-feature, spatially aware gate can selectively preserve structures while allowing changes, enabling flexible, task-matched translation without paired supervision.

Method: Introduce a learned per-feature gate within a GAN-free flow-matching framework. The gate uses a spatial prior derived from standardized distance between source features and the target feature distribution. It controls (i) initialization by mixing the real source latent with a task-matched corruption and (ii) transport timing during ODE integration. The corruption is task-matched: AdaIN-based (content-anchored) for structure-preserving translation and partially anchored for structure-changing translation. The gate can be overridden locally at inference via text or a detector without retraining.

Result: PRISM attains best Inception FID and KID on four of five benchmarks and competitive results on the fifth; in histopathology, it yields a nuclei-count ratio closest to the ideal, indicating a favorable balance between realism and structural preservation across diverse domains.

Conclusion: PRISM demonstrates that per-feature, spatially governed control in a GAN-free flow-matching framework enables effective unpaired translation with strong target realism while preserving important image structures, and offers flexible, inference-time overrides without retraining.

Abstract: Unpaired image-to-image translation must decide, per image, what to change and what to preserve without paired supervision. Many diffusion-based unpaired translators control preservation through a single global noise or guidance value applied across the image, which cannot separate content to keep from appearance to change. We present PRISM, a GAN-free flow-matching framework that replaces this global control with a learned per-feature gate. The gate's spatial prior is derived from each source feature's standardized distance to the target feature distribution, so features far from the target are freed while target-consistent features are preserved. The same gate controls both the initialization, which mixes the real source latent with a task-matched corruption, and the transport timing during Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) integration. The corruption is matched to the task, content-anchored (AdaIN) for structure-preserving translation and partially anchored for structure-changing translation, and the gate can be overridden locally at inference from text or a detector without retraining, preserving important structures of the original image while still generating realistic results. We evaluate PRISM on five natural and biomedical benchmarks (AFHQ cat->dog, CelebA-HQ appearance translation, day->night relighting, virtual staining, and breast frozen->permanent histopathology). Among the evaluated methods under a shared same-split protocol, PRISM attains the best Inception FID and KID on four benchmarks and a competitive result on the fifth, and on histopathology yields the nuclei-count ratio closest to the ideal, supporting a favorable balance between target realism and structural preservation.

</details>


### [103] [HoloCount: A Holistic Visual Counting Benchmark for MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06420)
*Jinhong Deng,Limeng Qiao,Guanglu Wan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces HoloCount, a three-level benchmark for visual counting to diagnose MLLMs' grounding and counting reliability, revealing performance gaps across semantic, analytical, and robustness tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the gap that existing counting benchmarks overlook complex logical, spatial, and adversarial failure modes, hindering reliable quantitative multimodal understanding.

Method: Presents a three-level taxonomy: Semantic Counting (atomic/property-based enumeration), Analytical Counting (logical/spatial/set-based reasoning), Robustness Testing (adversarial scenarios and grounded counter-priors). Evaluates >20 state-of-the-art MLLMs on HoloCount.

Result: Models perform well on perception tasks but degrade significantly on analytical and robustness tasks, revealing a persistent reliability gap; the benchmark maps current capabilities and guides future improvements.

Conclusion: HoloCount provides a diagnostically rich framework and dataset to push toward grounded, reliable multimodal counting; dataset available at the provided URL.

Abstract: Visual counting is a fundamental pillar of multimodal intelligence, requiring a seamless integration of fine-grained grounding and spatial reasoning. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success in qualitative scene understanding, their quantitative precision remains a significant bottleneck, often characterized by persistent numerical hallucinations. Existing counting benchmarks primarily focus on basic perception in simplified contexts, failing to capture the complex failure modes that emerge under logical constraints or adversarial conditions. To address these limitations, we introduce HoloCount, a holistic and diagnostically rich benchmark structured around a three-level hierarchical taxonomy. HoloCount evaluates MLLMs across: (1) Semantic Counting, focusing on atomic and property-based enumeration; (2) Analytical Counting, assessing logical composition through spatial and set-based reasoning; and (3) Robustness Testing, probing model integrity against adverse scenarios and grounded counter-priors, such as high-density scenes and linguistic biases. Through an exhaustive evaluation of over 20 state-of-the-art MLLMs, we reveal a critical performance gap: even top-tier models degrade significantly as tasks transition from perception to complex analytical reasoning and adverse scenarios. Our findings provide a systematic landscape of current MLLM counting capabilities and offer a roadmap for developing more grounded and reliable multimodal systems. The dataset is available at https://mm-mvr.github.io/HoloCount/.

</details>


### [104] [Toward Deployable Bangla Sign Language Recognition with Expert-Validated Data and a Lightweight Attention-Based Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06252)
*Saad Ahmed,Md Khalid Syfullaha*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A compact, expert-validated BdSL dataset (BdSL38) enables an efficient, on-device recognition model that rivals pretrained backbones with far fewer parameters, enabling practical accessibility for Bangla Sign Language users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable accurate, on-device BdSL recognition using a lightweight model trained from scratch on a high-quality, expert-validated dataset, addressing the limitations of controlled datasets and heavy pretrained backbones.

Method: A lightweight attention-based CNN with 298k parameters built from grouped bottleneck residual blocks, channel/spatial attention, multi-scale depthwise hand-feature block, dual pooling, and Swish activations; trained from scratch on RsBdSL38 (10,874 images across 38 BdSL signs); evaluated against ImageNet-pretrained efficient architectures under identical protocols; retrained on six public BdSL benchmarks; Grad-CAM with deletion-insertion and weight-randomization; signer-independent split; quantization to 0.48 MB for on-device inference.

Result: Achieves 96.37% accuracy on RsBdSL38 (five seeds, ±0.54%); 92.95–98.33% on six BdSL benchmarks, 97.04% on a merged corpus; 76.25% zero-shot on BdSL-38; ablation shows removing any architectural stage costs 7.6–89.3 points; signer-independent split yields 85.18%; quantized model at 0.48 MB runs in 3.98 ms per image on a 15.5 MB device footprint; dataset/code/models released.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that a purpose-built, lightweight model trained on expert-validated BdSL data can approach or match the performance of heavier pretrained models while enabling practical on-device deployment for BdSL recognition, benefiting accessibility and education.

Abstract: Deaf and hard-of-hearing people in Bangladesh communicate mainly through Bangla Sign Language (BdSL). Automatic BdSL recognition on personal devices could widen access to education and services. Existing systems use controlled-setting datasets without expert verification and heavyweight pretrained backbones unsuited to on-device use. We introduce RSBdSL38, 10,874 expert-validated images spanning all 38 BdSL hand signs, representing the 51 letters of the Bangla alphabet, recorded from real signers at three special-needs schools across Bangladesh. We propose a lightweight attention based convolutional network of 298,470 parameters, built from grouped bottleneck residual blocks, channel and spatial attention, a multi-scale depthwise hand-feature block, dual pooling, and Swish activations. Trained from scratch, it attains 96.37% accuracy (95.72% +- 0.54% over five seeds), within 1.08 percentage points of the best of nine ImageNet-pretrained efficient architectures under an identical protocol, using 8.5 to 68x fewer parameters and 1.3 to 21.7x fewer MACs. Retrained, it reaches 92.95 to 98.33% on six public BdSL benchmarks, 97.04% on a merged corpus, and 76.25% zero-shot on BdSL-38. Removing any architectural stage costs 7.61 to 89.30 points, against at most 3.17 for the training recipe. Grad-CAM with deletion-insertion and weight-randomization checks confirms that predictions follow the signing hand. A signer-independent split holding out 6 of 36 signers yields 85.18%. Quantized to 0.48 MB, it runs at 3.98 ms per image within a 15.5 MB footprint on a commodity smartphone. Together, RSBdSL38 and our from-scratch model turn benchmark accuracy into deployable accessibility at a fraction of pretrained-backbone cost; dataset, code, and models are released.

</details>


### [105] [MASS: Multiplayer World Models with Authoritative Shared State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06257)
*Ziqi Cai,Siqi Yang,Yimu Wang,Zixian Gao,Yunheng Liu,Shuchen Weng,Erwin Wu,Kaipeng Zhang,Boxin Shi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MAS introduces an authoritative shared state to decouple world dynamics from rendering in multiplayer video world models, improving state accuracy and cross-view consistency, scalable to large agent counts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video world models entangle world state with view-dependent latents, causing redundant computation, view inconsistencies, and poor scalability in multiplayer settings.

Method: A learned Logic Engine advances a global, authoritative typed state from joint actions without hand-written transitions, serving as the recurrent memory and synchronization reference; a learned Rendering Engine produces independent, on-demand views for requested cameras from this shared state.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art multi-view baselines on a matched multiplayer Snake benchmark in state accuracy and cross-view consistency; demonstrates scalability to 1,024 concurrent players for 10,000 recurrent steps.

Conclusion: Explicit, authoritative state modeling provides a practical foundation for scalable and consistent multi-agent world simulation.

Abstract: Current video world models struggle in multiplayer environments because they entangle world state with view-dependent visual latents, leading to redundant compute, view inconsistencies, and poor scalability. We propose MAS (Multiplayer world models with Authoritative Shared State) to resolve this limitation. Inspired by multiplayer game architectures, MAS disentangles world dynamics and view rendering. A learned Logic Engine advances a global, authoritative typed state from joint actions without any hand-written transition function, acting as the sole recurrent memory and synchronization reference. From this shared state, a learned Rendering Engine generates independent and consistent views for any requested camera on demand. This explicit disentangling allows MAS to achieve superior state accuracy and lower cross-view inconsistency compared to state-of-the-art multi-view baselines on a matched multiplayer Snake benchmark. It advances predicted worlds with 1,024 concurrent players for 10,000 recurrent steps. Our results show that explicit, authoritative state modeling provides a practical foundation for scalable and consistent multi-agent world simulation.

</details>


### [106] [OTLesMix: Wasserstein Barycenter and Optimal Transport Map for Synthetic Lesion Generation with Diverse Shapes and Locations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06264)
*Robin Trombetta,Carole Lartizien*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OTLesMix uses Wasserstein barycenters and optimal transport to synthesize diverse, realistic brain lesion samples, improving segmentation Dice by 2.9–6.6 points across three tasks and surpassing mix-based augmentation methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limited variability in synthetic lesion augmentation by generating diverse lesion shapes and locations to enhance segmentation performance.

Method: Introduce OTLesMix, a data augmentation approach that leverages Wasserstein barycenters and optimal transport plans to synthesize new samples from real brain lesion images, aiming for realistic and diverse augmentations.

Result: Dice score improvements of 2.9 to 6.6 points across three brain lesion segmentation tasks; outperforms state-of-the-art mix-based augmentation methods.

Conclusion: OTLesMix effectively increases lesion variability in synthetic data and improves segmentation performance, representing a promising augmentation strategy for medical imaging.

Abstract: The development of deep learning over the past decade has revolutionized medical imaging segmentation, allowing the extraction of precise descriptors from large volumes to characterize pathologies. Data augmentation is a technique widely regarded as a way to improve model training. It includes simple transformations like spatial operations or intensity modifications, but also more advanced synthesis techniques. Their goal is to generate new realistic samples from an existing dataset to diversify the images used during training. Among them, several propose different mixing strategies to combine real samples. However, one of their major shortcomings is to yield limited variability in terms of generated lesion shapes and locations. In this work, we introduce a novel image synthesis method, called OTLesMix, that leverages Wasserstein barycenter and optimal transport plan to generate realistic and diverse samples. We evaluated our method on three brain lesion segmentation tasks, on which it improves the Dice score compared to a model trained without synthetic data by 2.9 to 6.6 points, and outperforms state-of-the-art mix-based methods.

</details>


### [107] [TLNM: Externally Validated Tooth Detection, Numbering and Segmentation from Smartphone Photographs Using Mask R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06275)
*Arash Nedaei,Henna Tiensuu,Elina Väyrynen,Saujanya Karki,Jaakko Suutala*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A smartphone-image–based tooth localisation and numbering system using a Mask R-CNN achieves high accuracy on internal and external data, aided by color normalization and anatomical constraints; released as an open-source API to enable tele-dentistry in resource-limited settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public oral health screening is hampered by cost, access, and reliance on clinical-grade radiographs; consumer-grade images require robust pipelines for self-screening and tele-dentistry.

Method: A customised Mask R-CNN pipeline trained on 1,272 annotated smartphone images; includes a masked gray-world white-balancing color correction and an anatomically constrained detection layer to enforce structural validity and reduce false positives; evaluated via internal/external testing, ablation, and stability analyses; provided as a containerised open-source API.

Result: Internal: instance-mask AP@50 = 0.818; class-aware PQ = 0.780; operational F1 = 0.884; training stability SD across 10 runs = 0.009. External: instance-mask AP@50 = 0.901; class-aware PQ = 0.832; operational F1 = 0.928. Open-source containerised API available.

Conclusion: Smartphone imagery can support automated tooth-level mapping, offering a scalable, low-cost basis for remote screening and tele-dentistry in resource-constrained environments.

Abstract: Oral health issues affect billions globally, but the cost and limited access to professional dental care hinder preventive oral healthcare. Research relies on clinical-grade radiographs or intraoral camera images, unavailable for public self-screening. This study introduces a tooth localisation and numbering model for smartphone photographs. We developed a customised Mask Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (Mask R-CNN) pipeline trained on 1,272 annotated smartphone images. To address variability in patient-generated health data, the pipeline incorporates two domain-informed mechanisms: a masked gray-world white-balancing algorithm to mitigate artificial colour casts and an anatomically constrained detection layer to enforce structural validity and suppress false positives. Evaluation comprised four stages: internal held-out testing, independent external testing, a descriptive ablation study, and fold-based training stability analysis using the same internal test set. On the internal test set, the model achieved an instance-mask AP@50 of 0.818, class-aware PQ of 0.780, and operational F1 of 0.884. Training stability showed limited between-model variation: across ten runs, instance-mask AP@50 had a standard deviation of 0.009. On the external dataset, the model achieved an instance-mask AP@50 of 0.901, class-aware PQ of 0.832, and operational F1 of 0.928 despite differences in population, sensors, and acquisition protocols. The inference pipeline is available as an open-source, containerised API. These results demonstrate that consumer-grade smartphone imagery can support automated tooth-level anatomical mapping, offering a scalable, potentially low-cost foundation for remote screening and tele-dentistry in resource-constrained environments.

</details>


### [108] [UQ-Loc: Uncertainty-Aware LiDAR Scene Coordinate Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06307)
*Jacek Komorowski*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UQ-Loc adds uncertainty modeling to LiDAR-based scene coordinate regression (SCR), delivering calibrated per-voxel 3x3 covariances and improved 6-DoF localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SCR methods are deterministic and ignore aleatoric uncertainty, which can hinder robustness and informed decision-making in localization.

Method: Extend LightLoc with an anisotropic Gaussian covariance head predicting a full 3x3 positive-definite covariance per voxel. Train with a Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss plus a kNN-based spatial smoothness regulariser. Inference uses a modified SC2-PCR solver with uncertainty-weighted seed scoring and a Mahalanobis-distance inlier test.

Result: UQ-Loc achieves consistent improvements in 6-DoF localization accuracy and produces well-calibrated covariances, as evaluated via Expected Calibration Error (ECE).

Conclusion: Modeling uncertainty in LiDAR SCR yields more accurate and reliable localization; calibrated covariances enable better downstream decision-making, with ECE serving as an appropriate calibration metric.

Abstract: LiDAR-based Scene Coordinate Regression (SCR) maps point clouds directly to 3D scene coordinates, enabling precise 6-DoF localisation without explicit map retrieval. However, existing methods produce deterministic predictions, discarding aleatoric uncertainty that could improve robustness and downstream decision-making. We present UQ-Loc, which extends the LightLoc architecture with an anisotropic Gaussian covariance head that predicts a full 3x3 positive-definite covariance matrix per voxel. Training uses a Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss augmented with a kNN-based spatial smoothness regulariser, while inference employs a modified SC2-PCR solver with uncertainty-weighted seed scoring and a Mahalanobis-distance inlier test. We adopt Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as a principled metric for evaluating the quality of the predicted uncertainty. Experiments demonstrate that UQ-Loc achieves consistent improvement in 6-DoF localization accuracy while producing well-calibrated covariances.

</details>


### [109] [Does FLAIR super-resolution erase or hallucinate small white-matter lesions?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06311)
*Zahra Khodakarami,Yue Li,Pulkit Khandelwal,John Detre,Sandhitsu Das,Christopher Brown,David Wolk,Paul Yushkevich*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SR upsampling of thick-slice FLAIR improves WMH detection vs raw thick slices but mainly erases small real lesions; ECLARE best preserves small lesion signals, INR underperforms, and all SR reduces small-lesion content as slice thickness increases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate how super-resolution (SR) affects WMH content when upsampling thick-slice FLAIR for segmentation, to assess risks of lesion erasure or hallucination prior to clinical use.

Method: 29 ADNI subjects with manually segmented WMH. Each HR (1 mm isotropic) FLAIR degraded to simulated 3 and 5 mm through-plane. Up-sampled to HR using Multi-contrast INR, ECLARE (single-contrast self-supervised), and cubic interpolation. WMH segmentation evaluated using four methods (WMH-SynthSeg, segcsvd, MARS-WMH, TrUE-Net) under the most sensitive (MARS-WMH) with metrics: detection sensitivity, erasure rate (HR-detected lesions lost after SR), hallucination rate (predicted lesions not in manual or HR). Floor/ceiling defined by simulated thick slice and original HR, respectively.

Result: Dominant SR effect is erasure of small real lesions, increasing with slice thickness; nonetheless, SR reconstructions improved lesion detection over raw thick slices. ECLARE most effectively preserved small lesion signals at both thicknesses; INR did not outperform cubic interpolation.

Conclusion: SR can aid WMH detection but risks erasing small real lesions; selection of SR method matters. ECLARE shows promise for preserving small WMH signals, whereas multi-contrast INR may lead to greater lesion erasure. Further validation on larger samples and additional datasets is needed.

Abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH), bright regions on Fluid-attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) scans are associated with cerebrovascular pathology and neurodegeneration. FLAIR is usually acquired with thick slices in clinical settings, giving it poor through-plane resolution. Super-resolution (SR) is a widely used method for recovering an isotropic volume from an anisotropic scan. Yet whether applying it prior to WMH segmentation preserves lesion content remains unknown: a model may erase small real lesions or hallucinate absent ones. We used 1-mm isotropic high-resolution (HR) FLAIR scans from 29 individuals in the ADNI cohort, each manually segmented for WMH by an expert. Then, we degraded each to simulated 3 and 5 mm through-plane acquisitions. Multi-contrast implicit neural representation (INR), a single-contrast self-supervised model (ECLARE), and cubic interpolation were used to upsample them onto the HR grid. WMH segmentation from a simulated thick slice and the original HR FLAIR set the floor and ceiling, respectively, for the per-lesion analysis. Of four WMH segmentation methods (WMH-SynthSeg, segcsvd, MARS-WMH, TrUE-Net), we ran the analysis under the most sensitive one to small lesions on HR (MARS-WMH) with the evaluation metrics of detection sensitivity, erasure rate (HR-detected lesions lost after reconstruction), and hallucination rate (predicted components absent from both the manual and HR segmentation). The dominant effect of SR was erasure of small real lesions, not hallucination, and it increased with slice thickness, though every reconstruction still improved lesion detection over the raw thick slice. ECLARE recovered small lesion signal best at both thicknesses, while the INR was no better than cubic interpolation.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [110] [Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05159)
*Xi Wang,Kun Li,Xianyao Ling,Gang Yin,Liang Zhang,Jiang Wu,Wenbo Lei,Jun Xu,Annie Wang,Fu Zhang,Weizhe Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Agentic Nesting: encasing enterprise apps as autonomous AI agents in a nested hierarchy to enable cross-application orchestration via a central orchestrator and natural-language interface; introduces Application-as-Agent and Conversation-as-Integration paradigms with potential generalization to heterogeneous systems and large-scale data tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise ecosystems suffer data silos and process fragmentation due to heterogeneous systems; traditional integration approaches (ESB, API gateways, RPA) incur high coupling, maintenance costs, and limited intelligence—necessitating a more scalable, intelligent integration paradigm.

Method: Wrap legacy applications as autonomous AI agents exposed through digital proxies; organize agents in layered stewardship topologies (nested hierarchy) mirroring complex ecosystems; employ a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatch; provide a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and orchestration; advocate Application-as-Agent integration and Conversation-as-Integration interaction.

Result: Conceptual framework with architectural blueprint and design considerations; discusses potential benefits, generalization to heterogeneous systems and large-scale data applications; no empirical results reported in the abstract.

Conclusion: Agentic Nesting offers a paradigm shift from flat, middleware-centric integration to hierarchical, agent-based orchestration through natural-language interfaces; promises improved interoperability and intelligence across heterogeneous systems; future work suggested includes empirical validation and tooling for realization.

Abstract: Enterprise operations extensively rely on multiple heterogeneous business systems and information applications, which also result in severe data silos and process fragmentation. Enterprises have invested considerable financial and material resources in building these applications, however, effectively leveraging and orchestrating them remains a formidable challenge. Conventional approaches to enterprise application integration, encompassing middleware architectures such as Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), API gateway infrastructures, and Robotic Process Automation (RPA), suffer from inherent limitations like high architectural coupling, escalating operation and maintenance costs, and limited intelligence capabilities. This paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework in which existing enterprise applications are encapsulated as autonomous AI agents within a hierarchically nested structure. Rather than flat interconnection, agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies that mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems. The framework extracts a digital agent proxy from each legacy application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation, coordinates multiple agents through a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The main contributions of this paper are the proposition of the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, together with an exploration of the generalization potential of this methodology in scenarios encompassing heterogeneous system coordination, and large-scale data applications.

</details>


### [111] [The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05160)
*Saman Rahbar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric to quantify GWT-like ignition in transformer LMs by fitting a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer probe accuracy vs input signal strength and extracting the beta-hat index to indicate abrupt (ignition-like) vs graded transitions. Shows architecture-dependent differences across 11 models (five families), with high selectivity over spurious probes (9.6x), and reports several novel findings (e.g., FF transformers vs SSMs, iteration-axis ignition in Huginn-3.5B, a PELT-detected phase transition in Pythia-410M); but hypotheses linking ignition to scale or signal strength were not confirmed. Code is provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge Global Workspace Theory's prediction of all-or-none ignition with mechanistic interpretability in transformer models; provide a quantitative, comparably robust metric that can discriminate genuine linguistic structure from spurious probe capacity and compare ignition-like dynamics across architectures and training stages.

Method: Fit a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength; extract the sigmoid steepness (beta-hat) as the ignition index. Validate with shuffled-label controls to ensure selectivity for linguistic structure. Compare across 11 models (five architectures). Use Mann-Whitney U-tests for statistical contrasts; analyze along architecture, iteration vs depth axes, and training-time changes (PELT for phase transitions). Provide code for replication.

Result: Beta-hat is higher for feedforward transformers (89% above SSMs; p<1e-13, d=0.52). Mamba shows near-linear, suggesting absent global broadcast. Huginn-3.5B displays greater ignition along iteration axis than depth axis. Pythia-410M exhibits a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256, before induction-head formation. Ignition hypotheses related to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed. Overall, 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability are demonstrated, with the first bridge between GWT dynamics and mechanistic interpretability.

Conclusion: The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability in transformers, enabling architecture-wide discrimination of ignition-like dynamics. The accompanying code enables replication and broader application.

Abstract: We introduce the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models. The metric fits a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat: high values indicate abrupt, ignition-like transitions; low values indicate graded build-up. Across 11 models spanning five architecture families, shuffled-label controls demonstrate 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test). We find: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52), with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, demonstrating that recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along the recurrence dimension. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting transformer architectures may saturate available ignition mechanisms. The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized in the scaling literature. Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/ignition-index

</details>


### [112] [Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05168)
*Dayu Wang,Jiaye Yang,Weikang Li,Jiahui Liang,Yang Li,Deguo Xia,Jizhou Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Woodpecker Distillation improves strong LLMs by learning from contrastive local interventions (weak-model patches) that repair intermediate reasoning; the method distills a corrective future-token distribution into the strong model, outperforming imitation baselines on math reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning failures in large language models often originate from localized bugs in intermediate steps rather than general incompetence. These bugs can be repaired by brief patches that steer the model’s reasoning trajectory, suggesting a way to leverage such interventions to enhance performance.

Method:  contrastive analysis: compare successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same reasoning prefix; construct a corrective teacher distribution from the future token predictions induced by these patches; distill this signal into the strong model via a distillation objective that aligns the strong model’s future predictions with the corrective distribution.

Result: Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

Conclusion: Local, patch-based interventions can steer and reshape the future reasoning distribution of strong models; weak-to-strong distillation using contrastive corrective signals is an effective training paradigm for improving reasoning without solely relying on imitation of patches.

Abstract: Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite possessing the capability to solve them. We argue that many such failures arise from localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps rather than from global incompetence. We show that these bugs are frequently repairable: inserting a short patch generated by a weak probe model after the same strong-model reasoning prefix can redirect the trajectory toward a correct solution.
  However, this corrective effect is not reliably internalized by directly fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories, suggesting that the useful signal lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. We therefore propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. Our method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model.
  Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

</details>


### [113] [From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05203)
*Esra Zihni,Katryna Cisek,Hamzah Ziadeh,Hendrik Knoche,Robert Mikulik,John D. Kelleher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Guideline-based categorisation of continuous predictors can match continuous-model performance in most cohorts for 90-day stroke outcome prediction; one cohort shows a drop in accuracy; global feature importance remains stable, preserving prognostic hierarchy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine if clinicians' guideline-informed categorical encodings can replace continuous predictors in stroke-outcome models without sacrificing predictive performance, improving clinical interpretability.

Method: Head-to-head comparison of gradient-boosted models trained on continuous predictors versus fully categorised encodings using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds, evaluated on a multi-centre European registry across three treatment cohorts; assessment includes predictive performance and global feature importance.

Result: In two treatment cohorts, fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from continuous models; in one cohort, a significant drop in predictive accuracy is observed. Across cohorts, global feature importance rankings remain consistent between model types.

Conclusion: Guideline-based categorisation is a viable design option for stroke-outcome models, preserving the core prognostic factor hierarchy while enhancing interpretability; exceptions may occur in certain cohorts.

Abstract: Machine learning models achieve strong predictive accuracy for 90-day outcome prediction in acute ischaemic stroke, yet clinical adoption is limited by the misalignment of model explanations with clinicians' reasoning. Motivated by a clinician user study calling for clinical guideline-aligned cut-offs, we ask whether continuous predictors can be replaced by clinically informed categorical encodings without sacrificing performance. On a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, we compare standard and fully categorised gradient-boosted models, the latter using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. The fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from their continuous counterparts in two of the treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in predictive accuracy in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remain consistent, suggesting that discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors across all treatment groups. Guideline-based categorisation is thus a viable design choice for stroke-outcome models.

</details>


### [114] [SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05204)
*Jialuo Chen,Minghe Wang,Lingqi Jiang,Jianan Ma,Xinhao Deng,Xiaohu Du,Ruixiao Lin,Yunhao Feng,Linkang Du,Jingyi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILLTRACE introduces a multi-trace provenance framework for auditing LLM-agent skill reuse by extracting Expression, Implementation, and Operational traces, with an Operational trace modeled as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG); it achieves high AUROC and F1 on SKILLTRACE-BENCH and demonstrates scalability via a large wild audit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM-agent ecosystems increasingly package reusable, mixed-modality skills, traditional detectors (single-modality code or whole-package similarity) miss reuse that preserves only part of a skill; robust auditing of cross-modal reuse is needed.

Method: Extract three provenance traces (Expression, Implementation, Operational); represent Operational trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG); LLM assists only operational-trace extraction at ingestion; during audit, compare cached traces deterministically, calibrate against same-function strict negatives, report which trace supports reuse; evaluate on SKILLTRACE-BENCH with 820 transformed positives, 100 marketplace anchors, and 751 negatives; perform a 36,446-skill wild audit.

Result: Achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898 on SKILLTRACE-BENCH; wild audit shows trace-attributed evidence yields actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

Conclusion: Multi-trace provenance auditing enables more comprehensive and scalable detection of LLM-agent skill reuse by capturing textual, implementation, and operational structures; the SOG-based operational trace provides structured evidence to support audit decisions.

Abstract: LLM-agent ecosystems are rapidly growing around reusable skills: mixed-modality packages of metadata, natural-language instructions, code, tools, references, and operational workflows. As skills become marketplace artifacts, auditing their reuse is no longer the same problem as ordinary code clone detection. Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill. We present SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for LLM-agent skill reuse. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only the Operational-trace extraction, once at ingestion; at audit time SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports a reuse decision. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

</details>


### [115] [Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05205)
*Ziwei Zheng,Peiqiong Chen,Bang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR) introduces relation-level causal abstraction to generalize cause-effect knowledge from concrete, instance-level pairs. A multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system distills AECRs into two knowledge bases, and an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) injects these rules into CGEP to improve generalization, especially for rare/unseen events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome poor generalization of instance-level causal pairs on long-tail and unseen event combinations by abstracting causal relations into reusable rules.

Method: Develop AECR as generalized causal logic; use multi-agent CACI with similarity-constrained clustering to extract trustworthy AECRs from noisy data; construct two complete AECR knowledge bases; integrate AECRs into CGEP via AR-GCAE with rule-guided attention and gated representation fusion.

Result: Empirical results show that AECRs strengthen generalization in event causal reasoning and yield consistent improvements in event prediction, with the largest gains for rare and unseen events.

Conclusion: Abstract causal knowledge through AECRs provides a scalable, generalizable foundation for event-centric reasoning and enhances downstream predictive performance when integrated into neural encoders.

Abstract: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

</details>


### [116] [Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05206)
*Tarun Kumar S*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Otter is a compact 15.3M-parameter chess model that treats move prediction as a time-aware sequence, using a move-history encoder and a clock-pressure module. Trained on 6.1B positions from 117M Lichess rapid games, it achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 accuracy, outperforming Maia 2 with fewer parameters. Elo-bracket results peak at 57.38% (1900–1999). Code and models are released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Demonstrate that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential process improves human-mmove prediction, leveraging clock dynamics and recent move history instead of pure position-based prediction.

Method: A 15.3M-parameter Transformer-like model with two conditioning signals: (1) a move-history encoder conditioned on the last 20 moves; (2) a time-control module modulating predictions under clock pressure. Trained on 6.1B positions from 117M Lichess rapid games collected over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.

Result: Top-1 accuracy 55.23% and top-5 accuracy 90.95% in move prediction; outperforms Maia 2 with fewer parameters and less training data. Elo-bracket analysis shows peak accuracy of 57.38% in 1900–1999 bracket; results support time-aware sequential modeling.

Conclusion: Time-aware sequential modeling yields more human-like move predictions than position-only approaches, enabling a smaller model; results are public with code, trained models, and training logs released.

Abstract: Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

</details>


### [117] [SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05212)
*Zhixiang Liang,Yifei Liu,Yidan Huang,Haozhe Zhao,Beichen Huang,Jiaqi Wang,Nan Duan,Qiong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SearchAuditBench and SearchAuditor to audit and repair failures in long-horizon web-search agents; demonstrates improvement in end-to-end accuracy, but end-to-end pass rates remain modest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diagnosing failures in long-horizon search agents is hard due to error propagation across long, noisy traces; manual trace inspection is impractical; a benchmark and auditing framework are needed to localize, attribute, and repair failures with evidence-grounded judgments.

Method: Present SearchAuditBench: 1,243 failed trajectories from eight open-weight models across five benchmarks, average 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, expert-annotated with critical error step, root cause, and reference repair with rubrics. Propose SearchAuditor: a multi-perspective auditing framework that localizes, attributes, and repairs failures via evidence-grounded adjudication. Evaluate end-to-end pass rate across frontier models (e.g., GPT-5.5) and compare baselines.

Result: Baseline frontier-model GPT-5.5 yields 26.6% end-to-end pass rate; SearchAuditor achieves 32.3% and consistently outperforms baselines; enabling repairs to resume failed runs helps agents recover from errors.

Conclusion: Auditing with SearchAuditBench and SearchAuditor reduces human burden in diagnosing long-horizon agent failures and improves recovery via repairs, though overall pass rates remain below ideal levels, signaling room for further improvement.

Abstract: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

</details>


### [118] [PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05218)
*Ao Fu,Yi Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PD-GS introduces a phoneme-guided augmentation to 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses time-aligned phoneme tokens and a Linguistic Fusion Module to better capture articulation, reducing leaky-mouth artifacts and improving lip geometry while training from monocular video.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting often yields over-smoothed mouth motion and fails to respect hard articulatory constraints (e.g., bilabial closures). Self-supervised audio embeddings lack explicit, frame-aligned linguistic targets, causing missing discrete articulation events.

Method: Augment a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens from an ASR/forced-alignment pipeline. Introduce a Linguistic Fusion Module that adaptively gates and fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings. Train purely on monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision.

Result: On the HDTF benchmark, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces lip-closure violations on challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

Conclusion: Discrete phoneme guidance via the Linguistic Fusion Module complements continuous audio cues, enabling more accurate articulation in 3D talking-head synthesis while maintaining monocular-training efficiency.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

</details>


### [119] [When Privileged Guidance Misaligns: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05219)
*Junzhuo Liu,Weiwei Li,Jun Ling,Peng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Selective privileged on-policy distillation (SMRC-SD) matches teacher guidance to the student’s current state, avoiding state-reference mismatch and improving multi-turn task success on ALFWorld/WebShop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Privileged distillation can misguide when the student’s state diverges from the reference trajectory; applying guidance blindly harms learning. A state-compatible strategy is needed for interactive, sequential tasks.

Method: Introduce SMRC-SD: at each turn, decide whether the student’s current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Apply distillation only at matched states and construct a state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory. Evaluate on ALFWorld and WebShop, with ablations on routing and context.

Result: SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. On Qwen3-1.7B it raises task success from 0.746 to 0.865 on ALFWorld and from 0.574 to 0.693 on WebShop; ablations show the importance of locally supported turns and state-compatible context.

Conclusion: State-matched guidance is an effective, practical approach for on-policy distillation in interactive agents, mitigating state-reference mismatch while delivering tangible performance gains; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Privileged on-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multi-turn agents by allowing a synchronized teacher to re-score the student's response at every turn with access to training-only references, such as successful trajectories. In interactive environments, however, the student's preceding actions continually change the execution state. As the student takes different actions or completes subgoals in a different order, its rollout may reach states not covered by the reference, making the reference an unreliable source of guidance for the state actually reached. Applying privileged distillation indiscriminately therefore creates state--reference mismatch. This mismatch motivates a central objective: providing privileged reference guidance that remains compatible with the student's current execution state. We introduce State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD), which explicitly determines when and how a privileged trajectory should guide an on-policy student. At each turn, SMRC-SD verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Distillation is applied only at matched states, filtering out turns for which the reference lacks locally compatible guidance. For each matched state, SMRC-SD further constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory, grounding supervision in the state actually reached. Across ALFWorld and WebShop, SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from $0.746$ to $0.865$ on ALFWorld and from $0.574$ to $0.693$ on WebShop. Controlled routing and context ablations support both selecting locally supported turns and constructing state-compatible teacher context as contributors to these gains. Code is available at https://github.com/liujunzhuo/SMRC-SD.

</details>


### [120] [Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05224)
*Nick Oh,Fernand Gobet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Small-to-mid-scale LLMs trained on behavioral data can match large baselines in-distribution but require larger models to generalize to new task structure; ablations show stimuli/feedback content matter and choice history alone is insufficient; models may serve as noise-ceiling estimators, yet training paradigms bound their scope.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether LLMs trained on human behavioral data exploit task structure or statistical shortcuts, and how scaling and architecture affect in- and out-of-distribution performance.

Method: Train fourteen models (135M–14B params) across four architectures on Psych-101 (10.7M trial-level choices from 160 experiments). Systematically ablate four prompt channels (task instructions, stimuli, feedback, choice history) across 27 experiments and permute trial order to probe information sources.

Result: In-distribution: scale effect minimal; 0.6B–1B params match 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution: larger models gain advantages in generalizing to novel task structure. Stimuli/feedback content masking eliminates 75.7% of learned information and drops performance below chance; choice history alone does not explain performance. Permutation shows task invariance with independent trials but sensitivity when trial order depends on prior responses.

Conclusion: Small cognitively-tuned models can serve as noise-ceiling estimators for psychology experiments, but their applicability is limited by the training paradigms.

Abstract: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

</details>


### [121] [Project2Task: Graph-Guided Project-Level Planning for Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05225)
*Huirui Xu,Runtao Xu,Shuo Ren,Jiajun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Graph-guided project-level planning (Project2Task) decomposes long-horizon research into bounded, dependency-aware tasks via a directed lineage graph and task contracts; improves coherence and downstream execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-task or flat-task systems fail to capture long-horizon research structure and dependencies; need explicit, contract-based project-to-task planning to ensure coherence, avoidance of redundancy, and executable workflows.

Method: Introduce Project2Task that represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms arranged in a directed lineage graph; apply a Bernoulli block-model objective to choose horizontal/vertical/hybrid portfolio decompositions; generate bounded tasks with explicit ownership, repair overlaps, and emit dependency-aware contracts detailing objectives, inputs, artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order; contracts are executor-agnostic and integrate with downstream engines like AutoResearchClaw.

Result: On ten project briefs (~30 tasks), manuscript-based portfolio evaluation yields average quality score 7.15 versus 4.58 (Brief Baseline) and 5.31 (Topic-only). Integrating contracts with AutoResearchClaw raises downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759.

Conclusion: Explicit project-to-task planning produces coherent, non-redundant, executable research-task portfolios and enhances downstream task performance when paired with compatible executors.

Abstract: Research agents can increasingly search literature, propose hypotheses, generate code, run experiments, and draft manuscripts from a single topic. However, a research project is not merely a larger task: it is a long-horizon agenda that must be advanced through multiple bounded tasks with distinct but related objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences. Existing single-task systems often treat the project as one oversized task, produce a flat set of vague or overlapping tasks, or leave task boundaries and execution order to manual coordination. We introduce Project2Task, a graph-guided project-level planning layer for autonomous research. Given a project brief, it represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms and organizes them in a directed lineage graph. A lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Project2Task then generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and emits dependency-aware task contracts that specify objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. The contracts are independent of any particular downstream research executor and support integration of task outputs into a coherent project-level result. On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding roughly 30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gives Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw increases average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759. These results demonstrate the value of explicit project-to-task planning for producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable research-task portfolios.

</details>


### [122] [TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05228)
*Jin Liu,Steffen Thoma,Achim Rettinger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TriQua introduces adaptive fact modeling for LLM factuality: simple claims as standard triples; complex claims as hyperrelational facts with qualifiers; proposes TriQuaScore; improves evidence-based verification and provides fine-grained error localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The decompose-then-verify paradigm faces a trade-off: atomic facts often miss essential context, while broader statements lack granularity for precise verification. An adaptable representation is needed to preserve context without sacrificing atomicity.

Method: Propose TriQua framework: decompose claims into Simple-Triples and Hyperrelational facts with qualifiers; verification annotates errors at the triple/qualifier level; TriQuaScore quantifies factuality; empirical evaluation assesses alignment with human scores, decomposition quality, and verification performance against baselines.

Result: TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human factuality scores; TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality; outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

Conclusion: An adaptive, explainable factuality evaluation framework enabling precise retrieval and verification through fine-grained error localization; scalable to claims with varying complexity.

Abstract: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment. To address this, we introduce TriQua, a framework that flexibly models facts based on their complexity. Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves the necessary context for accurate retrieval and verification without sacrificing atomicity. Furthermore, TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection. Alongside the framework, we propose TriQuaScore to quantify the factuality of these structured fact units. Empirical evaluations show that TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

</details>


### [123] [Coherence-Oriented Dream Scene Visualisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05233)
*Azra Açıl,Simon Colton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) turns written dream descriptions into a four-panel, temporally coherent sequence of images by splitting the dream into four parts with an LLM, generating images with a text-to-image model, and regenerating mismatches; evaluated on 50 DreamBank descriptions using vision-language metrics (CLIP, DINOv2, Qwen2-VL).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Communicating emotionally intense dreams is difficult; a structured visual representation could improve comprehension, memory, and analysis of dreams, and provide a testbed for cross-modal coherence in dream-to-image pipelines.

Method: A four-stage pipeline: 1) use a large language model to split the dream description into four chronological parts; 2) generate images for each part with a text-to-image model ensuring visual coherence across the sequence; 3) re-generate any image that does not suitably match the corresponding text; 4) evaluate on 50 visualisations from DreamBank using objective metrics from CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL to assess quality, fidelity, and coherence.

Result: The abstract reports that DSV was evaluated over 50 visualisations and provides quality, fidelity and coherence results via the cited vision-language models, but does not provide specific numeric results in the abstract.

Conclusion: DSV demonstrates the feasibility of turning dream narratives into temporally coherent visual sequences and highlights objective, cross-modal metrics as a means to evaluate such systems; future work may refine segmentation, image coherence, and evaluation protocols.

Abstract: Dreams can be emotionally intense but difficult to communicate. We describe the Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) system which turns written dream descriptions into a temporal sequence of four panel images visualising the dream. This starts with a large language model prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. Then a text-to-image model produces images for each part with visual coherence maintained across the sequence, and DSV regenerates any image not suitably matching the text. We evaluate DSV over 50 visualisations from dream descriptions in DreamBank, and report quality, fidelity and coherence results via objective measures employing the CLIP, DINOv2 and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.

</details>


### [124] [Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05245)
*Muyang Ye,Tian Lan,Feihu Jiang,Yongshi Ye,Wuyunsiqin,Bin Zhu,Qianghuai Jia,Zhao Xu,Weihua Luo,Ye Wang,Jinyang Zhang,Longyue Wang,Lingfeng Bao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Search2Skill automates external-information gathering and distillation into reusable, structured skills for LLM agents, optimized via rubric-based RL for when/how to search and how to generate skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-evolving skill methods rely on the model's internal parametric knowledge, which is limited by domain conventions and procedures that may lie beyond what the model knows or can elicit. There is a need to bridge gaps by leveraging external sources and distilling evidence into reusable skills that transfer across models.

Method: Introduce Search2Skill: identify capability gaps in the agent, search external sources to address those gaps, and distill retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. The approach uses rubric-based reinforcement learning to jointly optimize when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills.

Result: Empirical evaluation across eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks shows Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under streaming and held-out protocols. Analyses indicate gains stem from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

Conclusion: Search2Skill provides a scalable framework for automatic skill acquisition that leverages external evidence to build abstract, reusable skills, improving expert-domain performance and generalization across models.

Abstract: Reusable skills, which encapsulate the procedural knowledge required to solve real-world professional tasks, offer LLM-based agents a path toward self-evolution in expert domains. Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone. To address this issue, we therefore propose a novel framework, Search2Skill, that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources to address them, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Specifically, Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills. Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under both streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

</details>


### [125] [LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05246)
*Jiahao Zhang,Yongzhi Tong,Zelin Fu,Pengde Zhao,Yanmei Jiang,Jiang Feng,Min Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LUNAR is the first cross-domain, longitudinal personalization benchmark for LLMs based on synthetic yet fidelity-aligned app-interaction histories, revealing that access to behavioral logs alone does not guarantee deep personalization and that effective personalization hinges on evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy management; direct retrieval of fine-grained records outperforms compressed memory, highlighting trade-offs between personalization and privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks focus on textual personas or isolated signals, lacking evaluation of cross-domain, longitudinal behavioral personalization grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities.
