Method: Introduce LUNAR with a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline built on real-world behavioral patterns to simulate longitudinal app histories across clothing, food, housing, and mobility. Evaluate 19 mainstream LLMs, comparing direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records versus compressed memory, and analyze the role of evidence selection and cross-domain integration under privacy constraints.

Result: Behavioral logs are necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization; neither larger context nor bigger models guarantee better personalization. Effective personalization requires selecting and integrating relevant cross-domain evidence. Direct retrieval of fine-grained records consistently outperforms compressed memory, but stronger personalization can threaten privacy.

Conclusion: Evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control are key challenges for personalized LLMs; LUNAR enables scalable evaluation and reveals fundamental trade-offs between personalization quality and privacy protection.

Abstract: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks primarily rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization, where responses must be grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. To address this gap, we introduce LUNAR, the first benchmark for evaluating how LLMs personalize responses from longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains, including clothing, food, housing, and mobility. To support scalable benchmark construction while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns, LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show that access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory, while stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection. These findings identify evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges for personalized LLMs.

</details>


### [126] [WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05248)
*Chunchao Guo,Jinpeng Li,Yang Li,Zilong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorldClaw presents a coarse-to-fine, agentic pipeline for open-world 3D scene generation that achieves global terrain coherence, rich local content, and editable assets through planning, semantic layouts, and render-based refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generate large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from text prompts while maintaining global spatial coherence, detailed local geometries, and editable assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse.

Method: A planning stage uses agents to translate prompts into a structured specification (regions, terrain, assets, materials, spatial relations). The system builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and region-aware height fields. For detail-demanding regions, it creates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and places them on the terrain; render-based agents refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts.

Result: WorldClaw outputs large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets, while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates scalable, open-world content generation with an agentic, coarse-to-fine pipeline that integrates planning, terrain synthesis, asset placement, and render-based refinement to produce editable, globally coherent 3D environments.

Abstract: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because a system must jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse. We present WorldClaw, a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework for open-world 3D scene generation. Planning agents translate a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. WorldClaw then builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on the terrain; render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts. Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

</details>


### [127] [Posture and Sustainment Optimization Under Adversarial Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05256)
*Amelie Norris,Alyssa Lee,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Posture optimization under adversarial threat using scenario-weighted and robust methods; outperforms greedy baselines in a 20-asset, 5-location setting via CEV and RobustCEV within a finite-horizon MDP framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address vulnerability of pre-commitment posture to geographic under-coverage and targeted adversarial threats by formalizing PSA as a finite-horizon MDP and introducing a scenario-weighted and adversarially robust optimization framework.

Method: Model PSA as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. Introduce Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer to maximize scenario-weighted posture efficiency. Develop RobustCEV that iterates against a Bayesian adversary updating its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Validate in three Indo-Pacific basing experiments with 20 assets and 5 locations; use paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition.

Result: Greedy baseline yields a 25.1% posture efficiency penalty and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under threat. CEV recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when threat distribution has geographic signal; 5–20 scenarios capture most gains. RobustCEV achieves up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer against adaptive adversaries with deceptive priors.

Conclusion: Scenario-weighted optimization and adversarial robustness substantially improve posture allocation over greedy heuristics, with gains validated statistically and shown to be structural rather than sampling artifacts. The approach highlights the importance of geographic coverage and threat dynamics in pre-commitment basing.

Abstract: Pre-commitment posture, the assignment of military assets to theater locations before conflict scenarios resolve, is a critical and formally unsolved problem in joint operational planning. Current practice relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value and ignore geographic coverage and are structurally vulnerable to adversaries that target high-strategic value locations. This paper presents a scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization engine for the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem, modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. We introduce the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which places assets by maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios, and the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Across three experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment with 20 assets and 5 theater locations, we demonstrate that: (1) the greedy baseline incurs a permanent 25.1% posture efficiency penalty due to geographic under-coverage and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated adversarial threat; (2) the CEV optimizer recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when the threat distribution carries a geographic signal, with a curated set of 5 to 20 scenarios sufficient to capture the majority of this gain; and (3) the RobustCEV extension recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer when an adaptive adversary employs a deceptive threat prior. All findings are validated using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, confirming that the performance gaps reported are structural properties of placement strategies rather than sampling artifacts.

</details>


### [128] [OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05263)
*Yidian Chen,Yingzi Gu,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty,Sharon Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OrchestraBench provides a failure-injection benchmark for multi-agent pipelines, introducing cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery to diagnose failure, recovery, and decomposition; results show policy differences, context dependence, and the need for detection/attribution for containment; framed as controlled mechanism probes rather than domain workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmark literature focuses on task accuracy; lacks diagnostic signals about where/how pipelines fail; need reproducible means to study failure propagation across routing decisions, recovery, and orchestration in production-like workflows.

Method: Seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows; evaluate routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests; use a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic; controlled mechanism probes with Claude agent over an arithmetic dependency chain; replicate across contexts (loan-approval) and across MAST modes (Sonnet, Opus, Haiku); analyze cascade radius, per-failure-mode recovery, and ablations (trusted-state repair).

Result: Keyword/flag router 0% on adversarial cases; intent-reasoning router 100%, matching oracle; three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation partially (0.30), latent/semantic modes never recovered (0.0); cascade radius increases with pipeline depth (0.9 to 4.7 for depths 3–7); blind retry reproduces latent faults and delays detection; trusted-state repair is main source of apparent containment; findings are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain workload claims.

Conclusion: The work provides a principled benchmark framework for diagnosing failure and containment in multi-agent pipelines, highlighting the need for detection and attribution, and showing that containment may rely on trusted-state signals; results generalize across contexts but depend on pipeline depth and mode.

Abstract: Multi-agent orchestration frameworks are moving from demos to production, yet benchmarks typically report task accuracy without diagnosing why a pipeline failed, where a cascade began, or which routing decision caused the breakdown. OrchestraBench evaluates failure, recovery, and decomposition through a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics and compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Controlled mechanism probes with a real Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted when the computation was reframed as a loan-approval workflow and across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku, although absolute rates shifted with context. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection. These results are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims.

</details>


### [129] [Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05266)
*Nathan S Johnson,Ian Abshire*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A comprehensive benchmark reveals that agent architecture choices affect microscopy task performance, but current heterogeneous tests do not predict performance on unseen tasks; proxies fail to generalize.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the nascent field of agentic control of physical infrastructure, evaluating how LLM-based microscopy agents generalize, and to understand design trade-offs across architectures, agents, and retrieval settings.

Method: A benchmark and trace-logging framework evaluating 1-, 2-, and 3-agent graph topologies; five LLMs; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and context parameters; 53 microscopy benchmarks; 105 agent configurations; 1,949 test runs; 49,109 RAG retrievals; analyze latency, token use, cost, and failure modes; additionally train surrogate models to predict performance.

Result: Clear differences in latency, token usage, cost, and failure modes across configurations; surrogate models trained on architecture and test results do not reliably predict performance on unseen tasks; benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison but do not support a task-independent global configuration model.

Conclusion: Benchmarks provide valuable diagnostic and comparative insight into agent architecture trade-offs for microscopy, but they reveal limited generalization to unseen tasks and no universal configuration rule; future work should pursue more task-conditioned or generalizable evaluation frameworks and understandability of failure modes.

Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

</details>


### [130] [CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05359)
*Jose A. Bird*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CASCADE predicts transcriptional responses to gene perturbations using ARACNe/MCP networks and validates directional concordance with copy-number–driven dosage proxies in TCGA, showing gene-specific success (e.g., MYC) but not universal, with notable LLM grounding limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Move beyond gene-membership validation to assess directional accuracy of predicted perturbation effects and evaluate whether natural-language queries can be accurately grounded to CASCADE APIs.

Method: Use focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage proxy for knockdown; compare predicted knockdown targets to expression differences (amplified vs non-amplified) across BRCA, COAD, and STAD in TCGA; replicate in METABRIC; benchmark against MSigDB; extend analysis to 15 additional genes; evaluate an LLM-based agent’s ability to map natural-language requests to CASCADE tool calls; analyze failure modes.

Result: MYC target predictions show strong concordance with real expression changes (BRCA 90.0%, COAD 72.0%, STAD 85.7%; all p<0.0013) and replicate in METABRIC (87.2%); performance exceeds permutation baselines but does not surpass existing knowledge of MYC/E2F biology; gene-specific effects observed across 15 genes with proliferation regulators tending to replicate while lineage-identity TFs and CCND2 fail; LLM grounding: 71.4% exact match for a local model and 85.7% for a larger model; some failures due to schema/gene-alias resolution; ambiguous queries lead to wrong perturbation type.

Conclusion: Directionality-aware CASCADE predictions can align with real tumor data for certain genes, indicating gene-specific validity and hedged performance; LLM grounding can be improved but demonstrates practical capacity to map queries to CASCADE calls; overall, CASCADE offers incremental but not universal predictive value, with clear limitations linked to gene identity and interpretation of perturbation type.

Abstract: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

</details>


### [131] [Counterfactual Analysis via Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05367)
*Zonghao Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GPT-3.5, with prompt engineering, can approximate traditional ML in predicting counterfactual ROI for online lending and generate coherent counterfactuals; performance closes in on gradient-boosted regression but does not exceed it in reported metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can perform counterfactual analysis to aid decision-making in online lending.

Method: Benchmark GPT-3.5 against advanced ML algorithms for predictive counterfactual ROI, apply prompt engineering to enhance GPT performance, and use GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under alternative interest rates.

Result: Prompt engineering boosts GPT predictions (R^2 from 1.97% to 2.84%), approaching but still below gradient-boosted regression (3.48%); GPT demonstrates logical coherence and causal reasoning in generating counterfactual ROIs.

Conclusion: LLMs are promising tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending and have potential broader applications in predictive and decision-making contexts.

Abstract: Counterfactual analysis aims to predict potential outcomes under hypothetical scenarios, offering valuable insights for decision-making. This paper investigates the application of large language models (LLMs), specifically the GPT-3.5 model, for counterfactual analysis. We focus on the online lending context, where the counterfactual return on investment (ROI) is crucial for evaluating different interest rate schemes. We begin by assessing the predictive performance of GPT and comparing it with advanced machine learning algorithms. The results show that prompt engineering can significantly enhance GPT's predictions, with the R-squared increasing from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. Subsequently, we utilize GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under a set of alternative interest rates. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, suggesting broader applications for LLMs in various predictive and decision-making contexts.

</details>


### [132] [DoctorAgents: an agentic framework to iteratively refine AutoML pipeline for small clinical temporal data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05375)
*Ruilin Wang,Bo-Hong Wang,Elizabeth Kourbatski,Jun Bai,Hegang Chen,Ziyang Song,Gilles Boire,Marie Hudson,Yue Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new AutoML paradigm for small clinical data where LLM-based agents iteratively reason and refine ML pipelines, improving performance and interpretability versus traditional AutoML.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical data are scarce, heterogeneous, and temporally complex, which makes reliable ML deployment challenging. Conventional AutoML relies on brute-force search over predefined spaces and often lacks explicit reasoning and memory, hindering performance, interpretability, and adaptability to clinical contexts.

Method: DoctorAgents employs specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement to autonomously construct and optimize end-to-end ML pipelines. It replaces exhaustive search with a reasoning-driven refinement loop, using textual gradient descent to backpropagate natural-language feedback for targeted updates without full search.

Result: Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines and yields more interpretable, task-specific representations.

Conclusion: Reasoning-driven, memory-enabled AutoML via agentic LLMs offers a scalable and interpretable approach for small clinical datasets, addressing key limitations of brute-force AutoML and enhancing reliability in high-stakes medical contexts.

Abstract: Clinical machine learning (ML) has the potential to support high-stakes medical decision-making, but reliable deployment is often constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporal complexity. Developing effective ML pipelines for such data remains time-consuming and error-prone, while existing automated machine learning (AutoML) systems only partially address this challenge because they largely rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory. We therefore reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. We propose DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines through specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement. DoctorAgents backpropagates natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent to perform targeted updates without exhaustive search. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.

</details>


### [133] [C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05381)
*Swapnanil Mukherjee,Agyeya Negi,Tanuja Ganu,Ponnurangam Kumaraguru*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new benchmark C^3PO evaluates cross-modal reasoning in MLLMs across video, audio, image, and text, exposing modality dominance as a key failure mode and showing humans outperform models by a large margin.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify brittleness in cross-modal reasoning due to modality bias and provide a diagnostic benchmark to study information composition and counterfactual conflict.

Method: Fully automatic data pipeline with 3,404 samples, IC/CC tasks, four-tier design, 25 templates, covering multiple modalities.

Result: Humans 88.64% accuracy; best model 73.17%; open-source models fail under conflict; attention analyses show high modality dominance; mid-layer entropy correlates with success; 56-point template gap.

Conclusion: Cross-modal reasoning requires sustained cross-modal attention; simply fusing modalities is insufficient; benchmarks reveal where and why models fail, guiding architectural improvements.

Abstract: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can process diverse sensory inputs, yet their reasoning remains heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. We introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text, evaluating two abilities: information composition (fusing dispersed evidence) and counterfactual conflict (resolving deliberate contradictions). C$^3$PO's paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design enable targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails. Built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates, C$^3$PO reveals that while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. Through attention probes, we find 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. The 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates reveals that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not combinations. These findings show multimodal perception does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature

</details>


### [134] [Adaptive Arena-based Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts for Open-Ended Care Plan Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05391)
*Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen,Hoang-Loc Cao,Phuc Ho,Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen,René Richard,Hung Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework (CANOE) for contestable care-plan generation using arena-based QBAF and human-in-the-loop contestation, with evaluation showing fine-tuned models outperform generic LLMs on clinical metrics and CANOE enhances explainability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monolithic LLM pipelines struggle with transparency and safety in multidisciplinary care planning; there is a need for transparent, contestable reasoning that can be audited and revised by humans.

Method: Five-module architecture: (1) complexity assessment to gauge problem scope, (2) adaptive team recruitment to assemble role-specialized agents, (3) role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), (4) human-in-the-loop contestation to challenge and revise arguments, and (5) care-plan synthesis with deterministic recomputation. Agents produce supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts resolved via arena-based clash resolution; acceptability scores propagate through the argumentation graph.

Result: Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge indicates medically fine-tuned models achieve strongest clinical correctness and safety; CANOE’s argumentative structure yields faithful explanations and allows human contestation.

Conclusion: CANOE offers a transparent, contestable, and deterministic framework for care-plan generation that integrates expert-driven argumentation with human oversight, demonstrating improved clinical correctness and safety through targeted model fine-tuning. Potential future work includes broader domain evaluation, scalability analyses, and integration with live clinical workflows.

Abstract: Care plan coordination demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines, where monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform in a transparent or safe manner. We present CANOE (Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts), a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that addresses these limitations through five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution before acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners may accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and the framework will deterministically recompute the final plan. Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

</details>


### [135] [Evaluating and Improving Pedagogical Fit in LLM-Based AI Tutors with the Pedagogical Suitability Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05411)
*Benjamin Barlog,Hudson Craig,Zedong Peng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI) to assess how well LLM tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and demonstrates PSI-guided regenerations improving weak cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation trends focus on answer correctness; instructional fit with learner state and curricular sequencing is under-measured and may drive tutoring effectiveness.

Method: Define six theory-informed sub-scores to form PSI, apply to 240 scenario-based evaluations of four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, Qwen3) using paired standard/defective prompts; use PSI-guided regeneration on 62 weak-performing cases.

Result: Baseline PSI differences across models are modest (0.557–0.638); models do not separate clearly by pedagogy. PSI is robust to prompt perturbations (Delta ≈ -0.002) with some sub-score trade-offs. PSI-guided feedback improves 51/62 weak cases (82.3%). Manual evaluation indicates pedagogically meaningful improvements.

Conclusion: Learner- and curriculum-aware alignment can matter more for effective tutoring than model category; PSI is measurable and improvable and can serve as a structured feedback signal for response improvement.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as AI tutors, but a correct answer is not always a pedagogically appropriate one. In classroom learning, effective help depends not only on correctness, but also on whether a response matches the learner's current foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus mainly on answer quality, leaving this instructional fit under-measured. We present the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores that evaluates how well LLM-generated tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and we further use PSI as a structured feedback signal for response improvement. We evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, and Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts, then apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol to 62 weak-performing cases. Baseline differences across the four tested models were modest overall (PSI range: 0.557 to 0.638), and open-weight and closed models did not exhibit a clear separation in pedagogical fit. Under the tested prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained largely stable (Delta = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. More importantly, PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak-performing cases: 51 of 62 cases improved (82.3%). Focused manual evaluation of the 62 PSI-selected weak cases provides initial evidence that the identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many PSI-guided regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement. These results suggest that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and that such alignment is both measurable and improvable.

</details>


### [136] [Negotiating Risk Boundaries in AI for Policing Through Mixed-Stakeholder Deliberation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05418)
*Mackenzie Jorgensen,Jo Reilly,Alex Sutherland,Miri Zilka*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A mixed-stakeholder workshop assesses 13 AI policing use cases for racial bias; finds broad openness to AI adoption but rejects recidivism risk assessment; racial-equity framing does not narrow deliberation; core questions center on usefulness, benefits, and universal reach; suggests integrating bias considerations into risk-benefit analysis (curb-cut effect).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address known racial bias risks in AI-enabled policing and the underrepresentation of affected communities in decision-making about AI adoption; evaluate whether AI tools deliver benefits fairly across populations.

Method: Mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop with 30 participants (community representatives, police officers, academics) evaluating 13 policing AI use cases, with explicit focus on racial bias; qualitative analysis of deliberations to identify concerns and reasoning patterns; comparison of equity-framed deliberation to baseline deliberations.

Result: Participants were broadly open to AI adoption; three use cases were rejected, notably recidivism risk assessment (objections targeted the premise). Foregrounding racial equity did not narrow deliberation; discussions converged on questions about tool effectiveness, genuine benefit, and universality of benefit; the deliberation reflected integrated risk-benefit reasoning akin to the curb-cut effect.

Conclusion: Embedding racial-bias considerations from the outset can enrich risk-benefit analysis of AI use in policing, but explicit equity framing may not constrain deliberations; future work should emphasize demonstrated effectiveness and equitable distribution of benefits across populations, and consider how to ensure minority communities reap true advantages.

Abstract: AI tools are being increasingly adopted in policing in the UK and worldwide. Racial bias is a known and well-documented risk, yet representatives of affected communities are rarely included in decisions about AI adoption. We present results from a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop bringing together 30 community representatives, police officers, and academics to assess the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with an explicit focus on racial bias. We found that participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright, most notably recidivism risk assessment, where objections targeted the premise rather than the implementation. Our analysis reveals that foregrounding racial equity did not narrow the deliberation. Instead, discussions gravitated toward a fundamental set of questions: does this tool actually work, will it deliver genuine benefit, and will that benefit extend to everyone? This integrated reasoning, reminiscent of the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, highlights the benefit of incorporating the racial bias lens into the risk-benefit analysis of AI use cases from the outset.

</details>


### [137] [SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05439)
*Yixuan Wang,Licheng Luo,Yu Fu,Kaidi Xu,Yue Dong,Mingyu Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A selective translation framework for NL-to-formal specifications that uses two black-box signals and conformal risk control to decide when to trust translations, with an anomaly detector for OOD inputs; demonstrated on STL, LTL, and SpaTiaL to improve reliability and enable abstention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable trustworthy NL-to-formal-spec translations by avoiding or abstaining from unreliable outputs in safety-critical settings, leveraging conformal prediction to bound risk.

Method: Two complementary black-box signals for reliability: (1) fidelity of back-translation to natural language, (2) dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence. These signals feed a distribution-free conformal risk controller that outputs accept/ abstain, plus an anomaly detector on instruction embeddings to reject OOD inputs before translation. The framework is language-agnostic across formal spec languages and evaluated on STL, LTL, SpaTiaL.

Result: Increased translation reliability and robustness across cross-tier shifts, with effective uncertainty-aware abstention and improved overall trust in NL-to-formal specification pipelines.

Conclusion: Establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may be unreliable and to abstain accordingly.

Abstract: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

</details>


### [138] [Stochasticity Is Not the Hard Part: Reduction and Complexity in Instructional Sequencing over Prerequisite DAGs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05455)
*Zonglin Han,Yichen Chen,Jiawen Jiang,Tongan Shi,Kristian A. Stevens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Stochastic instructional sequencing can be collapsed to a deterministic shortest-path on the lattice of prerequisite ideals, preserving optimal value and actions, but remains NP-hard in general; tractable regimes exist when transfer preferences align acyclically with prerequisites; a computable mΔ diagnostic bounds the value of sequencing; empirical data show both a easy regime with little benefit to optimize and a challenging regime where exact search (A*) scales linearly with problem size under a good heuristic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine when the order of instructional concepts matters, quantify the benefit of optimizing that order, and understand the computational complexity of finding optimal sequences under prerequisite constraints.

Method: Model instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path; prove an exact collapse to a deterministic shortest-path on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals; establish NP-hardness via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments; identify tractable special cases (joint acyclicity of transfer with prerequisites; fixed width enabling dynamic programming); introduce a computable diagnostic mΔ; evaluate on a large real dataset and constructed instances, comparing myopic versus optimal sequences and assessing search algorithms (A* with a consistent heuristic).

Result: The stochasticity can be eliminated exactly, reducing the problem to a deterministic shortest-path that preserves optimal values and actions. Despite this collapse, the problem remains NP-hard even under strong simplifications. If transfer preferences are jointly acyclic with prerequisites, any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal; fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time DP. The mΔ diagnostic bounds the potential value of sequencing before optimization. Empirically, 70,893 interactions show a 'doubly easy' regime with little room to gain from sequencing, while constructed challenging instances exhibit large myopic regret, though exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states.

Conclusion: General instructional sequencing under prerequisite constraints is computationally hard, but practical regimes exist where optimization adds little value and where efficient exact or heuristic search is feasible. The mΔ diagnostic provides a pre-optimization bound, guiding when sequencing should be pursued in practice.

Abstract: When a student must learn concepts connected by prerequisite dependencies, when does the order of instruction matter, and what does it cost to find the best one? We study instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem in which attempting a concept succeeds with a state-dependent probability and failure leaves the learner state unchanged. We first prove that this stochasticity can be eliminated exactly: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals, preserving optimal values and actions. The collapse removes stochastic complexity but not combinatorial complexity: optimal sequencing remains NP-hard -- via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments -- even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities at least $1/2$. Hardness is not uniform: when realizable transfer preferences remain jointly acyclic with the prerequisites, any topological order of the residual joint graph is optimal, and fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time exact dynamic programming. A computable diagnostic, $mΔ$, bounds the value of sequencing before optimization. On 70,893 interactions from an introductory CS course, the diagnostic certifies a doubly easy regime -- little value to optimize and little space to search -- while constructed transfer instances realize the challenging regime, where myopic sequencing suffers large regret yet exact A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states on that family.

</details>


### [139] [Recursive Synthesis for Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05466)
*Zhongzhi Li,Yucheng Shi,Zongxia Li,Ruhan Wang,Anhao Li,Zixun Huang,Junyao Yang,Lei Ke,Ninghao Liu,Haitao Mi,Leowei Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RST is a recursive, verified synthetic data pipeline that expands seed terminal-agent tasks into long-horizon tasks via iterative reference-solution extension, verifier/instruction realignment, sandbox validation, and seed recycling, achieving scalable data at low cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-quality long-horizon terminal-agent training data is expensive and difficult to scale with human authoring or LLM-only generation due to consistency constraints among instruction, environment, reference solutions, and verifiers.

Method: Starting from verified seed tasks, RST recursively extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for the next round. Over 15 rounds, 37,484 tasks are synthesized at ≈$0.05/task, with increasing task difficulty.

Result: Median reference solution length grows 67→374 lines; median executed commands grow 40→244; DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90% at R1 to 2.5% at R15. Rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories collected on synthesized tasks improve fine-tuning performance: Qwen3.5-27B and -122B-A10B gain up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench 2/Hard/Long-Horizon; agentic PPO increases scores to 49.44%, 32.00%, 22.07% (relative gains 20.0%, 41.2%, 21.9%). After 15 rounds, yield/validation remain stable, suggesting no ceiling in scale.

Conclusion: RST demonstrates scalable long-horizon terminal-task synthesis that maintains validation success across increasing difficulty, enabling practical utility for supervised fine-tuning and PPO-based training, with potential to scale beyond the reported rounds.

Abstract: High-quality long-horizon training data for terminal agents is expensive to produce, often costing hundreds to thousands of dollars per task, because each task must keep the instruction, environment, reference solution, and verifier mutually consistent. Human authoring does not scale, and direct generation with large language models (LLMs) often breaks these dependencies. We present Recursive Synthetic Terminal Tasks (RST), a recursive verified synthesis framework for constructing long-horizon terminal-agent tasks at scale. Starting from verified seed tasks, RST extends the reference solution, realigns the verifier and instruction to the new workflow, validates the result in a fresh sandbox, and reuses accepted tasks as seeds for subsequent rounds. Across fifteen recursive rounds, RST produces 37,484 synthesized terminal-agent tasks at roughly \$0.05 per task. Task difficulty increases substantially over rounds: the median reference solution grows from 67 to 374 lines, the median number of executed commands grows from 40 to 244, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro pass@4 drops from 90\% at $R_1$ to 2.5\% at $R_{15}$. To demonstrate training utility, we collect rejection-sampled Qwen3.5 trajectories on the synthesized tasks and use them for supervised fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on these trajectories improves Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B by up to 10 points on Terminal-Bench~2, Terminal-Bench Hard, and Long-Horizon Terminal Bench, while agentic PPO lifts Qwen3.5-27B to 49.44\%, 32.00\%, and 22.07\% on the three benchmarks, corresponding to relative gains of 20.0\%, 41.2\%, and 21.9\% over the base model. Moreover, after 15 rounds, the recursion shows no ceiling: synthesis yield and validation rates remain stable as difficulty keeps climbing, indicating that the process can continue well beyond the scale reported here.

</details>


### [140] [Innovation-Residual Auditing of Autonomous Analysis Agents: Localization, Detection Limits, Error Control, and Identifiability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05490)
*Ahmed Hassoon,Mark Dredze*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Auditing end-to-end autonomous data analyses by learning from sound analyses and flagging deviations depends crucially on how you score operations and how far back you reconstruct the intended analysis. There is a fundamental limit: very small errors cannot be attributed, and the detectability is dominated by the representation dimension rather than data volume.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As autonomous analytics perform end-to-end analyses with minimal supervision, there is a need to localize erroneous steps. Existing approaches learn from sound analyses to flag deviations; reliability of such audits has not been quantified.

Method: Compare per-operation surprisals under different reconstruction horizons (shortest preceding operation vs longer reconstruction of intended analysis). Quantify error spreading, derive procedures to control false positives under the assumption of exchangeable sound analyses, and analyze robustness to imperfect models and selection biases. Establish a limit on attribution for small-magnitude errors and relate detectability to representation dimensionality.

Result: Scoring choice determines localization: short-horizon scores localize errors one-to-one, while longer-horizon scores spread a single mistake across multiple operations. The study provides procedures to bound the false-flag rate under exchangeability, analyzes degradation under model misspecification and content-dependent review, and demonstrates a fundamental limit where very small errors are indistinguishable from normal variation; the limit improves only slowly with more data, being primarily constrained by representation size rather than data volume (e.g., a hundredfold data yields <2% improvement).

Conclusion: Audits of autonomous analyses face a representation-dimension bound that governs attribution granularity of errors. Practical auditing requires careful choice of horizon and exchangeability assumptions, and must account for potential selection biases; improving detectability will hinge on reducing representation complexity rather than simply expanding data.

Abstract: Autonomous agents now carry out entire data analyses, selecting cohorts, joining tables, and fitting models with little step-by-step supervision. When such an analysis turns out to be wrong, someone must determine which operation caused it. A recent approach does this without any labelled mistakes, learning instead from analyses known to be sound and flagging operations that depart from what that model predicts; how reliable such audits are has not been studied. This paper supplies that analysis. The choice of score determines whether an error can be localized at all. If each operation is scored by how surprising it is given the operation immediately preceding it, then operations that merely inherit an earlier error are indistinguishable from correct ones, so one mistake produces one flag; scores computed against a longer reconstruction of the intended analysis instead spread a single mistake across many operations. We quantify how far they spread, and how to choose the comparison length when an error accumulates gradually rather than at once. We then give procedures that control the proportion of falsely flagged operations within a single audited analysis, requiring only that sound analyses be exchangeable rather than that the fitted model be correct, and we quantify how much the guarantees weaken when the model is imperfect or when the analysis was selected for review in a way that depends on its content. Finally we establish a limit on what any such audit can report: errors below a certain magnitude cannot be attributed at all, being indistinguishable from ordinary variation among sound analyses. This limit falls so slowly as more sound analyses are collected that at the representation sizes now in use a hundredfold increase reduces it by under two percent, so the dimension of the representation rather than the volume of training data is the binding constraint.

</details>


### [141] [EcoAgent-Bench: Evaluating Economic Decision-Making in Budget-Constrained LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05519)
*Jie Wu,Ming Gong,Feixiang Cheng,Qinqin Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EcoAgent-Bench introduces price-aware tasks with explicit budgets to study economical decision-making in agents, including escalation, model-tier choice, and stopping. It contains 304 real-derived tasks across five families (from GAIA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue), evaluating seven LLM agents and four scripted controls in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings. Results reveal a misalignment between task completion and economical action, quantified by an economic-consistency score, and show that budget considerations are a distinct property from mere completion. The authors release the task bundle, pipeline, environments, and artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployment requires economical action selection as an intrinsic part of task solving, not just task completion. Traditional benchmarks treat resource use as an auxiliary statistic, but real usage involves budgeted decisions (whether to escalate, which model tier to use, and when to stop). This work argues for evaluating both accuracy and economic efficiency in agent benchmarks.

Method: The authors introduce 304 real-derived tasks organized into five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue. Each task specifies priced actions and a fixed budget, testing four decisions: avoid escalation, escalate when local evidence is insufficient, select a model tier, and stop on unsupported premises. Evaluations include seven LLM agents across tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, plus four oracle scripted controls. They report micro-averaged accuracy (one-sided policies) and a novel economic-consistency score, defined as the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups. A threshold-crossing budget sweep analyzes how escalation behavior changes with budget (e.g., GPT-5.4).

Result: Tool-API agents achieve only 3.9–24.0% micro strict success (max 7.3% economic consistency), often stopping too early or overspending on cheap tasks. A budget sweep can dramatically alter escalation rates (e.g., GPT-5.4 from 0% to 3%).

Conclusion: Budget-aware task solving is distinct from pure task completion. Economic-consistency metrics reveal vulnerabilities not captured by accuracy alone. The work provides a dataset, transformation pipeline, evaluation environments, and artifacts to study budgeted decision-making in agents.

Abstract: Agent benchmarks usually measure task completion and treat resource use as an auxiliary statistic. In deployment, however, the choice among a local lookup, broad search, composite research tool, stronger model, or human escalation is part of the task itself. We introduce EcoAgent-Bench, in which every task specifies priced actions and an explicit budget. Its 304 real-derived tasks span five families adapted from GAIA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, and test four decisions: avoiding unnecessary escalation, escalating when local evidence is insufficient, selecting a model tier, and stopping on unsupported premises. We evaluate seven LLM agents in tool-API and workspace-CLI settings, together with four oracle scripted controls. Micro-averaged accuracy rewards one-sided policies: always-escalate controls achieve high micro success while failing save-oriented tasks. We therefore also report an economic-consistency score (the worse of accuracy on upgrade-oriented and save-oriented family groups) which exposes this failure. Tool-API agents attain only 3.9-24.0% micro strict success (at most 7.3% economic consistency), often either stopping before warranted escalation or overspending on cheap tasks. A threshold-crossing budget sweep changes GPT-5.4's escalation rate from 0% to only 3%. These results show that completion under a budget and economical action selection are distinct properties. We release the task bundle, transformation pipeline, frozen evaluation environments, and integrity-bound result artifacts needed to study both.

</details>


### [142] [Hyper-ES: Effective Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning via Descent Direction Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05541)
*Yu Gu,Zhi Zheng,Yunpeng Ba,Xialiang Tong,Mingxuan Yuan,Zhenkun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hyper-ES uses a learned subspace of descent directions to enable CMA-ES to optimize LLM updates efficiently, mitigating high-dimensional ES inefficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full-parameter ES is ineffective for billion-parameter LLMs due to near-orthogonality of random perturbations to useful update directions in high dimensions; need a low-dimensional optimization path.

Method: Compute a compact adaptation subspace by performing a few gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain descent directions; form their span; apply CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace (search over combinations of meaningful directions).

Result: Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by about 1% across six mathematical reasoning datasets on Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones, with ~10% fewer gradient updates.

Conclusion: Subspace-based ES can leverage ES strengths in low-dimensional optimization to improve reasoning tasks in LLMs while reducing gradient-update cost; Hyper-ES demonstrates practical gains and provides code for reproducibility.

Abstract: Evolution Strategy (ES) is a promising alternative to gradient-based fine-tuning for resource-constrained Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. However, directly applying ES to billion-parameter LLMs is highly ineffective. In such high-dimensional parameter spaces, most random perturbations are nearly orthogonal to useful update directions, leading to unstable optimization. We propose Hyper-ES, a subspace-based ES framework that avoids the weakness of ES in full-parameter search while exploiting its strength in low-dimensional optimization. Instead of asking ES to discover useful directions from random perturbations in the LLM parameter space, Hyper-ES first performs a small number of inexpensive gradient-based fine-tuning runs to obtain descent directions. Although each direction may provide only a limited improvement on its own, their span forms a compact adaptation subspace that captures useful reasoning updates. Hyper-ES then applies CMA-ES to optimize layer-wise DARE-TIES merging coefficients within this subspace, allowing ES to search over combinations of meaningful descent directions rather than over arbitrary full-model perturbations. We evaluate Hyper-ES on three Qwen2.5-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill backbones across six mathematical reasoning datasets. Results show that Hyper-ES consistently outperforms GRPO-LoRA by 1% while requiring 10% fewer space-consuming gradient updates. Code at https://github.com/kuangrepi/Hyper-ES.

</details>


### [143] [SkillTV-Bench: Benchmarking How Well Judges Perform on Skill-Augmented Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05573)
*Zhi Han,Chenxi Zeng,Liuhaichen Yang,Zihan Guo,Ming Zhou,Yang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SkillTV-Bench (681 trajectories, 50 tasks, 11 domains) for skill-aware trajectory verification, and SkillTV-Evolve (JudgeSkill) with automated evolution; reports +14.8 pp accuracy and rollout-success gains; code at GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable robust evaluation of long-horizon, tool-enabled agent executions by accounting for task-time skills and inspectable artifacts, addressing the gap where prior benchmarks emphasize final outputs or static trajectories rather than integrated skill-aware verification.

Method: Develop SkillTV-Bench, a large-scale trajectory benchmark combining task-time skills with inspectable artifacts and environments; propose SkillTV-Evolve to externalize verification knowledge as a reusable JudgeSkill that guides an agent judge to plan inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts; implement an automated evolution loop on a separate development pool to refine JudgeSkill using misjudged cases.

Result: On SkillTV-Bench, refining JudgeSkill improves the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection, it raises selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts.

Conclusion: Skill-aware trajectory verification via SkillTV-Bench and JudgeSkill enhances measurement of long-horizon agent performance and offers reusable verification knowledge and data/code to the community.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly execute long-horizon tasks through tool use and environment interaction, shifting evaluation from final-response scoring to verification of complete executions. For skill-augmented agents, verification additionally requires the procedural knowledge encoded in task-time skills, because this knowledge indicates what evidence to inspect and which failures are task-critical. However, existing judge benchmarks often expose final responses or static trajectories, and rarely combine task-time skills with directly inspectable artifacts and environments. We therefore introduce SkillTV-Bench, a 681-case benchmark of real agent trajectories from 50 tasks across eleven domains, designed to evaluate skill-aware trajectory verification for both LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge methods. Additionally, we propose SkillTV-Evolve, which externalizes verification knowledge as a reusable JudgeSkill that guides an agent judge to plan targeted inspections and issue evidence-grounded verdicts. On a disjoint development pool, an automated evolution loop further refines the JudgeSkill using misjudged cases. On SkillTV-Bench, the refined skill increases the same agent judge's accuracy by 14.8 percentage points. In offline rollout-pool selection, it increases selected-trajectory success from 22.9% with one rollout to 45.5% with ten rollouts. The code and data are available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/SkillTV-Bench

</details>


### [144] [StepReflect: Structured UI Transition Reflection for Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05587)
*Linqiang Guo,Wei Liu,Li Gu,Yang Wang,Tse-Hsun,Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StepReflect is a locally deployable per-step GUI reflection model that uses explicit transitions and visual evidence, achieving strong transition accuracy and competitive task success with lower API costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address inefficiencies and misalignment of open-ended multimodal reflection with structured GUI state transitions in long-horizon mobile GUI tasks.

Method: A staged supervision pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference/reward refinement; models conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence; offline 8B model.

Result: 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, +11.83 pts vs zero-shot GPT-5.2 under the same input; online results: 3/4 agent configurations outperform baselines; within one success of GPT-5.2 Reflection in the remaining; reduced API costs across all four configurations.

Conclusion: StepReflect demonstrates a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

Abstract: Autonomous mobile GUI agents require accurate action reflection for reliable long-horizon execution. Existing approaches rely on open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action, which is costly and poorly matched to the structured nature of GUI state transitions. We propose StepReflect, which formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. StepReflect is trained through a staged pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement. Offline, the resulting 8B model achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, exceeding zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points under the same structured input. Online, across M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, and Seed-2.0-Pro, StepReflect achieves higher task success in three of four agent configurations and remains within one successful task of the GPT-5.2 Reflection Agent in the fourth. It also reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection in all four configurations. These results establish StepReflect as a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

</details>


### [145] [Epistemic Trustworthiness in Generative AI: A Normative Framework for Warranted Reliance in High-Stakes Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05602)
*Nimisha Karnatak,Max Van Kleek,Nigel Shadbolt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Epistemically warranted reliance in GenAI hinges on three constitutive conditions—epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice—applied to high-stakes domains. Failures under these conditions can cause harms not captured by traditional metrics like accuracy or fairness; the work proposes a normative framework and design/evaluation guidance aimed at warrants for reasoning, not just outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To specify when users are epistemically justified in using AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning, addressing a gap where existing frameworks focus on accuracy, fairness, safety, or trust but do not define warranted reliance as a distinct epistemic target.

Method: Philosophical synthesis of trustworthiness (competence, audience-orientation) into a constitutive normative framework comprising three conditions; supported by real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring to illustrate failures and harms; followed by design/evaluation implications.

Result: Establishes three jointly necessary, non-fungible conditions for epistemic warranted reliance: (1) epistemic humility (system communicates limits of its competence), (2) epistemic access (system enables inspection/question/contestation in context), (3) resistance to epistemic injustice (recognizes users as legitimate epistemic agents and avoids marginalization). Case analyses show how failures produce harms not captured by standard metrics; outlines implications for design and evaluation.

Conclusion: Advocates shifting from output-centric evaluation to epistemically warranted reliance, proposing design and evaluation practices that institutionalize humility, access, and justice to improve trustworthiness of GenAI in high-stakes domains.

Abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional contexts, where their outputs shape what users believe, how they reason, and what they treat as settled. This raises a central question for responsible AI: under what conditions is reliance on generative AI outputs epistemically warranted rather than behaviourally induced? Existing frameworks largely ask whether AI outputs are accurate, fair, explainable, safe, or trusted by users. These questions remain necessary, and each can contribute to warranted reliance. However, they do not directly specify warranted reliance as a distinct evaluative target: the conditions under which users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning. We argue that this requires an account of epistemic trustworthiness: what makes a system epistemically worthy of reliance. Drawing on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, we develop a constitutive normative framework comprising three jointly necessary and non-fungible conditions. First, epistemic humility requires systems to represent and communicate the limits of their competence. Second, epistemic access requires systems to enable users to inspect, question, and contest outputs in context. Third, resistance to epistemic injustice requires systems to recognise users as legitimate epistemic agents and avoid marginalising their knowledge and experience. Through real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring, we show how failures of epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice can produce consequential harms that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability do not address on their own. We conclude by outlining design and evaluation implications for GenAI systems organised around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone.

</details>


### [146] [Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05624)
*Bohan Jiang,Dawei Li,Yasin Silva,Huan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CAP is a framework to automatically detect preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS) in LLMs from a single response, enabling large-scale data collection and analysis; findings show PSRS rates from 5–56%, detection from text is feasible, but cross-model generalization to unseen models is challenging; dataset and code will be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sycophantic responses in LLMs can be harmful; automatic detection of PSRS from a single response is needed to study prevalence and enable mitigation.

Method: CAP collects labeled PSRS data by contrastive anchor probing across 17 LLMs, yielding 290,460 responses over 12 everyday-advice domains; analyzes prevalence, detectability, and cross-model generalization; evaluates PSRS detection from response text and models generalization to unseen models.

Result: PSRS rates span 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic; PSRS can be detected from text alone, but detectors must learn subtle patterns from training data; cross-model generalization performance drops on unseen models; initial approaches to address generalization are proposed; dataset and code to be released.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates the prevalence and detectability of PSRS, identifies cross-model generalization as a key challenge, and provides a data-and-code resource (CAP) for future research toward robust PSRS detection in LLMs.

Abstract: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in large language models (LLMs), and prior work has pointed out that some of them could be harmful. This paper focuses on one harmful sycophancy: preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where a model reverses an initial stance merely to align with a user's stated preference. While existing research mainly measures how sycophantic a model is, we go further and ask whether PSRS can also be detected automatically from a single response. To investigate this at scale, we introduce CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applying CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, we collect 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) How often does PSRS occur? (2) How well can it be detected? (3) How does detection generalize to unseen models? We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data. Because new LLMs appear rapidly, detectors inevitably encounter unseen models, making cross-model generalization an important framework goal. We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge. We will release our dataset and code to support future research.

</details>


### [147] [SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05628)
*Yuru Feng,Yaoqi Chen,Beidi Zhao,Qianxi Zhang,Xinjiang Wang,Jianan Lu,Zhirui Wang,Shusen Xu,Zengzhong Li,Qi Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillHEX is a closed-loop, hypothesis-driven, evidence-guided skill revision framework for LLMs that operates at test time under sparse rewards, using executable tests to produce dense diagnostic reward and a tree search over revision branches; it mitigates exploitation traps and outperforms previous methods on SkillsBench tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for autonomous, on-demand skill evolution during deployment with limited interactions and no training/validation data; sparse reward makes it hard to diagnose failures and avoid exploitation traps.

Method: Translate falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests; produce diagnostic evidence as dense reward without extra environment trials; use evidence to guide a search over persistent skill-revision branches; balance exploitation of supported edits and exploration of alternatives.

Result: Evaluated on 87 SkillsBench tasks; average pass rate 55.9% with GPT-5.3-Codex and 57.9% with Claude Opus 4.7 under five iterations; outperforms existing self-evolving methods.

Conclusion: SkillHEX enables robust, autonomous, test-time skill evolution under sparse rewards by coupling hypothesis-driven verification with evidence-guided search, reducing exploitation risk and improving success rates.

Abstract: Although agent skills equip LLMs with reusable procedural knowledge, manual maintenance suffers from high costs, unscalability, and misalignment. Real-world deployments thus require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time, constrained by limited interaction budgets and a lack of training or validation sets. This setting introduces a severe sparse reward challenge, where outcomes conflate multiple latent failure causes. Under such ambiguity, existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill are particularly vulnerable to an exploitation trap, allowing early misdiagnoses to exhaust limited trials along unproductive trajectories. To address this, we introduce SkillHEX, a closed-loop framework coupling hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. SkillHEX translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, producing diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides a search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing the exploitation of supported edits with the exploration of plausible alternatives. Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods and achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% and 57.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget, respectively.

</details>


### [148] [GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05948)
*Shuai Wang,Yaxin Feng,Xuekun Jiang,Shihan Tian,Ningyu Yan,Xing Shen,Chaoyang Lyu,Hui Wang,Yunsong Zhou,Hanqing Wang,Jiangmiao Pang,Yang Xiang,Xing Gao,Chunhua Shen,Weinan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAUGE is a real-world-grounded benchmark to jointly evaluate numerical simulators and generative video world models on physical fidelity, revealing no universally faithful engine and highlighting gaps in impulsive contact, fast textile motion, and volumetric deformation; video models capture equation forms but misestimate accelerations and timing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond perceptual similarity and human judgments in physics evaluation by providing a real-world-grounded, diverse, and instrumented benchmark that jointly tests simulators and video world models against real trajectories and calibrated physical metadata.

Method: 22 task families across rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects, grounded in real-world trajectories with calibrated metadata, uncertainty annotations, and task-specific observables. Evaluations include 14 task families on Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton using generalized trajectory errors, and 6 image-to-video models on 5 rigid-body tasks assessing physical-law consistency and temporal stability of inferred parameters.

Result: No single physics engine is uniformly faithful. Largest discrepancies observed in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. Video world models can reproduce the form of physical laws but may infer incorrect accelerations, momentum transfer, and oscillation timing.

Conclusion: GAUGE provides a foundation for developing more physically faithful simulators and world models for embodied intelligence, enabling targeted diagnostics and improvements across diverse physical phenomena.

Abstract: Physics engines facilitate large-scale training and evaluation for embodied intelligence, while generative video world models are emerging as implicit simulators of future states and interactions. However, existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation and rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments, providing limited insight into which physical principles or parameters are violated. We introduce GAUGE, a real-world-grounded diagnostic benchmark for jointly evaluating how numerical simulators and generative video world models reproduce or deviate from real-world physics. It comprises 22 controlled task families covering rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects.
