Then, this information is represented semantically using a BERT-based language model, after which the pair-wise similarity between courses can be computed. This information is then used by a Random Forest classifier to determine whether a candidate course abroad overlaps with a course already contained in the student's curriculum. We evaluate CourseGraph using (1) the Computer Science program at Eindhoven University of Technology, which contains information about courses with substantial overlap, and (2) six approved international programs from students enrolled in the Computer Science program at Lund University, including the corresponding decisions made by a curriculum administrator. The experimental results indicate that CourseGraph provides an effective approach for identifying overlapping courses and supporting curriculum alignment across universities.

</details>


### [174] [VLMs for Videogame Data Annotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05949)
*Katrin Schmid,Iuri Frosio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VLMs can annotate video game frames with reward signals but struggle with basic questions in racing games; effectiveness varies across genres; proposes output mixing and prompt optimization; sequence length, resolution, and batching impact quality and token usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Leverage VLMs to label frame sequences with rewards to enable conditioned training and offline RL in games, addressing data labeling bottlenecks and sim-to-real variability.

Method: Empirical evaluation of VLMs on video game frames, focusing on racing games; test their ability to answer basic questions; explore countermeasures (VLM output mixing, prompt optimization); study effects of input sequence length, resolution, and question batching on annotation quality and token consumption.

Result: VLMs often fail basic questions in racing games (and similar behavior across genres); countermeasures show potential; annotation quality degrades with longer sequences, higher resolutions, and batching affecting token usage; practical trade-offs identified.

Conclusion: VLM-based frame annotation for rewards is feasible but limited; implement mitigation strategies and optimize prompts; further research needed to improve reliability and efficiency.

Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have revolutionized how engineers approach complex problems in real-world applications. Their adoption in video games is on the other hand limited by the extreme variability of the synthetic scenarios and their poor compliance with real-world physics. Here we investigate the use of VLMs for annotating video game frame sequences with reward signals, a task with several potential applications including, among others, conditioned training and offline reinforcement learning. We show that VLMs often struggle to answer basic questions on racing video games (although we observed a similar behavior on other game genres) and discuss countermeasures such as VLM output mixing and prompt optimization. We also show how input sequence length, resolution, and question batching affect the annotation quality and its token consumption.

</details>


### [175] [Training a Conditioned Video Game Agent on a VLM Annotated Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05954)
*Katrin Schmid,Iuri Frosio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Annotate a video game dataset with Vision-Language Models to extract human-defined rewards, then use offline RL to train a conditioned agent to meet desired returns; discusses early experiments' difficulties and limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ease RL training in video games by avoiding hard reward engineering and game-engine access, addressing sparse rewards and opaque reward shaping.

Method: Annotate video-game dataset using VLMs instructed to extract rewards aligned with human-defined objectives; apply offline RL to train a conditioned agent that responds to specified returns.

Result: Offline RL can train a conditioned agent responsive to desired returns; however, early experiments reveal significant difficulties and limitations (e.g., reward extraction noise, off-policy issues, distributional shifts).

Conclusion: Promising approach to mitigate reward engineering and sparse rewards; success depends on reliable reward extraction via VLMs and robust offline RL methods; early results show challenges that require further refinement.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a powerful but far from easy-to-use technique for policy learning. In the specific case of video games, access to the game engine is required to get rewards for training (e.g. to collect rewards from the environment). Furthermore, the proper identification and weighting of the rewards generally requires a difficult trial-and-error approach. Lastly, rewards are often sparse and understanding how they eventually affect the learned policy is a non-trivial exercise. To ease these issues we propose annotating a video game dataset with Vision Language Models (VLMs) instructed to extract human defined rewards. We show that offline RL can then be used to train a conditioned agent that responds accordingly to the desired returns and we discuss the difficulties and limitations that emerged in our early experiments.

</details>


### [176] [Stability of Ranking-dependent Pair-wise Comparison Patterns in the Analytic Hierarchy Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05958)
*Vitaliy Tsyganok,Sergii Kadenko,Oleh Andriichuk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Three incomplete ranking-dependent pairwise comparison patterns in AHP (Best-Worst, Best-Second Best, and Maximum Difference) are compared for stability to expert errors; simulations identify the most stable incomplete pattern and show potential for reducing comparisons without sacrificing credibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the quality of expert data and reduce the number of comparisons in ranking-based decision support by leveraging ordinal information and analyzing stability to expert judgments in AHP-like methods.

Method: Analytically compare the three incomplete patterns, derive conditions for comparable stability against expert errors, and perform simulation-based experiments to evaluate performance and robustness.

Result: Identified conditions under which the three methods can be compared in terms of stability; simulations reveal relative stability and allow ranking of methods; determined the most stable incomplete pattern and demonstrated potential to reduce comparisons without loss of credibility.

Conclusion: Incomplete ranking-dependent patterns can be viable, stable options in decision support under uncertainty; provides guidance for selecting an incomplete pattern to balance stability and effort in AHP-like frameworks.

Abstract: The paper addresses several ranking-dependent decision support methods. Ordinal information on compared objects can be used to improve the quality of expert data during estimation and help reduce the number of comparisons that the experts need to perform. In the paper we compare three incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison patterns which can be used in the Analytic Hierarchy Process - Best-worst method, Best-Second Best (Top 2) method, and the original maximum difference method. The first two comparison patterns (and respective methods) are incomplete, while the third can be a complete one. We determine conditions under which these three methods can be compared in terms of stability to expert errors. We also present the results of a simulation-type experiment, in which the three methods are compared. The research allows us to define the most stable incomplete ranking-dependent pair-wise comparison pattern and reduce the number of comparisons without loss of credibility of expert session results. The research contributes to algorithmic, cognitive, and applied aspects of decision support in uncertain environments.

</details>


### [177] [Temporal Bridges for Spatial Resolution: Enhancing Climate Data Super-Resolution with Bidirectional Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05981)
*Yichen Zhang,Yixiong Xiao,Congxi Xiao,Jingbo Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment for climate data super-resolution (SR), using Paired Latent Mapping for spatial alignment/noise reduction and Bidirectional Temporal Alignment to exploit temporal correlations, achieving superior SR performance on large-scale real-world data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-resolution climate data are costly; existing SR methods rely mostly on spatial info and ignore temporal correlations; climate data are stochastic/noisy, making temporal alignment challenging; a tailored framework is needed to leverage implicit temporal structure for better SR.

Method: Proposes Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional alignment. Key components: (1) Paired Latent Mapping for spatial alignment and latent-space denoising by unifying latent spaces; (2) Bidirectional Temporal Alignment training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames to capture temporal correlations; (3) Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution that jointly optimizes the framework for climate data SR.

Result: Empirical evaluation on large-scale real-world climate datasets shows superior SR performance of the proposed framework compared with baselines.

Conclusion: The framework effectively captures implicit temporal correlations in climate data and improves SR quality, addressing limitations of prior single-frame approaches and ineffective traditional temporal alignment methods.

Abstract: High-resolution climate data is crucial for meteorological predictions and for informing decision support across diverse domains. However, the acquisition of such high-resolution climate information is often prohibitively costly, necessitating the development of data-driven meteorological prediction models. These models aim to generate fine-grained climate data from low-resolution inputs, a process termed climate data super-resolution (SR). Nevertheless, recent advancements in deep learning for climate data SR have primarily focused on leveraging single-frame spatial information, largely neglecting the temporal correlations between different time frames that could enhance SR outcomes. Furthermore, climate data are inherently stochastic and noisy, rendering widely used temporal alignment methods, such as optical flow models, ineffective in this context. Consequently, the development of a framework tailored for climate data SR that effectively captures implicit temporal correlations remains an unresolved challenge. To this end, we propose a novel Temporal-Enhanced framework with bidirectional temporal alignment. In essence, our framework establishes a temporal bridge to enhance spatial resolution in climate data SR through bidirectional alignment, leading to improved SR performance. Within this framework, Paired Latent Mapping achieves spatial alignment and noise reduction by unifying latent spaces. Then a Bidirectional Temporal Alignment captures temporal correlations by training forward and backward networks on consecutive latent frames. Temporal Enhanced Super-resolution then optimizes the entire framework for climate data SR. Experiments on large-scale real-world datasets demonstrated the superior performance of our framework.

</details>


### [178] [AgentOPSD: Recursive Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05987)
*Zi-Han Wang,Zhengxi Lu,Zhiyuan Yao,Jinyang Wu,Jie Wu,Zhengzhou Cai,Yueqing Sun,Ziang Ye,Linji Hao,Qi Gu,Xunliang Cai,Yongliang Shen,Yujiu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A critic-free, turn-level credit assignment method (AgentOPSD) for long-horizon RL that recursively updates a Bayesian belief state from token-level teacher-student log-prob gaps to reweight outcomes into turn-level signals, identifying pivotal turns; yields state-of-the-art results without extra critics or rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Credit assignment in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks is challenging; existing RL with verifiable rewards struggles to credit pivotal decisions; privileged self-distillation provides supervision but lacks a principled sequential credit mechanism.

Method: AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space, producing a principled reweighting of sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals and identifying pivotal turns via marginal belief revision; it is critic-free and requires no extra rollouts.

Result: Evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA with Qwen2.5 models at 3B and 7B; outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines; achieves 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B; ablations attribute gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive updates.

Conclusion: Turn-level aggregation plus history-dependent recursive belief updates are the key drivers of performance; AgentOPSD is compatible with standard policy optimization, requires no critic or extra rollouts, and demonstrates strong gains across multi-domain agentic tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards constructs trajectory-level advantage estimates, yet it often fails to credit the few pivotal decisions that determine outcomes in long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks. Recent work introduces privileged self-distillation for credit assignment, providing denser supervision, but it remains unclear how such local signals should represent sequential credit. We propose AgentOPSD, a critic-free, recursive method for turn-level credit assignment in agentic reinforcement learning. AgentOPSD aggregates token-level teacher-student log-probability gaps into turn-level evidence and recursively updates a Bayesian belief state in log-odds space. This yields a principled reweighting scheme that converts sparse outcome supervision into turn-level credit signals and identifies pivotal turns through the marginal belief revision between consecutive states. The method is fully compatible with standard policy optimization and requires neither an additional critic nor extra rollouts. We evaluate AgentOPSD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA using Qwen2.5 models at two scales (3B and 7B). AgentOPSD outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, achieving 89.1% success on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies attribute the gains to turn-level aggregation and history-dependent recursive belief updates.

</details>


### [179] [OPERA: Operator-residual feedback for reliable autonomous optical experiments with language-model agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05990)
*Ning Xu,Xiang Zheng,Fuqiang Zhong,Huadong Wang,Xiaolong Wu,Zhiyuan Liu,Hui Ning*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPERA: an operator-residual framework for autonomous optical experiments where operators enact executable changes and residuals report deviations from physical constraints. This physics-aligned feedback reduces wasted experiments, improves task success, and transfers from digital twins to real instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scores used to guide autonomous experimentation can diverge from physical success; there is a need for interpretable, physics-grounded feedback that aligns agent actions with measurable physical outcomes and resource efficiency.

Method: Represent experimental actions as optical operators that are executable changes to measurement/control/reconstruction. Use operator-residuals to quantify departures from specified physical conditions. An agent uses both feedback streams to select/combine/generate operators, with performance evaluated against a withheld physical reference. Validation across three optical tasks; transfer from digital twins to three optical instruments.

Result: Score-only feedback boosted scores but often did not improve physical outcomes (23.6–39.0% of decisions). Operator-residual feedback increased the likelihood of reaching/maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. Protocols optimized in digital twins transferred to real instruments, with repeated experiments showing reduced projection budgets in structured-light reconstruction.

Conclusion: Coupling executable operators with physically interpretable residuals yields decisions guided by measurable physical evidence, improving task success and resource efficiency and showing transferability from digital models to real optical systems.

Abstract: Autonomous agents choose actions using scores that may not reflect experimental success. We developed OPERA, an operator-residual framework for optical experiments. It represents experimental actions as optical operators and evaluates their outcomes using physically interpretable residuals. Operators specify executable changes to measurement, control or reconstruction, while residuals report departures from specified physical conditions. The agent uses both to select, combine or generate operators, and physical performance is evaluated independently against a withheld reference. Across three optical tasks, score-only feedback produced score increases without physical improvement in 23.6--39.0\% of decisions, compared with 0.9--1.9\% for operator-residual feedback. Operator-residual feedback increased the probability of reaching and maintaining task targets and reduced experimental budgets. Protocols selected in digital twins were transferred to three optical instruments, and repeated experiments showed a lower projection budget in structured-light reconstruction. Together, operators and residuals guide autonomous decisions using measurable physical evidence.

</details>


### [180] [Hybrid Machine Learning Framework for Herd-Level Cattle Growth Pattern and Weight Gain Forecasting in Grazing-Based Production Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06001)
*Muhammad Riaz Hasib Hossain,Rafiqul Islam,Shawn R. McGrath,Md Zahidul Islam,David W. Lamb*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid ML framework for herd-level cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing; cascade GB→RF→NN architecture achieved best predictive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular observations which hinder livestock growth forecasting; a robust, accurate herd-level forecast is needed to inform management decisions under heterogeneous sensing conditions.

Method: Utilized weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors collected 2022–2024 in southeastern Australia. Created structured forecasting datasets and generated herd-level trajectories via temporal aggregation of animal-level predictions. Evaluated four hybrid architectures (residual, stacked, cascade, ensemble-assisted) against ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU baselines. Independent testing assessed performance across forecasting horizons. Performed feature importance analysis.

Result: Cascade GB→RF→NN architecture achieved best performance: test R^2 = 0.889, RMSE = 21.319 kg, MAE = 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures showed greater robustness than recurrent models under sparse observations. Forecast error increased with longer horizons. Key predictors: animal age, rainfall, and temperature.

Conclusion: The proposed hybrid framework supports feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions in heterogeneous sensing environments.

Abstract: Commercial grazing systems yield irregular livestock observations, which challenge cattle growth forecasting. This study developed a hybrid machine learning framework for herd level cattle weight forecasting using automated sensing observations collected between 2022 and 2024 in southeastern Australia. Weekly live weight observations, demographic variables, and lagged environmental predictors were integrated into structured forecasting datasets. Herd level forecasting trajectories were generated through temporal aggregation of animal level predictions. Four hybrid architecture families were evaluated, including residual, stacked, cascade, and ensemble assisted frameworks. ARIMA, LSTM, and GRU models were used as comparative baselines. Independent testing demonstrated strong predictive agreement across multiple forecasting horizons. The cascade GB to RF to NN architecture achieved the best performance, with a test R^2 of 0.889, RMSE of 21.319 kg, and MAE of 15.462 kg. Hybrid architectures maintained greater robustness than recurrent sequential models under sparse observation conditions. Forecasting error increased progressively across extended prediction horizons. Feature importance analysis identified animal age, rainfall, and temperature as dominant predictors influencing herd level growth forecasting. The proposed framework may support feed allocation, grazing management, and livestock marketing decisions under heterogeneous sensing environments.

</details>


### [181] [HERALD: Counterfactual Audits and Minimal Repairs for Proof-of-Retrieval Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06012)
*Zhuowen Liu,Bohan Cui,YinShang Guo,Yuting Wang,Hao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HERALD is an offline auditing framework that tests search-agent citation integrity under identical-question interventions, revealing that targeted citation-strengthening can evade detectors; shows partial robustness improvements but persistent vulnerabilities, especially on MuSiQue, and sparse detector coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure that search-agent rewards reflect true evidence retrieval and to guard against citation laundering; existing metrics can misalign with actual evidence provenance, motivating an offline, controlled audit that disentangles scoring, learning signal, and policy transfer.

Method: Introduce HERALD: offline audit with exact-same-question interventions; separate candidate-visible from oracle information; enumerate detector contracts before policy optimization; perform a complete 2^3 ablation; evaluate on four Qwen3-8B pools drawn from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue; test against search deletion, fake IDs, and label-free laundering; measure empirical ASR, EM non-inferiority, citation precision/recall, and attackability; analyze across pool rules, a BM25 attacker, and four models; assess training-time detector presence and effects on learning signal.

Result: R0 rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds; targeted strengthening of L (citing non-retrieved corpus passages) is observed as the inclusion-minimal repair with R[L] achieving zero empirical ASR and a 0.50% cluster upper bound; gaps persist under various settings; under 5M-token matched training, R[L] meets EM non-inferiority on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue; equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve (by 2.02 and 1.46 points); unsupported citations drop (1.69 points); laundering attackability drops on 2Wiki and MuSiQue; natural L is not reduced; the detector is present in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories; overall, HERALD demonstrates separation of robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

Conclusion: HERALD provides a principled offline auditing framework that can disentangle scoring from policy learning and uncover specific vulnerabilities (citation laundering via L-strengthening) while also delivering partial robustness gains; however, detector coverage remains sparse and some benchmarks (MuSiQue) remain vulnerable, indicating the need for broader hardening and integration of robust detection into training.

Abstract: Search-agent rewards mix answer quality, citation grounding, tool cost, and anti-hacking terms; a high score therefore need not imply that cited evidence was retrieved, and added penalties can cancel. We introduce HERALD, an offline audit that applies exact same-question interventions, separates candidate-visible from oracle information, and enumerates detector contracts before policy optimization. On four Qwen3-8B pools from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, $R_0$ rejects search deletion and fake IDs, but a label-free citation-laundering attack succeeds. A complete $2^3$ ablation identifies targeted strengthening of $L$---citing a corpus passage absent from the retrieved evidence---as the observed inclusion-minimal repair: $R[L]$ has zero empirical ASR with a 0.50% one-sided cluster upper bound. The gap persists across pool rules, a visible BM25 attacker, and four models; broader hardening remains vulnerable when the attack removes an oracle support-ID penalty. Under strict 5M-token matched training evaluated on 256 paired questions per benchmark, $R[L]$ meets the EM non-inferiority gate on HotpotQA and 2Wiki but not MuSiQue. Equal-suite citation precision and support recall improve by 2.02 and 1.46 points, unsupported citations fall by 1.69, and laundering attackability falls on 2Wiki and MuSiQue. Natural $L$ is not reduced, and the detector appears in only 18 of 58,368 training trajectories. HERALD thus separates robust scoring, sparse learning signal, and policy transfer.

</details>


### [182] [From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06020)
*Jiale Han,Xiang Li,Jing Qian,Wenyuan Gu,Pin Gao,Ye Luo,Hongyuan Zha,Dacheng Tao,Benyou Wang,Lin William Cong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Economic World Models (EWMs) as a six-level generative framework to simulate economics from the inside, surveys current work, identifies gaps, and offers an implementation blueprint and resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create high-fidelity, endogenous economic simulations with heterogeneous agents, beliefs, and adaptive institutions that can train AI, support decision-making, and serve as safety substrates.

Method: Defines a six-level capability ladder (from fixed-rule agent worlds to self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins), conducts a systematic literature survey, translates the agenda into an implementation blueprint, and releases curated papers/resources.

Result:  finds concentration of work at lower levels; higher-level features such as self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms are rare; provides a blueprint and resources to accelerate development of economic sandboxes.

Conclusion: EWMs offer a path toward high-fidelity sandboxes and AI safety substrates; the work flags the need for endogenous institutions, empirical alignment, and robust mechanisms, and delivers an actionable roadmap to advance the field.

Abstract: Economic World Models (EWMs) are generative economic models that simulate how economies evolve from within by modeling heterogeneous agents, their beliefs and actions, and the market and institutional mechanisms through which their interactions produce aggregate outcomes. This paper develops an implementation roadmap for building economic world models as generative engines in which heterogeneous agents act, interact, adapt, and co-evolve with markets and institutions, thereby producing economic dynamics from the inside. We organize EWM systems into a six-level capability ladder, from fixed rule-based agent worlds to adaptive and LLM-based agent worlds, self-evolving agents, evolving institutional worlds, and sim-to-real economic twins aligned with real observations. A systematic literature survey across these levels reveals that existing work remains concentrated in lower-level agent and simulation environments, while systems with self-evolving agents, endogenous institutions, persistent empirical alignment, and validated economic mechanisms remain rare. By translating the EWM agenda into an implementation blueprint, this paper aims to accelerate the development of the next generation of economic simulation environments that can serve as high-fidelity sandboxes for human decision-makers and as training, planning, evaluation, and safety substrates for AI agents. We release a curated paper list and related resources to support future research.

</details>


### [183] [Integrating Implicit and Explicit Relational Biases through Graph-Based Multiple Instance Learning: A Case Study in Skin Lesion Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06037)
*Rafał Buler,Jakub Buler,Maciej Bobowicz,Michał Grochowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A dual-level relational framework for image classification combining self-supervised implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based relational modelling, achieving state improvement on skin lesion benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling to better capture inter-patch dependencies and relational structure in imagery, particularly for medical imaging tasks.

Method: Baseline EfficientNetB3; introduce patch-based convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relations via self-supervised reconstruction; extend with explicit graph-based relational modelling by organizing embeddings into grid, random, and k-NN graphs and applying graph attention networks (GAT); grid-structured GAT yields strongest gains.

Result: ISIC-2018: baseline 76.17% balanced accuracy; implicit 77.12%; grid-structured GAT 79.27%. ISIC-2019: implicit 59.84%; implicit+explicit 60.67%.

Conclusion: Combining implicit patch-level relational modelling with explicit graph-based message passing improves performance over baseline and implicit-only approaches, with grid-structured GAT providing the best results among tested topologies.

Abstract: Relational inductive biases are essential for capturing structural dependencies among data. This study investigates a dual-level relational framework for image classification, bridging the gap between implicit representation learning and explicit structural modelling. We begin by establishing a baseline using an EfficientNetB3 architecture. To move beyond standard convolutional biases, we adopt a patch-based strategy, employing a convolutional masked autoencoder to learn implicit inter-patch relationships through self-supervised reconstruction. We then extend this approach by incorporating explicit relational modelling, organizing the learned embeddings into various graph topologies, including grid-based, random, and k-nearest neighbour structures. Experimental results on the ISIC-2018 and ISIC-2019 skin lesion diagnosis benchmarks show that combining implicit inter-patch modelling with explicit graph-based message passing yields the best performance. On the ISIC-2018 test set, the baseline model achieves a balanced accuracy of 76.17%, which improves to 77.12% with implicit patch-based relational modelling. The fully integrated grid-structured Graph Attention Network further increases performance to 79.27%. Similarly, on ISIC-2019, the implicit approach reaches 59.84% balanced accuracy, while the combination of implicit and explicit modelling yields 60.67%.

</details>


### [184] [When History Lies: Evaluating and Improving Tool Use under Misleading Multi-Turn Histories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06057)
*Xiaoqing Wu,Xingyu Fan,Feifei Li,Wenhui Que*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Polluted historical traces can hijack tool-use policies in dialogue-driven agents. A synchronized bench (Original/Polluted/Oracle) isolates failure modes, and an Oracle-conditioned teacher-to-student transfer with soft supervision yields strong, scalable policy transfer, achieving state-of-the-art tool-use accuracy on Qwen3-1.7B and robust generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the vulnerability where accumulated but obsolete history can mislead policy decisions in tool-calling agents; establish evaluation benchmarks and training strategies to ensure robust policy behavior under history perturbations and to enable reliable-state transfer.

Method: Introduce bench with Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views; eleven gold-preserving interventions to diagnose failures in decision state, entity binding, and interface execution; propose Oracle-conditioned teacher policy transfer to a student observing polluted history via soft supervision on student prefixes; evaluate on Qwen3-1.7B with varying teacher sizes; compare against Gold-SFT, Oracle sequence distillation, and off-policy token distillation.

Result: Ours achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy on Qwen3-1.7B, surpassing Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle distillation (82.3%), and off-policy distillation (85.0%). An 8B teacher raises a 1.7B student to 91.9%; an 8B student reaches 93.0%. Results generalize to clean histories, unseen functions, regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop QA.

Conclusion: History reliability is a distinct bottleneck for tool use; reliable-state policy transfer via Oracle-conditioned teacher supervision is effective and scalable, with strong generalization to new contexts and tasks.

Abstract: Tool-calling agents infer task state from accumulated dialogue and tool traces. In persistent interactions, however, historical traces may remain structurally valid and semantically plausible after they cease to be authoritative for the current request. We show that such history can hijack a policy the model already possesses: on Qwen3-1.7B, pollution flips 32.1% of decisions that are correct under the original trajectory and frequently induces reuse of corrupted entities or interface conventions. We introduce bench, a paired benchmark with synchronized Original, Polluted, and Oracle State views that preserve the system policy, current tools, latest request, and gold next action. Eleven gold-preserving interventions isolate failures in decision state, entity binding, and interface execution across complete calls and non-call decisions. We further propose ours, which transfers an Oracle-conditioned teacher policy to a student observing only polluted history through soft supervision on student-generated prefixes. On Qwen3-1.7B, ours achieves 87.0% Balanced Tool-Use Accuracy, outperforming Gold-SFT (66.3%), Oracle sequence distillation (82.3%), and off-policy token distillation (85.0%). The method scales consistently: an 8B teacher raises the same compact 1.7B student to 91.9%, while an 8B student reaches 93.0%. The resulting policies further transfer to clean histories, unseen functions, independently regenerated evaluation contexts, external tool-use benchmarks, and noisy multi-hop question answering. These results establish history reliability as a distinct tool-use bottleneck and demonstrate reliable-state policy transfer as an effective and scalable solution.

</details>


### [185] [Signal or Spurious Cue? A Randomized Audit of Survey-Country Metadata in LLM Social Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06085)
*Yifan Lyu,Xinran Li,Jiaqi Qiao,Xiujuan Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Metadata about country of origin can shape LLM forecasts; verified country cues improve predictive accuracy, whereas random-label disclosure rarely attenuates country-directed effects; a large dataset (PROV-FORECAST) is released for further study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether country-related metadata improves individual-response forecasts by LLMs and whether making the label origin explicit or random affects bias, using controlled within-record audits across multiple models, countries, and targets.

Method: Within-record audit with a primary 72-record panel testing opaque vs disclosed-random labels across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. Additional non-overlapping mixed-coverage panel and cross-panel checks. Measured country-direction uptake (effect size ~0.214 for both label conditions), attenuation (0.0003, 95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]), and Brier loss reduction from verified country (0.040, 95% CI [0.024, 0.056]). Assessed random-label regret (not significantly negative). PROV-FORECAST releases 14,400 item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

Result: Key findings include: (1) both opaque and disclosed-random labels yield a similar country-direction shift of 0.214; (2) attenuation between pre- and post-disclosure effects is negligible and uncertain (0.0003, CI crosses zero); (3) verified country metadata reduces Brier loss by 0.040, indicating improved probabilistic accuracy; (4) random-label regret is not significantly positive or negative; (5) results persist in a non-overlapping mixed-coverage panel; (6) verified metadata shows utility on selected targets; (7) disclosure does not reliably attenuate random-label uptake across panels.

Conclusion: Country-origin metadata can improve forecast accuracy when verified, but simply disclosing random labels does not reliably attenuate country-directed uptake. The study provides a substantial dataset (PROV-FORECAST) to enable replication and further exploration of metadata effects on LLM forecasts.

Abstract: Survey-country metadata can improve an LLM's forecast of an individual response when informative, yet the same cue may redirect the forecast when assigned at random. A within-record audit tests whether disclosing a random label's uniform, record-independent origin reduces its country-directed uptake, and whether verified survey country lowers held-out Brier loss. Independent population anchors and recorded human answers measure direction and consequence across five fixed API models, six countries, and seven development-selected targets. In the primary post-review 72-record panel, opaque and disclosed-random labels each produced country-direction shifts of 0.214. Paired attenuation was 0.0003 (95% CI [-0.0157, 0.0166]). Verified country reduced Brier loss by 0.040 (95% CI [0.024, 0.056]), while random-label regret included zero. A non-overlapping mixed-coverage consistency panel retained positive disclosed-random movement and verified utility, while attenuation remained uncertain. On the selected targets, verified metadata was useful in both panels, but disclosure did not reliably attenuate random-label uptake. PROV-FORECAST contains 14,400 paired item-level probability distributions from the corrected panel.

</details>


### [186] [Evaluating Investment Logic in Large Language Models: A Real-World Benchmark Towards Personalzied Financial Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06108)
*Yuanhong Jiang,Jingjie Zou,Zhenghong Lin,Xusheng Yu,Qiqi Huang,Shuai Jia,Shijie Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InvestLogicBench is a process-native benchmark that uses a P→E→R→D→O trace over 201k decisions from 151 real investors to evaluate LLMs on grounded, profile-consistent financial reasoning; results show high logical plausibility but weak event grounding, advocating a data-system interface with versioned profiles and decision ledgers for consequential agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial LLM evaluations emphasize static QA or end results, failing to assess whether actions align with investors’ profiles and reasoning. There is a need for a benchmark that captures agency, personalization, and temporal causality to properly assess consequential agents in finance.

Method: A dataset of 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors, with episodes instantiated as P→E→R→D→O traces (Profile, Events, Reasoning, Decision, Outcome). The release provides profiles, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Evaluation across four leading LLMs measured logical plausibility, event grounding, and return/process quality.

Result: Logical plausibility scores are high (≈4/5) but event grounding is weak (≈0.8–2.8/5); there is a mismatch between return quality and process quality. The study reveals polished but poorly grounded reasoning, which traditional outcome-only or static QA evaluations obscure.

Conclusion: P→E→R→D→O should serve as a data-system interface with versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance is positioned as a stress test for broader personalized, consequential AI agents.

Abstract: Investment competence is inherently personalized: the same market evidence can justify different actions for investors with different goals, horizons, portfolios, and risk boundaries. Yet financial LLMs are evaluated either by static question answering or by terminal profit and loss. The former omits agency; the latter cannot reveal whether a profitable action was grounded, profile-consistent, or merely lucky. We ask whether the community is using the wrong ruler for consequential agents.
  We introduce \textsc{InvestLogicBench}, a process-native benchmark containing 201,247 documented decisions from 151 real-world investors. Each episode instantiates a \textbf{P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O} trace: investor \textit{Profile}, observable market \textit{Events}, investment \textit{Reasoning}, executable \textit{Decision}, and delayed \textit{Outcome}. The release includes profile construction, point-in-time event binding, structured logic, horizons, outcomes, and post-mortems, and supports comprehension, profile-conditioned generation, and end-to-end replay. Across four leading LLMs, logical plausibility remains near 4/5 while event grounding is only 0.8--2.8/5; return and process quality also disagree. These results expose polished but weakly grounded reasoning that outcome-only evaluation hides. We further argue that P$\rightarrow$E$\rightarrow$R$\rightarrow$D$\rightarrow$O should be a data-system interface, requiring versioned profiles, temporal provenance, inspectable retrieval, decision ledgers, and replayable outcomes. Finance is our stress test for a broader class of personalized, consequential agents.

</details>


### [187] [ECHO: A Locally-Deployable Agentic Health Assistant with Temporal Memory, Safety Guardrails, and Speech Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06110)
*Abdulkadir Külçe,Alihan Esen,Cağla Fikir,Berke Kurt,Kuzey Arar,Gökhan Ercan,Faik Boray Tek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A locally-deployable, privacy-preserving conversational health assistant (ECHO) combines an agentic chatbot (ReAct + LangGraph) with 17 clinical tools, cross-session memory via a temporal knowledge graph, a two-stage safety system, and a multimodal emotion/depression/pain assessment; it runs offline on consumer hardware and achieves strong tool-use, safety, and modality performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable robust, private, long-term chronic care management with offline operation, rigorous safety, and cross-session memory, addressing privacy concerns and regulatory compliance in health assistants.

Method: Agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph; 17 clinical tools; temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; two-stage safety layer: (1) rule-based for crisis signals and jailbreak attempts (<1 ms), (2) a signed graph neural network (GNN) with APPNP-style propagation classifying boundary-case clinical intent; 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query Turkish health dataset; multimodal speech assessment module using Whisper encoding + BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion to estimate emotion, depression, and pain; full web app running on consumer hardware with no external data transmission, supporting GDPR and KVKK compliance.

Result: Tool-execution pass rate of 94.9% across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini; safety metrics include 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on Turkish queries; mean macro F1 of 0.652 for emotion/depression/pain estimation; zero-shot LLM baselines (e.g., Llama 3.3 70B) are outperformed; system is privacy-preserving and offline.

Conclusion: ECHO demonstrates a cohesive, offline-capable health-assistant stack that integrates73 cross-session memory, safety, and multimodal assessment to support long-term chronic care while meeting privacy regulations; strong tool-use and safety performance indicate viability for deployment in privacy-sensitive settings, albeit results are dataset-specific (Turkish) and benchmark-driven.

Abstract: This paper presents ECHO (Enhanced Care \& Health Observer), a locally-deployable conversational health assistant for long-term chronic care management. ECHO integrates three complementary software modules developed under shared supervision as a unified system. The core module is an agentic chatbot built on a ReAct loop orchestrated via LangGraph, equipped with 17 clinical tools and a temporal knowledge graph for persistent cross-session memory; it achieves a 94.9\% tool-execution pass rate across a 59-scenario benchmark with GPT-5 Mini. A two-stage hybrid safety layer intercepts all incoming queries: a rule-based layer handles explicit crisis signals and jailbreak attempts in under 1ms, while a signed graph neural network (GNN) with APPNP-style propagation classifies boundary cases by clinical intent, achieving 88.8\% accuracy and 90.6\% unsafe recall on a 2,537-query annotated Turkish health dataset while outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines including Llama 3.3 70B. A multimodal speech assessment module combining Whisper acoustic encoding and BERT text encoding with cross-attention fusion estimates emotion, depression, and pain, reaching a mean macro F1 of 0.652. The full system is implemented as a web application that can run entirely on consumer hardware, with no patient data transmitted to external services, supporting compliance with GDPR and KVKK.

</details>


### [188] [From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06112)
*Manideep Dhar,Ritwik Singh,Sharat Chandra Kumar Manikonda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Presents a hospital-specific, compliance-first Agentic AI architecture with three layers—Agent Orchestration, Compliance/Policy, and Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric—integrated into Hospital Information Management Systems. Demonstrates end-to-end triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging on synthetic data with a ready-to-deploy prototype, aiming for scalable, ROI-focused AI across on-prem, hybrid, and cloud deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current hospital AI deployments are isolated and non-scalable, with 70-80% of AI pilots failing to scale due to governance gaps, data fragmentation, and missing integration blueprints. A unified, governance-centric architecture is proposed to unlock enterprise value.

Method: Propose a multi-layer architecture (Agent Orchestration Layer, Compliance and Policy Layer, Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric) and integrate them into existing hospital AI platform models. Uses a synthetic yet structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open prototype to demonstrate end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging across clinical, operational, and financial domains.

Result: Demonstrates end-to-end orchestration with simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. Provides a ready-to-deploy prototype and argues for a governance-driven pathway to scalable, ROI-focused hospital AI platforms across on-prem, hybrid, and cloud deployments.

Conclusion: Offers a pragmatic blueprint for hospital leadership to move from ad hoc tools to a globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform, adaptable to various deployment models and capable of aligning AI with regulatory and security standards.

Abstract: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

</details>


### [189] [Mind the Gaps: Mixture-of-Minds for Human Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06115)
*Pranav Dahiya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Anacreon introduces a targeted audience-simulation model that preserves individual heterogeneity within a narrow domain by learning authorship embeddings, clustering around seed people, and training cluster-specific adapters on a 12B base, achieving state-of-the-art ordinal alignment (0.775) on a large external survey with reduced biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the limitations of population-level accuracy and the flattening of heterogeneity in LLM simulators, and to enable faithful individual-level predictions that can still yield aggregate insights.

Method: 1) Learn an authorship embedding to separate individuals. 2) Cluster a real qualitative corpus around seed people. 3) Train a dedicated adapter for each cluster (a mixture of minds) on Gemma 4 12B. 4) Harvest demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, augmented with a chain-of-emotion. 5) Reduce prompt brittleness by shuffling response options. 6) Balance the training distribution to reduce positive bias.

Result: On a large external survey, Anacreon achieves state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775 with a small residual bias, indicating strong individual-level predictive fidelity within the tested domain.

Conclusion: A promising step toward deriving aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals by combining mixture-of-minds adapters with careful data augmentation and bias-mitigating strategies, demonstrated within a narrow, well-specified domain.

Abstract: Predicting how a population will answer a new question is a long-standing goal. Statistical methods succeed at the level of the mass but falter at the level of the individual. Large language model simulators inherit this gap. They recover a population's central tendencies while flattening its heterogeneity, and they carry social biases and prompt brittleness that distort individual predictions. This paper introduces Anacreon, an audience simulation model that targets the individual level within a narrow, well-specified domain. Anacreon learns an authorship embedding that separates individuals, clusters a real qualitative corpus around seed people, and trains a dedicated adapter for each cluster, a mixture of minds, on a Gemma~4 12B base. It harvests demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, and augments each record with a chain-of-emotion. It reduces prompt brittleness by shuffling response options and reduces positive bias by balancing the training distribution. On a large, externally sourced survey, Anacreon reaches a state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775, the individual-level accuracy measure on which the field has converged, with a small residual bias. The work is a step toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals.

</details>


### [190] [Poli-Bias: Understanding and Measuring Large Language Model Biases in International Political Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06123)
*Massi-Nissa Abboud,Aladin Djuhera,Elena Cabrio,Holger Boche*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Poli-Bias is a counterfactual auditing framework that detects political bias in LLMs by swapping country identities in paired prompts; it decomposes disparities into five interpretable dimensions and reveals systematic effects across 13 diverse LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Measuring political bias in LLMs is challenging because bias can appear in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning and cannot be captured by a single metric. A fine-grained, interpretable audit tool is needed to detect country- and user-identity effects on responses.

Method: Introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework that compares responses to paired prompts with country identities swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. It decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions and evaluates across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes.

Result: Across 13 LLMs, country identities and user affiliations systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Poli-Bias provides a fine-grained framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs.

Conclusion:  Poli-Bias offers a precise, decomposed audit framework to detect and analyze political bias in LLMs, enabling researchers to pinpoint where and how unequal treatment arises across countries and user affiliations.

Abstract: Measuring political bias in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as it can manifest through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that are difficult to capture with a single metric. In this work, we introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework for measuring whether LLMs treat legally equivalent conflict scenarios differently depending on the countries involved. Poli-Bias compares responses to paired prompts in which country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than reducing bias to a single judgment, our framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, revealing how and where unequal treatment manifests. Across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes, we find that country identities and user affiliations can systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Our results thus establish Poli-Bias as a fine-grained framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs.

</details>


### [191] [Contextual Information Policy Optimization for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06128)
*Xingyu Guo,Wei Chen,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CIPO is an RL framework that aligns reasoning with external evidence use by giving dense turn-level credit to evidence-informed actions, combining this with a global reward to preserve answer correctness, reducing prior-driven reasoning and improving performance across multiple benchmarks without extra reward models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation focuses on final accuracy or intermediate progress, not grounding of post-retrieval actions in evidence, leading to prior-driven reasoning and confirmation bias in knowledge-intensive tasks.

Method: Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO) assigns turn-level credit to reasoning actions influenced by retrieved evidence and combines an evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward, without requiring human annotations or an additional reward model.

Result: Empirical results on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show reduced prior-driven reasoning and strong performance on most tasks.

Conclusion: CIPO effectively discourages evidence-detached guesses and promotes reasoning trajectories where retrieved facts guide or revise subsequent reasoning while preserving answer correctness.

Abstract: Search agents extend large language models beyond static parametric memory by enabling them to acquire and use ex ternal evidence during multi-step reasoning. For knowledge intensive tasks involving complex or evolving information, their reliability depends not only on retrieving relevant ev idence but also on using it to guide subsequent reasoning. However, existing methods primarily reward final-answer cor rectness or intermediate progress, without directly assessing whether post-retrieval actions are grounded in the retrieved evidence. This misalignment encourages prior-driven reason ing: agents form conclusions based on internal knowledge and use retrieval mainly to confirm them, resulting in confirma tion bias and inefficient evidenceuse.Toaddressthisissue, we propose Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO), an evidence-oriented reinforcement learning framework that explicitly aligns policy optimization with external evidence use. CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning ac tions influenced by retrieved information, while combining this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward to pre serveanswercorrectness.Withthismanner,CIPOdiscourages evidence-detached guesses and promotes reasoning trajecto ries in which retrieved facts can guide or revise subsequent reasoning. Importantly, CIPO requires neither human process annotations nor an additional reward model. Extensive exper iments on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show that CIPO reduces the prevalence of prior-driven rea soning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.

</details>


### [192] [FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06144)
*Bo Deng,Kang Zhou,Lifan Guo,Chongyang Tao,Xuanren Chen,Chenggang Xie,Renzhao Liang,Feng Chen,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FinEvo-Bench is a longitudinal, real-case-grounded benchmark with 120 tasks across 20 business scenes to evaluate self-evolution in finance agents. It shows evolving agents improve task scores and reduce compliance issues, with different scaffolds contributing varying gains; rubric-based feedback outperforms reference feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap in evaluating cross-task transfer and long-horizon professional performance in AI agents by using real-case procedures and compliance rubrics in financial workflows; quantify self-evolution gains across independent task streams.

Method: Four self-evolving agent scaffolds (based on Qwen3.7-Max) are evaluated over three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams across 20 business scenes containing six related cases each. Institution-provided procedures define operations and constraints; case facts are drawn from institution-provided or publicly documented sources. Outputs are scored by Claude Code (Claude Opus 4.6). Paired non-evolving controls measure self-evolution gains. Analyses include within-scene rank comparisons and ablations on memory vs. skill evolution. 

Result: Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) with 0.09 compliance issues per task; Codex records the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Overall, evolution raises scores by 9.33–19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12–0.44 per task across scaffolds. Within-scene ranks 4–6 show larger gains than ranks 1–3 by 6.10–8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution yields higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only or combined memory-skill evolution. Rubric feedback improves scores and reduces compliance issues more than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively prior experience translates into later improvement.

Conclusion: FinEvo-Bench provides a dual benchmark for professional performance and self-evolution, enabling assessment of how retained experience translates into future task performance and compliance within realistic financial workflows.

Abstract: Most agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task helps with later tasks. Existing self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. We introduce FinEvo-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark with 120 real-case-grounded tasks, 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Institution-provided professional procedures define the required operations and constraints. Eligible institution-provided and publicly documented cases supply the task facts. Each scene contains six related but substantively distinct cases that share a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for task quality and financial compliance. We compare four self-evolving agent scaffolds using the same Qwen3.7-Max backbone and three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate each scaffold's self-evolution gain from retained experience, while an independent Claude Code scoring agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 evaluates all outputs. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task); Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task. Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution. Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively an agent turns prior experience into later improvement.

</details>


### [193] [PaDoc: Layout-Grounded Parallel Decoding for Document Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06146)
*Hao Yu,Jiabo Zhan,Kang Liu,Linnan Zhao,Dongxu Yue,Rui Chen,Jinglin Wang,Chong Sun,Chen Li,Jing Lyu,Chun Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PaDoc is a layout-grounded end-to-end document parser that enables concurrent decoding of layout and region content by treating the layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation, reducing decoding depth and enabling parallelism within a single MLLM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional end-to-end parsers serialize the entire page into a single autoregressive sequence, which forces long decoding paths, while crop-based two-stage parsers sacrifice full-page context and require repeated visual processing; a method that preserves full-page context with region-level parallelism is desirable.

Method: Introduce a prefix-conditioned factorization under a region-sufficiency assumption, enabling the layout stream and regional content branches to advance concurrently. Implement this inside a single multilingual large language model (MLLM) using packed variable-length ancestor attention to keep training-compatible visibility, and use masked parallel decoding to create branches that a vLLM backend serves concurrently with shared-prefix cache reuse.

Result: On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc achieves an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and an Overall score of 94.24 among end-to-end parsers, with Text Edit 0.038 and Formula CDM 95.59. On a 384-page subset with an A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser across five concurrency levels, delivering 67.4-118% higher valid-page throughput and 39.2-54.9% lower P95 latency than a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline.

Conclusion: PaDoc demonstrates that layout-grounded, branching decoding within a single MLLM can retain full-page context while achieving substantial speedups and competitive accuracy, outperforming traditional end-to-end baselines; further work could assess generalization, memory trade-offs, and applicability to other document modalities.

Abstract: End-to-end document parsers provide a unified interface, but serialize page layouts and regional contents into one autoregressive sequence. This formulation forces independent regions onto a decoding path whose length grows with the total content, whereas crop-based two-stage parsers expose region-level parallelism at the cost of repeated visual prefills and fragmented page context. To retain full-page context while removing dependencies, we propose PaDoc, a layout-grounded parser that treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, we derive a prefix-conditioned factorization in which the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing the decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. We realize this factorization within a single MLLM: packed variable-length ancestor attention preserves the visibility under standard next-token training, while masked parallel decoding creates branches that the evaluated vLLM backend serves as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse. On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc attains an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, a top-tier Overall score of 94.24 together with the best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset and one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4-118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2-54.9% relative to a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Longin-Yu/Padoc

</details>


### [194] [CogVis: Must Open-Vocabulary Change Detection Perceive the Scene Anew for Every Query?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06150)
*Zijie Wang,Chen Zhong,Wei He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CogVis reformulates Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) as a perception-memory-verification pipeline, decoupling temporal perception from semantic decisions via a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP), calibrating category-dependent thresholds with a Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC), and filtering candidates with an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF). It achieves state-of-the-art results across seven benchmarks and boosts inference throughput by 28.50%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-vocabulary change detection requires recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Existing methods often entangle temporal evidence, semantic discrimination, and region verification, leading to unstable outputs and redundant computation. A perception-memory-verification approach inspired by human change perception aims to stabilize decisions and improve efficiency.

Method: Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) extracts a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features to decouple temporal evidence from semantic decisions. Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) dynamically estimates image-query-specific decision thresholds to compensate for category-dependent score shifts. Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability.

Result: CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven benchmarks, spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment. It also improves inference throughput by 28.50% by sharing scene-level change perception across queries.

Conclusion: By decoupling temporal perception from semantic categorization and introducing memory-guided calibration and adaptive filtering, CogVis provides robust, efficient OVCD with strong generalization across tasks.

Abstract: Earth-surface monitoring requires change detection models capable of recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) addresses this need. However, existing methods often entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, causing unstable results and redundant computation. Inspired by human visual change perception, we propose CogVis, a cognitive memory-guided framework that reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm. CogVis first employs a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) to extract a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features, thereby decoupling temporal evidence from semantic category decisions. A Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) then compensates for category-dependent score shifts by dynamically estimating an image-query-specific decision threshold. Finally, an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability. Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment show that CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated datasets. By sharing scene-level change perception, CogVis further avoids repeating category-agnostic temporal perception across queries and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

</details>


### [195] [iARCS: Iterative Agentic RL for Controllable 3D Scene Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06161)
*Saugat Adhikari,Ashok Prasad Neupane,Pramish Paudel,Ajad Chhatkuli,Danda Pani Paudel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: iARCS uses iterative agentic RL with universal-reward pretraining and LLM-generated reward programs to adapt a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements, improving constraint fidelity while maintaining diversity and data usefulness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap where synthetic 3D scenes are realistic but fail to satisfy task-critical functional constraints (accessibility, traversability, spatial rules) needed for downstream embodied AI/training.

Method: Two-stage: (1) universal-reward pretraining to enhance physical plausibility and layout quality; (2) task-specific fine-tuning using reward programs generated by large language models and refined iteratively from training feedback; operates within an iterative agentic RL loop.

Result: Improved constraint fidelity for walkability, reachability, and clearance tasks; effective constraint optimization for task-specific needs; competitive scene diversity; synthetic data from iARCS improves a base generator's performance as a practical data source.

Conclusion: Agentic RL with LLM-driven reward programs can align synthetic scene generation to user-task requirements, making the data more usable for downstream tasks and enhancing the base generator's utility.

Abstract: Synthetic 3D scene generation is increasingly used as a data source for computer vision and embodied AI, but existing generators often optimize perceptual realism without reliably satisfying task-critical functional constraints. This mismatch limits the usefulness of synthetic data for downstream training, where accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance are often essential. We present iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework that adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements. iARCS uses a two-stage strategy: universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, followed by task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined from training feedback. Experiments show improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity. We further show that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, supporting its value as a practical synthetic data generation tool rather than only a controllable scene editing method.

</details>


### [196] [Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06167)
*Modhurita Mitra,Jan-Willem Versteeg,Maarten D. Schermer,Shiva Nadi Najafabadi,Marie L. De Bruin,Lourens T. Bloem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Schema-based, zero-shot, single-call IE framework using generative AI with path-based semantic evaluation; achieves high accuracy (F1>90% on 12/14 attributes) and ~30x speed-up on NICE HTA documents; generalizable across models, orgs, languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To extract complex, hierarchical information from unstructured documents efficiently and consistently, addressing variability and evaluation against gold standards, enabling automated, semantically grounded comparison.

Method: A domain-specific schema encodes knowledge to guide extraction in a single zero-shot model call. A path-based semantic matching algorithm aligns nested, variable-cardinality attributes with the gold standard. Semantic comparisons of attribute values are performed by generative AI, classified by a rubric into exact, semantic, useful, or non-match. Validated on NICE HTA documents using Claude Opus 3; tested across different AI models, HTA organisations, and languages.

Result: Extracted 12 of 14 attributes with F1 > 0.9. Attribute extraction time was ~30x faster than a human expert. Demonstrated generalisability across AI models and HTA organisations and languages.

Conclusion: The framework provides a unified, scalable approach to structured information extraction from unstructured text with high accuracy and efficiency, transferable across models and domains, and suitable for HTA and related fields.

Abstract: We present a schema-based framework for extracting complex, structured information from unstructured text documents using generative AI, followed by automated semantic evaluation of the extracted information against a gold standard. The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.
  In the evaluation step, we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard. We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.
  We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of $>$90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was $\sim$30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert. We further demonstrate generalisability of this framework across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

</details>


### [197] [MicroEvo: Knowledge-Guided LLM Sampling for Efficient Microarchitecture Design Space Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06183)
*Jia Xiong,Runkai Li,Chenxu Niu,Guangyuan Gao,Changwen Xing,Yifan Zhang,Xinlai Wan,Jieran Cui,Chen Bai,Yusheng Hua,Ying Wang,Ming Ling,Xi Wang,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MicroEvo) for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization improves Pareto-front quality and search efficiency, with iterative knowledge accumulation and adaptive search directives; scalable to industrial cores; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Microarchitecture search spaces are large and expensive to evaluate; existing methods often ignore architectural dependencies and fail to learn from iterative search, leading to wasted evaluations and poor Pareto convergence.

Method: Couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search. Includes LLM-driven evolutionary operators, a Pareto-aware tree policy balancing Pareto contribution and diversity, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism to extract and reuse optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt search behavior online.

Result: Pareto-front quality improved by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II; 10.6x higher search efficiency; demonstrated scalability to an industrial-scale core.

Conclusion: MicroEvo provides a knowledge-guided framework for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization that leverages LLMs and MCTS with adaptive knowledge reuse, achieving better Pareto performance and efficiency; code at the linked repository.

Abstract: Microarchitecture design space exploration suffers from expansive search spaces and expensive PPA evaluation, leaving only a small simulation budget for design decision-making. Existing methods perform blind search without considering microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn from the iterative search effectively, leading to wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence. In this paper, we propose MicroEvo, a knowledge-guided framework that couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. MicroEvo combines LLM-driven evolutionary operators, a Pareto-aware tree policy that balances Pareto contribution and diversity, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt the search behavior online. Experiments show that MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency, and also demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/GEAR-SEU/MicroEvo-ICCAD-26.

</details>


### [198] [Comparative Approaches to Agent Retrieval over Large Skill Libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06196)
*Indivara Kolluru,Nathan Sportsman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hybrid lexical-dense ranker for on-demand skill loading outperforms a typed knowledge-graph approach; added structure does not improve retrieval and can reduce reach due to pre-filter topology; author-written queries inflate perceived performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently selecting and loading skills from a large library is costly. The study investigates whether structural supervision (a knowledge graph with prerequisites and data flow) benefits retrieval beyond a strong ranker.
