Method: Compare two systems on 690 skills and 117 realistic queries: (1) a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading; (2) a typed knowledge graph encoding relations like prerequisites, data flow, and ordering. Evaluate the graph as a substitute for extra ranked results at a fixed token budget, test an LLM-generated edge layer, analyze reachability and a pre-filter topology bound, and compare author-written queries versus realistic queries.

Result: Hybrid ranker retrieves the correct skill within top five in 73.5% ± 8.0% of cases; about 25% remain unserved. The graph approach performs worse by -11.2 points (p = 0.0007). LLM-generated edge layer adds no improvement over free neighbors. 73% of missed queries are not reachable through the graph. 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker already surfaced. Graph enriches semantics but does not extend retrieval reach. Author-written queries overstate hit@5 by up to 44 points, potentially hiding these results.

Conclusion: Structural interdependence does not universally improve retrieval over a strong ranker; the benefit of adding structure depends on pre-filter topology and reachability constraints. The work provides a mechanistic account of when structure helps and identifies conditions under which it can be beneficial.

Abstract: Agents backed by large skill libraries must decide which skills to load and in what order. Loading the entire library into context is expensive and provides no structure for autonomous sequencing. We study two systems for this problem over a corpus of 690 skills: a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading, and a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations such as prerequisites, data flow, and ordering. On a set of 117 realistic, non-echoing queries, the hybrid ranker retrieves the correct skill within the top five in 73.5% +/- 8.0 of cases, leaving roughly a quarter of queries unserved. When used as the design intended (substituting graph neighbours for additional ranked results at matched token budget), the graph is significantly worse (-11.2 points, p = 0.0007). Its LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over neighbours obtained free from a local embedding pass, and 73% of the queries the ranker misses are not reachable through the graph at all. We attribute this to a pre-filter topology bound. Because the graph's candidate edges are drawn from the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches, 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker had already surfaced together. The graph can enrich relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. We further show that evaluating on author-written queries overstates hit@5 by up to 44 points, which would have hidden these results entirely. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of why added structure does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker, and identify the conditions under which adding structural interdependence into the retrieval is optimal.

</details>


### [199] [EnvACE: Internalizing Environment Dynamics via World Rehearsal for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06197)
*Zishan Xu,Zhiyuan Yao,Yuxin Chen,Yifu Guo,Zhengxi Lu,Yuquan Lu,Jinyang Huang,Yan Xu,Yasheng Wang,Weinan Zhang,Xingshan Zeng,Weiwen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EnvACE trains LLM agents with world rehearsal, replacing external environments with an internal agent world model learned via alternating action and simulated environment responses, enabling better long-horizon tool use and transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on costly, hard-to-ground external environments for training long-horizon tool-using agents; enable scalable, internal grounding of action–environment dynamics.

Method: Policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it generates a tool call, then plays the environment to produce the response, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response; both roles are optimized end-to-end with task-success rewards, yielding an internal world model.

Result: Outperforms environment-scaling baselines across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench; gains consistent across model scales; test-time private rehearsal provides further gains under a moderate budget; code released publicly.

Conclusion: World rehearsal provides a scalable pathway for training LLM agents, yielding an internalized world model that supports decision making and extends training beyond external environments.

Abstract: Training large language model agents for long-horizon tool use typically relies on interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, whose construction and verification are costly, or on external simulators that are difficult to ground. We introduce EnvACE, an agentic reinforcement learning method that replaces external environment interaction during training with world rehearsal. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it first generates a tool call, then plays the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. Through world rehearsal, the policy internalizes the relationship between actions and their environment responses in its parameters, yielding an agent world model that directly supports decision making. Across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in the overall evaluation. Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction. Our findings establish world rehearsal as a new path toward scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Within-yao/EnvACE.

</details>


### [200] [TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06223)
*Yixiong Xiao,Congxi Xiao,Jingbo Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TS-RAG introduces retrieval-augmented generation for time series forecasting by designing special reference tokens to fuse input sequences with retrieved similar sequences, yielding state-of-the-art performance on real-world benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limited data, smaller model scales, and limited generative capabilities in time series forecasting; leverage retrieval-augmented generation to inject external, relevant sequence information.

Method: A TS-RAG framework that retrieves similar time series sequences and uses specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from retrieved sequences with the input, enabling robust capture of temporal dynamics; avoids naive concatenation of references.

Result: Experimental results show consistent state-of-the-art performance on several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

Conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of retrieval-augmented generation for time series forecasting and outlines the benefit of a token-based fusion mechanism for integrating external references.

Abstract: While deep learning models, particularly transformer-based architectures, have shown impressive performance in time series forecasting, the application of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this domain remains limited. Since RAG has proven effective in enhancing the capabilities of large language models by incorporating relevant external information, retrieving similar time series sequences as references might also improve accuracy in time series forecasting tasks. However, most time series models are constrained by limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and a lack of the extensive generative capabilities found in large language models. Simply concatenating reference sequences into the prompt, as done in language models, may not yield the expected results. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, TS-RAG, which leverages RAG to enhance forecasting performance. The framework introduces specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from the input sequence with that from retrieved similar sequences, enabling a more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

</details>


### [201] [DASH: Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons for On-Policy Self-Distillation of Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243)
*ZhiYan Hou,Xinyu Tang,Hongyan An,Jianjin Zhang,Weizhen Wang,Yunyun Han,Gengsheng Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Haiyun Guo,Wenbin Hu,Jinqiao Wang,Yafeng Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DASH introduces divergence-adaptive supervision horizons for on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) to exploit temporal structure in token-level supervision, improving mathematical reasoning across model scales without extra forward passes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address sparsity and underutilization of temporal context in OPSD where all local divergences are weighted equally; exploit history of discrepancies to tailor supervision.

Method: Compute the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean, map it to adaptive gates, and use these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation, thereby adjusting token-level supervision weights according to divergence evolution.

Result: DASH yields improvements over vanilla OPSD across three math reasoning benchmarks and three model scales; gains achieved without additional forward passes, reusing existing teacher and student distributions; code provided.

Conclusion: Adaptive, temporally aware distillation supervision can better leverage divergence dynamics during generation, enhancing reasoning performance with minimal extra cost.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models using automatically verifiable outcome signals, but these signals are typically sparse and at the sequence-level. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mitigates this sparsity by querying a privileged teacher at student-visited prefixes and providing dense token-level distributional supervision. Although this dense supervision alleviates signal sparsity, we find that standard OPSD still underexploits the temporal structure of the rollout. It assigns every local divergence the same coefficient, regardless of its position or the divergence sequence in which it occurs. In on-policy autoregressive generation, the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories, reflecting different evolutions of the mismatch between the teacher and student. Since the local scalar alone cannot distinguish these temporal contexts, standard OPSD cannot adapt its token-level weights to the realized discrepancy sequence. To address this limitation, we propose Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons (DASH). DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean to an adaptive propagation gate and then uses these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation. By doing so, DASH adjusts token-level supervision weights according to how local divergences evolve during generation. Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show that DASH improves over our matched vanilla OPSD reruns on every benchmark at all three scales. DASH reuses the teacher and student distributions that OPSD already computes, so the gains require no additional teacher or student forward pass.
  Code: https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD

</details>


### [202] [Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06265)
*Omid Bazgir,Md Nasir,Jacob Hoffman,Yang Yang,Manu Agrawal,Anusua Trivedi,Vinay Rao Dandin,Chris Gibbons,Christine Swisher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Suggests explicit utility-constrained realism enhancement for synthetic clinical benchmarks; demonstrates with a Synthea-based care-gap benchmark; two deterministic revisions improve realism metrics while staying above a utility floor; naïve densification fails; realism and fidelity are related but distinct.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Privacy-sensitive healthcare data are hard to access, and synthetic benchmarks can pass utility checks yet remain structurally unrealistic. The work formalizes realism improvement as a constrained optimization where realism increases without dropping below an operational utility threshold.

Method: Instantiate a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients subjected to demonstration electronic health record workflows and processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is quantified via missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment. Compare two deterministic revisions against a naive densification control to assess impact on realism while maintaining utility above a floor. Analyze relationship between internal realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference.

Result: Two deterministic revisions improve realism panels (e.g., more realistic missingness, actionable rows, and population alignment) while remaining above the utility floor. A naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. Internal realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct concerns.

Conclusion: Synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly with utility treated as a constraint rather than as sufficiency for realism; alignment between realism and source fidelity is important but separable, guiding benchmark design under privacy constraints.

Abstract: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents can pass existing utility checks and still remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are hard to access. We study how to improve such benchmarks without breaking the downstream utility checks already used in practice.
  We formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes should increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. We instantiate this idea on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients exercised through demonstration electronic health record workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured through missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment.
  The baseline benchmark is extremely thin: sampled-pair missingness is 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while remaining above the current utility floor, whereas a naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. We further show that internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives. These results suggest that synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as one constraint rather than as sufficient evidence of realism.

</details>


### [203] [The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06270)
*Zhiheng Wang,Bo Peng,Lai Wei,Chaochao Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Visual tool-use via crop-and-zoom in multimodal LLMs yields limited causal benefits; a causal audit reveals two failure modes and an 'illusion' where aggregate gains do not reflect causal contribution across rollouts; only a calibrated minority benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determine whether returned visual evidence causally affects answers and diagnose miscalibration in thinking-with-images systems; bridge gap between observed performance gains and causal contribution.

Method: Model a causal graph for visual tool-use, then perform policy-level, trajectory-level, and step-level interventions; define Visual Evidence Gain; compare tool-use vs direct inference; corrupt/replace observations; evaluate across six models and five perception benchmarks; provide code.

Result: Policy miscalibration with two failure modes: Calling Without Looking (observations do not causally affect answer) and Looking Without Planning (informative observations but incoherent call schedule). Trajectory analysis attributes gains to a Calibrated minority; overall illusion of tool-use: aggregate gains not causally effective across rollouts.

Conclusion: Causal auditing uncovers the illusion of visual tool-use; to realize genuine benefits, align tool-use with causal pathways and improve calibration; code available for replication.

Abstract: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm equips multimodal LLMs with active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom. However, models using these operations often achieve only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at substantially higher token cost. They may also repeatedly crop irrelevant regions and fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. We ask whether the returned visual evidence causally affects the answer. To answer this question, we formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. We then audit it through interventions at the three levels: policy (comparing tool-use with direct inference), trajectory (corrupting all observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix). Our step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates the contribution of each returned observation. Across six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks, we uncover policy miscalibration with two failure modes. In Calling Without Looking, returned observations have no causal effect on the answer. In Looking Without Planning, observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes the policy-level accuracy gain and shows that the gain is concentrated in a Calibrated minority. We term this discrepancy the illusion of visual tool-use: despite aggregate accuracy gains, visual tool-use is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauAudit.

</details>


### [204] [QuanTiMedAI: Quantum-Enhanced Time-Series Model guided by Agentic AI for Cardiac Arrest Mortality Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06294)
*Mutasim Fuad Sarker,Adiba Rahman Namira,Wafa Binte Alam,Md Adnan Arefeen,Mahzabeen Emu,Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework called QuanTiMedAI combines agentic LLM-guided feature discovery with a compact quantum recurrent network to predict cardiac arrest mortality from ICU time-series data, achieving AUROC 0.852 on MIMIC-IV with only 605 parameters and outperforming a state-of-the-art baseline; ablation confirms each architectural choice, suggesting quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can surpass classical RNNs with far fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current mortality predictions in ICU for cardiac arrest rely on static early-admission summaries, ignoring temporal deterioration and recovery. There is a need for temporally aware, data-efficient models that can leverage high-dimensional clinical data, potentially via integrated agentic AI and quantum-enhanced methods.

Method: Use an agentic large language model to guide feature discovery/selection from clinical data, then feed the selected features into a compact quantum recurrent network designed for time-series mortality prediction. The model includes nonlinear feature enhancement via quantum architecture and is evaluated on a MIMIC-IV cardiac arrest cohort. An extensive ablation study analyzes the contribution of each architectural component.

Result: Quantum-enhanced architecture achieves AUROC 0.852 using 605 parameters, roughly 2.9% better than the current state-of-the-art baseline for this task. The method demonstrates competitive predictive performance with a fraction of the parameters and outperforms conventional feature selections.

Conclusion: Agentic LLM-guided feature discovery combined with quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can yield superior performance with substantially fewer parameters than classical approaches, and temporal modeling of ICU data is advantageous for mortality prediction in cardiac arrest.

Abstract: Cardiac arrest remains one of the most lethal conditions encountered in intensive care units. Despite the growing availability of electronic health record data, existing mortality prediction studies in this population largely depend on static summaries derived from early admission. Such approaches ignore the temporal progression of physiological deterioration and recovery that unfolds throughout a patient's ICU stay. To address this limitation, we introduce QuanTiMedAI, a quantum-agentic framework developed for cardiac arrest mortality prediction using agentic AI guided quantum enhancement time series model. The proposed system combines an agentic large language model (LLM) for clinically informed feature discovery with a compact quantum recurrent network for temporality aware mortality prediction. Our findings demonstrate that agentic LLM-guided feature selection consistently outperforms conventional feature selection approaches, and the proposed quantum architecture achieves competitive predictive performance through nonlinear feature enhancement while keeping the number of parameters very low. Through extensive experimentation on a MIMIC-IV cohort of cardiac arrest patients, QuanTiMedAI's quantum-enhanced architecture attains an AUROC of 0.852 using only 605 parameters, an improvement of approximately 2.9\% over a current state-of-the-art baseline for this task. A structured ablation study systematically validates the contribution of each architectural design choice. These results show that quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can exceed classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters.

</details>


### [205] [Bias Analysis of L2 Speaking Assessment Systems Using Concept Activation Vectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06300)
*Arya Labroo,Mengjie Qian,Kate Knill*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Extends Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to analyze bias in L2 speaking assessment models, comparing a text-based BERT grader and a Whisper-based multimodal grader. Introduces sparse autoencoder (SAE)–based CAVs to improve linear recoverability of concepts. Finds that concept recoverability and influence depend on representation and architecture; SAEs improve linear recoverability but attenuate activation-space sensitivity, underscoring the need to distinguish concept existence from influence when auditing bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure fairness of transformer-based L2 speaking graders in high-stakes settings by diagnosing whether internal representations encode bias-relevant concepts and whether those concepts influence scores; address the challenge of interpretability in complex embeddings.

Method: Apply CAVs to two models (text-based BERT grader and Whisper-based multimodal grader). Assess whether a concept is linearly encoded in activation space and whether it influences scores via gradient-based sensitivity. Compare standard CAVs with SAEs to learn CAVs in a sparse latent space and map them back to activation space.

Result: Concept recoverability (whether a concept exists in representations) depends on the model/representation; concept influence (sensitivity) is architecture-dependent. SAEs yield more linearly recoverable concepts but reduce the activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers.

Conclusion: Auditing bias in L2 speaking assessment requires distinguishing whether a concept is present in internal representations from whether it affects outputs. Model choice and representation shape both the recoverability and measured influence; SAEs aid interpretability but may dampen detectable sensitivity, implying careful interpretation of fairness audits.

Abstract: Automatic speaking assessment systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings to mark second language (L2) learners' speaking tests, making it critical to show that their scores depend on speaking proficiency rather than irrelevant speaker attributes such as first language (L1) or age. Transformer-based foundation models have improved the accuracy of these L2 speaking graders, but their black-box representations make fairness and interpretability analysis more difficult. Building on prior work that used Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to detect bias towards unwanted attributes (`concepts') in feature-based graders, we extend CAV-based analysis to two neural speaking assessment systems: a text-based BERT grader and a speech-and-text multimodal grader based on Whisper. CAVs represent human-interpretable concepts as directions in a model's activation space, allowing us to distinguish between whether a concept is encoded in a model's internal representations and whether it influences the predicted score, the latter quantified using a gradient-based sensitivity metric. Since CAVs rely on linear separability, which is less likely in complex neural embedding spaces, we also investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide cleaner concept directions by learning CAVs in a sparse latent space and mapping them back to activation space. Our analysis shows that concept recoverability depends strongly on the representation and architecture being probed, rather than on the concept alone. Sensitivity to concepts is also architecture-dependent. SAEs make concepts more linearly recoverable, but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers. These findings highlight the need to distinguish concept recoverability from concept influence when auditing bias in speaking assessment systems.

</details>


### [206] [HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06301)
*Varun Ursekar,Apaar Shanker,Yash Maurya,Shehab Yasser,Vijay S. Kalmath,Veronica Chatrath,Yuan Xue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HarnessOpt-Bench provides a standardized, end-to-end benchmark to measure harness optimization performance of LLM-based optimizers under expensive, stochastic evaluation, revealing that optimizer quality can exceed harness quality and gains vary across tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No common protocol exists to quantify frontier LLMs' ability to autonomously optimize harnesses (prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration). A scalable, discriminative benchmark is needed to evaluate progress and enable fair comparisons.

Method: An optimizer model (an LLM) paired with a coding harness receives a seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and archives candidate versions. The study compares 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers across 4 downstream tasks and 111 scored runs, using both a shared coding harness and native harnesses.

Result: Optimizer models exhibit larger performance separation than the coding harnesses they act through; native harnesses are not consistently superior; gains vary substantially by task and seed regime. The study establishes harness optimization as a measurable, discriminative capability with substantial room for improvement across the space of tasks and seeds.

Conclusion: Harness optimization is a measurable, discriminative capability with large potential for improvement. The benchmark enables cross-model, cross-harness comparison and highlights variability across tasks and seed configurations.

Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed within agentic systems, their capabilities depend not only on the model weights but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code surrounding them. This makes automated harness optimization -- the iterative and evaluation-guided improvement of a harness by an AI system -- both an important route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability for AI systems themselves. Yet the community lacks a common protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task. We introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer, an LLM paired with a coding harness, receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by its normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition that remains inaccessible throughout search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters target-agent resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. We evaluate 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers both under a shared coding harness and under their native harnesses across 4 downstream tasks, over 111 scored runs. Experiment results show that optimizer models separate more than the coding harnesses they act through, native harnesses are not consistently superior, and gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes. These results establish harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with large space for improvement.

</details>


### [207] [Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06305)
*Sagar Tamang,Ayush Vyas,Tabarakul Hazarika*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Embedding-free, table-aware retrieval (READ) for long financial documents yields substantial gains over embedding-based dense retrieval, but BM25 remains competitive; the work emphasizes transparent, deterministic document navigation over opaque similarity scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long financial documents (financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns) expose structural failures of chunk-based embedding retrieval, particularly unit propagation (lakh vs crore) and fragile chunk boundaries. The paper argues for auditable, structure-aware search to enable reliable, reproducible question answering.

Method: READ: a three-operation, deterministic retrieval loop—normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads—exposed via the Model Context Protocol to produce replayable audit trails. Comparison against dense embedding retrieval and a top-k tool; analysis includes statistical tests (Holm-adjusted p-values).

Result: On 51 verified questions, READ achieves 58.8% accuracy versus 15.7% for dense retrieval (p_Holm = 2e-5); a tuned version of READ reaches 35.3% with a 23.5-point advantage (p_Holm = 0.017). A top-k tool yields 27.5%. BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ in some settings, indicating the embedding-based advantage is not universal.

Conclusion: Embedding-free, agentic retrieval with explicit structural handling can outperform embedding-based retrieval in long, structured documents; the gains rely on interface design and deterministic reading rather than pure iteration. BM25 remains a strong baseline in this domain; results suggest focusing on structure and auditability for retrieval in technical documents.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

</details>


### [208] [TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06346)
*Yunjia Qi,Zehua Yin,Xintong Shi,Hao Peng,Songyuanyi Lu,Yixian Liu,Richeng Xuan,Yuhong Liu,Zhichao Hu,Xiaozhi Wang,Lei Hou,Bin Xu,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrajDebug is a framework for error-lifecycle tracing in LLM-based agentic systems that identifies the earliest error in long trajectories using multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based scrutiny, paired with TrajErrBench (486 annotated failed trajectories) for evaluation; results show superior performance and actionable diagnostics, with code/data to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To tackle cascading errors, long-trajectory debugging challenges, and the difficulty of attributing final failures to earlier steps in LLM-driven agents. The work targets improving error localization and attribution to guide debugging and improvement of agent success.

Method: Introduce TrajDebug, featuring multi-granularity history compression to summarize long histories, evidence-based error identification to locate root causes, and error lifecycle tracing (resolution status and terminal impact). Build TrajErrBench from existing Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro annotations. Evaluate across diverse agent benchmarks against baselines; provide actionable feedback and a release plan for code/data.

Result: TrajDebug achieves the best overall performance compared to existing baselines on multiple benchmarks; diagnostics yield actionable guidance for improving downstream agent success; application studies demonstrate practical benefits.

Conclusion: The framework offers a practical, scalable approach to error localization and attribution in long-horizon LLM agentic tasks, with a sizeable annotated benchmark to support reproducibility and further research; code and data will be released to facilitate adoption.

Abstract: LLM-based agentic systems have shown remarkable capabilities in complex domains, while suffering from cascading errors and difficulty in debugging. Critical error detection aims to locate the earliest error step in a failed trajectory that is responsible for the final failure. However, progress faces two main challenges. First, long trajectories make it difficult to identify individual errors, since the evidence for judging a step may be scattered across distant instructions, observations, and prior context. Second, failed trajectories often contain multiple local errors with different downstream effects, only some of which remain responsible for the final failure. In this work, we propose TrajDebug, an error-lifecycle tracing framework that addresses long-trajectory error discovery with multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification, and supports critical attribution by tracing each error's resolution status and terminal impact. We further construct TrajErrBench, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories from Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro, covering realistic tool-use and coding scenarios. Experiments across diverse agent benchmarks show that TrajDebug achieves the best overall performance over existing baselines, and application studies further demonstrate that its diagnoses provide actionable feedback for improving downstream agent success. We will release the codes and data to facilitate further research.

</details>


### [209] [Challenges in Evaluating Explanation Methods for Static and Evolving Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06351)
*Jerzy Stefanowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The abstract surveys gaps in evaluating Explainable AI (XAI), illustrating DetoxAI for bias detection and concept unlearning, and discusses human-grounded evaluation, adaptation to concept drift, counterfactuals, and the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the insufficient and fragmented evaluation in XAI and the need for robust assessment across bias detection, concept drift, and evolving data contexts.

Method: Uses DetoxAI as a running example for bias and concept unlearning; presents a human-grounded evaluation of image-class explanations; discusses methods to adapt explanations to streaming data with concept drift; shares experiences with counterfactuals; and connects these issues to the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.

Result: Provides qualitative insights and experiential perspectives on evaluation challenges; no reported quantitative results in the abstract; highlights practical difficulties and considerations for future evaluation frameworks.

Conclusion: Emphasizes persistent evaluation gaps in XAI and the need for integrated, human-centered, drift-aware evaluation approaches that account for the co-evolving data, models, and explanations.

Abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) with respect to insufficient evaluation. They are illustrated through the DetoxAI image recognition system for bias detection and concept unlearning. Then, an example of a human-grounded evaluation of methods for explaining image classification is presented. The paper further explores methods for adapting explanations to evolving data streams with concept drift. Experiences with adapting counterfactuals for this problem are discussed. Finally it is related to the challenges of tracking the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.\footnote{This paper has been accepted for a publication in J.Nalepa (ed) Explainable AI in Space. Proceedings of EASi 2026 Workshop at IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Bremen, Springer CCIS vol 3107 (2016).}

</details>


### [210] [The Low Frequency Trap: Video Language Models Fail at Simple Event Bookkeeping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06361)
*Sarvesh Baskar,Zikui Cai,Shayan Shabihi,Anirudh Satheesh,Muhammad R. Islam,Udari Madhushani Sehwag,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trace-grounded parametric profiling introduces executable event traces to evaluate event counting in controlled video tasks, revealing systematic temporal reasoning failures and poor fidelity in high-count/high-frequency regimes; increasing sampling yields limited improvements; evaluation shifts from aggregate accuracy to diagnostic insights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world video benchmarks mix event count, rate, duration, and complexity, hindering isolation of failure modes. A method to audit events against ground-truth executable traces can diagnose temporal reasoning limits beyond final accuracy.

Method: Three controlled tasks (bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, categorical state transitions) with varying event count N and frequency F while keeping rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace for capability-surface estimation and timestamp-level evaluation across 2,190 videos.

Result: Findings include a staged temporal failure: at 80% reliability, persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5–1 Hz are counted reliably, while transient blinks yield no reliable positive-count region. In high-count/high-frequency regimes, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and 18.1% of true events are recovered. Increasing sampling rate boosts Bounce Ball accuracy (19.6%→29.3%) but sequence agreement with ground truth remains only 3.7%. Prompt strategies offer limited gains; real-world evaluations show similar concentration at low event counts.

Conclusion: Trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy to a detailed diagnostic of where temporal reasoning fails, enabling finer-grained analysis of model capabilities and failure modes.

Abstract: Real-world video benchmarks provide broad coverage, but their fixed clips entangle event count, rate, duration, and visual complexity, making failure modes hard to isolate. While existing programmatic benchmarks offer better control, they score only the final answer rather than auditing reported events against executable ground truth. To bridge this gap, we introduce trace-grounded parametric profiling for event counting in three controlled video tasks: bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, and categorical state transitions. Across 2,190 videos, we vary event count N and frequency F while holding rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace for capability-surface estimation and timestamp-level evaluation. Our results reveal a staged temporal failure. At an 80% reliability threshold, Gemini 3.6 Flash reliably counts persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5 and 1.0 Hz, yet demonstrates no reliable positive-count region for transient blinking events. Thus, event representation dictates whether a model initially accesses evidence -- a limitation that compounds as count and frequency increase. In the high-count, high-frequency regime, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and the model recovers just 18.1% of true events. To test if visual access is the primary bottleneck, we increase sampling rate. Although this boosts Bounce Ball accuracy from 19.6% to 29.3%, the reported sequence agrees with ground truth only 3.7% of the time. Extra frames can therefore inflate final scores without producing faithful event recovery. Different prompting strategies yield similarly limited gains, and real-world video evaluations show the same concentration of success at low event counts. Ultimately, trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy metrics to a detailed diagnostic of where temporal reasoning fails.

</details>


### [211] [Tracing the Heart: An Evidence-Linked Pipeline for Heart-Failure Feature Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06366)
*Soorya Ram Shimgekar,Michelle Hu,Dorisa Shehi,Daniel Kang,Roy Ka-Wei Lee,Koustuv Saha,Christian Poellabauer,Christopher Lee,Sajeev Singh,Piyum Zonooz,Navin Kumar,Zeeshan Ahmed,Priyadarshini Kachroo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: nMAS automates heart-failure EHR feature engineering using an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded multi-agent pipeline; increases phenotyping AUROC; features are structured and rubric-scored with provenance; validated on synthetic 500-record dataset; single-institution validation; external validation needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EHR feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI (≈39–45% of data scientists’ workload). Heart failure requires integrating fragmented EHR data with guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and LLM approaches offer limited automation, maintainability, and traceability. There is a need for auditable, scalable, and maintainable automated feature engineering.

Method: Developed Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering. Evaluated on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS produced 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM.

Result: Added aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and from 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping. Independent LLM-based rubric assessment scored features at 81.5% of maximum points for evidence support and methodological soundness. 132 structured features and 70 rubric-scored features were generated; evaluation limited to a single institution and external validation is needed.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data. However, evaluation was restricted to one institution, and external validation is necessary to establish generalizability and real-world impact.

Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI, accounting for 39-45% of data scientists' workload. This is especially pronounced in heart failure, which affects an estimated 6.7 million U.S. adults and requires integrating fragmented EHR data with disease-specific, guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and large language model (LLM)-based approaches offer only partial automation with limited maintainability and evidence traceability. We developed the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering, and evaluated it on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM. Adding the aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping, and an independent LLM-based rubric assessment of evidence support and methodological soundness scored the features at 81.5% of maximum points. These results demonstrate the feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data, though evaluation was limited to a single-institution cohort and external validation is needed.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [212] [MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05196)
*Adam Simson,Ankush Dutta,Quang Bui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Open, reproducible benchmark (MS-MLB) for MS vs healthy classification from whole-blood RNA; leakage-controlled pipeline; Gradient Boosting achieves top scores (AUC-ROC ~0.989, MS Research Score 93.83); not clinically validated; available at GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a transparent, reusable framework for evaluating ML methods on MS blood transcriptomics and to enable fair comparisons across models on a common dataset (GSE17048). Although blood RNA may contain disease signal, ML classifiers cannot replace clinical diagnosis; a benchmark helps assess methodological progress.

Method: Use the public GSE17048 dataset transformed into an MS vs healthy control task. Evaluate multiple algorithms under a leakage-controlled pipeline with nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout, bootstrap CIs, ROC/PR analysis, calibration metrics, and an MS Research Score. Provides an external model submission pathway within the framework.

Result: Gradient Boosting ranked first on the holdout set with MS Research Score 93.83, AUC-ROC 0.989, sensitivity 0.950, specificity 0.778, F1 0.927, Brier 0.050. The benchmark emphasizes reproducibility and external submission; the score is for research comparisons only and not clinically validated. MS-MLB is claimed to be the first open benchmark for MS vs healthy using GSE17048 with an external submission pathway.

Conclusion: MS-MLB offers a reproducible, open benchmark for comparing ML models on MS blood transcriptomics and establishes a standardized evaluation pipeline. While performance is high, clinical validity remains unproven, and generalizability beyond GSE17048 requires further validation.

Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

</details>


### [213] [When Do Corrective Features Help? An Agent for Corrective Feature Discovery on Black-Box Forecasters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05207)
*Fangxin Wang,Ziyi Zhang,Diyi Zhuang,Langzhou He,Shiyu Wang,Baichuan Mo,Philip S. Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRAFTER introduces corrective residual features for frozen forecasters by combining a compositional input-channel search and an LLM-assisted feature generator, filtered by a validation gate. It yields strong, dataset-wide gains across six backbones and backends, robust to fine-tuning, and enables attribution of gains to feature sources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frozen pretrained forecasters exhibit systematic failure modes that are costly to fix via retraining. The goal is lightweight, interpretable post-hoc corrections using corrective features that model the failure process rather than the data-generating process.

Method: Two generators mine residuals: (1) a compositional search over raw input channels; (2) an LLM that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects candidates; accepted features are used by a light corrector applied on top of the frozen backbone. The pipeline is source-agnostic and benchmarked against dedicated feature-engineering systems.

Result: Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER outperforms all dedicated feature-engineering systems for every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement of the corrector-alone baseline and reducing the weakest backbone error by up to 27%. Gains persist across multiple LLM backends and even when added on top of fine-tuned backbones.

Conclusion: Corrective residual feature discovery via CRAFTER is effective, generalizes across datasets, backbones, and LLMs, and provides a robust, attribution-friendly post-hoc correction framework for frozen forecasters.

Abstract: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to repair through fine-tuning. We study corrective feature discovery: mining interpretable features of a frozen forecaster's residual to drive a lightweight post-hoc corrector. Prior automated feature engineering models the data-generating process; corrective features instead model the model-failure process. We present CRAFTER (Corrective Residual Agent with Feature-based Temporal Exploration and Reasoning), which keeps the backbone frozen and mines its residual with two complementary generators: a compositional search over the raw input channels, and a large language model (LLM) that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of its origin, and a validation-selected corrector applies the accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. This source-agnostic pipeline also allows prior feature-engineering systems to be evaluated under identical conditions, making CRAFTER an instrument for attributing forecast improvements to the feature source alone. Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reducing the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. These gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

</details>


### [214] [PPDL: LLM-Based Flows as Probabilistic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05234)
*Louis Mandel,Guillaume Baudart,Mandana Vaziri,Martin Hirzel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Probabilistic language to program LLM-based flows that quantify and propagate uncertainty, enabling experimentation with inference scaling without extra code; demonstrated via experiments and a Rocq theorem prover case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of accuracy measures and confidence signals in LLM-driven pipelines, especially across multi-step flows and tool interactions.

Method: Introduce a probabilistic programming language to specify LLM-based workflows; formalize uncertainty propagation across calls; permit exploration of different inference scaling strategies within the flow's logic without code changes; evaluate via experiments and a case study.

Result: Shows that uncertainty can be quantified and propagated through LLM flows; demonstrates practical applicability with a theorem-proving agent for Rocq, validating the approach and potential efficiency gains.

Conclusion: Provides a framework to build more reliable LLM-powered applications by integrating probabilistic uncertainty management into the flow, with demonstrated feasibility and avenues for broader evaluation.

Abstract: Building reliable applications that leverage large language models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge. While LLMs offer impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, their outputs often lack accuracy and provide no clear measure of confidence. This uncertainty compounds in flows of multiple calls to LLMs and other tools, making it difficult for developers and end-users to trust the results. This paper introduces a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows. It enables developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty throughout the application's flow, and experiment with different inference scaling techniques without adding a single line of code beyond the flow's logic. We present an experimental study to demonstrate this capability, and a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.

</details>


### [215] [Decoupling Perception from Description: Computation-Grounded Representation Alignment between Multivariate Time Series and Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05238)
*Xinran Feng,Yi Xie,Chao Zhang,Ruikun Li,Wanyun Ling,Ziyue Li,Chenxi Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A computation-grounded, 4B-parameter model (CGTime) decouples perception from description to enhance multivariate time-series understanding, achieving state-of-the-art multivariate facts despite being smaller than baseline LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Label quality for time-series-language alignment is limited by single-variable labels and by LLMs' weak perception of complex multivariate patterns; cross-variable dynamics require a different paradigm to be scalable and reliable.

Method: Compute an array of statistics deterministically from open-source multivariate series; have an LLM verbalize these precomputed facts. Perception is handled via computation; description via language.

Result: CGTime surpasses larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding: best multivariate fact score 0.283 (vs 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano); Holm-corrected paired tests show significance against all baselines; also yields more accurate verifiable numerical facts and broader statistical coverage in captions.

Conclusion: Decoupling perception from description yields a reliable, realistic, and scalable approach for multivariate time-series-language tasks; computation-grounded design enables improved factual accuracy and cross-variable reasoning.

Abstract: Training multimodal models to align time series with language runs into a self-supervision trap. The usual recipe asks an LLM to read a series and write a description, so label quality is capped by the perceptual skill the model is supposed to learn. The data can never teach more than the labeler already knows. A second gap makes this worse: most datasets use a single variable, but the patterns that matter (cross-channel correlation, lead-lag structure, co-occurring anomalies) appear only with several variables, right where the labeling LLM's limits are most exposed. These two problems create a trilemma: existing methods are reliable, realistic, or scalable, but none achieves all three. We resolve this by decoupling perception from description. Deterministic code computes a set of statistics from real, open-source multivariate series; the LLM verbalizes those precomputed facts. Perception, which LLMs do poorly, is handled by computation, while the LLM handles expression. This produces CGTime, our 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model. CGTime outperforms far larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding tasks: it attains the best multivariate fact score on our held-out benchmark (0.283 vs. 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano), a gap that survives Holm-corrected paired significance tests against every baseline. It also states verifiable numerical facts in generated captions more accurately and covers a broader range of statistical properties.

</details>


### [216] [Disentangling 3D Modeling from Spatial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05242)
*Haoze Sun,Jiequan Cui,Qingshan Xu,Richang Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR) separates 3D perception from reasoning by using off-the-shelf perception models to create explicit 3D evidence, and fine-tuning an LLM (via LoRA) to reason over this evidence, achieving competitive spatial reasoning without large-scale 3D VQA training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern perception models excel at estimating continuous 3D geometry while LLMs excel at compositional and symbolic reasoning. A modular approach that leverages both strengths may improve interpretability, efficiency, and scalability compared to end-to-end 3D+reasoning models.

Method: Reconstructs the physical world into structured 3D evidence using existing perception modules, then fine-tunes an LLM with LoRA to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence, without requiring extensive 3D VQA training or complex tool policies.

Result: DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks, while offering improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency due to the explicit separation of perception and reasoning.

Conclusion: Explicitly disentangling perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence, enabling modular components and interpretable reasoning over explicit 3D evidence.

Abstract: In this work, we explore an alternative paradigm for spatial reasoning by explicitly disentangling 3D perception from reasoning, rather than jointly acquiring implicit 3D perception and reasoning through large-scale training. Our key observation is that modern perception models excel at estimating continuous 3D geometry, whereas large language models (LLMs) are particularly effective at compositional and symbolic reasoning. Motivated by these complementary strengths, we propose the Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR), a simple yet effective framework that reconstructs the physical world into structured 3D evidence using off-the-shelf expert perception models and fine-tunes an LLM with LoRA to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence. Without large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies, DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks. Beyond its strong performance, DiSR offers improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency, demonstrating that explicit separation of perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative paradigm to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence.

</details>


### [217] [Marginal Matching Does Not License Factorized Sampling: Auditing Conditional Style Leakage in Factorized Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05243)
*Duong Bach,Hai Nguyen Hong,Cuong Do*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Matching the style latent to a Gaussian prior via its marginal distribution does not guarantee independence from class labels; a factorized sampling criterion has four conditions, and eliminating one is necessary but not sufficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Critically examine the common practice in factorized generative models of enforcing independence by matching the latent style z_s's marginal to a Gaussian prior; show that this constraint does not constrain the class-conditional distributions, enabling class information leakage.

Method: Theoretical decomposition of the four conditions for genuine factorization; empirical evaluation on a case-study model and four latent baselines, measuring marginal and conditional statistics, using MMD, linear probes for class labels, clustering accuracy, and external class-conditional generation; robustness checks under perturbations; evaluation of mitigation strategies (post-hoc conditional prior, empirical style bank) across two datasets.

Result: Demonstrates that zero marginal (global) MMD does not imply independence from class labels; z_s remains highly predictive of the label (74%–100% accuracy via a linear probe; clustering accuracy 99.15%). External class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time; leakage persists under multiple perturbations (capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, supervision) across two datasets.

Conclusion: Marginal distribution matching is insufficient to certify independence from class labels. It is necessary to address all factorization conditions, and reporting only marginal statistics is insufficient to validate the claimed factorization in latent variable models; mitigation can reduce leakage in some metrics but not fully eliminate within-class dependence.

Abstract: Factorized generative models commonly regularize a latent style variable z_s by matching its marginal distribution to a fixed Gaussian prior and interpret this as evidence that the style representation is independent of class information. We show that this interpretation is incorrect. Matching only the marginal distribution places no constraint on the class-conditional distributions, allowing the latent style to remain highly predictive of the label despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate. We derive an exact decomposition showing that this mismatch is one of four conditions required for factorized sampling, and demonstrate that eliminating it is necessary but not sufficient to obtain the intended factorization.
  Empirically, our case-study model and four representative latent baselines achieve near-zero global MMD while still allowing a linear probe to recover class labels with 74%--100% accuracy (10% chance level). Our model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy, whereas externally evaluated class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage remains under six independent perturbations involving model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, and supervision across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%--46%, although they leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior improves externally evaluated class generation to 0.97 on MNIST without retraining but reaches only 0.41 on CIFAR-10, while an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that no divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels, and that reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

</details>


### [218] [PRISM: Priority-aware Rubric Internalization via Structured Multimodal Data Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05249)
*Xiaomin He,Dongling Xiao,Jiahao Xie,Ruiqi Lu,Qianle Wang,Zhongbin Guo,Wanxuan Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PRISM introduces a rubric-based executor for multimodal instruction following, with an accompanying evaluation suite (PRISM-Eval) and data synthesis pipeline. A 10K-sample dataset yields substantial Strict accuracy gains while preserving general performance, transferring across models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple, unevenly weighted requirements. Current training data treat instruction following as answering a single self-contained question, leaving a gap in multi-rule, priority-aware execution.

Method: PRISM uses a four-stage data synthesis pipeline to create persona-task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. PRISM-Eval employs deterministic Loose and Strict metrics based on fixed labels to evaluate multi-rule compliance without inference-time judges.

Result: On PRISM-Eval, Qwen3-VL-4B improves from 9.5% to 30.1% Strict accuracy with 10K samples; general benchmark performance is preserved; gains transfer to four open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures.

Conclusion: Structured rubric supervision enables scalable multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following, bridging the gap between real-world requirements and current single-question evaluation.

Abstract: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet most multimodal training data still reduce instruction following to answering one self-contained question. We study this gap through \textbf{rubric comprehension}, which casts the model not as a generator measured against rubrics but as an \textbf{executor} that follows them: given an image and a typed, prioritized rubric, the model must verify each rule before producing an overall judgment. To support this setting, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a four-stage data synthesis framework that produces persona--task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. We further introduce \textbf{PRISM-Eval}, whose Loose and Strict metrics use deterministic matching against fixed labels and therefore require no inference-time judge model. With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5\% to 30.1\% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks, and the gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures, suggesting that structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following.

</details>


### [219] [Beyond Full-Model Rollback: AuroSFT for Adapter-State Multi-Task Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05250)
*Yue Han,Ziniu Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AuroSFT provides a parameter-efficient, mergeable adapter-based alternative to multi-task SFT (msft), freezing the backbone and using adapters with a rank-bounded, mergeable update to improve accuracy while reducing checkpoint costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-task SFT, tasks often have different optimal generalization times; treating heterogeneous data as a single optimization can be suboptimal. Full-model checkpoints (as in msft) incur significant storage, restoration, and deployment costs.

Method: Freeze the pretrained backbone, train injected adapters; roll back adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks and continue with the remaining active mixture. At each layer, adapters apply an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor rather than to the sample representation; the update remains linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection.

Result: Under retained-backbone evaluation, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy, outperforming the msft baseline at 59.85% across five backbones; it also achieves higher accuracy on all backbones. Code is available at an anonymous repository.

Conclusion: AuroSFT delivers higher accuracy with parameter efficiency by converting the carried state into mergeable adapters, reducing checkpoint costs while maintaining performance across diverse backbones.

Abstract: Multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often casts a heterogeneous data mixture as a single optimization problem, even though different tasks may reach their best generalization at different times. msft exposes this mismatch through task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but its original formulation materializes the scheduler state as full-model checkpoints, making stage transitions costly to store, restore, and deploy. This paper introduces AuroSFT, a parameter-efficient framework that recasts the carried state of overfitting-aware multi-task SFT as a compact, mergeable adapter state. AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone, trains only injected adapters, rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks, and continues on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor rather than to the sample representation. The resulting update remains linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection. Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy, compared with 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy on all five backbones. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroSFT-80D1.

</details>


### [220] [Beyond Rotations: AuroOFT for Expressive Quantized Orthogonal Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05253)
*Yue Han,Dianlin Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AuroOFT extends quantized orthogonal fine-tuning by adding a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer, enabling input-dependent nonlinear corrections while preserving quantization compatibility and initialization identity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of qoft’s linear orthogonal updates by introducing nonlinear, input-dependent corrections without sacrificing stability or quantization compatibility.

Method: Attach a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer; map activations to an RMS-normalized compact latent space; employ adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating; zero-initialized up projection ensures identical behavior to qoft at initialization; orthogonality is a branch-level stability property, not of the full nonlinear layer.

Result: Under matched data, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 by 1.30–2.70 percentage points on 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, surpasses QLoRA by 6.52–10.62%, and reduces trainable parameters by 32.3–44.7% relative to QLoRA in representative scales.

Conclusion: AuroOFT yields better performance with substantially fewer trainable parameters while maintaining quantization-compatible training; it preserves stability properties of the qoft branch and adds nonlinear corrections; code is available in an anonymous repository.

Abstract: Quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models by learning structured activation rotations before frozen quantized weights. However, its task-specific updates remain constrained to linear orthogonal transformations, limiting input-dependent nonlinear corrections. We introduce AuroOFT, which keeps qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch while attaching a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. AuroOFT maps activations into an RMS-normalized compact latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. The zero-initialized up projection makes AuroOFT functionally identical to qoft at initialization, while orthogonality remains a branch-level stability property rather than a property of the combined nonlinear layer. Under matched data, optimization, decoding, and parser protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over matched qoft by 1.30-2.70% on the 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA in representative scales. The small exam-style multiple-choice math set is treated only as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroOFT-F3FD.

</details>


### [221] [An Emerging Retail Portfolio Management Application: Personalized, Tax-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Goals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05255)
*Ramin Pishehvar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A pre-deployment RL-driven robo-advisor prototype that provides personalized, tax-aware, broker-integrated portfolio recommendations via a FastAPI backend and explicit user goals, showcasing a three-phase RL stack (self-supervised cross-asset encoder, Mixture-of-Experts policy with an intent router, and a LoRA personalization adapter) tested end-to-end with Alpaca in paper-trading and 14-day walk-forward backtests, plus practical engineering lessons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retail investors lack access to personalised, tax-aware portfolio management and to institutional-grade systems due to cost, complexity, and required tech stacks; the work aims to close this gap with a fully integrated, auditable, and testable prototype that can eventually scale to real end users.

Method: An integrated application consisting of a FastAPI backend and web dashboard where users express goals in natural language. The system routes goals to six investment mandates and generates live portfolio recommendations from a three-phase RL stack: (1) a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, (2) a Mixture-of-Experts allocation policy with a learned intent router, and (3) a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations using an individual’s brokerage behavior without retraining the core model. The system is end-to-end tested against Alpaca (paper trading), supports multi-user auth, a preview-before-apply flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain. It reports 14-day walk-forward backtests with bootstrapped CIs as pre-deployment validation rather than production performance and shares practical engineering lessons for RL systems built on live data sources.

Result: The work delivers a functionally complete prototype with end-to-end integration and testing, a concrete deployment path, and preliminary validation via 14-day walk-forward backtests. It provides architectural and operational insights (e.g., inactive integration paths, API call failures, and empirical verification over checkpoint metadata) that are valuable for applied RL with live data.

Conclusion: The project presents a credible, incremental approach to bringing institutional-grade personalization and governance to retail investors, emphasizing empirical validation and transparent pre-deployment status while outlining clear next steps for full deployment and broader generalization.

Abstract: Retail investors lack access to the kind of personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients take for granted -- existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, and institutional-grade systems require account minimums and technology stacks unavailable to individual investors. We present a fully built, integration-tested application that closes this gap: a FastAPI backend and web dashboard that let a user describe an investment goal in plain language (e.g. "I want steady growth but need to sell some shares next month for a down payment"), routes that goal to one of six investment mandates, and produces a live, broker-integrated portfolio recommendation from athree-phase reinforcement learning system -- a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations from an individual's revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against a live brokerage API (Alpaca, paper-trading mode), including multi-user authentication, a trust first preview-before-apply confirmation flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain, but has not yet been opened to real end-users; we report this honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment application with a concrete path to full deployment, alongside 14-day walk-forward backtests (bootstrapped confidence intervals included) as preliminary, pre-deployment validation rather than production performance. We also report several practical engineering lessons -- silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata -- that we believe generalize to other applied RL systems built on external, live data sources.

</details>
