### [222] [Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Post-Wildfire Debris-Flow Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05265)
*Quinn Ledingham,Zhengsen Xu,Yimin Zhu,Zack Dewis,Mabel Heffring,Saeid Taleghanidoozdoozan,Motasem Alkayid,Megan Greenwood,Lincoln Linlin Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Systematic benchmarking of 15 ML models for post-wildfire debris-flow prediction; TabPFN leads unaugmented performance; SHAP highlights short-duration rainfall metrics; synthetic augmentation via TabPFN samples boosts performance (except CNN); provides a framework combining benchmarking, interpretability, and augmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hazard prediction in recently burned basins is difficult due to overlap in feature space, limited data, and the need for interpretable models. The study aims to benchmark models, identify driving features, and assess synthetic data augmentation to improve predictive performance.

Method: Basins-scale observations of post-wildfire debris-flow events from the western United States. Evaluated 15 models, including TabPFN, using repeated stratified cross-validation. Measured predictive performance with threat score. Used SHAP to determine feature importance. Explored synthetic data augmentation by generating TabPFN-based samples and re-evaluating models.

Result: TabPFN achieved the highest unaugmented threat score (0.637); best tree-based models were close. SHAP identified short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation as the most influential features; burn severity and terrain features contributed less. Synthetic augmentation improved performance for all models except CNN, with the largest boost among deep learning models (+0.041).

Conclusion: The study offers a comprehensive framework combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation to advance post-wildfire debris-flow prediction.

Abstract: Prediction of post-wildfire debris flows is critical for mitigating hazards to communities, infrastructure, and resources during intense rainfall in recently burned areas. However, identifying reliable machine learning models is complicated by overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, the need for model interpretability, and limited training data. This paper addresses these challenges through a systematic evaluation of machine learning models in terms of predictive performance, feature importance, and synthetic data augmentation. Using basin-scale observations of post-wildfire debris-flow events across the western United States, we compare 15 models, including the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). Repeated stratified cross-validation shows that TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented performance with a threat score of 0.637, closely followed by the best tree-based models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to identify the features driving predictions, revealing that short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation consistently rank highest, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. We further evaluate synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address the scarcity of debris-flow observations. Synthetic augmentation improves the performance of all models except CNN, with the largest mean threat score increase of +0.041 among the deep learning models. By combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation, this work provides a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction.

</details>


### [223] [Rectifying Geometric Misalignment: Online Source-Free Adaptation for Class-Imbalanced EEG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05315)
*Shiwen Chu,Shanglin Li,Motoaki Kawanabe,Reinmar Kobler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OSPDIM is a source-free online UDA method for EEG BCIs that addresses label shift on SPD manifolds by introducing a manifold-constrained bias in tangent-space mapping, optimized via information maximization. It operates online without batch statistics and outperforms standard Riemannian baselines under severe class imbalance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In EEG-based BCI, covariate shifts across subjects/sessions degrade generalization. Riemannian alignment like RCT assumes balanced priors, but real online settings exhibit label shift, causing geometric misalignment. A online, source-free method is needed to correct distributions on the SPD manifold.

Method: Introduce a manifold-constrained bias parameter in the tangent-space mapping of SPD matrices. Optimize this bias via information maximization to correct geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Operates online without relying on global batch statistics (source-free). Bias is estimated and corrected on-the-fly, leveraging SPD geometry.

Result: 2D SPD simulations show that OSPDIM rectifies misalignment where centering fails. In motor imagery data, OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, especially under challenging online adaptation with severe class imbalance.

Conclusion: OSPDIM provides a robust, plug-and-play solution for online UDA in BCI that handles label shift on SPD manifolds without batch statistics, improving performance in real-time, imbalanced data streams.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) often require unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to generalize across subjects and sessions. While Riemannian alignment methods like the Riemannian Centering Transformation (RCT) are effective for handling covariate shifts, they implicitly assume balanced class priors. However, in realistic online BCI scenarios, the label distributions vary dynamically (label shift), causing standard alignment techniques to geometrically misalign the target data distributions. In this work, we propose OSPDIM (Online SPD manifold information maximization), a source-free online UDA framework designed to address label shifts on the Riemannian manifold. OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping, which is optimized via information maximization to correct the geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods relying on global batch statistics, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly. Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually demonstrate that OSPDIM successfully rectifies the misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets show that OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, particularly in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance, offering a robust solution for practical, plug-and-play BCI systems.

</details>


### [224] [QEvict: Recoverable Quantized KV Eviction for Attention-Drift-Robust Long-Context Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05326)
*Ayushman Garg,Akshita Gupta,Shaswata Bhattacharya,Abhishek Gupta,Sandeep Kumar,Manoj Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel three-tier KV-cache eviction scheme, QEvict, addresses the brittleness of binary evictions by enabling recoverable eviction and dequantization, improving long-context retention under fixed memory budgets for autoregressive LLM inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV-cache memory is a bottleneck in autoregressive LLMs. Traditional eviction policies erase tokens irreversibly, which can be detrimental as attention patterns evolve during decoding; there is a need to preserve broader historical context without exceeding memory limits.

Method: Introduce diagnostics Future Missed Mass and Global LIR to quantify future attention on discarded states. Propose QEvict: a three-tier KV-cache management scheme with (1) high-confidence windows stored in full precision, (2) intermediate windows stored in a quantized recoverable tier, and (3) low-confidence windows deleted. During decoding, cumulative attention updates window importance; when a quantized window regains importance, it is dequantized and promoted to full precision, under a fixed memory budget.

Result: QEvict preserves broader historical context while maintaining exact precision for the most important regions, leading to improved retention of information. It outperforms representative eviction and quantization baselines on long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks by reducing missed attention and improving information retention.

Conclusion: Recoverable eviction with dequantization balances precision and memory, enabling broader historical context under fixed budgets and enhancing performance on long-context tasks; the approach is conceptually sound and broadly applicable, though effectiveness may depend on thresholding and task distribution.

Abstract: Autoregressive large language model inference is increasingly constrained by the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache. A dominant line of work reduces this footprint by evicting tokens that appear unimportant under attention-derived scores. However, such policies make an implicit irreversible decision: once a token is evicted, it cannot become useful again. We show that this assumption is brittle during decoding. Token and window importance drift as generated queries evolve, causing standard eviction policies to permanently discard states that later receive substantial attention under the full-cache model. To characterize this behaviour, we introduce Future Missed Mass and Global LIR, two diagnostics that measure future attention assigned to discarded states and the reactivation of historically inactive regions. We propose QEvict, a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces binary retain-or-delete eviction with recoverable eviction. QEvict maintains high-confidence windows in full precision, stores intermediate windows in a quantized recoverable tier, and deletes only the lowest-confidence windows. During decoding, cumulative attention scores update window importance and when a quantized window becomes important again, it is dequantized and promoted to the full-precision. Under a fixed memory budget, this design preserves broader historical context while retaining exact full precision for the most important regions. Across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, QEvict consistently improves over representative eviction and quantization baselines, reducing missed attention and improving information retention

</details>


### [225] [DG-FedReuse: Proxy-Gradient-Gated Cached-Update Reuse with Matched Sparse Uplink Accounting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05358)
*Rahil Aftab,Vineet Kumar Rakesh,Soumya Mazumdar,Tapas Samanta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DG-FedReuse is a simulator-level mechanism enabling age-decayed cached update reuse in federated learning, with strict cache-age and fresh-client quotas, plus an adaptive Top-K update encoding. It demonstrates substantial uplink data savings but limited generalization claims and parameter-bound sensitivity, without proving end-to-end benefits or superiority over existing stale-update methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce communication overhead in federated learning by reusing stale client updates under a principled age-decay rule, while maintaining accuracy and respecting freshness constraints.

Method: Introduce DG-FedReuse: select clients contribution of age-decayed cached updates when a head-gradient discrepancy proxy stays below a round-dependent threshold. Enforce a hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota. Use adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation for fresh updates. Evaluate on six image-classification datasets with 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5), across three seeds.

Result: At 90 rounds, modeled uplink data-field saving is 83.36-85.42% vs 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg. Seed-aligned accuracy differences: -5.29 to -0.14 pp. Best test accuracies under checkpointing: -2.38 to +0.45 pp vs matched FedAvg. Dense-model-downlink symmetry reduces saving to 41.68-42.71% and gains to 3.24-4.27 pp, showing dependence on accounting boundary.

Conclusion: The work characterizes the reuse rule within the simulator and does not establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime/energy savings, faster convergence, nor clear superiority over stale-update or lazy-aggregation approaches.

Abstract: Federated learning repeatedly incurs local optimization and model-update transmission. We study DG-FedReuse, a simulator-level mechanism that allows selected clients to contribute age-decayed cached updates when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy remains below a round-dependent threshold. A hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota constrain reuse, while fresh updates use an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. Experiments cover six image-classification datasets, 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5), and three seeds. At a common 90-round budget, DG-FedReuse yields 83.36-85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving, compared with 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg; the seed-aligned accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies obtained under test-controlled checkpointing are retained only as exploratory archival evidence and range from -2.38 to +0.45 percentage points relative to matched FedAvg. A symmetric dense-model-downlink sensitivity reduces the headline saving to 41.68-F42.71% and the incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg to 3.24-4.27 percentage points, demonstrating the dependence of communication conclusions on the accounting boundary. The study characterizes the proposed reuse rule in the implemented simulator; it does not establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime or energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

</details>


### [226] [Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) for Predictive Latent Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05371)
*Hailong Jiang,Emran Hossain,Feng Yu,Jianfeng Zhu,Guilin Zhang,Wulan Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs): a quantum-inspired framework for predictive world modeling with structured latent states and measurement-inspired decoding. Establishes core properties (classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, structured compactness) and evaluates complex-valued and density-matrix-like variants on elementary cellular automata, finding local predictive benefits for complex-valued models but limited long-horizon rollout for density-matrix variants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explore whether quantum-inspired representations and inductive biases (complex-valued latents, density-matrix-like states) can yield more structured, efficient, and accurate world models for prediction, simulation, and planning beyond classical vector/probability-based approaches.

Method: Propose Quantum-Structured World Models with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding. Formalize three foundational properties, instantiate two variants (complex-valued and density-matrix-like), and evaluate against strong classical baselines on elementary cellular automata.

Result: Complex-valued QSWMs exhibit promising local predictive performance; density-matrix-like variants show limitations for long-horizon rollout. Classical baselines remain competitive, highlighting areas where quantum-inspired structure helps and where it does not.

Conclusion: Quantum-inspired structured latent representations can provide useful inductive biases for world modeling, particularly for short-horizon prediction. Further work is needed to improve long-horizon stability and to understand when different quantum-inspired parametrizations are advantageous.

Abstract: World models learn latent states that summarize interaction histories, evolve over time, and support prediction, simulation, or planning. Most existing world models represent these states using classical vectors, probability distributions, recurrent hidden states, or transformer activations. In this paper, we introduce Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a quantum-inspired framework for predictive world modeling with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. We study whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory, such as complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents, provide useful inductive biases for world modeling. We establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. We then instantiate complex-valued and density-matrix-like QSWM variants and evaluate them on elementary cellular automata against strong classical baselines. Results show promising local predictive potential for complex-valued QSWMs, while also revealing limitations in long-horizon rollout, density-matrix variants

</details>


### [227] [Spectral Distillation: From Nonlinear Dynamics to Linear State-Space Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05416)
*Liane Galanti,Devan Shah,Shlomo Fortgang,Elad Hazan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A convex-learn-then-distill pipeline learns a compact linear state-space model for nonlinear dynamics with provable guarantees; OSF yields an implicit spectral predictor, which is distilled into an explicit LDS with dimension-free error decomposition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome non-convex system identification for nonlinear dynamics and obtain a provable, compact linear representation that is valid in hindsight.

Method: Learn an implicit spectral predictor via Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method; then perform spectral-to-LDS distillation to obtain an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system; analyze error as distillation term plus OSF term governed by Luenberger complexity; guarantees depend on observer complexity, not latent dimension.

Result: Theoretical guarantee: average prediction error splits into exponentially small distillation error and OSF learning error; dimension-free with respect to latent nonlinear dimension. Empirical results on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show competitive or superior compact LDS predictors compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Proposes the first end-to-end provable pipeline to extract a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics via convex learning followed by distillation, with potential for efficient, interpretable dynamics modeling.

Abstract: Can nonlinear dynamical systems be learned through a compact linear state-space representation, without directly solving a non-convex system-identification problem? We give a provable pipeline for doing so. Starting from observations of an unknown nonlinear dynamical system, we first learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer for the system. We then apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system. Our main theorem shows that the average prediction error of the distilled LDS decomposes into an exponentially-small distillation term and the OSF learning term governed by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free: it depends on observer complexity rather than on the latent dimension needed to represent the nonlinear system. To our knowledge, this yields the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show that the train-then-distill pipeline produces compact LDS predictors that match or outperform directly trained baselines.

</details>


### [228] [Perturbation Sensitivity at Convergence: A Simple Signal for Identifying Spuriously Correlated Samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05419)
*Nilesh Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A convergence-time signal enables identifying samples tied to spurious correlations without group annotations; a fixed input perturbation reveals fragile samples, enabling rebalancing that significantly improves worst-group accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ERM models trained on data with spurious correlations fail on subpopulations; lack of group annotations makes identifying affected samples challenging; existing early-training signals require group labels for intervention timing.

Method: After convergence, use a fixed input perturbation; samples whose predictions flip are classified as fragile (likely spurious-examples) while others align with a shared rule. Use these detected samples to rebalance training without any group labels or early-stopping hyperparameters; requires two forward passes per training example per iteration. No group annotations at any stage; no early epoch intervention.

Result: On Waterbirds, worst-group accuracy improved from 57.3% to 80.8% using the detected samples; with true group labels, the accuracy reaches 85.8%.

Conclusion: The approach enables effective group-robustness improvements without group annotations or early-stopping signals, nearing oracle performance and offering a practical alternative for mitigating spurious correlations.

Abstract: Models trained by empirical risk minimization on data containing spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy while failing on subpopulations where the correlation does not hold. Existing methods for identifying the affected samples without group annotations rely on signals from early training, which requires locating the epoch at which to intervene, a hyperparameter typically selected using group-labeled validation data. We show that a usable signal is available after convergence, when loss no longer distinguishes the two populations. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared rule, while the remaining samples are fit through configurations specific to individual inputs and are correspondingly more fragile. Applying a fixed perturbation to a converged model's inputs flips the predictions of the latter far more often than the former. The resulting procedure requires two forward passes per training sample, no group annotations at any stage, and no early-stopping epoch. Using the detected samples to rebalance training raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, against 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

</details>


### [229] [IFlowNets: Extending Generative Samplers to Learn Strategies in Incomplete Information Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05422)
*Conor M. Artman,Nicholas Di,Scott Perkins*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Information Flow Networks (IFNs) by extending Adversarial Flow Networks to incomplete information games; introduces IFlowNets as a strictly more general framework that yields valid densities and training objectives; reports preliminary results showing competitive speed/performance versus OS-MCCFR and RL baselines in three standard games.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap in generative sampling frameworks for incomplete information games, ensuring valid density estimation of player strategies and a coherent training objective, addressing limitations of existing AFlowNets in such settings.

Method: Extend AFlowNets to incomplete information games to form IFNs, identify inadmissible constraints when translating complete-information GFlowNets to incomplete-information settings, formulate IFlowNets that generalize AFlowNets and yield valid densities and objectives, provide theoretical analysis, and present preliminary experiments in three standard game environments comparing against OS-MCCFR and RL-based methods.

Result: IFlowNets achieve performance and speed comparable to or better than OS-MCCFR and standard RL methods across three standard game environments.

Conclusion: IFlowNets offer a strictly more general framework for generative flow networks in incomplete information games with valid densities and training objectives, supported by theoretical insights and encouraging preliminary empirical results; further work needed on broader benchmarks and deeper theoretical guarantees.

Abstract: While many algorithms blend reinforcement learning (RL) with counterfactual regret (CFR) methods to leverage tradeoffs in computational speed and performance, there are fewer investigations into generative sampling frameworks in game theoretic applications in incomplete information games. We extend a generative flow network framework, Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets), to incomplete information games, called Information Flow Networks (IFNs). We prove that previously established constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities (corresponding to player strategies) and a valid training objective. We show that our proposed generalization, IFlowNets, alleviates this issue and strictly generalizes AFlowNets. In preliminary results for three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in performance and speed.

</details>


### [230] [Why the Third Axis Is Freedom](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05423)
*Michael Timothy Bennett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: XM introduces multiple outputs per comparison (K) and reframes exploration as a fundamental 'freedom' objective; theoretical and empirical work shows freedom drives generalization, and increasing K enhances or saturates measured freedom, with XM outperforming MDL-based selection in many cases; conclusion: freedom is the true end, XM the means, especially under distribution shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reassess exploratory objectives in generative training, challenging MDL as the sole constraint and identifying the true objective that yields better generalization across tasks.

Method: Formalize Explorative Modeling (XM) with K outputs per comparison; derive the average XM loss as a function of miss probability raised to K; provide a formal proof linking weak models to better generalization; conduct Forward XM experiments varying K; train XM candidate pools and compare validation selection against a freedom selector using unlabelled parent contexts; evaluate under distribution shift.

Result: XM loss depends on miss probability to the power K; for K>1, match probability increases with freedom; empirically XM tends to optimize freedom; larger or saturated freedom observed with higher K in Forward XM; freedom selector wins 29/30 cases; generative expressivity acts as a proxy and is not the sole driver of generalization; selecting for freedom improves XM under distribution shift.

Conclusion: Freedom is the underlying objective driving generalization, not merely generative expressivity; XM is a means to maximize freedom; optimization for freedom yields robust performance and outperforms MDL-based selection in many scenarios.

Abstract: In generative training, a model produces an output and is penalised for its difference from an example. With one output per comparison, a model that produces one common answer can outperform a model retaining a broader repertoire. Explorative Modeling (XM) produces $K$ outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, claiming exploration as a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Here I show the third axis is actually freedom, meaning the weakness of the constraint implied by a model's behaviour. Previous work showed freedom is a property of function rather than form. Parameters, architecture, minimum-description-length (MDL), and data can vary while the behavioural constraint remains unchanged. It was formally proved that weakest models are likeliest to generalise, and freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500\% in induction experiments. I prove average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power $K$. For $K>1$, match probability rises with freedom. I then demonstrate empirically that XM optimises for freedom. In a Forward XM experiment, larger $K$ increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. I trained XM candidate pools and compared validation selection with a freedom selector that read unlabelled parent contexts. Freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy for freedom, that discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalisation significance. XM is a means, freedom an end, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.

</details>


### [231] [EvoHarness-RL: Learning Self-Evolving Runtime Harness for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05446)
*Xuying Ning,Dongqi Fu,Tianxin Wei,Hanqing Zeng,Yuanchen Bei,Bingxuan Li,Zihao Li,Qifan Wang,Xiang Shen,Yifan Wu,Jiayi Liu,Hong Li,Yinglong Xia,Xiangjun Fan,Hanghang Tong,Jingrui He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoHarness-RL learns offline harness policies to construct and online-manage external harness state for long-horizon LLM agents, enabling selective external-state access and achieving high task success; reveals harness annealing and harness evolution dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: External-state management is essential for stateful, long-horizon tasks, but current approaches rely on ad hoc prompts or domain-specific conventions. Noise in interaction traces makes state formation from experience challenging; a trainable, policy-driven harness policy can coordinate with external workspaces.

Method: Introduce EvoHarness-RL with Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as the policy-facing harness state. Use supervised harness fine-tuning to teach the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, followed by cost-aware GRPO reinforcement learning to learn coordination policies for selectively reading, updating, and consolidating state during long-horizon tasks. Evaluated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM.

Result: The approach achieves 96.9% task success. It reveals two dynamics: (i) harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns and reduces frequent harness calls in favor of selective external-state access, and (ii) harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation yield a compact, task-adaptive state substrate for the external workspace.

Conclusion: Trainable harness policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces can benefit long-horizon agents beyond merely adding more tools or larger memories; this approach enables efficient, policy-driven management of external state.

Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly rely on external execution support to maintain state, track progress, invoke tools, verify outcomes, and reuse experience across interactions. However, effective harness use raises two coupled challenges: state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access. Existing agents usually handle both through prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions, leaving the external workspace and its usage policy manually engineered. To address this, we study the problem of harness policy learning, where agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution. We introduce EvoHarness-RL, which exposes Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, while cost-aware GRPO explores coordination policies to selectively read, update, and consolidate that state during long-horizon interaction. Instantiated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM, EvoHarness-RL reaches 96.9% success and reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into the model policy and shifts the agent from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access, and harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate. These results suggest that long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories.

</details>


### [232] [Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotopes for Identifiable and Refinable Predictive Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05454)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ) for decomposing uncertainty into discrete mode, bounded drift, and stochastic noise; provides closed-form likelihood, cross-step coupling via a shared bounded generator, and multi-modal conformal inference; identifiability up to permutation and distinct density relative to Gaussian mixtures; empirically competitive with same-encoder baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real prediction tasks exhibit multiple, distinct uncertainty sources (mode choice, bounded systematic drift, irreducible noise) that are not cleanly captured by Gaussian mixtures or convex-conformal predictors. An output head that jointly models these sources and yields tractable likelihood and conformal guarantees is desirable.

Method: Model the three uncertainty sources as three generators of a zonotope: a binary generator for discrete mode, a bounded generator for drift within the chosen mode, and a stochastic generator for irreducible noise. The same bounded generator is shared across prediction steps, creating algebraic coupling of future predictions. Compute a closed-form likelihood via convolution of the generators. Prove identifiability of the three generators up to permutation. Show the resulting HProbZ density is not representable by any finite Gaussian mixture. Provide per-mode analytic risk and distribution-free, multi-modal conformal sets at inference. Evaluate against baselines with same encoder and mixture heads on representative benchmarks.

Result: The HProbZ head yields a representation that captures discrete mode, bounded drift, and stochastic uncertainty in a unified, tractable form. It provides a closed-form likelihood, stepwise coupling that propagates information across future predictions, and analytic per-mode risk and conformal sets. Empirically, it performs competitively or better than same-encoder mixture baselines and offers structural properties absent in mixtures or convex-conformal predictors.

Conclusion: HProbZ delivers joint modeling of heterogeneous uncertainty sources with tractable likelihood and conformal inference, along with identifiability guarantees and a density not representable by finite Gaussian mixtures. This composition yields advantages over traditional mixture or convex-conformal approaches and enables richer, multi-modal predictive reasoning.

Abstract: Probabilistic prediction heads in neural networks typically output either a Gaussian mixture or a single conformal region. Neither separates the distinct sources of uncertainty often present in real prediction tasks: a discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within the chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. We introduce the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), an output head that represents these three sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, and admits a closed-form likelihood by convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, so observing one step refines the predictive distribution at every remaining step in a single forward pass. We establish that the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and that an HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. The same shared structure provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks supports the effectiveness of the design relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

</details>


### [233] [Matrix Zonotopic Attention: A Context-Adaptive Value Projection for Set Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05472)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The abstract analyzes an asymmetry in multi-head attention: input-dependent routing (softmax) vs input-independent value projection, introduces Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) as a target complexity measure, and shows depth benefits depend on TDOF. It proposes Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) to incorporate a context-adaptive value projection via a matrix-zonotope family, preserving initialization equivalence to standard MHA and permutation equivariance. Empirical results show selective gains on high-rank, sparsely combinatorial targets and limited gains on aggregate-statistic targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand the representational and depth-related limitations of standard multi-head attention for permutation-invariant set targets and develop a principled extension that adapts value projections to context while preserving symmetry properties.

Method: Theoretical depth-separation analysis; define Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) for target operators; prove depth requirements for context-rigid attention scale with TDOF; introduce Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) with a center matrix plus input-dependent gated generator matrices; show that initialization recovers standard MHA and that permutation equivariance is preserved; provide a data-driven reachability interpretation; empirical evaluation on set-prediction tasks.

Result: TDOF-guided depth separation; MZAttn matches standard MHA at initialization and preserves permutation equivariance; offers a data-driven mechanism to represent more complex targets; experiments corroborate that benefits appear for targets with high-rank, combinatorial dependence and are limited for aggregate-statistic targets where standard attention already performs well.

Conclusion: Adaptive, context-dependent value projections via matrix-zonotopes extend MHA’s expressivity to complex target operators without sacrificing key properties; the practical advantage depends on the target’s TDOF; practitioners should select MZAttn over MHA when the target exhibits high-rank, sparsely combinatorial dependence.

Abstract: Multi-head attention combines an input-dependent softmax routing with an input-independent linear value projection, so the per-sample operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is the same for every input set. We study the consequences of this asymmetry for permutation-invariant set targets. We introduce the Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) of a target operator, a complexity measure counting the input-dependent directions an exact representation requires, and present a depth-separation analysis showing that context-rigid attention needs depth proportional to the target's TDOF, whereas a single layer with a context-adaptive value family can represent the same target. Building on this analysis, we propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), which replaces the fixed value projection with a context-adaptive matrix-zonotope family: a centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices weighted by input-dependent gates. The construction reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialisation, preserves permutation equivariance, and admits a data-driven reachability interpretation. Experiments on a range of set-prediction tasks are consistent with the TDOF prediction that the architectural advantage is selective: it appears on targets that depend on the input set in a high-rank, sparsely combinatorial way, and is small on aggregate-statistic targets where parameter-matched standard attention is already competitive.

</details>


### [234] [KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05475)
*Zhaowei Han,Xiang Zhang,Bing Han,Kai Liu,Danqi Hu,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KV-Skill introduces an external factorized operator design space for frozen LMs, enabling either text-derived or reward-learned skills that plug via a shared interface without prompting changes, improving task performance across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The two common ways to encode task knowledge—prompt-based text and weight updates—are limited: prompts require interpretation each use and weight changes are hard to load/share. There is a need for portable, separable skill representations that can be attached to a frozen backbone via a lightweight interface.

Method: Two complementary paths: (1) Registration — convert an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and train a shared per-backbone interface; (2) Reward learning — learn a compact latent operator from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. The approach does not add prompt positions. Evaluated across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, compared against baselines like SkillOpt and SoftSkill, and against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA.

Result: KV-Skill consistently improves the effectiveness of procedural knowledge; on Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, Registration yields 77.2 accuracy vs 23.4 for source text skill, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward budgets, KV-Skill outperforms seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. Post-hoc analysis shows text-derived operators maintain most benefits with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while random directions fail. A shared interface can host three independently loadable KV-Skills without forgetting.

Conclusion: Task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed independently of the backbone, enabling modular, transferable skills that remain loadable and retain performance across tasks.

Abstract: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 23.4 for the source text skill, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, one shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill

</details>


### [235] [Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05571)
*Mohammad Asadi,Soheil Hor,Bardiya Akhbari,Jack W. O'Sullivan,Tahoura Nedaee,Layne C. Price,Raviteja Anantha,Euan Ashley,Ehsan Adeli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training-free alignment (Align-RAG) for retrieval-augmented forecasting with frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs); per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift of retrieved windows enable dynamic in-context use without training adapters, outperforming trained fusion modules on Chronos-Bolt across seven datasets and improving zero-shot MSE on additional TSFMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Question the need for learned fusion modules in retrieval-augmented forecasting and show that frozen backbones can utilize retrieved context via simple, closed-form alignment, potentially simplifying and improving performance.

Method: Apply per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before feeding into a frozen backbone, requiring no learned parameters. Evaluate on Chronos-Bolt against state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapters; also test zero-shot performance on four other frozen TSFMs. Compare prediction shifts to a closed-form ridge predictor and use futures-shuffle control to rule out futures-averaging.

Result: Align-RAG outperforms the trained retrieval adapter on Chronos-Bolt across seven datasets (average MSE improvement of 3.75%). It also yields 2.5%–13.7% improvements in zero-shot MSE across four additional frozen TSFMs without per-backbone tuning. Alignment-induced prediction shifts track a closed-form ridge predictor on same pairs, with futures-shuffle control ruling out futures-averaging.

Conclusion: Frozen TSFMs inherently support dynamic in-context use of retrieved data; closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before training any fusion modules. Code is provided.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented forecasting promises to adapt frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to new domains without fine-tuning, but recent methods typically rely on learned fusion modules, i.e., trained adapters that merge retrieved examples into the backbone's forecast, based on the assumption that frozen backbones cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own. We show this assumption is unnecessary. We introduce Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies a closed-form per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter a frozen backbone's context. With no learned parameters, Align-RAG outperforms the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on a frozen Chronos-Bolt on all seven datasets of the standard benchmark (avg -3.75% MSE), showing that the gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without any training. Align-RAG further improves zero-shot MSE on four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone with no per-backbone tuning. To probe why alignment helps, we compare the frozen backbone's prediction shift under aligned demonstrations to the closed-form ridge prediction shift on the same pairs. We find that aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out a futures-averaging account. Together, these results indicate that frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals, and that closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained. Code available at: https://github.com/masadi-99/align-rag

</details>


### [236] [LC-GRPO: Bridging Train-Inference Gap for Flow-Based GRPO with Langevin Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05600)
*Yingqing Guo,Hui Yuan,Zijian He,Mengdi Wang,Zheng Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LC-GRPO introduces Langevin-corrected rollouts for flow-based GRPO, aligning stochastic training with deterministic ODE inference to reduce sampling mismatch and improve RL performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrepancies between stochastic SDE rollouts used in training and the deterministic ODE solver used at test-time cause sample quality degradation and inefficient policy optimization; a method is needed that preserves marginals and tractable likelihood without extra score models.

Method: Rollouts consist of two steps per transition: (i) an inference-aligned ODE Euler step, and (ii) a Langevin correction targeting the marginal at the resulting timestep. The score is obtained from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model, and the transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with tractable likelihood. Theoretically, one Langevin correction reduces Wasserstein distance from an imperfect Euler step; at matched randomness, the transition can surpass Euler–Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE.

Result: Empirical results show LC-GRPO improves reward optimization across SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

Conclusion: LC-GRPO offers a principled, effective way to reconcile stochastic training with deterministic inference in flow-based GRPO, backed by theoretical guarantees and demonstrated gains on text-to-image and text-to-video tasks.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models are typically sampled by solving a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), whereas online reinforcement learning requires stochastic rollouts for policy exploration and optimization. Existing GRPO methods for flow models therefore replace the inference-time ODE with a stochastic differential equation (SDE) during training. Although the ODE and SDE share the same marginal distributions in continuous time, their finite-step discretizations can differ substantially. In particular, SDE rollouts often become blurry as the exploration noise increases, creating a mismatch between the samples used for reinforcement learning and those generated by the test-time ODE sampler. We introduce LC-GRPO, a flow-based GRPO framework with Langevin correction. Each rollout transition first takes an inference-aligned ODE Euler step and then applies a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The required score is recovered directly from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model, while the resulting transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood for policy optimization. We theoretically show that, under suitable conditions, one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step. At a matched randomness level, we further show that the proposed transition can be more accurate than the standard Euler--Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo demonstrate that LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

</details>


### [237] [GAUGE: Granularity-Adaptive Counterfactual Gating of Evidence for Incomplete Multimodal Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05608)
*Yunping Shi,En Yu,Kairui Guo,Jie Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GAUGE is a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification that performs fine-grained evidence control without retraining, by imputing missing modalities, encoding inputs into unit-level evidence, and using Taylor-based counterfactual scores to modulate evidence via additive biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Incomplete multimodal data in real-world settings; coarse imputation and fusion risk retaining misleading components and suppressing reliable ones within the same recovered modality.

Method: Impute missing modalities with a frozen imputer; encode observed and recovered inputs as fine-grained evidence units; compute prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores for replacing each unit with a reference, all in a single forward–backward pass; map scores to continuous gates and convert them into additive attention-logit biases to modulate unit-level evidence without changing the backbone.

Result: GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across six benchmarks under diverse incomplete-input settings.

Conclusion: GAUGE offers a principled, scalable approach for fine-grained evidence control in incomplete multimodal classification, with a Taylor remainder analysis characterizing the first-order approximation error.

Abstract: Multimodal classification typically assumes all modalities are available, yet real-world inputs are often incomplete. Imputation and dynamic fusion can mitigate such incompleteness, but existing methods operate at a coarse modality level and thus cannot retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, compromising prediction reliability. To address this issue, we propose GAUGE, a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification. GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes observed and recovered inputs uniformly as fine-grained evidence units. Rather than intervening on each unit explicitly, GAUGE scores the counterfactual effect of replacing every unit with a reference representation through prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores, all obtained in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates, which are converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without altering the backbone architecture. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across diverse incomplete-input settings. Furthermore, a Taylor remainder theoretical analysis characterizes the error of the first-order approximation relative to the exact counterfactual effect, establishing GAUGE as a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness.

</details>


### [238] [Reasoning Errors Have a Region and a Direction in the Residual-Stream Trajectory of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05660)
*Hamed Damirchi,Ignacio Meza De la Jara,Damith Ranasinghe,Yuhang Liu,Javen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A three-stream detector for evaluating reasoning in LMs, combining motion signals with restricted state views to outperform displacement-based and single-layer probing baselines on unseen reasoning benchmarks, and even correlating with factual correctness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reliably distinguish sound reasoning from flawed reasoning in language models by addressing the limitations of trajectory-based methods that discard essential state context.

Method: A three-stream detector: (1) motion from layerwise residual-stream displacements, (2) a coarse region reader via vector quantization, and (3) a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This restores sufficient state context to interpret motion without full-state probing.

Result: Outperforms displacement-only state-of-the-art by up to 12% and single-layer probing by up to 21% on unseen reasoning benchmarks. Also reads factual completion and fact verification better than competing detectors. Ablations show motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals.

Conclusion: State-conditioned motion reading with restricted state views is a superior signal for reasoning validity, balancing context and privacy of the state, outperforming static-state and full-state probing approaches.

Abstract: As language models are increasingly used for tasks that require verifiable reasoning, reliably distinguishing sound reasoning from flawed reasoning has become an important practical problem. Recent trajectory-based methods seek this signal in layerwise residual-stream displacements, which capture how representations change while attenuating some stable, token-specific information. However, displacement omits the state from which an update originates, whereas restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. We identify this trade-off and propose a three-stream detector that combines motion with two restricted views of location. A coarse region reader based on vector quantization and a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This design restores enough state context to interpret the motion without returning to full-state probing. On reasoning benchmarks unseen during training, our method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state of the art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also reads factual completion and fact verification, ahead of every detector we compare against, which places the signal on correctness rather than on a kind of reasoning. Ablations further show that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals. These results suggest that reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone.

</details>


### [239] [Potential Matching Optimal Transport: Continuous Normalizing Flows for Exact $p$-Wasserstein Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05666)
*Lishuo Zhang,Ruizhi Huang,Yang Yu,Lei Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PMOT: potential-flow OT framework for general p-costs (c_p(x,y)=||x-y||^p) using a scalar potential to parametrize CNF velocity in a generalized Benamou–Brenier form. Employs a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges between model endpoints to train the potential gradient, while permitting flexible terminal distribution matching. Zero-loss exactness: under mild regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou–Brenier OT optimality system and recovers the p-optimal transport map and dynamics. Empirically: learns p-specific maps that align with p-OT references on synthetic benchmarks; competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data; MMD-based color transformation shows flexible sample-based terminal matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalized optimal transport with p-costs is theoretically rich but challenging to implement. The authors propose PMOT, a potential-flow framework that reparameterizes the CNF velocity via a scalar potential within the generalized Benamou–Brenier formalism. The goal is exactness of the OT solution under mild assumptions and practical flexibility in terminal distributions across tasks (density modeling and color transformation).

Method: Define a CNF velocity field via the gradient of a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou–Brenier formulation for exponent p. Train the potential gradient using a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by model endpoints, enabling end-to-end learning while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching.

Result: Zero-loss exactness: under stated regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness, any zero-loss solution satisfies the OT optimality system and recovers the corresponding p-OT map and dynamics. Empirically, PMOT learns p-specific maps that agree with p-OT references on synthetic benchmarks; remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model for high-dimensional tabular data; MMD-based color transformation demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

Conclusion: PMOT offers a principled potential-flow approach to general p-cost OT with a strong exactness guarantee and flexible terminal matching capabilities, yielding accurate p-specific transport maps and competitive density/modeling performance across domains.

Abstract: We introduce Potential Matching Optimal Transport (PMOT), a potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost optimal transport with $c_p(x,y)=\|x-y\|^p$. PMOT parameterizes the CNF velocity field with a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou--Brenier form for the chosen exponent $p$. It trains the potential gradient with a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching. Our main result establishes zero-loss exactness: under the stated regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou--Brenier optimality system and recovers the corresponding $p$-optimal transport map and dynamics. On synthetic benchmarks, PMOT learns $p$-specific maps that agree with the corresponding $p$-matched OT references. It also remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and an MMD-based color transformation experiment demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

</details>


### [240] [When Does Consensus Mean Correctness? Measuring the Agreement-Accuracy Coupling with Semantics-Preserving Re-Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05670)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RENDEQ is a render-equivalence generator for scientific figures to study the coupling between agreement under perturbations and model correctness in open-weight vision-language models. Re-rendering-based perturbations improve accuracy and reliability versus resampling; agreement can outperform a token-log-probability baseline on most models but can be reversed by pipeline issues or when optimizing for agreement reduces error diffuseness; key finding: the value of agreement depends on error diffuseness and may harm performance if overemphasized.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To obtain a direct, parameter-free measure of whether agreement across perturbations tracks correctness. Scientific figures provide a controlled setting where redrawing yields semantically equivalent images with a deterministically known ground truth, enabling exact error localization that natural-image perturbations lack.

Method: Construct RENDEQ to generate render-equivalence sets by re-rendering figures from underlying data via a program. Evaluate on three open-weight vision-language models (VLMs) across three independent instantiations. Compare re-rendering to resampling as perturbations. Benchmark agreement (the model’s concordance across renders) against an evidence-carrying baseline (mean token log-probability). Analyze which style factors (e.g., plotting library) drive dispersion. Investigate the effect of fine-tuning on cross-render consensus.

Result: Re-rendering outperforms resampling in both accuracy and reliability across the tested models. Agreement-based signals beat mean token log-probability on two of three models and tie on the third; a buggy replication traced to a rendering-pipeline failure explains a discrepancy with a prior result. The remaining dispersion across perturbations is concentrated in one style factor (the plotting library), far exceeding other factors and noise. Fine-tuning on cross-render consensus inverts the effect: accuracy declines in all five replication runs, opposite to published results on natural images. Overall, agreement certifies correctness only when errors are diffuse; an objective that rewards agreement can destroy that diffuseness.

Conclusion: Agreement can be a useful reliability signal, but its effectiveness is conditional on the diffusion of errors across perturbations. Render-based perturbations provide a principled means to study this coupling, revealing that naive optimization for agreement can harm performance by reducing error diffuseness. Diagnosing and controlling error structure is essential when using agreement as a training or evaluation signal.

Abstract: A model's agreement across perturbed inputs is used both as a label-free reliability signal and as a self-training target, on the premise that agreement tracks correctness. That coupling is rarely measured directly: natural-image perturbations preserve meaning only by assumption, and no exact answer key localizes errors. Scientific figures remove both obstacles, a figure is drawn from data by a program, so redrawing it yields images that are semantically equivalent by construction and share a programmatically exact answer. We build RENDEQ, a generator of such render-equivalence sets, and measure the coupling on three open-weight VLMs, checking every finding across three independent instantiations. Re-rendering beats resampling on both accuracy and reliability. Agreement beats an evidence-carrying baseline, mean token log-probability, on two of three models and ties on the third, reversing an intermediate, buggy replication traced to a rendering-pipeline failure. The dispersion behind this is concentrated in one style factor, the plotting library, more than double the next-largest factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Fine-tuning on the model's own cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy falls in every one of five replication runs, the opposite sign to published results on natural images. Agreement certifies correctness only above a threshold set by how diffuse a model's errors are, and an objective that rewards agreement destroys exactly that diffuseness.

</details>


### [241] [Consistency Has a Computable Blind Spot: A Commutation Theory of Label-Free Reliability for Vision-Language Figure Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05675)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a theory of label-free reliability for vision-language models using invariance and equivariance. Identifies a computable blind spot where certain errors commute with edits; introduces matched edits, cyclic relabeling, and a label-free detector (Equivariance-Consistency Score) and the REND-EQUIV dataset; validates across models and data, and explains metamorphic-testing inversions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable label-free detection of reading errors in vision-language models by formalizing invariant and equivariant structure; address blind spots where perturbations fail to reveal errors.

Method: Formalize when an error is invisible (edits commute, joint centralizer concept); define matched edits and their completeness for affine reading errors; show no swap-edit suite is complete for label permutations, with cyclic relabeling closing much of that gap; instantiate Equivariance-Consistency Score (ECS) as a training-free detector; release REND-EQUIV pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets over identical data.

Result: Empirical support across three models and hand-labeled data; predicted ordering holds, and a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation rather than implementation; cyclic relabeling yields gains on real data; explains a known inversion in classifier metamorphic-testing literature as a joint property of relation and fault class.

Conclusion: Detectability in reading errors is inherently a joint property of the relation and fault class; the proposed ECS and REND-EQUIV framework provide a label-free, training-free detector and illuminate where and why blind spots occur.

Abstract: Label-free reliability for vision-language models rests on invariance: perturb the input and a faithful reader's answer should not change. This has a known blind spot, a systematic misreading survives the perturbation and gets certified wrong, which we show is computable, not just real: an error is invisible to an edit exactly when the two commute, so the errors a suite cannot reach form its joint centralizer, a set that shrinks as edits are added and can be written down rather than guessed at. We act on the complementary relation, equivariance: edit a figure's data and the correct answer must change by a computable amount. Two matched edits are provably complete for affine reading errors; no suite of swap edits is complete for label permutations, and cyclic relabeling closes most of that gap. We instantiate the theory as the Equivariance-Consistency Score, a label-free, training-free detector, and release REND-EQUIV, pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets over identical data. The predicted ordering holds across three models and a hand-labeled population immune to the one circularity in how it is selected; a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation, not to any implementation; and cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted gain on a matched real sample. The same characterization explains a reported inversion of this ordering in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is a joint property of the relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

</details>


### [242] [SEAM: Global consistency beyond local accuracy in scientific machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05702)
*Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan,Bum Jun Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEAM introduces a generator-agnostic framework to assess global explanation admissibility by aligning local explanations across regions; uses a finite explanation-sheaf SEAM-Ω, identifying obstructions on overlaps, exact repairs or residual-attributions, and separating inconsistency from non-identifiability under distribution shift across PDEs and FNO monitoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Local explanations validate models only within subdomains; this is insufficient to guarantee a globally coherent scientific explanation. A global consistency audit is needed to assemble local explanations into a single admissible account.

Method: Construct SEAM-Ω as a finite explanation-sheaf: each region is represented by a structured explanation with state, closure, observation channels, and optional contract metadata; compare neighboring explanations on overlaps to derive channel-resolved objections; convert disagreements into obstructions; perform exact feasibility repairs restricted to accounts' permitted revisions; if exact repair is unavailable, provide residual-aware regularized records with empirical attribution; separate inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitor generators under distribution shift; prove theorems on minimum-cost intervention and contract-detectability; demonstrate across nineteen experiments using synthetic PDE systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator monitoring.

Result: SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps, and provides a global explanation-consistency audit; demonstrates robustness to distribution shift across multiple experiments involving PDEs and FNOs.

Conclusion: SEAM adds a global explanation-consistency audit to existing solvers and learning models, enabling evaluation of whether locally derived explanations form a coherent global scientific account and guiding interventions when inconsistencies are found.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning commonly validates models at the level of a subdomain, a benchmark split, or an explanation for one prediction. Yet such local checks cannot establish whether the resulting explanations can be assembled into one globally admissible explanation. We introduce Scientific Explanation-Admissibility Machines (SEAM), a generator-agnostic framework that makes this local-to-global consistency question computable across regions, sensors, regimes, and model components. The finite explanation-sheaf instantiation SEAM-$Ω$ represents each region by a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels together with optional contract metadata; compares neighboring explanations on their overlaps; and converts disagreement into a channel-resolved obstruction. This obstruction locates inconsistency and tests competing declared accounts by restricting each repair to the revisions that one account permits. Exact feasibility refutes or retains an account; when exact repair is unavailable, residual-aware regularized records provide a separately labeled empirical attribution. The framework also separates inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitors learned generators under distribution shift. We establish theorems for minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability, together with companion results for identifiability and closure recoverability. Across nineteen experiments involving synthetic partial differential equation systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator (FNO) monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, and attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps. SEAM adds a global explanation-consistency audit to existing solvers and learning models, testing whether their local explanations form a coherent scientific account.

</details>


### [243] [Spectral Aliasing Pretext: A novel task for Self-Supervised fault diagnosis in rotating machinery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05705)
*Victor Gialis,Maxime Metz,David Esteve,Abdenour Soualhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAP is a self-supervised pretraining method using spectral aliasing with undersampling, enabling linear probing to outperform supervised fine-tuning for fault diagnosis on CWRU with limited labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeled data for machinery fault diagnosis is scarce in industry. Self-supervised learning on unlabeled vibration data can learn robust, transferable representations without destructive data augmentations.

Method: Undersample signals to produce folded spectra, then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. The pretext task enforces learning of frequency-domain invariants related to faults, avoiding aggressive augmentations.

Result: On the CWRU dataset, SAP produces stable, highly discriminative representations. In linear probing, it achieves high classification performance with only a small fraction of labeled data and low variance; full fine-tuning does not yield more stable or better results.

Conclusion: SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis when labeled data are limited.

Abstract: Deep learning is a new way for machinery fault diagnosis but requires extensive labeled data, a scarce resource in industrial settings. We propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP), a self-supervised learning method that pretrains models on unlabeled vibration data by exploiting spectral aliasing. We deliberately undersample signals to create folded spectrum, then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. This pretext task forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults, without potentially destructive augmentations. Experiments on the CWRU dataset show that SAP learns stable and highly discriminative representations. In a linear probing setting, SAP quickly achieves very high classification performance with only a small fraction of labeled data and low variance. In contrast, full fine-tuning, including fully supervised training, does not lead to more stable or better results. Overall, these findings suggest that SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis with limited labeled data.

</details>


### [244] [CircuitSteer: Geometrically Aligned Multi-Layer Steering via Sparse Autoencoder Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05732)
*Mehrshad Saadatinia,Parsa Razmara,Ardalan Aryashad,Ali Abbasi,Seyedarmin Azizi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CircuitSteer identifies multi-layer semantic circuits using Sparse Autoencoders and feature flow circuits, synthesizes dense steering vectors from sparse features, and performs multi-point interventions to robustly steer LLM behavior while preserving fluency across tasks and model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current steering methods rely on fixed, single-layer interventions (e.g., CAA) that may not sustain behavioral changes across layers or across semantically diverse inputs. There is a need for multi-layer, geometry-consistent control that distributes steering across circuits in a model.

Method: Build a feature flow circuit via feature co-activation and alignment of decoder directions; use Sparse Autoencoders to extract multi-layer subcircuits responsible for target behaviors; synthesize dense steering vectors from sparse features; apply multi-point interventions to guide the internal semantic trajectory. Evaluate on toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal across two model families with contrastive examples.

Result: CircuitSteer consistently achieves fluency-preserving interventions, outperforming baselines that either degrade text quality or fail to cover complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal. Demonstrates robustness across models and datasets and claims unique coverage via multi-layer circuit steering and geometric alignment of features. Code is available.

Conclusion: Multi-layer circuit steering with geometric alignment yields more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions, indicating extended potential for scalable alignment of LLMs through distributed circuit manipulation.

Abstract: Controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for AI alignment. Existing steering methods, such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), typically rely on fixed single-layer interventions derived from aggregate activation differences. These methods impose a single intervention across semantically diverse inputs and often fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers, limiting the effectiveness of the steering. In this work, we introduce CircuitSteer, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and manipulate coherent semantic circuits distributed across multiple layers. By constructing a feature flow circuit based on feature co-activation and the geometric alignment of decoder directions, we isolate the specific multi-layer subcircuits responsible for a target behavior. We then synthesize dense steering vectors from these sparse features and apply multi-point interventions to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory. We evaluate CircuitSteer using contrastive examples across a diverse set of tasks, including toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal, spanning two model families. Across all models and datasets, CircuitSteer is the only method to consistently produce fluency-preserving interventions; competing methods either sacrifice text quality or lack coverage, failing entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal.
