These results demonstrate that multi-layer circuit steering, enabled by enforcing geometric alignment among selected features, yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions. Code is available at https://github.com/mehrshad-sdtn/CircuitSteer.

</details>


### [245] [Multivariate Time Series Forecasting needs Cross Variable Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05742)
*Kuiye Ding,Yifan Hu,Hanchen Wang,Hao Xue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CvLoss is a plug-in structural regularizer for multivariate time-series forecasting that enforces cross-variable residual consistency via a cross-variable graph, addressing the objective gap of Direct Forecasting and improving performance across backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct Forecasting (DF) objectives can be mismatched when future variables exhibit cross-variable and lagged dependencies. There is an objective gap because DF does not explicitly constrain cross-variable structure in forecast residuals.

Method: Introduce CvLoss, a plug-in regularizer that constructs a cross-variable graph over forecast residuals and penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences across forecast patches, capturing both synchronous and asynchronous interactions.

Result: Empirical evaluations show CvLoss improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms standard learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

Conclusion: CvLoss provides a principled, model-agnostic means to enforce cross-variable consistency in forecasts, addressing the objective gap and enhancing forecasting performance.

Abstract: Multivariate time series forecasting presents unique challenges because future variables often co-evolve under shared system dynamics. While existing studies mainly focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations, dependencies among future values are much less explored. Specifically, modern forecasting models largely follow the Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm, generating multi-step forecasts with point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain cross-variable structure. In this work, we show that the DF objective is mismatched in the presence of cross-variable and lagged dependencies, revealing an objective gap. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{C}ross-\textbf{V}ariable \textbf{Loss} (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that constrains forecast residuals on a cross-variable graph. CvLoss penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions. Our experiments show that CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

</details>


### [246] [Equipment-centric workpiece localization in near real-time using deep learning-based vision and event-driven finite state machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05744)
*Dohyeon Kong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Equipment-centric vision framework for continuous workpiece localization in hot forging, using multi-camera 3D equipment coordinates, event-driven FSMs, and a keypoint-guided 3D CNN to detect handling events with strong accuracy and moderate latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for continuous traceability and process coordination in hot forging, where extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing disrupt direct tracking.

Method: Infer floorplan-wide 3D equipment coordinates from static 2D cameras; recognize grasp and release events; validate via event-driven finite state machines; integrate a keypoint-guided attention mechanism within a 3D CNN to focus on functionally relevant equipment regions; provide visualization of transfers and quantitative analysis of operations.

Result: 100% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window; mean localization error 317.8 mm; mean system latency 21 seconds.

Conclusion: Bridges vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning, enabling visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations, thereby supporting traceability and process coordination in hot forging.

Abstract: Continuous workpiece localization is essential for traceability and process coordination in hot forging, but direct tracking is unreliable because of extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. This study presents an equipment-centric framework that infers workpiece locations from handling equipment observed by multiple static 2D cameras. The framework estimates floorplan-space 3D equipment coordinates and recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism integrated into a 3D convolutional neural network improves activity recognition by focusing on functionally relevant equipment regions. Evaluation in an operational hot forging factory achieved 100\% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, a mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and a mean system latency of 21 seconds. The framework connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning and supports visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations.

</details>


### [247] [Accelerating nanodrug development in continuous flow systems using informed prediction models based on low-cost surrogate nanoparticles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05761)
*Kai Dahms,Eilien Heinrich,Jochen Schmid,Michael Bortz,Iryna Savych,Regina Bleul*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A shape-constrained predictive model for nanoparticle size and PDI across processing conditions improves prediction accuracy and reduces experimental screening in microfluidic liposome/LNP synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Nanoparticle properties are highly sensitive to process parameters and lack of predictive frameworks leads to costly, iterative experimentation.

Method: Develop and validate a shape-constrained predictive model using controlled microfluidic synthesis data for liposomes and lipid nanoparticles across varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous/organic mixing ratios; integrate experimental data with expert knowledge to impose shape constraints and test with minimal empirical data.

Result: The shape-constrained model accurately predicts nanoparticle size and dispersity across process conditions and reduces reliance on extensive experimental screening.

Conclusion: Shape-constrained modeling enables rational, efficient process development for nanomedicine manufacturing, by providing reliable predictions with limited experimental data.

Abstract: The development of nanotherapeutics often involves extensive empirical optimization due to the sensitivity of nanoparticle properties, such as size and polydispersity index (PDI), to minor changes in process parameters. Factors like formulation concentration, flow rates, and mixing ratios can significantly influence clinical efficacy and therapeutic outcomes. The absence of predictive mathematical frameworks has made iterative experimental screening necessary, increasing both costs and development time.
  This study introduces and validates a predictive modeling approach based on shape constraints, aiming to enhance the estimation of nanoparticle characteristics across various process conditions. Using controlled microfluidic methods, liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios.
  The shape-constrained model, informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge, was subsequently validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data. Results reveal that shape-constrained modeling facilitates accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows. This framework supports rational and efficient process development for manufacturing nanomedicine systems.

</details>


### [248] [Neuro-Symbolic Closed-Loop Control of Laser Powder Bed Fusion with an In-Loop Ontology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05773)
*Gisuk Hong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Geometry-conditioned neuro-symbolic control for laser powder bed fusion; ontology-driven closed loop with GP-uncertainty bounds reduces dross by mapping depth-to-width ratio to observable width; feasible and adaptable via ontology edits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To control unmeasurable melt-pool depth (overhang dross) and quality in LPBF by integrating symbolic reasoning with data-driven constraints in a closed-loop controller.

Method: A standards-aligned ontology inside the control loop; description-logic reasoner converts objectives/constraints into references/bounds; depth→width mapping via geometry- and power-dependent ratio with GP; constraint selection (lack-of-fusion floor, monotone guard, energy-density cap); per-scan small QP; Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to IN625 NIST AM-Bench; runs on geometric context changes.

Result: Eliminates dross with geometry-blind controller; holds dross at zero with small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring; degrades gracefully under plant mismatch; retargets to new alloys by editing ontology data rather than code; ratio calibration is principal next step.

Conclusion: Demonstrates architectural feasibility and adaptability; ontology-driven extensions enable constraint-aware control in additive manufacturing.

Abstract: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which a standards-aligned ontology operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe, and a description-logic reasoner converts them into the references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross, a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality yet cannot be measured during the build, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width, with the ratio and its calibrated uncertainty supplied by a Gaussian process. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints-adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, a monotone guard beyond the calibrated range, and an energy-density cap where a process window is declared while running only on changes of geometric context and otherwise leaving a single small quadratic program on the per-scan path. In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture eliminates the dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code. The results establish architectural feasibility, experimental calibration of the ratio is the principal next step.

</details>


### [249] [GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05783)
*Paweł Batorski,Przemysław Spurek,Paul Swoboda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GROM is a one-shot, exact analytical unlearning method for LLMs that updates targeted weights via a closed-form ridge-regression formula using gradient-free forward passes, achieving faster unlearning with strong forgetting-utility trade-offs and robustness to quantization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address inefficiency and incomplete removal in gradient-based iterative unlearning, avoiding masking and susceptibility to quantization, by delivering a fast, exact solution.

Method: Formulate unlearning as a ridge-regularized least-squares problem and derive a closed-form additive update for selected weight matrices. The update is computed from forward passes only (no backpropagation) and applied in one shot to suppress unwanted content while preserving retained-data behavior.

Result: GROM runs in seconds, orders of magnitude faster than fine-tuning, and achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News, and WMDP. It reduces computational overhead without harming overall model performance and resists low-bit quantization attacks that reintroduce erased content.

Conclusion: The approach removes targeted content from weights rather than masking it, offering a robust, efficient, exact unlearning solution with publicly available code.

Abstract: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

</details>


### [250] [Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05797)
*Stefan Krsteski,Charlotte Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks reveals that commonly used AUC can mask poor estimates; token-level entropy provides a useful predictive signal; residuals between expected and observed difficulty identify hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility, enabling better benchmark calibration and curricula design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecast task difficulty before costly simulations to guide benchmark design, calibration, and progressive training, especially in long-horizon domains where trial-and-error is computationally expensive.

Method: Systematic study across 17 benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. The paper assesses ex ante difficulty using predictive signals (notably token-level entropy) and analyzes residuals between expected and observed difficulty to diagnose environment issues and evaluate proxy metrics like AUC.

Result: Findings include: (1) AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates; (2) token-level entropy is a useful predictor of difficulty; (3) residuals between expected and observed difficulty expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

Conclusion: Ex ante difficulty prediction is feasible across diverse agentic domains. Incorporating token-level entropy improves predictive accuracy, and residual analysis serves as a diagnostic tool for identifying environment problems, aiding benchmark calibration and curriculum construction.

Abstract: Task difficulty dictates an agent's likelihood of success, and estimating it without rollouts means forecasting this directly from a task description before executing costly simulations in stateful environments. Reliable estimates would therefore allow environment designers to calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula. This becomes increasingly important as agents move into long-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error is a severe computational bottleneck. Prior work on early prediction is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments, often relying on narrow features and inaccurate evaluation metrics. We study \textit{ex ante} difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We show that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and show how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

</details>


### [251] [Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Reinforcement Learning for Visual Continuous Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05989)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OG-SPR is a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation dynamics. It uses two auxiliary objectives—multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction—with lightweight adapters to avoid over-constraining the shared representation, achieving improved sample efficiency and state-of-the-art results on 28 DM Control Suite tasks, especially in hard domains like dog and humanoid.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art dynamics-based representation learning in visual RL relies on either latent self-prediction or observation-prediction. Each objective can be insufficient alone and may misalign temporal predictability with observation grounding. A hybrid approach could leverage the strengths of both while mitigating their weaknesses.

Method: Proposes Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR): a model-free visual RL framework that learns representations via two auxiliary objectives. 1) multi-step latent self-prediction to enforce temporal predictability in latent space, 2) next-observation prediction to ground representations in observation dynamics. To avoid over-constraint, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing latent predictive signals without forcing direct self-prediction on the shared representation.

Result: Empirically, OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive methods across 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

Conclusion: Jointly optimizing latent temporal predictive signals and observation-grounded objectives yields more sample-efficient representations for visual RL. The adapters mitigate potential over-constraint and enable benefits from latent self-prediction without forcing it directly on the shared representation, suggesting a robust design for complex visual control tasks.

Abstract: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Recent dynamics-based representation learning methods have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-free visual RL by learning dynamics-aware representations through auxiliary prediction performed either in latent space (self-prediction) or observation space (observation prediction). However, state-of-the-art methods from both categories still struggle on challenging visual control tasks when training data is limited. We posit that relying on either predictive objective alone may be insufficient. In contrast, observation prediction grounds learned representations in observation-level dynamics, but does not directly regularize the temporal predictability of latent representations over extended horizons. In this paper, we propose Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR), a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation-level dynamics. OG-SPR incorporates two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. We empirically show that directly imposing latent self-prediction on the shared representation may over-constrain it and does not necessarily improve performance. To address this issue, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite show that OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

</details>


### [252] [Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05819)
*Alfred M. Pastor,Maribel Castillo,Jose M. Badia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A learning-to-rank approach selects GPU-efficient contraction plans for tensor-network simulations, achieving better plan quality than baselines; performance is partly backend dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tensor-network contraction on GPUs exhibits large performance variance across plans; the plan search space is large and manual tuning is impractical, necessitating automated plan selection to reduce overall cost.

Method: Represent each contraction plan by structural features derived from its contraction sequence; train gradient-boosted rankers (listwise and pairwise) using GPU timing measurements; evaluate on diverse circuit families with in-distribution and shift test sets; compare to random and MinFill baselines; analyze cross-GPU generalization by training on one GPU and testing on another without retraining.

Result: Rankers generally identify better plans; the listwise model provides the strongest decision quality; performance is fairly robust across GPUs, though not perfectly stable; source-trained models retain useful decision quality on a different GPU, indicating partial transferability; results support Learning to Rank as a practical method to reduce contraction-plan search, with some backend dependence remaining.

Conclusion: Learning to Rank is a practical approach to reduce contraction-plan search cost, offering transferable plan quality across GPUs but with performance nuances tied to hardware specifics.

Abstract: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining. The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.

</details>


### [253] [Evidential Rule Learning for Interpretable Classification with Abstention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05859)
*Javier Fumanal-Idocin,Javier Andreu-Perez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FERL is a fast, interpretable fuzzy-rule learner that outputs evidential decisions with built-in abstention. It achieves strong accuracy, stable evidential outputs (Lipschitz), and competitive OOD/concept-bottleneck performance across tabular and vision datasets without post-hoc calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for interpretable classifiers that quantify evidence and can abstain, avoiding post-hoc calibration and opaque rules; improve reliability in deployment.

Method: Learn deterministic fuzzy-rule models whose outputs are evidential (belief, plausibility) derived from fuzzy memberships in a single pass; no extra calibration head, no hold-out set; prove Lipschitz stability; compares to state-of-the-art rule learners.

Result: On 30 tabular datasets, FERL achieves +2.6 percentage points average accuracy over the second-best method; native credal-set predictions yield higher utility-discounted accuracy (u65/u80 ≈ 0.80/0.83) vs naive credal (0.79/0.80) and higher coverage; OOD near-tabular detectors achieve AUROC 77.7 vs 77.4 baseline; on CUB/AwA2 concept-bottleneck tasks, within 2.3 AUROC of strongest detector; best AwA2 AUPR-Out and novel-class rejection; can name anomalous attributes.

Conclusion: FERL demonstrates that evidential, interpretable fuzzy-rule models can rival or exceed existing rule learners in accuracy while providing reliable abstention and evidence-based decisions, with strong stability and cross-domain performance; it offers a practical, transparent alternative to post-hoc calibration and opaque models.

Abstract: Interpretable classification often requires more than accurate predictions for real-life deployment: models should be transparent about the evidence behind their decisions and abstain when they cannot decide reliably. We introduce Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL), a method that learns interpretable, accurate fuzzy rule models whose outputs are evidential. Unlike post-hoc calibration, FERL's belief, plausibility, and abstention capabilities arise directly from the fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, with no auxiliary head, held-out set, or repeated inference. Our theoretical analysis further shows that FERL is Lipschitz stable, which means that its evidential outputs vary smoothly with the input. Against state-of-the-art rule learners, FERL is statistically significantly more accurate across a 30 tabular-dataset benchmark ($+2.6\%$ average accuracy over the second best). Its native set predictions attain the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers ($u_{65}/u_{80}=0.80/0.83$ vs.\ $0.79/0.80$ for the naive credal classifier), at higher set coverage ($0.92$ vs.\ $\le0.82$). FERL also matches dedicated out-of-distribution detectors on tabular near-OOD detection ($77.7$ vs.\ $77.4$ AUROC for the strongest baseline). Under detector-class-disjoint concept-bottleneck evaluation, its it is within $2.3$ AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector on both CUB and AwA2, while attaining the best AwA2 AUPR-Out ($68.3$) and novel-class rejection ($57.2$), while being able to name which attributes are anomalous.

</details>


### [254] [Beyond Feature Importance: A Comparative Analysis of Pattern Detection Methods in Cluster Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05880)
*Benjamin Connor,Anna Jurek-Loughrey,Lu Bai,Muhammad Fahim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Common post-hoc methods (RF surrogate with permutation importance, LIME, PCA) can recover relevant features in clustering but fail to consistently detect all injected pattern types; reveals a gap and need for dedicated pattern-detection methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interpreting clustering outcomes is crucial, especially in healthcare; existing explainability tools focus on feature importance or local explanations rather than pattern-level cluster interpretation; synthetic data with predefined patterns enables controlled evaluation.

Method: Evaluate three techniques on synthetic datasets with injected patterns; use a Random Forest surrogate with permutation feature importance, LIME, and PCA to identify pattern-related features; assess ability to recover injected patterns.

Result: Each method can recover relevant features but none consistently detects all pattern types; performance is pattern-type dependent.

Conclusion: Highlights the gap between explainability tools and pattern-level cluster interpretation; motivates development of dedicated pattern-detection methodologies.

Abstract: Interpreting clustering outcomes remains a fundamental challenge in data analysis, particularly in domains such as healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. While numerous explainability techniques exist, they are primarily designed to assess feature importance or provide local instance-level explanations rather than to identify structured patterns present within clusters. This work presents a comparative evaluation of commonly used post-hoc analysis methods for pattern detection in clustering results. To enable controlled evaluation, we introduce a suite of synthetic datasets in which predefined patterns are systematically injected. Three widely used techniques are evaluated: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis. Results demonstrate that although each method can successfully recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. These findings high- light a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, motivating the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies.

</details>


### [255] [Alternating Levenberg-Marquardt Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-Enhanced Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05892)
*Yulun Wu,Matthieu Barreau,Miguel Aguiar,Karl H. Johansson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FALM-PINN decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting to overcome spectral bias and representation–coefficient coupling in PINNs, using a Fourier-enhanced basis learned in an upper level and a Levenberg–Marquardt-based nonlinear least-squares fit of projection coefficients in a lower level; proven global convergence; shows substantial accuracy gains on challenging high-frequency/nonlinear PDEs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs struggle with high-frequency/multi-scale and strongly nonlinear PDEs due to spectral bias and the entanglement of representation learning with coefficient fitting. A decoupled optimization aims to mitigate these issues and improve accuracy and robustness.

Method: An alternating optimization framework (FALM-PINN): (upper level) learns a Fourier-enhanced basis to enrich the latent space with high-frequency components; (lower level) solves a nonlinear least-squares problem by fitting projection coefficients on this basis using the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm; for linear PDEs, the method reduces to a single-step convex problem; the approach applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems.

Result: Global convergence of the alternating training scheme is proven for both nonlinear/coupled and linear cases; numerical experiments on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show relative L2 errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: FALM-PINN provides a robust framework that effectively mitigates spectral bias and representation–coefficient coupling in PINNs, offering convergence guarantees and substantial accuracy gains across challenging PDEs, with applicability to general nonlinear and coupled systems.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often fail to accurately resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency or multi-scale solutions, as well as strongly nonlinear problems. Two factors underlie this difficulty: spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to underfit high-frequency features; and representation-coefficient coupling, the entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization objective. In this work, we propose the Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg--Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN), an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, while the lower-level problem resolves the coupling by fitting the projection coefficients on this basis, solving a nonlinear least-squares problem with the Levenberg--Marquardt algorithm. The framework applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems, and reduces to a single-step convex optimization problem for linear PDEs. We prove global convergence of the alternating training scheme in both cases. Numerical examples on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show that FALM-PINN achieves relative $L^2$ errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [256] [CohortHijack: Robustness of Single Cell Annotation to Companion Cell Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05900)
*Arash Vashagh,Yasmin Vashagh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CohortHijack demonstrates that the composition of a query cohort can be manipulated to alter refined labels in single-cell annotation without changing the target cell's expression, revealing a new robustness vulnerability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether popular single-cell annotation refinements (label smoothing via neighbors or cluster voting) can be manipulated without altering the target cell, thereby assessing robustness of these pipelines.

Method: Introduce CohortHijack: remove selected non-target cells from the query cohort while keeping the target expression profile, baseline prediction, and trained model intact. Compare random vs structured removal; employ greedy, multi-start, and beam search. Evaluate on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM. Also test CellTypist majority voting. Perform ablations disabling neighborhood refinement.

Result: Structured removal outperformed random on Paul15. Multi-start search altered 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes under 0.4%. Ablations showed the effect disappears when neighborhood refinement is disabled. In CellTypist voting, independent predictions remained stable, but refined labels changed with small companion-cell removals.

Conclusion: Query cohort composition constitutes a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation. Robustness audits should consider cohort perturbations, and defenses should monitor or constrain neighborhood-refined predictions to mitigate such attacks.

Abstract: Many single-cell annotation tools refine an initial cell label using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. We study whether this refinement can be manipulated without changing the target cell. We introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. We evaluate random and structured removal methods, together with greedy, multi-start, and beam search, on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Structured removal was consistently stronger than random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. We also evaluated CellTypist majority voting, where independent predictions remained unchanged across all evaluations, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals. These findings identify query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation.

</details>


### [257] [BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05928)
*Yuhao Wang,Zelin Zang,Yuxuan Liu,Zhen Lei,Stan Z. Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BioM-JEPA extends JEPA to block-level gene representations in single-cell data, improving representation quality and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tackle sparsity and depth-bias in single-cell transcriptomics by predicting representations of graph-connected gene blocks (protein associations and coexpression evidence) rather than individual genes.

Method: A student network predicts target-block representations from the remaining genes; a slowly updated teacher supplies the block targets from the full observed gene set. Uses linear attention for efficiency. Block definitions derived from protein associations and coexpression data. Evaluated on CellBench and hPancreas with various diagnostics including perturbation-response and canonical pathway alignment.

Result: Block-level predictions yield embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth than token-prediction, random-block, or reconstruction controls. Frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings preserve expression, pathway, and neighborhood information and achieve the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among models. Diagnostics align with pancreatic programs. In a one-epoch hPancreas run (batch size 8), BioM-JEPA achieved 5.75x higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76x higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation.

Conclusion: Graph-connected gene blocks are effective prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology, enabling robust, scalable representations that retain biological information and improve efficiency.

Abstract: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes. Here we present BioM-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that instead predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network infers each target-block representation from the remaining genes in a cell, while a slowly updated teacher supplies the corresponding target from the full observed gene set. Under the reported extraction procedure, block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth in the tested diagnostics than token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls. Across CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among the evaluated models. Representation diagnostics were also consistent with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional relationships between genetic perturbations. Linear attention avoids constructing a quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrix; in a matched one-epoch hPancreas experiment at batch size 8, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75-fold higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76-fold higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation. Together, these results support graph-connected gene blocks as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology.

</details>


### [258] [How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05980)
*Sid Ali Hamideche,Louis Adrien Dufrene,Quentin Lampin,Guillaume Larue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Linear or simple mappings can align some, but not all, heterogeneous text embeddings; latent universality is not a given, as compatibility depends on architecture, pooling, objective, and data distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess cross-model latent communication and test claims of universal latent structure across independently trained text encoders in realistic settings.

Method: Experimentally evaluate cross-space alignment with lightweight translators (primarily linear mappings) across nine embedding models varying in architecture, pooling, and training objective. Use CKA to measure representational similarity, and assess downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval to gauge practical compatibility.

Result: Simple translators reveal meaningful shared structure for some compatible model pairs and enable transfer in those cases, but fail for others. Compatibility is not universal; it depends on architecture, training objective, pooling strategy, and data distribution.

Conclusion: Heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings; universal latent universality is not supported in realistic settings. More nuanced or model-aware alignment methods may be required for robust AI-to-AI latent communication.

Abstract: We investigate whether simple transformations can translate representations across heterogeneous text embedding models. Understanding how independently trained models organize semantic information is an enabler for AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text. Focusing on lightweight translators such as linear mappings, we test the literature hypothesis of latent universality in a realistic text setting beyond simplified benchmarks. Across nine embedding models differing in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective, we evaluate compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval. Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Overall, the results show that heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in some literature.

</details>


### [259] [THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05982)
*Pui Chung Siu,Claudia Cabrera,Mani Mudaliar,Arkaitz Zubiaga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Temporal heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph (THBKG) tracks target–disease links over time to predict Phase II→III progress using evidence profiles at decision time; graph propagation yields strong performance, especially for cases lacking direct evidence, and enables explainable predictions with a path-based explainer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inadequate target–disease linkages account for a large fraction of Phase II failures. Current knowledge graphs cannot reconstruct the evidence profile as it appeared at past decision dates, hindering retrospective validation and decision-making.

Method: Construct THBKG with 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, each edge timestamped by the year its evidence changed. Define a decision-aligned benchmark: predict, at Phase II entry, whether a target–disease pair advances to Phase III using evidence datable before the decision. Apply graph propagation on the temporal graph and use a path-based explainer on the decision-time subgraph to decompose predictions into the underlying evidence landscape.

Result: Graph propagation outperforms direct-evidence baselines, achieving relative success of 4.3–4.5 among the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The majority (72.8%) of pairs have no direct evidence at decision time, yet the encoders rank these above chance by propagating through intervening biology. A path-based explainer provides interpretable, decision-time explanations. THBKG is released for continual retrospective validation and exploratory study.

Conclusion: THBKG enables retrospective, decision-aligned evaluation of therapeutic hypotheses and provides explainable predictions for target–disease progressions, addressing a key gap in past-evidence profiling and supporting ongoing hypothesis validation.

Abstract: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

</details>


### [260] [A Unified Risk View of Uncertainty: Posterior Risk for Disentanglement and Evaluation Beyond Proxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05995)
*Frieder Wizgall,Georg Tirpitz,Moritz Seiler,Kerstin Ritter,Bálint Mucsányi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Defines uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk and launches a theory-backed, semi-synthetic benchmark to disentangle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty without proxy tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inconsistent definitions of epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty and lack of ground-truth uncertainty make evaluation difficult; proxies like OOD detection fail to provide complete uncertainty targets.

Method: Proposes uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, combining Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-induced deviations. Builds a benchmark using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes to compute oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty; avoids proxy metrics to enable fine-grained analysis.

Result: The benchmark enables direct computation of oracle uncertainties and reveals that high predictive accuracy does not imply good uncertainty disentanglement; shows meaningful method differences and sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

Conclusion: Provides a theory-grounded framework for evaluating and disentangling uncertainty estimates, enabling precise assessment of uncertainty quality beyond predictive performance.

Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are critical in safety-sensitive applications, where understanding the sources of predictive uncertainty is essential. This often requires disentangling epistemic uncertainty from aleatoric uncertainty, yet these uncertainty types are not defined consistently across the literature, making it difficult to assess whether a method produces accurate uncertainty estimates. Evaluation is further complicated by the fact that ground-truth epistemic uncertainty is typically unavailable. Existing benchmarks therefore mostly rely on proxy tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not provide complete ground-truth uncertainty targets and offer limited insight into the structure and quality of uncertainty estimates. We propose a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, the expected loss of a predictor under the distribution of plausible ground-truth functions given the data. This view combines Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-dependent deviations from the posterior mean, capturing effects such as misspecification and optimization error. This formulation constitutes the foundation of a theory-backed benchmark that enables direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes. By avoiding proxy evaluations, the benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of uncertainty estimates. Empirically, we find that accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals practically useful differences between methods, identifying approaches with meaningful alignment to oracle uncertainty targets while exposing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

</details>


### [261] [Do Tabular Foundation Models Agree with Themselves?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06004)
*Christian Klötergens,Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi,Lars Schmidt-Thieme,Tom Hanika*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TFMs do not produce faithful joint distributions; they fail key consistency checks (marginalization and factorization) across tasks and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is no ground-truth joint distribution for real-world tabular data; assessing the faithfulness of TFMs’ joint predictions requires synthetic consistency criteria that can be checked against available marginals and factorization orders.

Method: Define two tests—marginalization consistency (marginals equal the directly predicted marginals) and factorization consistency (joint distribution invariant to factorization order). Evaluate TFMs on classification and regression across multiple tabular datasets, checking these properties for autoregressive multivariate construction.

Result: Every TFM evaluated violates both marginalization consistency and factorization consistency for both classification and regression across all datasets.

Conclusion: Current TFMs may not yield faithful joint distributions; existing autoregressive assembly methods fail these fundamental distributional tests, motivating rethinking of training/evaluation of TFMs and development of models that satisfy these consistency properties.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are currently the best approach to tabular prediction problems. They are constructed as transformers that approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution based on a pre-training prior. These univariate predictors can be converted into multivariate ones autoregressively by sampling one target and adding it to the features.
  However, the faithfulness of the resulting joint has not been investigated. Furthermore, TFMs cannot be evaluated against the posterior itself, at least not on real-world datasets, because the ground-truth distribution is unknown. We therefore propose asking a different question: could a model's predictions result from any joint distribution? To answer this question, we pose two requirements that any such model must satisfy. The first is marginalization consistency, which demands that marginalized conditionals are equal to directly predicted marginals. The second is factorization consistency, which demands that different factorization orders result in equal joint distributions. Every TFM that we evaluate violates both of these requirements for both classification and regression across all datasets.

</details>


### [262] [ProDVI: Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06015)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProDVI uses language-model-generated executable Python functions encoding coarse dynamics to pretrain the RL value network with synthetic transitions, improving sample efficiency without needing datasets, simulators, or meta-learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model-free RL is highly sample-inefficient due to learning from scratch. Access to precollected data, high-fidelity simulators, or related-task meta-learning is often unavailable. ProDVI seeks a resource-light way to bias representations with dynamics priors derived from LLMs.

Method: Prompt a code-generating language model to produce executable Python functions that encode coarse environment dynamics. Use these functions to generate synthetic transitions, then train an auxiliary dynamics-prediction objective to pretrain the state-action encoder of the value network within an actor-critic framework. The programs are only for pretraining and need not faithfully simulate the real environment; online RL will correct deviations.

Result: Empirical evaluation on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite shows that ProDVI improves the sample efficiency of model-free RL algorithms.

Conclusion: Programmatic dynamics priors sourced from LLMs can provide dynamics-aware initialization for RL value networks, reducing sample complexity and enabling quicker online adaptation, with robustness to imperfect priors since online learning can adjust.

Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) is notoriously sample inefficient. One contributing factor is that RL agents are typically initialized from scratch, forcing them to acquire task-relevant knowledge through online interaction. Existing approaches obtain informative initializations through pre-collected datasets, high-fidelity simulators, or meta-learning over related tasks, but these prerequisites may be difficult to access or even unavailable. In this paper, we propose Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization (ProDVI), a framework that leverages the commonsense and domain knowledge encoded in large language models to initialize RL agents without relying on these resources. Specifically, ProDVI prompts a code-generating language model to produce executable Python functions that encode coarse hypotheses about environment dynamics. These functions are then used to generate synthetic transitions. Based on these transitions, we construct an auxiliary dynamics prediction objective to pretrain the state-action encoder of the value network in an actor-critic framework. The learned representation provides dynamics-aware inductive biases before online RL begins. Importantly, the generated programs are used only for representation pretraining and are not required to faithfully simulate the target environment. While the generated programs may be inaccurate, their induced initialization can be corrected through online learning from real transitions and rewards. Experiments on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite tasks show that ProDVI can effectively improve the sample efficiency of model-free RL algorithms.

</details>


### [263] [BioKD: Selective Physiology-to-Video Knowledge Distillation via Reliability Gate for Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06023)
*Bojing Hou,Ruohao Li,Yitong Zhu,Hongjun Liu,Luwen Yu,Yuyang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reliability-aware physiology-to-video knowledge distillation framework (BioKD) improves video-based emotion recognition by using physiological signals as privileged training information and a reliability-gated, progressive distillation strategy, achieving improved performance on DEAP/AMIGOS with no inference-time overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome limitations of video-only emotion recognition in the presence of ambiguous social cues and to eliminate the need for intrusive physiological sensing at inference by leveraging privileged physiological signals during training.

Method: BioKD trains a video-based student model with physiology-to-video distillation using a sample-wise reliability-aware gating mechanism and a progressive distillation schedule to mitigate negative transfer from unreliable physiological supervision; no additional inference-time overhead and no requirement for physiological sensing during deployment.

Result: Empirical evaluation on DEAP and AMIGOS shows consistent improvements in valence and arousal recognition under both trial-wise and subject-wise evaluations; example figures include 68.01% trial-wise arousal accuracy on DEAP and 65.29% under subject-wise evaluation; analyses indicate reduced overconfident teacher errors and superiority over entropy-only weighting; inference-time overhead remains unchanged.

Conclusion: Reliability-aware progressive distillation effectively leverages privileged physiological information to produce robust, non-intrusive video representations for affective recognition, with improved performance and no inference-time costs.

Abstract: To address the limitations of video-based emotion recognition under ambiguous or socially masked behavioral cues, as well as the poor deployability of physiological signals, this paper proposes a reliability-aware physiology-to-video knowledge distillation framework, termed BioKD. The proposed framework leverages physiological signals as privileged information during training to guide a video-based student model in learning deep affective representations, while relying solely on non-intrusive video inputs at inference time. To cope with the high noise and instability of physiological teacher supervision caused by inter-subject variability, signal artifacts, and temporal inconsistency, BioKD incorporates a sample-wise reliability-aware gating mechanism together with a progressive distillation strategy. By adaptively regulating the strength of knowledge transfer, the framework suppresses negative transfer induced by unreliable physiological supervision and enables more stable cross-modal distillation. Experiments on DEAP and AMIGOS show that BioKD consistently outperforms representative baselines under both trial-wise and subject-wise evaluation protocols for valence and arousal recognition. For example, BioKD achieves 68.01\% on DEAP (trial-wise arousal) and 65.29\% under the more challenging subject-wise setting, demonstrating improved performance under a subject-independent evaluation setting. Further analyses show that BioKD effectively mitigates overconfident teacher errors and outperforms an entropy-only weighting strategy, confirming the importance of explicitly modeling supervision reliability. In addition, BioKD introduces no additional inference-time overhead relative to the same video student architecture and removes the need for physiological sensing and multimodal synchronization.

</details>


### [264] [Hybrid-Adaptive Thread Tuning to Mitigate Simulation Execution Bottlenecks in High-Performance Reinforcement Learning Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06025)
*Jiming Su,Hantao Hua,Lujia Yin,Yiping Yao,Feng Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoThread uses a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) to predict thread counts for RL inference, constrained by a finite-source M/M/1 queue model and refined via load-aware online fine-tuning, yielding significant speedups and throughput gains over static and state-of-the-art baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Simulation-in-the-loop RL inference suffers from dynamic, workload-sensitive overhead due to thread configuration; existing multithreading strategies cannot match resources quickly enough, causing contention and reduced throughput.

Method: Hybrid adaptive thread-tuning framework. A PINO-based predictor estimates optimal thread count, constrained by a finite-source M/M/1 queue model to reflect arrival/service dynamics. Online load-aware fine-tuning compensates for prediction errors, enabling fast, real-time resource adjustment within the RL inference loop.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows an average speedup of 18.4% over static strategies. Throughput is 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively. Execution time is reduced by up to 83.8% compared with state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: AutoThread effectively mitigates simulation bottlenecks in RL inference by integrating a physics-informed predictor with queueing constraints and online adaptation, delivering robust performance improvements; code and dataset are publicly available.

Abstract: In simulation-in-the-loop decision-making systems, reinforcement learning (RL) inference is often constrained by simulator-side execution overhead, where workloads are highly dynamic and sensitive to runtime thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match thread resources before or during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput. Through empirical analysis, we identify the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time as the key factor determining the optimal thread count. Building on this insight, we propose AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method for mitigating simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. AutoThread employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor and incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide prediction, enabling fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It further performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation. Experiments show that AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4\% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8\% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/suchenjm/AutoThread.

</details>


### [265] [Dynamic Graph Prompting via Topology-Routed Mixed-Curvature Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06031)
*Quanxin Wang,Xuanting Xie,Bingheng Li,Xingtong Yu,Shuo Wang,Ruiyi Fang,Zhao Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CurvPrompt introduces a topology-routed, geometry-aware prompting framework for dynamic graphs, using a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts with topology-aware routing to adapt representations for few-shot learning and node classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dynamic-graph prompting relies on a single embedding space, but temporal evolution alters local topology and degree heterogeneity, causing geometry under-adaptation and suboptimal representations.

Method: A bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each with a learnable prompt; topology-aware gate routes node–time instances to a sparse subset of experts, creating a personalized mixed-curvature representation. Soft routing is used during pre-training to learn a continuous topology-geometry mapping, while downstream adaptation employs hard Top-K routing with uniform weights for stability and efficiency.

Result: Empirical evaluation on four benchmark datasets shows substantial improvements in few-shot link prediction and strong, consistent performance on node classification, validating the need for geometry-adaptive prompting in dynamic graphs.

Conclusion: Geometry-adaptive prompting across multiple curvature spaces enables personalized, efficient representations for dynamic graphs, addressing geometry under-adaptation and improving performance in label-scarce regimes.

Abstract: Dynamic graph prompting freezes a pre-trained temporal backbone and adapts it to label-scarce downstream tasks using lightweight prompts. However, existing methods operate within a single, fixed embedding space. In this work, we reveal that temporal shifts in local clustering and degree heterogeneity actively reorganize the edge curvature spectrum---indicating that the optimal representation geometry dynamically evolves with local topology over time. We formalize this unaddressed mismatch as geometry under-adaptation. To overcome this limitation, we propose CurvPrompt, a topology-routed geometry prompting framework for dynamic graphs. Instead of relying on a single space, CurvPrompt maintains a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each paired with a learnable prompt. A topology-aware gate dynamically routes each node--time instance to a sparse subset of experts, constructing a personalized mixed-curvature representation. To ensure parameter efficiency and training stability under extreme label scarcity, CurvPrompt employs soft routing during pre-training to build a continuous topology--geometry mapping, and transitions to hard Top-K routing with uniform weights during downstream adaptation. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets show that CurvPrompt significantly advances few-shot link prediction while delivering strong, consistent performance on node classification tasks, validating the necessity of geometry-adaptive prompting.

</details>


### [266] [Does Latent Context Help? A Controlled Evaluation of Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Arctic Shipping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06105)
*Vaishnav Vaidheeswaran,Dilith Jayakody,Biruk Ambaw,Jaswanth Kumar,Md Mahbub Alam,Gabriel Spadon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Nonlinear shared reward outperforms linear reward by 50.9% in held-out likelihood; per-vessel latent context degrades performance; observed route/environment features explain most variation; multiple metrics yield different model rankings; recommends testing feature explainability before adding latent context for trustworthy AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess interpretability and robustness of IRL-based reward models for AI-assisted Arctic navigation, specifically whether latent contexts capture hidden preferences or merely re-encode observable factors, in safety-critical settings.

Method: Empirical comparison among three reward models (linear shared, nonlinear shared, nonlinear with vessel-specific latent context) using 3,186 AIS voyages across 9 Arctic seasons (200 vessels). Evaluate held-out likelihood, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer; perform context probes and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation to assess dependence on observable features; analyze model rankings via multiple metrics.

Result: Nonlinear shared reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% vs linear baseline; adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%; vessel-level variation largely explained by observable route/environmental features; different metrics yield different model rankings; latent context not needed for trustworthy AI in this setting.

Conclusion: Before adding per-vessel latent context, verify that observed features account for behavioral variation; use multiple evaluation metrics; latent context may be counterproductive; this approach strengthens trustworthiness of AI in safety-critical domains.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a framework for recovering such rewards from vessel trajectories, while recent meta-IRL methods introduce latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity. However, it remains unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode information already available in the observed state. We conduct a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing a linear shared reward, a nonlinear shared reward, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. The nonlinear reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, whereas adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation show that apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Moreover, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer yield different model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric is sufficient to evaluate learned rewards. These findings motivate testing whether the observed route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation before adding per-vessel latent context. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

</details>


### [267] [Kastor: An efficient fine-tuning strategy for generative emulation of PDE simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06107)
*Guillaume Couairon,Alexis Jacq,Yu-Han Wu,Renu Singh,Yana Hasson,Quentin Berthet,Romuald Elie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Kastor combines a large-stride causal autoregressive model with a non-causal temporal super-resolution network and a Mean Prediction Regularization (MPR) to convert deterministic physics foundation models into efficient, accurate generative surrogates for PDE-like simulations, improving stability, spectral fidelity, and computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address error accumulation in long-horizon auto-regressive surrogates and the challenge of capturing stochasticity, while reducing compute cost and preserving physical fidelity.

Method: Two-stage inference: (1) large-stride causal AR model for fast, coarse temporal steps; (2) non-causal temporal super-resolution network to refine temporality without drift. Training with Mean Prediction Regularization (MPR) enforcing the deterministic mean under null noise; spatial gradient matching to boost physical fidelity. Evaluated on diverse simulation datasets from The Well benchmark, compared against Walrus finetuning.

Result: Significant improvements in forecasting accuracy, spectral fidelity (power spectrum density), and computational efficiency. Reported 42.9% average reduction in forecasting error relative to a Walrus-based reference; 8/10 datasets outperform Walrus on VRMSE.

Conclusion: Kastor offers a unified, scalable framework to turn deterministic physics foundation models into high-quality generative surrogates, achieving superior performance across multiple metrics and datasets compared to established baselines.

Abstract: Machine learning offers a promising avenue to accelerate physical simulations by replacing computationally expensive traditional Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solvers with fast, differentiable surrogate models. However, standard auto-regressive ML emulators often suffer from error accumulation over long horizons and struggle to capture the stochasticity of complex physical systems. In this paper, we propose Kastor, a comprehensive methodology to adapt a deterministic physics foundation model into a highly efficient and accurate generative surrogate. First, we introduce a two-stage inference scheme that combines a large-stride causal auto-regressive model with a non-causal temporal super-resolution network, significantly reducing error accumulation while minimizing computational cost. Second, we present Mean prediction regularization (MPR), a novel training objective that constrains the generative model to predict the deterministic distribution mean under null noise conditioning. This regularization dramatically improves the performance and stability of both Functional Generative Networks (FGN) and diffusion-based emulators. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating spatial gradient matching improves the accuracy and physical fidelity of the simulations as measured by power spectrum density. Extensive evaluations on diverse simulation datasets of the benchmark The Well show that with these components, our model outperforms competing methods in forecasting accuracy, spectral consistency, and computational efficiency. Our model achieves a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting compared to our reference based on the Walrus finetuning methodology, and outperforms Walrus for 8 out of 10 datasets on variance-normalized RMSE (VRMSE).

</details>


### [268] [Is Self-Pretraining really useful to improve diagnosis in medical Time Series?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06122)
*Omar Coser,Antonio Orvieto,Paolo Soda,Loredana Zollo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-PreTraining (SPT) yields consistent gains for transformer-based medical time-series across uni- and multivariate data, especially with deeper models, without task-specific changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether SPT benefits observed in long-context transformers extend to medical time-series tasks with varying modalities and data availability.

Method: Train transformer models from scratch and with SPT using four masking-based objectives to promote temporal and cross-modal representations; evaluate on three medical time-series tasks (Camargo rehabilitation robotics, Non-EEG Stress, Gait Parkinson's Disease); vary model depth and compare performance; analyze both multivariate and univariate inputs.

Result: SPT improves classification accuracy by 0–6 percentage points across datasets, masking strategies, and architectures; gains amplify with deeper models; benefits observed even with univariate inputs; improvements generalize across modalities/datasets and improve robustness in data-limited settings.

Conclusion: SPT is a simple, general pre-training strategy that enhances transformer performance on medical time-series without task-specific architectural changes, offering improved robustness and accuracy in data-limited clinical environments.

Abstract: Inspired by recent evidence that transformer architectures benefit from Self-PreTraining (SPT) on long-context benchmarks, we investigate whether similar gains extend to multimodal, multivariate, and even simple univariate medical time series. Our objective is to assess the impact of SPT on the performance and scalability of transformer-based models across diverse medical applications, particularly under limited data conditions. We evaluate transformer architectures on three representative medical time-series tasks: rehabilitation robotics (Camargo dataset), stress detection (Non-EEG Stress), and Parkinson's disease detection (Gait Parkinson's Disease). Models are trained either from scratch or through SPT using four masking-based objectives designed to promote temporal and cross-modal representation learning, and we systematically vary model depth to examine how capacity interacts with pre-training benefits. Across datasets and configurations, SPT consistently improves classification accuracy by 0-6 percentage points depending on masking strategy, dataset and architecture, with gains observed not only in multivariate settings but also when models are restricted to simple univariate inputs. The improvements increase for deeper models that can better exploit the enriched temporal representations learned during pre-training. These findings indicate that SPT is a simple and general strategy that enhances transformer performance on medical time-series tasks without requiring task-specific architectural changes, supporting its potential to improve robustness and accuracy in data-limited clinical settings.

</details>


### [269] [LLM Inference Under Bursty Workload Distribution: Modifying the WAIT Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06135)
*Anjali Gangadhar Katageria,Shobha Rani,Raghu Nandan Sengupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An online intensity-estimation extension to the WAIT scheduling algorithm adapts to time-varying arrivals, using MMPP-based workloads; it yields higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM with comparable latency in bursty traffic scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world traffic to LLM services is bursty and non-Poisson, so schedulers based on constant-rate Poisson arrivals are fragile; a lightweight, knowledge-free method to adapt to variable demand is needed.

Method: Extend the WAIT algorithm with online estimation of request intensity from observed interarrival times; evaluate using Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP) synthetic workloads with diverse request types; compare via simulation against Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, and vLLM.

Result: The proposed method achieves higher throughput than the baselines in low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency, based on simulation with MMPP-based workloads.

Conclusion: An online, lightweight adaptation to arrival-rate dynamics improves throughput under bursty traffic without harming latency, demonstrating practical viability for dynamic LLM-serving environments.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude are widely used for information retrieval and problem-solving. Recent work has focused on improving scheduling algorithms to boost throughput while maintaining low latency. However, these approaches often assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates - an assumption that fails to reflect the inherently bursty and dynamic nature of real-world traffic. We propose a lightweight extension to the state-of-the-art WAIT algorithm [1], which adapts to time-varying arrival rates without prior traffic knowledge. The proposed algorithm performs online estimation of request intensity based on observed interarrival times. Using Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types, we conduct a simulation-based evaluation demonstrating that the proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve [2], ORCA [3], and vLLM [4] in the evaluated low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.

</details>


### [270] [SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06137)
*Yi He,Zhengkang Guan,Anpeng Wu,Peng Cui,Fei Wu,Kun Kuang*

Main category: cs.LG
