TL;DR: SkillTFM is a training-free adaptation framework for tabular foundation models that uses a verifiable, extensible skill bank and gated skill evolution to handle distribution shifts and heterogeneous feature semantics, aiming to improve predictive performance without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address distribution shifts and task-specific patterns in tabular data while avoiding costly fine-tuning and additional labeled data.

Method: Introduce a verifiable and extensible skill bank that couples boundary evidence identification (characterizing task structure and base-model failure) with gated skill evolution (retrieving and extending reusable skills with explicit validation).

Result: Empirically, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128–0.142 and raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898 on simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting; effectiveness generalizes across different TFM backbones.

Conclusion: A training-free adaptation framework that generalizes across TFMs by leveraging boundary-aware skill evolution, enabling more practical deployment under distribution shifts.

Abstract: Tabular data are ubiquitous in real-world applications and are crucial for data-driven prediction and decision-making across science, industry, finance, healthcare, and public services. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose tabular learning, offering reusable predictors across diverse datasets and substantially reducing the need for task-specific training, tuning, and model development. However, their practical deployment remains constrained by distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns that are difficult to capture without costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data.
  To this end, we propose SkillTFM, a training-free system that shifts TFM adaptation from parameter updates to the gated evolution of agentic skills. The core of SkillTFM is a verifiable and extensible skill bank that couples boundary evidence identification with gated skill evolution: the former characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns, whereas the latter retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation. Across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128--0.142, raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898. Furthermore, experiments across TFM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of SkillTFM.

</details>


### [271] [Threshold-Based Early Stopping of Accumulations in Neural Networks with Binary Activation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06177)
*Quentin Luquet de Saint-Germain,Massil Ait Abdeslam,Jean Pierre David*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training early-stopping for binary neural networks (BNNs) to skip unnecessary accumulations without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce compute in BNNs by exploiting that many later contributions do not change the final sign of the accumulated sum, enabling substantial reduction in dot-product operations for constrained deployments.

Method: Analyze running partial sums of binary activations on the training data, predict the final sign as soon as it becomes determined, using an idealized weight ordering for counting operations; no model parameters are retrained.

Result: On VGG11 with CIFAR-10, removes 86.6% of accumulation terms in the deepest convolution with only 0.37-point accuracy loss; removing 25% of full-network arithmetic when applied to the three deepest convolutions together, with a 1.36-point accuracy drop.

Conclusion: The approach yields substantial computational savings in binary neural networks with modest accuracy degradation and without retraining, by leveraging early termination of accumulations based on observed sign stability.

Abstract: Binary neural networks are very attractive for constrained deployment, enabling small footprint and low-power inference. For binary activations, the dot products become sign-controlled additions or subtractions, but the number of operations is unchanged. Indeed, every neuron or output channel still accumulates all of its input, even though only the sign will be retained, which is often wasteful. As the accumulation progresses, the running partial sum frequently drifts so far from zero that its final sign becomes highly predictable long before the last term is reached; every contribution evaluated after that point changes the value of the sum but not the final output activation. This paper turns this observation into a post-training early-stopping mechanism. We characterize the behavior of the running accumulations on the training dataset and use this information to predict the final sign as soon as possible. No model parameter is retrained. We count the number of operations under an idealized ordering of weights. On VGG11 applied to the CIFAR-10 dataset, the method removes $86.6\%$ of the accumulation terms of the deepest convolution for a $0.37$-point accuracy drop, and $25\%$ of the full-network arithmetic when used on the three deepest convolutions simultaneously, for a $1.36$-point drop.

</details>


### [272] [SAGA: Score-Weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment for Low-Resource Nordic Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06179)
*Hoda Fakharzadehjahromy,Emil Wiman,Andreas Bueff,Hafsteinn Einarsson,Fredrik Heintz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGA uses dependency‑parser supervision to guide preference optimization, replacing human labels and improving grammatical quality for Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål with GPT-SW3-1.3B.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on costly human preference annotations for language-model alignment in morphologically rich, low‑resource languages by leveraging available parsers.

Method: Convert parser judgments into delta‑DPO preference pairs, combine parser quality with lexical diversity into a composite reward, filter low‑information pairs via a reward‑gap criterion, and monitor reward hacking. Applied to GPT‑SW3‑1.3B across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål; evaluation uses parse success, independent Stanza evaluation, and native speaker pairwise preferences.

Result: Danish parse success rises from 69.0% to 93.8%; Icelandic shows a +4.5 percentage‑point improvement on Stanza evaluation (three‑run mean +3.3 points); native speakers prefer SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons; Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 percentage points.

Conclusion: Parser‑derived supervision is a practical alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low‑resource languages where high‑quality dependency parsers are available.

Abstract: Preference optimisation has proven effective for improving large language models but typically relies on costly human preference annotations. Extending these methods to morphologically rich, low-resource languages remains challenging because such annotations are scarce. We present SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment), a parser-guided preference optimisation framework that replaces human labels with dependency-parser supervision. SAGA converts parser judgements into preference pairs for delta-DPO, combines parser quality with lexical diversity in a composite reward, filters low-information pairs using a reward-gap criterion, and monitors reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision. Across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål using GPT-SW3-1.3B, SAGA consistently improves grammatical quality without requiring human preference labels. Danish parse success increases from 69.0% to 93.8%, Icelandic achieves a +4.5 percentage-point improvement on an independent Stanza evaluation (three-run mean +3.3 percentage points) while native speakers prefer SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons, and Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 percentage points. These results demonstrate that parser-derived supervision is a practical alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers are available.

</details>


### [273] [Continual Learning in Transition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06216)
*Zhiyan Hou,Dan Zhang,Tao Feng,Liyuan Wang,Wei Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Hongyan An,Junfeng Fang,Haokai Ma,Zhaohui Xu,Haiyun Guo,Jinqiao Wang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a tri-axial framework (When/How/Where) to analyze continual learning, signaling a shift from parameter-centric updates to system-level adaptation, and surveys methods across these axes including on-policy, test-time learning, and external components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CL has traditionally focused on parameter-centric updates. The abstract argues for a broader, system-level view and a formal tri-axial framework to capture ongoing, cross-stage evolution in learning mechanisms.

Method: Conceptual analysis and systematic survey using three axes (When, How, Where). Classifies methods along these axes (off-policy, on-policy, beyond-gradient optimization; pre-training, post-training, inference-time; internal parameters vs external constraints) and synthesizes key challenges and directions.

Result: Introduces and anchors a tri-axial framework for CE (continual learning), demonstrates how existing methods map onto this space, and discusses transition trends, challenges, and future research directions.

Conclusion: There is a paradigm shift from parameter-centric CL to system-level adaptation, necessitating broader research into update mechanisms, external components, and inference-time strategies; highlights future directions and unresolved challenges.

Abstract: Classical continual learning (CL) has primarily focused on enabling models to update and retain knowledge through parameter-centric mechanisms, e.g., training strategies, architectural designs, and weight adaptation. However, emerging paradigms are reshaping the scope of CL beyond this traditional model adaptation view. For instance, on-policy learning broadens the space of update mechanisms; test-time training extends CL from the training phase to inference; and external harness components such as memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols extend the evolutionary boundaries of model capabilities far beyond the static parameter space. Collectively, these developments indicate a transition from parameter-centric learning toward system-level adaptation. To characterize this transition, we examine the evolution of continual learning through three dimensions: When, How, and Where learning occurs. The How dimension encompasses off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient optimization mechanics. The When dimension captures evolution across pre-training, post-training, and inference-time stages. The Where dimension delineates updates occurring within internal parameters versus external structural constraints. Anchored by this tri-axial framework, we systematically survey representative methods, trace the ongoing transition of continual learning, and discuss the key challenges, broader implications, and future directions arising from this paradigm shift.

</details>


### [274] [Timestep-Conditioned Transformers for Global Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06241)
*Sam Levang,Fran Bartolic,Ty Dickinson,Chase Dwelle,Paulius Rauba,Viktor Cikojevic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GEM-3 introduces a probabilistic global weather model that uses explicit multi-timestep inference with a single trained weight set, enabling configurable timesteps at inference and improved rollout stability via mixed-timestep training; it uses a ~134M parameter neighborhood-attention transformer on an equirectangular grid, delivering near-state-of-the-art medium-range probabilistic skill and efficient training/inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed autoregressive timesteps force a trade-off between short-range accuracy and long-range stability. A flexible timestep at inference and multi-timestep training aim to balance predictability and usability across forecast horizons, with improved rollout stability.

Method: Train with mixed timesteps; at inference, configure the timestep with the same weights; architecture: lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer (~134M params) on an equirectangular grid, building on GEM-2; multi-timestep inference to handle multiple horizons; results include probabilistic forecasts and decision diagnostics.

Result: Achieves near-state-of-the-art medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training and inference, and decision-relevant diagnostics; demonstrates practical forecasting system balancing horizon-specific predictability and usability.

Conclusion: Explicit multi-timestep inference with a single weight set, plus mixed-timestep training, yields a flexible and stable forecasting system that covers a broad horizon while maintaining efficiency and actionable diagnostics.

Abstract: Existing machine-learning weather forecasting models rely on predetermined and fixed autoregressive timesteps. The choice of model timestep involves a fundamental trade-off: shorter timesteps (e.g. 1 to 6 hours) finely resolve atmospheric dynamics within the diurnal cycle but increase error accumulation for a given forecast horizon, while longer timesteps (e.g. 24 hours) reduce error accumulation but limit the usability of short-range forecasts where sub-daily predictability is high. In this work, we present GEM-3, a probabilistic global weather model that addresses this trade-off through explicit multi-timestep inference. With a single set of trained weights, the model timestep can be configured at inference time to balance predictability and usability across a broad forecast horizon. Additionally, we find that mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability relative to timestep-specialist models. Under the hood, GEM-3 is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer with ~134M parameters on an equirectangular grid with a number of architectural advancements beyond its predecessor GEM-2. The result is a practical forecasting system that couples near-SOTA medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training and inference, and decision-relevant diagnostics.

</details>


### [275] [A Six-Dimensional Taxonomy of Post-Training Adaptation Techniques with Applications in AI Governance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06246)
*Fardin Afdideh,Fernando Seoane,Farhad Abtahi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A survey that unifies post-training adaptation methods under a six-dimension taxonomy, enabling consistent comparison, documentation, and governance across model classes and deployment contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training adaptation literature is fragmented across technique families, model classes, and usage contexts, hindering fair comparison, replication, and governance of modified models.

Method: Proposes a six-dimensional taxonomy organized by mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, and model type; distinguishes terms like fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, and prompting; traces evolution across ML paradigms; maps relationships among techniques (inheritance, supersession, hybridization, layered deployment); synthesizes vocabulary and practice for documentation and governance; identifies open challenges.

Result: A unified, extensible vocabulary and framework that clarifies how adaptation methods relate, supports model-change tracking and governance, and provides a basis for evaluating and describing post-training modifications across traditional, foundation, and multimodal models.

Conclusion: Open challenges include evaluation and reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows; the taxonomy offers a structured foundation but requires ongoing updates to cover emerging methods.

Abstract: Post-training adaptation has become central to modern machine learning practice and includes techniques such as retraining, fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, alignment, retrieval augmentation, model editing, unlearning, calibration, and Multimodal Instruction Tuning. However, the literature remains fragmented across technique families, model classes, and deployment contexts, making it difficult to compare methods or describe how a trained model has been modified. This survey synthesizes the post-training adaptation literature and introduces a six-dimensional taxonomy organized by mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, and model type. The taxonomy distinguishes commonly conflated terms such as fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, and prompting, and shows how adaptation strategies evolve from traditional machine learning through deep learning, foundation models, large language models, and multimodal large language models. It also maps relationships among techniques, including inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks. The resulting vocabulary can support technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis. The survey concludes by identifying open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows.

</details>


### [276] [MetaboLLM: a metabolomics-specialized large language model for biochemical knowledge integration and predictive metabolite graph construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06253)
*Dohyun Ku,Min Gu Kwak,Francisco J. Pasquel,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Domain-specific LLMs (MetaboLLM) with retrieval and continual pretraining improve metabolomics knowledge tasks; MetaboLLM-GIN translates outputs into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction, achieving high AUCs in CABG-stress hyperglycemia and postmenopausal hormone-regimen tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metabolomics knowledge is dispersed across heterogeneous resources, hindering translation into predictive, interpretable representations; need methods that unify knowledge and enable patient-level predictions.

Method: MetaboLLM uses continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval. MetaboLLM-GIN converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for prediction via a graph isomorphism network. Evaluation spans four backbone families, on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, plus external benchmark; includes retrieval-based graph generation and comparisons to baseline and non-retrieval LLM configurations.

Result: MetaboLLM outperforms base and medically adapted models on knowledge, relational, and description tasks; transfers to an external benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieves highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia after CABG (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs from unadapted/non-retrieval LLMs. Model interpretation yields biologically meaningful insights.

Conclusion: Domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive, interpretable metabolite graph representations, enabling improved patient-level predictions and broader applicability.

Abstract: Metabolomics knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous resources and remains difficult to translate into predictive representations. We developed MetaboLLM, a metabolomics-specialized large language model adapted through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval, together with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using a graph isomorphism network. Across four backbone families, MetaboLLM outperformed corresponding base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction after coronary artery bypass grafting (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs generated from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM configurations. Model interpretation further produced biologically meaningful findings in both applications. These results show that domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations.

</details>


### [277] [RxnCLF: Contrastive Transformation-Aware Reaction Foundation Model for Improved Reactivity Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06259)
*Yiting Zheng,Cheng Fang,Anthony Donofrio,Haote Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A condensed reaction graph with self-supervised contrastive learning to create a transformation-aware reaction representation (RxnCLF), improving yield prediction across reaction classes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reaction yield prediction is data-scarce and space-sparse; existing encodings (string, fingerprint, graph) poorly capture transformations, limiting generalization for complex substrates.

Method: Construct a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that unifies reactant and product information; pretrain on 1.7M Pistachio reactions using a contrastive self-supervised objective to learn a transformation-aware latent space; fine-tune on Buchwald–Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary datasets for C–N coupling and amide formation; compare against graph and sequence baselines.

Result: RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines, achieving the best performance (R2) across multiple yield-prediction benchmarks; demonstrates a scalable, interpretable transformation-focused representation.

Conclusion: CRG-based RxnCLF acts as a scalable reaction foundation model with potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and enable downstream tasks such as regio-/enantioselectivity prediction and reaction-condition optimization.

Abstract: Reaction yield prediction remains challenging because labeled data are scarce and reaction space is both combinatorially large and sparsely populated, limiting the generalization of existing reaction representations. String-, fingerprint-, and graph-based reaction encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, making accurate prediction difficult for reactions with complex substrates. We propose reaction contrastive learning foundation (RxnCLF), a self-supervised contrastive framework for reaction representation learning. RxnCLF is built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that unifies reactant and product information into a single graph, enabling the model to learn explicit and enriched transformation structure rather than disconnected graphs. Pretrained on 1.7 million Pistachio reactions, RxnCLF learns a compact and continuous latent space that captures both reaction-center features and broader side chain contexts, making it transformation-aware and chemically interpretable. Fine-tuned on multiple yield prediction benchmarks, including Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary HTE C-N coupling and amide formation datasets, RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines, improving R2 and achieving the best performance overall. Our results highlight the promise of CRG-based RxnCLF as a scalable reaction foundation model, with the potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream reaction informatics tasks, including regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

</details>


### [278] [Hypothesis Testing with Conditional Queries: Learnability and the Value of Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06262)
*Zonghuan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A characterization of learnability and adaptivity gaps in conditional-query testing on a finite alphabet. Learnability holds iff there is positive separation in the two classes' pairwise conditional probabilities; zero separation yields a fixed worst-case error of 1/2 for any finite query budget. An adaptive tester of T queries can be emulated by a randomized non-adaptive procedure using O(N^2 (T + log(1/ρ))) pre-selected pair queries, whose transcript is within ρ in total variation of the adaptive transcript. A matching lower bound shows Ωε(N^2) non-adaptive queries for a family with constant adaptive complexity, implying a worst-case adaptivity gap of Θε(N^2). Interaction therefore yields a quadratic, but not exponential, reduction in test complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify how much adaptivity helps in distinguishing distribution classes under a conditional-query model on a finite alphabet, and determine the exact adaptivity gap and learnability criteria.

Method: 1) Derive a separation-based criterion for learnability in the conditional-query model. 2) Construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure that pre-selects pair queries and simulates the adaptive transcript with total-variation closeness. 3) Prove a matching lower bound by exhibiting a family with constant adaptive cost but Θ(N^2) non-adaptive cost. 4) Analyze consequences for the adaptivity gap, yielding Θε(N^2).

Result: Learnability occurs exactly when the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities; if separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error remains 1/2 for any finite budget. The authors provide an O(N^2(T+log(1/ρ))) non-adaptive procedure that, with pre-chosen queries, simulates the adaptive transcript within ρ in total variation. They also present a family showing a lower bound Ωε(N^2) for the non-adaptive complexity with constant adaptive complexity, establishing the worst-case adaptivity gap as Θε(N^2).

Conclusion: Interaction in this conditional-query setting yields quadratic improvements over fixed non-adaptive strategies but does not produce exponential gains; the learnability criterion fully characterizes when improvement is possible and the size of the adaptivity gap is Θε(N^2).

Abstract: Model evaluations may fix all tests before observing any responses or select later tests using earlier responses. We study this choice in a conditional-query model on a finite outcome space $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|=N$. We first ask which pairs of distribution classes can be reliably distinguished. We then ask how many additional queries are required to match an adaptive tester when all queried events must be fixed in advance. We show that learnability holds if and only if the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities. When this separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error is exactly $1/2$ at every finite query budget. For any $T$-query adaptive policy and any $ρ\in (0,1)$, we construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using $O(N^2(T + \log(1/ρ)))$ pair queries chosen before any response is observed. Its simulated transcript is within $ρ$ in total variation of the adaptive transcript, uniformly over all distributions in the model. We also construct a matching family with constant adaptive query complexity and $Ω_\varepsilon(N^2)$ non-adaptive query complexity. Consequently, the worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap is $Θ_\varepsilon(N^2)$. Thus interaction can reduce the required number of tests by a quadratic factor, but the apparent exponential branching of an interactive evaluation does not yield an exponential query advantage.

</details>


### [279] [The Tamed Subgradient Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm beyond Convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06283)
*Iosif Lytras,Nikolaos Makras,Sotirios Sabanis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new subgradient-based Langevin sampler (SG-TULA) for non-smooth, non-convex potentials with superlinear gradient growth is proposed. It yields explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein-2 convergence guarantees and excess risk bounds, with demonstrated applicability to GPT-2 pretraining where it competes with AdamW/Muon while providing verifiable guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sampling and optimization under non-smooth, non-convex potentials with superlinear gradient growth is challenging; smoothing approaches add bias and lack finite-sample guarantees. A method operating directly on subgradients with controlled growth aims to provide explicit, dimension-aware non-asymptotic guarantees.

Method: Introduce Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA) that discretizes Langevin diffusion using subgradients. Use taming to handle superlinear gradient growth, yielding a stable, explicit scheme. Derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 with all constants explicit in dimension and inverse temperature. Provide excess risk estimates for associated optimization. Verify assumptions with explicit constants for a regularized pretraining potential of a GPT-2 lineage and analyze a boosted coordinate-wise variant.

Result: Non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 are established with explicit constants depending on dimension and inverse temperature, improving rates for subgradient-based Langevin methods. Excess risk bounds for the corresponding optimization problem are obtained. The framework is validated on a regularized GPT-2 pretraining potential, and a boosted coordinate-wise SG-TULA variant pretrains GPT-2 competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, a comparison with no existing non-asymptotic guarantees.

Conclusion: SG-TULA advances sampling and optimization in non-smooth, non-convex, superlinear regimes by delivering explicit finite-sample guarantees and practical competitive performance on large-model pretraining. It invites further refinement of constants, broader potential classes, and extensive empirical validation.

Abstract: We study the problem of sampling from target distributions whose potentials are simultaneously non-smooth, subject to superlinear gradient growth, and non-convex. We introduce the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discretisation of the Langevin diffusion that operates directly on subgradients, without relying on computationally demanding smoothing procedures. To handle the superlinear regime, taming techniques are employed to produce a stable, explicit scheme. We derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, with all constants tracked explicitly in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving upon the currently known rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms. We further provide excess risk estimates for the associated optimisation problem. We verify the assumptions, with explicit constants, for the regularized pretraining potential of a LLM in the GPT-2 lineage and the boosted coordinate-wise variant of SG-TULA pretrains the former competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees are presently available.

</details>


### [280] [Surv-IPTB: An Attention-Based Model for Estimating Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit with Survival Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06288)
*Lev V. Utkin,Stanislav K. Kogan,Andrei V. Konstantinov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An attention-based Surv-IPTB framework estimates individualized probability of treatment benefit in survival analysis by reframing IPTB as pairwise binary classification, handling censoring with imprecise probabilities, and using learnable attention over pairwise comparisons. Demonstrates robust performance on synthetic nonlinear datasets, outperforming T-/S-learner baselines with traditional models; code is publicly available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of estimating individual treatment benefit (IPTB) in survival analysis under censoring. Existing meta-learners (T/S-learner) with standard survival models may falter in nonlinear or complex feature spaces and under varying censoring. Proposes an attention-based, pairwise comparison framework with imprecise probabilities to quantify uncertain treatment effects.

Method: Reformulate IPTB estimation as a binary classification over pairwise comparisons across treatment and control groups. Use an attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations to flexibly aggregate comparisons. Model handles right-censoring via imprecise probability representations, assigning interval-valued probabilities to uncertain effects and learning soft class probabilities for censored cases. Evaluate on synthetic nonlinear datasets (spiral, bell-shaped, circular feature spaces) with varying censoring rates and treatment effects; compare against meta-learner baselines using random survival forests, Cox PH, and Beran estimators.

Result: The approach yields robust performance across censoring rates and treatment effect strengths, maintaining accuracy in nonlinear scenarios where traditional methods degrade. It consistently outperforms T-learner and S-learner baselines with standard survival models. The framework is scalable and statistically principled for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings.

Conclusion: Attention-based Surv-IPTB provides a scalable, principled solution for estimating IPTB under censoring in survival analysis, with strong empirical results on synthetic nonlinear data and publicly available code.

Abstract: This work presents a novel attention-based framework for estimating the Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit (IPTB) in survival analysis contexts. The proposed model, called Surv-IPTB, directly quantifies the probability that a specific patient will experience extended survival time under treatment versus control. We reformulate IPTB estimation as a binary classification problem, leveraging pairwise patient comparisons across treatment and control cohorts. The framework incorporates a principled handling of right-censored observations through imprecise probability representations, where uncertain treatment effects are characterized by interval-valued probabilities. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations enables flexible, data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons, while simultaneously learning soft class probabilities for censored cases. Through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with complex nonlinear structures, including spiral, bell-shaped, and circular feature spaces, we demonstrate that our approach maintains robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths. The model consistently outperforms meta-learner baselines (T-learner and S-learner) equipped with random survival forests, Cox proportional hazards, and Beran estimators, particularly in challenging nonlinear scenarios where conventional methods exhibit significant degradation. The results establish the proposed attention-based framework as a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings. The code implementing the model is publicly available.

</details>


### [281] [BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291)
*Johann Birnick,Rayan Saab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BaKron is an efficient two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian-based quantization solver that achieves O(m+n) sequential steps and O(mn(m+n)) total work, matching GPTQ's cubic scaling while leveraging richer curvature information via anti-diagonal parallelism and divide-and-conquer; modular with respect to the base quantizer and Hessian estimator; supported by benchmarks and efficient Hessian computations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need to enable two-sided curvature-aware neural network quantization without prohibitive cost. GPTQ uses one-sided information; two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian captures output-coordinate correlations but is expensive when applied naively to the weight matrix.

Method: BaKron employs anti-diagonal parallelism and a recursive divide-and-conquer construction to solve the two-sided adaptive-rounding problem on an m x n weight matrix. It reduces total work from O(m^2 n^2) to O(m n (m+n)) while requiring only O(m+n) sequential steps, and is modular with respect to the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator. The work includes benchmarks, a survey of Hessians BaKron can use, an efficient Hessian-computation technique, and experimental evaluation.

Result: BaKron matches the cubic scaling of GPTQ while exploiting the richer curvature information from two-sided Hessians, significantly reducing computational cost relative to naive two-sided approaches. It is validated with practical benchmarks across a range of Hessians and demonstrated to be compatible with existing two-sided adaptive rounding frameworks (BoA, YAQA).

Conclusion: BaKron offers a practical, modular, and scalable solver for two-sided curvature-aware quantization, enabling efficient use of richer Hessian information in neural network quantization. The approach is empirically validated and opens avenues for broader Hessian choices and quantizers.

Abstract: We accelerate a family of algorithms for neural network quantization whose geometry is informed by any Kronecker-factored approximation of the Hessian. GPTQ-style adaptive rounding typically uses one-sided information derived from input activations. Two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations can additionally capture correlations across output coordinates, but applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally expensive. Building on the two-sided adaptive-rounding formulation used by BoA and YAQA, we introduce BaKron, an efficient solver that combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction. For an $m\times n$ weight matrix, BaKron uses $O(m+n)$ sequential steps while reducing the total work from $O(m^2n^2)$ to $O(mn(m+n))$. Thus, it matches the cubic scaling of GPTQ while exploiting richer curvature information. Moreover, BaKron is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator. We also provide practical benchmarks, consider a range of Hessians that BaKron can be called with, find an efficient technique to compute these Hessians, and evaluate the algorithm experimentally.

</details>


### [282] [On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296)
*Yijiang Li,Bingyang Wang,Yijun Liang,Yunjie Tian,Di Fu,Nuno Vasconcelos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: U-OPSD enables self-distillation using only the model’s own generations via internal consistency, generating a pseudo-solution through multi-rollout majority voting and shortest pseudo-solution conditioning to distill into the model’s longest incorrect prefixes, achieving competitive gains across benchmarks compared to supervised GT-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on external supervision for self-distillation and enable genuine self-improvement by learning from the model’s own outputs without ground-truth or external guidance.

Method: Sample multiple rollouts, form a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. Condition a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution and distill it into prefixes of the model’s longest incorrect completion to correct itself where it is confidently wrong.

Result: Consistently improves base models across diverse benchmarks and training settings, matching or surpassing supervised methods with GT (e.g., OPSD, GRPO). In AIME24/AIME25/HMMT25/MATH500/AMC23, gains of 8.5% and 10.7% in non-thinking mode at 4B/8B; surpasses OPSD by ~3% and ~2%. In thinking mode, on par with OPSD (slightly better at 4B) and surpasses GRPO.

Conclusion: U-OPSD demonstrates that self-distillation can be effectively achieved on-policy using only a model’s own outputs, delivering competitive gains without GT or external signals and offering a viable alternative to supervised distillation approaches.

Abstract: On-policy (Self-)Distillation (OPD / OPSD) has shown strong potential for post-training large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods still rely heavily on external supervision, including ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or guidance from larger models, and therefore fall short of genuine "self"-distillation. In this study, we show that on-policy self-distillation can be achieved using only a model's own generations via internal consistency. We propose Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation (U-OPSD). U-OPSD first samples multiple rollouts and constructs a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. It then conditions a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution and distills it into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, allowing the model to correct itself precisely where it is confidently wrong. Across diverse benchmarks, base models, and training settings, U-OPSD consistently improves over the base models and matches or surpasses supervised methods with ground truth (GT), such as OPSD and GRPO. On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23, U-OPSD improves over the base model by 8.5% and 10.7% on Qwen3 non-thinking mode at the 4B and 8B scales, respectively, and outperforms OPSD by an average of 3.2% and 2.3%. In thinking mode, U-OPSD remains on par with OPSD, outperforming it by 0.9% at 4B and matching it at 8B, while surpassing GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1%, respectively.

</details>


### [283] [RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310)
*Chenglong Wang,Ziming Zhu,Yifu Huo,Bei Li,Qiaozhi He,Yan Ding,Xiaoyang Hao,Yuxin Gao,Tianhua Zhou,Xiaojia Chang,Tongran Liu,Jingbo Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RRC (Ranking-based Reward Construction) enables generative reward models to produce more effective RL signals by deriving rewards from relative preferences rather than scalar scores, using self-competitive ranking and anchor-guided ranking; it yields consistent gains on open-ended chat and reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative reward models excel at ranking but RL commonly relies on scalar rewards, causing a mismatch. Transitioning to ranking-based rewards can provide richer feedback and stabilize training.

Method: Introduce two ranking strategies: (1) self-competitive ranking: compare sampled responses to create relative preferences; (2) anchor-guided ranking: use a small set of reference (anchor) responses to scale ranking-based rewards. Rewards are derived from pairwise or relative rankings rather than absolute scores, integrated into RL training.

Result: Empirical results show substantial improvements over existing reward construction methods across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains in RL performance using generative reward models.

Conclusion: Ranking-based reward construction bridges the gap between ranking-centric generative reward models and scalar RL signals, improving RL training efficiency and performance; code is available at the provided GitHub link.

Abstract: Recent advances in reward modeling show a paradigm shift from discriminative reward models to generative reward models. However, despite their strong capabilities in response ranking, generative reward models have not realized their potential in reinforcement learning (RL). Our analysis reveals that this limitation arises from a mismatch between the comparative nature of generative reward modeling and the scalar scoring paradigm adopted by existing RL algorithms. To bridge this gap, we propose a Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) approach, which enables generative reward models to provide more effective RL learning signals by deriving rewards from relative preference rankings. RRC introduces two complementary strategies: self-competitive ranking, which exploits comparisons among sampled responses, and anchor-guided ranking, which enables scalable ranking-based reward construction with a small set of reference responses. Experiments across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches. Our code can be found at https://github.com/wangclnlp/RRC.

</details>


### [284] [CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06352)
*Fanzhe Meng,Guoxin Chen,Jiale Zhao,Shuang Sun,Zhiyu Lin,Wayne Xin Zhao,Ruihua Song,Ji-Rong Wen,Kai Jia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CalibForge autonomously synthesizes terminal tasks by calibrating solver behavior (multi-solver and contrastive calibration) to identify solver-relative learnable tasks; a large calibrated task set is created and improves model performance on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Executable and verifiable tasks are insufficient alone; need tasks whose solvability depends on solver settings to produce effective, transferable learning data.

Method: Autonomous synthesis of terminal tasks guided by verified solver behavior. Two calibration strategies: (1) multi-solver disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, and (2) contrastive calibration targeting a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation. These establish a solver-relative learnable zone and yield 5,431 calibrated tasks.

Result: Calibrated tasks provide stronger supervision than baselines; models trained on the full set achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, with up to 24.71pp, 27.68pp, and 30.04pp improvements on Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Pro, and Doc2Repo respectively.

Conclusion: Solver-relative learnability is a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent-training data, with CalibForge producing a large, diverse task set that improves cross-domain performance.

Abstract: Training terminal agents requires executable and verifiable tasks that are not merely solvable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Executable validation establishes feasibility, yet does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting. In this paper, we present CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks through adversarial solver calibration. Multi-solver calibration targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, whereas contrastive solver calibration targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation; both operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Using CalibForge, we construct 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Our ablations show that both strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring and validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the corresponding base model reach 24.71 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 points on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 points on Doc2Repo. Together, these results support solver-relative learnability as a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data.

</details>


### [285] [An Optimal Agnostic PAC Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06363)
*Markus Engelund Mathiasen,Jian Qian,Nikita Zhivotovskiy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A learner for binary classification with finite VC dimension achieves a statistically optimal agnostic PAC risk bound, matching the known lower bounds (up to universal constants) for all L* and δ.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resolve the (agnostic) sample complexity of PAC learning for finite VC classes by providing a learner with optimal excess risk bounds.

Method: Propose a learning algorithm and prove a high-probability excess risk bound: L(h_hat) ≤ L* + c ( sqrt{ L*(d+log(1/δ))/n } + (d+log(1/δ))/n ) with probability at least 1-δ.

Result: The bound is statistically optimal up to universal constants; matches Devroye–Györfi–Lugosi lower bounds, thus settling the sample complexity for agnostic PAC learning at fixed L*.

Conclusion: The paper establishes that, for finite VC dimension d, agnostic PAC learning is settled (up to universal constants) with a learner achieving the stated risk bound for all δ in (0,1/2].

Abstract: Let $H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^X$ be a class of finite VC dimension $d\ge1$. Writing $L$ for the binary risk and $L^*=\min_{h\in H}L(h)$, we construct a learner achieving the statistically optimal risk bound: from an i.i.d.\ sample of size $n$, for every $0<δ\le 1/2$, with probability at least $1-δ$, \[
  L(\widehat h)
  \le L^*+ 7\cdot10^8\left(
  \sqrt{\frac{L^*(d+\log(1/δ))}{n}}
  +\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}
  \right). \] This settles the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning up to universal constants at every fixed $L^*$, matching the lower bounds of Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi [A Probabilistic Theory of Pattern Recognition, Springer, 1996].

</details>


<div id='cs.RO'></div>

# cs.RO [[Back]](#toc)

### [286] [VLAff: Vision-Language-Affordance Model for Unified Actionable Affordances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05215)
*Jihoon Oh,Kento Kawaharazuka,Kei Okada*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes EgoAffordance dataset and VLAff—an embodied-to-agnostic framework using egocentric human videos, 3D reconstruction, and a vision-language foundation model to predict and execute visual, grasp, and trajectory affordances for zero-shot robot manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address embodiment mismatch between humans and robots by learning object-centric, embodiment-agnostic affordances. Leverages large-scale human egocentric videos and 3D reconstruction to extract actionable affordances, enabling scalable, cross-domain robot learning.

Method: Use egocentric videos with state-of-the-art 3D Structure-from-Motion and hand mesh reconstruction to extract visual, grasp, and trajectory affordances. Build EgoAffordance dataset (204K episodes; 5.6M visual affordances; 11.6M grasp/trajectory affordances). Develop VLAff, a vision-language foundation model that learns cross-modal correlations across affordances. Given a visual observation and instruction, VLAff outputs visual affordance heatmaps, grasp poses, and trajectories, which are then converted into executable actions using 3D scene information.

Result: VLAff achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual affordance prediction and demonstrates applicability to real robots, including zero-shot manipulation and affordance-guided robot learning.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates that an embodiment-agnostic, cross-modal foundation model can translate human-derived affordances into executable robotic actions, with a large-scale dataset enabling robust, scalable robot learning across tasks and objects.

Abstract: Learning manipulation skills from human videos is promising for scalable robot learning. However, the embodiment mismatch between humans and robots makes this challenging. One promising solution is to learn object-centric actionable affordances that are embodiment-agnostic. In this work, we propose a framework that leverages egocentric human videos with state-of-the-art 3D Structure-from-Motion and hand mesh reconstruction to extract actionable affordances such as visual, grasp, and trajectory affordances that explicitly encode where to interact, how to grasp, and how to move. We construct EgoAffordance, a large-scale dataset comprising 204K episodes with 5.6M visual affordances and 11.6M grasp and trajectory affordances. Building on this, we introduce VLAff, a large vision-language model-based unified foundation model that learns cross-modal correlations across all actionable affordances. Given a visual observation and instruction, VLAff generates visual affordance heatmaps, grasp poses, and trajectories, which are then converted into directly executable actions by utilizing 3D scene information. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that VLAff not only achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual affordance prediction, but can also be effectively applied to real robot applications such as zero-shot manipulation and affordance-guided robot learning.

</details>


### [287] [A System for Train Condition Monitoring and Structural Health Assessment of Rail Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05221)
*Maximilian Posner,Martin Dazer,Daniela Lauer,Robert Winkler-Höhn,Mathilde Laporte,Tobias Herrmann,Martin Köppel*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: AI-enabled structural sensing for real-time rail vehicle condition monitoring and impact detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enhance safety, maintenance, and design optimization for mainline rail as GoA4 deployments face safety and environmental challenges; current perception systems miss impact and overrun events.

Method: Integrates structural sensor data with AI-based data analysis to detect impacts, structural damage, and driving-over events in real time; supports condition-based maintenance and long-term data analytics for design optimization.

Result: Feasibility demonstrated; potential improvements in operational safety, predictive maintenance, and data-driven design optimization; supports progression toward automated operation in mainline rail.

Conclusion: An AI-augmented structural sensing framework can enable safer operations and facilitate transition to GoA4 in mainline rail, while informing vehicle design and maintenance strategies.

Abstract: The ongoing digitalization of rail systems and the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) are fundamentally transforming the design, operation, and maintenance of rail vehicles. While fully automated operation at Grade of Automation 4 (GoA4) is well established in metro systems, its deployment in mainline rail remains limited. This is primarily due to stringent safety requirements and the complexity of open operational environments. Current perception systems based on cameras, radar, and lidar are effective in detecting objects but provide limited capability for reliably identifying impacts, collisions, and driving-over events. This paper presents a novel approach for real-time vehicle condition monitoring and impact detection that integrates structural sensor technologies with AI-based data analysis. The proposed framework addresses three key applications: (1) automated detection of impacts, structural damage, and driving-over events, (2) condition-based maintenance enabled by continuous monitoring, and (3) long-term data analytics to support vehicle design optimization. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approach and highlight its potential to enhance operational safety, enable predictive maintenance strategies, and support the transition toward fully automated operation in mainline rail systems

</details>


### [288] [Failing Gracefully: Mitigating Impact of Inevitable Robot Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05313)
*Duc M. Nguyen,Saad A. Ghani,Andrew Marshall,Allison Andreyev,Gregory J. Stein,Xuesu Xiao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes a safety-aware planning framework for service robots, combining a probabilistic-impact safety formulation with FailBench, a MuJoCo-based simulator to study failure modes and improve robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Failures in household service robots are inevitable and can have safety-critical consequences; a systematic approach to evaluate and mitigate such failures is needed for safe deployment.

Method: Define a safety formulation that jointly considers the probability and severity of failure-induced interactions; quantify entity-specific impact to guide planning; develop FailBench to simulate failures (sensing issues, actuator malfunctions) in MuJoCo for controlled experiments.

Result: Framework and simulator establish a foundation for safer, more robust motion planning and learned policies; the abstract does not report empirical results.

Conclusion: Together, they enable safer deployment in real-world homes and provide a platform for future evaluation and policy learning under diverse failure scenarios.

Abstract: Service robots operate in household environments shared with humans, pets, and everyday objects, where they are highly susceptible to failures such as software crashes, hardware degradation, or unpredictable interactions. While roboticists strive to minimize failures, some remain inevitable, making it critical to mitigate their potential consequences for safe and reliable deployment. This paper introduces a novel safety formulation that evaluates both the probability of impactful interactions between robots and surrounding entities during failures, and the severity of their outcomes. By quantifying the impact of failures on different entities, our approach enables robots to make informed planning decisions that balance safety with task efficiency. To support systematic evaluation, we also present FailBench, a MuJoCo-based simulation framework for studying robot-environment interactions under diverse failure modes, including sensing issues and actuator malfunctions. Together, our safety formulation and FailBench provide a foundation for developing safer and more robust motion plans and learned policies in real-world household environments.

</details>


### [289] [Unified Planning-Learning Framework for Robust UUV Navigation Under Partial Observability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05365)
*Md Ether Deowan,Eleni Kelasidi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An observation-only autonomy framework for UUVs that fuses onboard sonar-derived occupancy mapping, clearance-constrained global planning, and a risk-aware RL-based local policy, with latent-state learning and BT-based distillation, evaluated in Sophia? Isaac Sim with multi-seed experiments showing improved robustness and safety under partial observability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Navigate dynamic, partially observable underwater environments safely and robustly by integrating perception, planning, and learning. Leverage explicit planning cues (time-to-collision, clearance) while learning reactive control and compact environmental representations; provide reproducible methodology for UUV autonomy.

Method: Construct occupancy maps from onboard sonar and depth images; adopt a clearance-constrained global planner for long-horizon structure; employ a reinforcement learning policy for short-range tracking and reactive avoidance; learn a compact latent state representation from onboard sensors encoding environment structure, obstacle dynamics, and uncertainty; apply behavior tree distillation with staged supervision to improve safety and training stability; use an uncertainty-calibrated distillation mechanism to reweight teacher guidance based on online latent-model uncertainty, emphasizing uncertain regimes; retain TTC and clearance cues as explicit features in planning and local policies; evaluate with a reproducible multi-seed protocol in high-fidelity Isaac Sim simulation, benchmarking against BT-only and standard RL baselines.

Result: Demonstrates improved robustness and safety under dynamic conditions; provides a unified hybrid planning-learning architecture and reproducible methodology for robust UUV autonomy under partial observability.

Conclusion: Proposes a general, reproducible pipeline that combines explicit planning cues with learning-based perception and control, enabling robust UUV autonomy in dynamic underwater environments with partial observability.

Abstract: This paper presents an observation-only autonomy framework for Unmanned Underwater Vehicles (UUVs) navigation in dynamic underwater environments that integrates persistent occupancy mapping, global clearance-aware planning, and risk-aware local control. The proposed pipeline constructs occupancy maps solely from onboard sonar and depth image observations, adapts a clearance-constrained global planner (GP) to provide long-horizon structure, and integrates a reinforcement learning (RL) policy to handle short-range tracking and reactive avoidance. To further support decision-making under partial observability, the system learns a compact latent state representation from onboard sensor data, encoding environmental structure, obstacle dynamics, and uncertainty. Behavior tree (BT) distillation with staged supervision is introduced to improve safety and training stability, while an uncertainty-calibrated distillation mechanism reweights teacher guidance using online latent-model uncertainty, emphasizing uncertain regimes during learning, with time-to-collision (TTC) and clearance cues remaining explicit in planning and local policy features. To demonstrate the efficacy of the framework, a reproducible multi-seed evaluation protocol is established in high-fidelity GPU-accelerated simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Sim, and performance is benchmarked against BT-only and standard RL baselines. The results obtained demonstrate improved robustness and safety under dynamic conditions, thus providing a general pipeline with a unified hybrid planning learning architecture and a reproducible methodology for robust UUV autonomy under partial observability.

</details>


### [290] [World-to-Wrist: Task-Conditioned Future Wrist Modeling for Fine-Grained Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05369)
*Yuhao Pan,Haosong Peng,Zhengshen Zhang,Zhengyang Yan,Yalun Dai,Fushuo Huo,Chujie Wang,Tianyu Qi,Xiucheng Wang,Nan Cheng,Wenchao Xu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes World-to-Wrist VLA (W2-VLA) with task-conditioned future wrist modeling, plus W2-CoT annotations, yielding improved fine-grained and contact-sensitive manipulation at >80 Hz across single-arm and bimanual setups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models typically treat main-view and wrist-view observations as parallel inputs, neglecting how wrist-local interactions evolve under the global task context, which harms fine-grained manipulation.

Method: W2-VLA contextualizes latent modeling tokens as a compact interface between the vision-language model and the wrist predictor; conditioned on this interface and observed wrist history, the predictor forecasts future wrist latents that inform action prediction. W2-CoT is a synthesis pipeline producing structured annotations describing manipulation progress, physical transition cues, and wrist-local evidence to supervise the latent interface.

Result: Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks show improved fine-grained and contact-sensitive manipulation for both single-arm and bimanual settings, while maintaining action-generation rates above 80 Hz.

Conclusion: W2-VLA, with task-conditioned future wrist modeling and W2-CoT annotations, enhances VLA-based manipulation by better anticipating wrist-local dynamics and preserving high-speed action generation.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often treat main-view and wrist-view observations as parallel visual inputs, overlooking their distinct roles in robot manipulation. Fine-grained manipulation, however, benefits from anticipating how wrist-local interactions may evolve under the global task context. To address this limitation, we present World-to-Wrist VLA (W2-VLA), a VLA model for fine-grained robot manipulation with task-conditioned future wrist modeling. Given current multi-view observations and a task instruction, W2-VLA contextualizes a set of latent modeling tokens as a compact interface between the vision-language model and the wrist predictor. Conditioned on this interface and the observed wrist history, the predictor forecasts future wrist latents, which are transformed into future-aware context for action prediction. In addition, we introduce W2-CoT, a synthesis pipeline that produces structured annotations describing manipulation progress, physical transition cues, and wrist-local evidence. These annotations provide auxiliary supervision that shapes the task-conditioned latent interface. Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved fine-grained and contact-sensitive manipulation across both single-arm and bimanual settings, while maintaining action-generation rates above 80 Hz.

</details>


### [291] [Sliding Sensors: Configurable Confidence in State Estimation for Continuum Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05410)
*Ella Walsh,Spencer Teetaert,Eric Diller,Timothy D. Barfoot,Jessica Burgner-Kahrs*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Mechanically reconfigurable sensing shapes state estimation uncertainty in continuum robots by longitudinally translating a sensor, improving task-relevant confidence and reducing full-body shape estimation error versus a fixed-tip sensor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimation uncertainty in continuum robots is spatially non-uniform in uncertain environments; global accuracy is not always the priority; the goal is sufficient confidence at task-relevant locations along the robot.

Method: Concept hardware design enabling longitudinal translation of a sensor within a continuum robot; experimental demonstration comparing a sliding sensor to a fixed-tip sensor.

Result: State estimation confidence can be reconfigured by sensor location; sliding the sensor over time reduces full-body shape estimation errors compared to a single fixed tip sensor.

Conclusion: Mechanically reconfigurable sensing enables uncertainty shaping in state estimation for continuum robots and is feasible, with potential improvements for task-adaptive sensing.

Abstract: Continuum robots often operate in uncertain environments, where accurate state estimation is essential for safe interactions. Estimate uncertainty is inherently spatially non-uniform: confidence varies depending on where measurements are available. Global estimation accuracy is not always the top priority, but rather achieving sufficient confidence at task-relevant locations along the robot. This extended abstract introduces mechanically reconfigurable sensing enabling uncertainty-shaping in state estimation for continuum robots. We present a concept hardware design demonstrating the feasibility of longitudinal translation of a sensor within a continuum robot. We demonstrate that state estimation confidence can be reconfigured by varying the sensor location, and show a reduction of full-body shape estimation errors when sliding the sensor back and forth over time, compared to a single fixed tip sensor.

</details>


### [292] [ARGUS: Aligning Robot Scene Geometry Under Shifting Views with Large 3D Vision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05579)
*Rishik Sathua,Haonan Chen,Katherine Driggs-Campbell*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ARGUS is an observation pre-processing pipeline that aligns multi-view observations to a canonical viewpoint using large-scale 3D vision models, decoupling geometry from viewpoint to improve learning efficiency of visuomotor policies; it achieves 4–6x faster convergence and better performance in both limited-view and view-diverse regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policy learning for robot manipulation is hindered by entanglement of scene geometry with camera viewpoint, reducing generalization across viewpoint-diverse datasets (e.g., DROID, BridgeV2). An invariant, canonical representation of observations could improve data efficiency and transfer.

Method: ARGUS preprocesses image observations with large-scale 3D vision models to reproject or align them into a canonical viewpoint before feeding them to downstream visuomotor policies, thereby simplifying the observation space and reducing viewpoint-related variance.

Result: Empirical results show consistent improvements over prior approaches across datasets with varying viewpoint diversity, in both limited-view and view-diverse training settings; convergence is 4–6x faster when learning from viewpoint-diverse data.

Conclusion: Using large-scale 3D vision models for observation alignment reduces the learning burden on visuomotor policies, enabling more efficient learning from large-scale, viewpoint-diverse robot datasets.

Abstract: Large-scale visuomotor policies have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of robot manipulation tasks. However, despite this success, manipulation polices often entangle scene geometry with the corresponding viewpoint, learning where objects lie in an image rather than where it lies in the task space. This entanglement inherently limits the corresponding policy's ability to learn from viewpoint-diverse datasets (ex. DROID, BridgeV2) and generalize beyond the viewpoints captured in their training data. In this work, we present ARGUS, an observation pre-processing pipeline that uses large-scale 3D vision models to align image observations from arbitrary camera viewpoints into a canonical viewpoint before passing it to downstream visuomotor policies. Experiments across training datasets with varying levels of viewpoint diversity, from fixed multi-view camera configurations to highly varied camera placements, show that our method consistently outperforms prior approaches across both limited-view and view-diverse training regimes. In efficiency comparisons, ARGUS demonstrates an ability to learn from view-diverse data, converging to high success rates 4-6x faster than previous methods by leveraging a simplified observation space. Overall, our findings show that leveraging large-scale 3D vision models reduces the learning burden on visuomotor policies, enabling more efficient learning from large-scale, viewpoint-diverse robot datasets.

</details>


### [293] [PathCover: A Fast Convex Decomposition along a Path via Randomized Iterative Space Partitioning (RISP) on Point Clouds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05586)
*Kunal S. Narkhede,Abhijeet M. Kulkarni,Guoquan Huang,Ioannis Poulakakis*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PathCover offers a real-time corridor generation framework using a randomized RISP algorithm to build obstacle-free convex polytopes directly from raw LiDAR data in expected linear time, enabling safe MPC/trajectory optimization with finite termination and progress guarantees; exhibits ~10x speedups over state-of-the-art while preserving corridor volumes and is validated in simulation and hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous navigation requires fast, reliable generation of obstacle-free regions at sensor rate. Existing corridor generators fail to meet real-time constraints, hindering real-time planning and safety guarantees.

Method: Introduce PathCover, driven by RISP, a randomized algorithm that constructs convex polytopes directly from raw point cloud data under a mild probabilistic elimination condition. It produces sequences of overlapping, obstacle-free polytopes that constrain downstream MPC/trajectory optimization, with proven finite termination and progress guarantees along obstacle-free reference paths; validated on LiDAR data and integrated with simulation and hardware experiments.

Result: Demonstrates order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable corridor volumes on synthetic and real LiDAR datasets. Validated in high-fidelity quadrotor simulations and real-world deployment on a quadrupedal robot using live LiDAR perception.

Conclusion: PathCover provides a practically viable, theoretically sound real-time corridor generation framework, enabling robust, fast planning for constrained navigation and scalable to complex environments.

Abstract: Autonomous robot navigation requires the rapid generation of obstacle-free regions for trajectory planning. However, existing corridor generators struggle to meet real-time, sensor-rate computational constraints. To resolve this bottleneck, we introduce PathCover, a framework driven by RISP; a novel randomized algorithm that constructs convex polytopes directly from raw point cloud data in expected linear time under a mild probabilistic elimination condition. PathCover generates sequences of overlapping, obstacle-free polytopes that safely constrain downstream MPC and trajectory optimization. We mathematically guarantee that the algorithm terminates in finite steps while ensuring continuous progress along any obstacle-free reference path. Extensive benchmarks on synthetic and real-world LiDAR datasets demonstrate an order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable corridor volumes. The complete pipeline is validated via high-fidelity quadrotor simulations and physical deployment on a quadrupedal robot navigating constrained environments using live LiDAR perception.

</details>


### [294] [Search-Aided Joint Agent-Environment Reinforcement Learning for Robust Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding with Rotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05588)
*He Jiang,Jingtian Yan,Yulun Zhang,Yimin Tang,Tanishq Duhan,Rishi Veerapaneni,Guillaume Sartoretti,Jiaoyang Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A novel Search-Aided Joint Reinforcement Learning (SJRL) framework for Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding with realistic LMAPF-R2 constraints, combining a single-step planner (Causal PIBT) with a joint RL objective where the environment learns graph edge costs to guide agents via backward Dijkstra; outperforms Causal-PIBT on dense maps and scales to a mixed-reality warehouse with 8 real and 248 virtual robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address realistic constraints in LMAPF (robust safety and in-place rotation) that are often neglected by oversimplified kinematic models, thereby accelerating coordination in highly constrained environments and enabling closer real-world deployment.

Method: Augment neural policies with Causal PIBT to resolve collisions and propagate intentions; propose a unified RL framework that jointly optimizes agent and environment policies; the environment policy learns graph edge costs to provide global movement guidance, enabling backward Dijkstra search for planning; evaluated on high-density maps and in a mixed-reality warehouse.

Result: SJRL achieved significant improvements over the strong baseline Causal-PIBT across multiple high-density maps; validated in a challenging mixed-reality warehouse with 8 physical robots and 248 virtual robots.

Conclusion: The integration of a single-step search-based planner with a learnable environment payoff yields robust performance under realistic LMAPF-R2 constraints, with demonstrated scalability to dense, real-world-like robotic deployments and potential for real-world deployment with further refinements.

Abstract: Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding (LMAPF) requires repeatedly planning collision-free paths for agents that continuously receive new goals upon reaching their current ones. While many learning-based planners have been proposed for LMAPF, most rely on oversimplified kinematic assumptions that may overlook motion constraints critical to real-world performance. In this work, we study a more realistic LMAPF model derived from many real-world automated warehouse systems, termed LMAPF-R2, which incorporates robust safety constraints and in-place rotation constraints. These constraints substantially increase coordination difficulty, particularly in highly constrained spaces. To address these challenges, we propose Search-Aided Joint Reinforcement Learning (SJRL). We first augment neural policies with Causal PIBT, a single-step search-based planner that resolves agents' collisions and propagates their intentions. We then introduce a unified RL formulation that jointly optimizes agent and environment policies, where the environment policy learns graph edge costs to provide global movement guidance via backward Dijkstra search. Experiments demonstrate that SJRL achieves significant improvements over the strong search-based planner, Causal-PIBT, across multiple high-density maps. We further validate SJRL in a challenging mixed-reality warehouse environment with 8 physical robots and 248 virtual robots.

</details>


### [295] [KILVO: Kinematic-Inertial-LiDAR-Visual Odometry with Robust Multimodal Adaptation for Humanoid Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05647)
*Jixin Gao,Fucheng Liu,Teng Zhang,Fusheng Zha*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: KILVO is a kinematic-inertial-LiDAR-visual odometry framework for humanoid robots that fuses joint encoders, IMU, LiDAR, and camera via an asynchronous-sequential error-state Kalman filter; it uses inertial prediction, high-rate leg kinematics constraints, and sequential exteroceptive updates (LiDAR geometry priors then photometric visual terms), with multimodal adaptation and a compact contact estimator; demonstrated across multiple robots and scenarios with strong robustness and real-time performance; code released on GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humanoid robots demand robust, real-time odometry under diverse sensor conditions and potential sensor degradation. Existing fusion methods struggle with asynchronous data, leg/knee constraints, and sensor failures. This work aims to integrate proprioceptive and exteroceptive cues in a resilient, high-rate framework tailored for humanoids.

Method: Propose KILVO: an asynchronous-sequential hybrid ESIKF that propagates state with IMU, includes leg kinematics as proprioceptive constraints at high rate, and updates exteroception sequentially: first LiDAR-based geometric priors, then visual photometric error. Joint encoders, LiDAR, and camera are fused; a compact contact estimation module shares information with the state estimator to enhance robustness, enabling multimodal adaptation to sensor failures.

Result: Extensive experiments on public datasets and real-world humanoid robots show competitive accuracy, efficiency, and output rates with strong robustness to sensor degradation and failures, outperforming some state-of-the-art fusion methods in humanoid settings. GitHub code/datasets released.

Conclusion: KILVO provides a robust, real-time, multi-sensor odometry solution for humanoid platforms, leveraging asynchronous fusion and proprioceptive constraints, with demonstrated resilience to sensor faults and realistic gait scenarios.

Abstract: This article presents a kinematic-inertial-LiDAR-visual odometry for humanoid robots, called KILVO. Tailored to the platform features, requirements, and real-world complexity, it fully utilizes the sensors commonly equipped on humanoid robots, including joint encoders, IMU, LiDAR, and camera, within an asynchronous-sequential hybrid error-state iterated Kalman filter (ESIKF). Specifically, inertial data are used for prediction, leg kinematics are processed asynchronously at a high rate and provide proprioceptive constraints, while exteroception is updated sequentially, first by registering LiDAR points for geometric priors and then by updating the visual component via photometric errors. Moreover, the framework is elaborately designed with multimodal adaptation for resilience to sensor failures. A compact contact estimation module is also developed, sharing information with state estimation without additional sensors.
