Extensive experiments on public datasets and in the real world across multiple humanoid robots, gait patterns, and scenarios demonstrate that KILVO achieves highly competitive accuracy, efficiency, and output rates, with strong robustness against sensor degradation and failures, making it more suitable for humanoid robots than state-of-the-art fusion methods. Our code and datasets are released on GitHub.

</details>


### [296] [JoyAI-RA 0.5: Scaling Robot Manipulation Learning via Dual Action Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05674)
*JoyAI-RA Team*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: JoyAI-RA 0.5 presents a Vision-Language-World-Action framework with dual action alignment to fuse heterogeneous data (human ego, simulation, real robots) for scalable manipulation; shows strong real-world AgiBot results and data-driven scaling with more human pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address scarcity and heterogeneity of robot data; naive pooling leads to negative transfer; need to leverage abundant human egocentric video and bridge supervision/embodiment gaps.

Method: Proposes implicit action alignment to infer latent actions from visual transitions; explicit alignment uses canonical action representation and camera-frame end-effector actions to ground human and robot trajectories; combines world-dynamics priors with visual semantics; inner-outer RL loop for task adaptation and policy improvement.

Result: Real-world AgiBot benchmark, strong performance on seen tasks and unseen variations; task score scales with volume of human pretraining; no plateau observed; human data becomes primary axis.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that abundant but weakly labeled human experience can be converted into transferable training signals for manipulation; highlights the potential of human video to scale capabilities.

Abstract: Robot data is scarce, so generalist policies need to learn from heterogeneous sources, including human egocentric video, simulation, and real robots, which differ in supervision and embodiment, with action labels missing or mutually incompatible. Human egocentric data scale best but sit farthest from robot data, and naive pooling causes negative transfer rather than knowledge sharing. We propose JoyAI-RA 0.5, a generalist Vision-Language-World-Action (VLWA) framework that couples physical world-dynamics priors with visual semantics and scales manipulation learning across such data via dual action alignment. Implicit action alignment infers latent actions from visual transitions, enabling action-free human, simulation, and robot data to guide a latent-action-conditioned world model in learning physical dynamics. Explicit alignment grounds reliable human and robot trajectories in a unified physical action space through a canonical action representation and camera-frame chunk-relative end-effector actions. An inner-outer-loop reinforcement stage then pairs efficient task adaptation with foundation-policy improvement. On a real-world AgiBot benchmark, JoyAI-RA performs strongly on both seen tasks and unseen variations. The task score improves consistently as the volume of human egocentric pretraining data increases and shows no sign of plateauing at our largest scale. This suggests that abundant but weakly labeled human experience can be converted into a transferable training signal, making human video not merely a weak auxiliary source but a primary axis along which manipulation capability can be scaled. Project page can be found at https://joyai-ra-05.github.io/.

</details>


### [297] [Nonvisual Classification of Ground-Condition by Artificial Proprioception in an Amoeba-Inspired Autonomous Walking Robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05684)
*Hyoto Yamaguchi,Zenji Yatabe,Seiya Kasai*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Nonvisual ground-condition classification for a four-legged robot using proprioceptive sensing and reservoir computing to distinguish flat vs rough terrain, enabling real-time gait switching; robust to motion-induced sensor fluctuations; includes sensor contribution analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable robust locomotion without vision by inferring terrain from proprioceptive signals, reducing reliance on image processing.

Method: Integrates a three-axis accelerometer, eight foot pressure sensors, and reservoir computing (RC) to classify ground condition (flat vs rough). Evaluates performance under dynamic walking and analyzes each sensor's contribution to the classification. Demonstrates real-time gait adaptation based on inferred terrain.

Result: High classification accuracy despite large sensor fluctuations during walking; successful on-site gait switching in response to ground condition; insights into the role of individual sensors in the decision.

Conclusion: Shows feasibility of nonvisual terrain classification using multimodal proprioception and RC for adaptive locomotion, with potential for more robust, vision-free navigation and further exploration of sensor contributions.

Abstract: Nonvisual classification of ground condition based on a multimodal sensing approach was investigated for an amoeba-inspired autonomous walking robot. To classify ground condition without image sensing and processing, we implemented artificial proprioception by integrating a three-axis accelerometer, eight foot pressure sensors, and reservoir computing (RC). Even when large fluctuations in the sensor outputs are caused by dynamic motions of a four-legged robot in walking, our system can classify the ground condition, flat or rough, with high accuracy. We demonstrate on-site switching of walking gait depending on ground condition in the robot. We also discuss the contribution of each sensor to ground condition classification.

</details>


### [298] [Hijacking Robots with a Piece of Paper: A Systematic Study of Physical Prompt Injection in VLM-Controlled Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05715)
*S. M . Bhagya P. Samarakoon,M. A. Viraj J. Muthugala,W. K. R. Sachinthana,Mohan Rajesh Elara*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Systematic study of physical prompt injection in vision-language–controlled robots. Introduces a four-category taxonomy and a 20-prompt benchmark across layouts and commands; attacks show non-trivial success on three frontier VLMs; analyzes reasoning traces; evaluates three defenses (prompt filtering, two-stage verification, text masking) with substantial effectiveness; defenses reduce risk but may hinder reading in-scene labels and require trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify and mitigate security risks from in-scene textual prompts acting as indirect prompts to VLM-based robotic planning, a realistic attack surface as VLMs are increasingly used in autonomous tasks.

Method: Four-category taxonomy (indirect signage, task redefinition, authority impersonation, conflict injection); 20 attack prompts tested across three physical scene layouts and three command formulations; evaluated on three frontier VLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B); 5,670 trials; analysis of reasoning traces; evaluation of three defenses: prompt-based defense (75-100% effective, model-dependent), two-stage verification (85-100%), pre-processing text masking (100%).

Result: Attacks succeed at 27.0%, 29.4%, and 5.0% across the three models; authority-impersonating and negation attacks transfer across all models; models exhibit model-specific defense behaviors (explicit rejection in Gemini; perceptual inattention in GPT-4o); defenses substantially reduce risk (75-100%, 85-100%, 100% respectively) while preserving general task capabilities; however, defenses may impair reading-in-scene labels.

Conclusion: Vision-language–driven robotic planning is meaningfully vulnerable to human-readable physical signage, but simple defenses can substantially mitigate risk with manageable trade-offs in task performance.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as planners in robotic systems, where they translate natural-language commands into executable actions grounded in visual scene understanding. This tight coupling between perception and instruction-following introduces a new attack surface: adversarial text placed within the robot's visual field can act as an indirect prompt injection into the VLM's reasoning stack. We present a systematic study of physical prompt injection attacks against VLM-controlled sorting, introducing a four-category taxonomy, indirect signage, task redefinition, authority impersonation, and conflict injection, instantiated as a benchmark of 20 attack prompts evaluated across three physical scene layouts and three command formulations that vary in destination specificity and rule explicitness. Across 5,670 trials on three frontier VLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B), attacks succeed at 27.0%, 29.4%, and 5.0% respectively, with authority-impersonating and negation attacks transferring across all three models. Analysis of reasoning traces reveals that successful compromise is nearly always conscious (99.9% acknowledgment rate), and that models defend through structurally different mechanisms, explicit rejection for Gemini, perceptual inattention for GPT-4o. We evaluate three simple mitigations: prompt-based defense (75-100% effective, model-dependent), two-stage verification (85-100%), and pre-processing text masking (100%). Our findings show that VLM-controlled manipulation is meaningfully vulnerable to human-readable physical signage, and that simple defenses substantially reduce risk, though defense choice involves trade-offs. The defenses preserve general task capabilities in our benchmark, but they may impair tasks that require reading in-scene labels.

</details>


### [299] [ATP: Anatomical Torque with Passivity-based Control Framework for Safe Upper-Limb Exoskeleton Assistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05723)
*Yu Chen,Gong Chen,Xiang Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Anatomical Torque with Passivity-Based Control (ATP) for upper-limb exoskeletons, integrating a reinforcement-learning muscle controller, online torque refinement, and a cable-driven, energy-tank–based passivity controller; demonstrates safe, generalizable torque assistance with EMG improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend anatomical torque assistance from lower-limb to complex, nonperiodic upper-limb movements, ensuring safety, generalization across tasks, and formal passivity guarantees.

Method: 1) Scalable musculoskeletal simulation trains a unified RL muscle controller that generalizes across upper-limb movements and outputs anatomical reference torques. 2) Online torque-refinement adapts references, suppresses tendon-induced spikes, and includes a learned anomaly score for safe assistance. 3) Interaction torque controller delivers assistance via a cable-driven compliant exoskeleton; an energy tank preserves passivity and provides torque-tracking guarantees, with theoretical analysis. 

Result: Simulations and real-world experiments show accurate tracking of long-duration motion sequences and generalization to real-time movements; accurate torque tracking while preserving passivity; the system resumes tracking after energy-tank replenishment. An EMG study with five participants shows reduced target-muscle activity during static and dynamic tasks compared with gravity compensation and open-loop assistance, up to 48% reduction in a dynamic multi-joint task.

Conclusion: ATP offers a safe, generalizable framework for upper-limb exoskeleton assistance with formal passivity guarantees and demonstrated muscle activity reductions; supports real-world applicability and warrants further validation on larger cohorts.

Abstract: Providing assistance across diverse movements is a central objective of exoskeletons, and anatomical knowledge can enable responsive support that generalizes across tasks. However, anatomical assistance has mainly been studied for lower-limb exoskeletons, where periodic, weight-bearing motions impose lower demands on torque precision. Extending such assistance to complex, nonperiodic upper-limb movements remains challenging. This paper proposes Anatomical Torque with Passivity-Based Control (ATP) for safe upper-limb exoskeleton assistance. First, a scalable musculoskeletal simulation framework trains a unified reinforcement-learning muscle controller that generalizes across upper-limb movements and generates anatomical reference torques without complex biomechanical computations. Second, an online torque-refinement scheme adapts the reference to diverse movements, suppresses tendon-induced spikes, and incorporates a learned anomaly score for safe and comfortable assistance. Third, an interaction torque controller delivers assistance through a cable-driven compliant exoskeleton without constraining motion to predefined trajectories, while an energy tank preserves passivity with theoretical guarantees on torque tracking and system passivity. Simulations and real-world experiments show accurate tracking of long-duration motion sequences and generalization to real-time human movements. The controller achieves accurate torque tracking while preserving passivity and resumes tracking after energy-tank replenishment. An EMG study with five participants further shows reduced target-muscle activity during static and dynamic tasks compared with gravity compensation and open-loop assistance, with reductions of up to 48% relative to movement without the exoskeleton in a dynamic multi-joint task.

</details>


### [300] [Near-sensor Computing for Rapid Visuotactile Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05725)
*Zhengying Zhu,Ruilin Zhang,Runze Hu,Chenxi Xiao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Near-sensor, streaming spectral Poisson solver enables deterministic, low-latency tactile geometry reconstruction with modest power, improving reaction time over host-based processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce power, data-transfer overhead, and scheduling latency in visuotactile sensing to enable faster, more reliable tactile responses in robotics.

Method: Implement a spectral Poisson solver as a fully streaming hardware pipeline (near-sensor). Operate at 166 MHz; process 128x128 frames with no data-dependent branching or iterative convergence to ensure deterministic latency (0.211 ms to first depth value). Measure across 15 contact geometries.

Result: First depth value after 35,107 cycles; fixed latency 0.211 ms. Depth error of 0.17% of peak contact depth across geometries. Reflex loop time: 28.3 ± 4.9 ms (near-sensor) vs 169.9 ± 27.8 ms (host). Power consumption: ~347 mW for the core. Demonstrates accurate, energy-efficient, deterministic tactile geometry suitable for rapid responses.

Conclusion: Near-sensor reconstruction with a streaming spectral Poisson solver delivers accurate, energy-efficient, and deterministic tactile geometry with significantly faster reflexes than host-based processing, validating the approach for real-time robotic tactile control.

Abstract: Visuotactile sensors reconstruct dense contact geometry from measured surface gradients, but host-based processing increases power consumption and introduces data-transfer delays and variable scheduling latency, limiting the sensing and response speed of robotic systems. To address these limitations, we implement a near-sensor computing framework that includes a spectral Poisson solver as a fully streaming hardware pipeline. The computational core logic has an estimated power consumption of 347 mW and achieves high throughput without data-dependent branching or iterative convergence, thereby providing deterministic latency. Operating at 166 MHz, the pipeline produces the first depth value of each 128x128 frame 35,107 cycles after receiving the first input pixel, corresponding to a fixed latency of 0.211 ms. Across 15 contact geometries, the reconstructed depths differ from a double-precision reference by 0.17 % of the peak contact depth. On-chip decisions based on these reconstructions close a robot protective reflex loop in 28.3 +/- 4.9 ms, compared with 169.9 +/- 27.8 ms for an equivalent host-based loop using the same actuator. These results demonstrate that near-sensor reconstruction can provide accurate, energy-efficient, and deterministic tactile geometry on timescales suitable for rapid robotic contact responses.

</details>


### [301] [In-Context VLA: Endowing Vision-Language-Action Models with Language via In-Context Post-Training and Agentic Tool Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05738)
*Jiarui Yang,Wen Huang,Jiale Zhang,Maowei Hu,Hang Guo*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CoT text reasoning degrades low-level control in VLA models; introduce in-context post-training and agentic tool-use to ground language, yielding better task performance and efficiency across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA systems trained by imitation on static observations struggle when asked to reason with language; ungrounded CoT can hurt timing and action quality. A grounded-language approach may better support real-time manipulation.

Method: 1) In-context post-training: inject perceptual evidence as structured context and supervise only on actions. 2) Agentic tool-use interface: policy queries open-vocabulary detectors, monocular depth, and a vision-language model to acquire task-relevant information. 3) Data engine: generates diverse, paraphrased, and evidence-conditioned spatial descriptions to train the policy to interpret unseen language.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance and efficiency across RoboCasa-GR1, SimplerEnv, LIBERO simulators and 8 real-world robot manipulation tasks, outperforming CoT-based approaches under matched configurations.

Conclusion: VLA benefits from grounded language rather than free-form language generation; the proposed framework enables robust, efficient manipulation by grounding language in perception and action.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become the dominant recipe for generalist manipulation, yet they are almost universally trained by behavior cloning: a policy imitates expert action chunks conditioned on a static image and a fixed instruction. A natural remedy is to inject explicit reasoning through textual chain-of-thought (CoT). We show, both empirically and analytically, that free-form textual CoT degrades low-level control: the reasoning it produces is ungrounded, its latency breaks closed-loop timing, and, crucially, the reasoning and action tokens are optimized against conflicting objectives so that the policy learns to narrate rather than to act. We argue that what a VLA needs is not the ability to generate language, but the ability to consume grounded language. To this end we introduce \textbf{\ourmethod{}}, a framework that endows a VLA with language competence through (i) in-context post-training, in which perceptual evidence is injected as structured context and the model is supervised only on actions, and (ii) an agentic tool-use interface, in which the policy queries open-vocabulary detectors, monocular depth, and a vision--language model to actively acquire task-relevant information. Rather than emitting a single templated caption, our data engine produces diverse, paraphrased, and evidence-conditioned spatial descriptions, so that the policy learns to interpret language it has never seen verbatim. Across the RoboCasa-GR1, SimplerEnv, and LIBERO simulation benchmarks, together with 8 real-world robot manipulation tasks, our method consistently achieves SOTA results in both performance and efficiency when compared with CoT-based approaches under matched configurations.

</details>


### [302] [Acoustic-driven millimetric helical robot: ultrasonic synergistic manipulation in confined fluidic environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05746)
*Hanlin Wang,Xin Wang,Xinwei Wei,Jiaxu Liu,Le Wang,Shengze Cai,Chao Xu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A coordinated multi-acoustic-field strategy enables millimeter-scale helical robots to be propelled and maneuvered using acoustic radiation forces and acoustic streaming, validated by simulations and experiments including in vitro vessel tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scale non-contact acoustic manipulation from micro/nano to millimeter robots in confined biological environments where propulsion is inefficient, enabling versatile biomedical mobility.

Method: Integrates acoustic radiation forces with acoustic streaming through coordinated fields; conducts multiphysics simulations; performs experiments on millimeter-scale helical robots; semi-autonomous navigation; in vitro porcine venous vessel tests.

Result: Demonstrates planar navigation, inclined climbing, and vertical motion; ultrasonic synergy improves maneuverability; successful unidirectional and reciprocating motion under confinement; provides mechanistic insight into millimeter-scale acoustic micromanipulation.

Conclusion: Shows feasibility of scaling acoustic micromanipulation to the millimeter regime and supports biomedical applications requiring versatile, controllable robotic mobility in confined environments.

Abstract: Acoustic field-driven manipulation provides a non-contact and non-invasive strategy for controlling microscale and nanoscale objects, yet its extension to millimeter-scale robots was limited by insufficient propulsion efficiency in confined biological environments. Here, a coordinated multi-acoustic-field approach is introduced, which harnesses the synergistic action of acoustic radiation forces and acoustic streaming flows to enable controlled locomotion of millimeter-scale helical robots and enhance propulsion. Multiphysics simulations captured the dynamics of millimeter-scale helical robots under combined acoustic fields, and experimental validation demonstrated their locomotion capabilities, including planar navigation, inclined climbing, and vertical motion. Semi-autonomous navigation experiments further confirmed that ultrasonic synergy substantially improved maneuverability. In vitro tests in porcine venous vessels demonstrated that coordinated acoustic fields supported both unidirectional and reciprocating motion under biologically relevant confinement. These findings provide mechanistic insight into scaling acoustic micromanipulation to the millimetre regime and support biomedical applications requiring versatile and controllable robotic mobility.

</details>


### [303] [XEWorld: Can Action-Conditioned World Models Generalize to Unseen Robot Embodiments?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05799)
*Yixiang Chen,Jiabing Yang,Yuan Xu,Qisen Ma,Keji He,Peiyan Li,Kai Wang,Ziheng He,Xiangnan Wu,Jing Liu,Nianfeng Liu,Yan Huang,Liang Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: XEWorld shows current action-conditioned world models mostly memorize visual patterns rather than physical dynamics, failing zero-shot cross-embodiment generalization; even few-shot adaptation induces catastrophic forgetting, indicating need to decouple appearance from dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether world models truly learn transferable physical dynamics by testing on unseen robot embodiments in identical scenes, addressing a key gap where models may rely on visual similarity.

Method: Introduce XEWorld: a controlled cross-embodiment testbed that isolates embodiment by evaluating held-out robots in physically identical scenes. Systematically analyze how models render unseen embodiments, their ability to map joint actions to visual trajectories, and their capacity to predict dynamic changes from static observations; evaluate zero-shot generalization and few-shot adaptation with attention to catastrophic forgetting.

Result: Findings indicate models function as 2D visual pattern matchers, with generalization governed by visual similarity rather than physical kinematics. They struggle to translate abstract joint actions into coherent trajectories and to predict dynamics from static inputs. Zero-shot success requires heavy pixel-space cues and temporal alignment; even with few-shot adaptation, there is catastrophic forgetting of seen embodiments.

Conclusion: Current architectures fail to generalize physical dynamics across visual appearances. Achieving true cross-embodiment generalization requires architectural innovations that disentangle physical dynamics from visual appearance.

Abstract: Action-conditioned world models are promising learned simulators for robotic manipulation, yet evaluating them exclusively on training robots fails to reveal whether they capture physical dynamics or merely memorize visual patterns. To answer whether a model can faithfully render a robot it has never seen, we introduce XEWorld, a controlled cross-embodiment testbed for world models that isolates embodiments by evaluating held-out robots within physically identical scenes. Our systematic analysis uncovers a shared architectural bottleneck: current models act primarily as 2D visual pattern matchers whose generalization is governed by visual similarity rather than physical kinematic similarity. Driven by this limitation, they struggle to translate abstract numeric joint actions into coherent visual trajectories, and fail to predict dynamic visual changes from static initial observations. Consequently, successfully rendering an unseen embodiment zero-shot strictly requires heavily grounded cues, specifically pixel-space actions and explicit spatial-temporal alignment. Even when bypassing this zero-shot barrier via few-shot adaptation, the forced appearance recovery triggers catastrophic forgetting of seen embodiments. Together, these failures expose a critical inability to apply learned physical dynamics to novel visual appearances, highlighting that achieving true cross-embodiment generalization requires architectural innovations that decouple visual appearance from underlying physical dynamics.

</details>


### [304] [Coordinated Multi-Robot Disassembly for Makespan Optimization of Large-Scale Assemblies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05830)
*Niklas Hargus,Andreas Orthey,Marc Toussaint*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CoMuDi coordinates multi-robot disassembly in confined spaces by integrating ST-RRT* into a temporal-constrained task-and-motion planning framework, yielding higher success rates and shorter makespans on large assemblies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Disassembly in restricted workspaces requires synchronized, collision-free, time-efficient planning for multiple robots; existing TM planning methods struggle with large-scale tasks and tight temporal dependencies.

Method: Constructs compound pick/place/exit tasks from a team, assembly, and dependency graph; propagates temporal constraints to optimize start/end times; embeds space-time RRT* (ST-RRT*) to minimize task arrival times; compares against standard RRT* with varying time bounds; evaluates on six assemblies (≤49 pieces, ≤9 robots).

Result: ST-RRT*-enabled CoMuDi achieves higher success rates and shorter makespans; reduces idle times; demonstrates scalability to large assemblies.

Conclusion: CoMuDi with ST-RRT* is an effective, scalable approach for coordinated multi-robot disassembly in confined environments, providing reliable planning and efficient schedules.

Abstract: Multi-robot task and motion planning for disassembly tasks requires robots to operate in confined workspaces while coordinating their motions with other robots. To tackle this problem, we propose a planning method called coordinated multi-robot disassembly (CoMuDi). CoMuDi coordinates a team of robots for disassembly tasks. The input is a team of robots, an assembly of objects, and a dependency graph. Based on this information, we create compound tasks for pick, place, and exit motions. By propagating temporal constraints, we ensure that each robot can start and end their tasks as early as possible while avoiding collisions with nearby robots. By integrating the space-time RRT* planner (ST-RRT*) into CoMuDi, we ensure that individual tasks minimize arrival time and thereby help us minimize overall makespan. We compare the performance of CoMuDi using both ST-RRT* and RRT* planners with varying time bounds, demonstrating that the combination of CoMuDi and ST-RRT* leads to a higher success rate while minimizing makespan. Finally, we evaluate CoMuDi on six assemblies with up to 49 pieces and up to 9 robots. In those scenarios, we show that CoMuDi returns robot paths that exhibit low idle times, thereby demonstrating that CoMuDi can reliably solve large-scale assemblies.

</details>


### [305] [SkillMemo: Expert-guided Skill Memory Framework for Compositional Embodied Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05970)
*Changyuan Wang,Chubin Zhang,Zhenyu Wu,Runhao Li,Angyuan Ma,Ke Chao,Yinan Liang,Xiuwei Xu,Ziwei Wang,Yansong Tang,Jiwen Lu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes SkillMemo, a memory-augmented framework for long-horizon embodied manipulation that decomposes demonstrations into latent skills via MoE segmentation and stores skill primitives in an episodic memory; retrieves and fuses skills to improve DP and VLA, achieving SOTA and strong compositional generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome scarce large-scale embodied trajectory datasets and poor compositional generalization in out-of-distribution tasks by explicitly modeling reusable skill structures and long-horizon dependencies.

Method: 1) MoE-based expert-guided trajectory segmentation to produce skill primitives; 2) Skill-level episodic memory storing compact key-value representations; 3) Inference-time retrieval of relevant skills and fusion with current gating to bias action predictions.

Result: Empirical evaluation on simulation and real-world manipulation tasks shows consistent improvements for DP and VLA backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance and strong OOD compositional generalization, outperforming π_{0.5}.

Conclusion: Memory-augmented latent skill decomposition is effective for long-horizon embodied tasks, enabling robust generalization and leveraging reusable skill structures to augment existing visuomotor models.

Abstract: Embodied visuomotor models, including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have demonstrated promising performance on robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their potential remains fundamentally constrained by the scarcity of large-scale embodied trajectory datasets, leading to insufficient compositional generalization in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios with limited capability to capture reusable skill structures. To address this limitation, we propose Skill-Based Memory (SkillMemo) framework that implicitly decomposes long-horizon demonstrations into latent atomic skills and integrates skill-level features into a dynamic episodic memory bank for solving compositional tasks. Specifically, we first introduce an expert-guided trajectory segmentation module built upon a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which implicitly partitions trajectories into distinct skill primitives represented by learned gating coefficients. We further design a skill-level episodic memory architecture that stores compact skill representations as retrievable key-value pairs. During inference, the memory bank retrieves the most relevant skill primitives which are subsequently fused with the model's current gating distribution, providing a robust contextual prior to refine action predictions. Extensive experiments on the simulation benchmark and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that SkillMemo consistently enhances both DP and VLA backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance and outperforming $π_{0.5}$, while exhibiting strong compositional generalization to unseen task configurations.

</details>


### [306] [TRACE: Learned Proprioceptive Odometry for Legged Robots under Unreliable Contact Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05975)
*Taehyeon Kong,Woojin Kim,Jemin Hwangbo*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TRACE is a robust, end-to-end proprioceptive odometry estimator for legged robots that uses tokenized robust attention and a foot-aware cross-attention module to fuse IMU and leg data, with physics-inspired losses and sim-to-real transfer techniques; it achieves reduced position drift across diverse terrains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unreliable contact degrades legged odometry; manual thresholds are brittle; need an end-to-end approach leveraging onboard sensors with better generalization and sim-to-real transfer.

Method: End-to-end estimator predicting relative pose and body velocity from history of IMU and joint measurements; foot-aware cross-attention adaptively weights IMU and leg tokens without manual contact/slip thresholds; direct supervision with two physics-inspired auxiliary losses promoting kinematic consistency and proper use of leg information; policy randomization during simulation; partial real-world fine-tuning of temporal encoder and prediction head.

Result: Consistent reductions in position drift vs classical filtering-based, hybrid, and pure learning baselines across indoor/outdoor terrains; ablations confirm impact of training objectives, policy randomization, and real-world fine-tuning, especially under unreliable contacts and sim-to-real mismatch.

Conclusion: TRACE improves robustness to unreliable contacts and enhances sim-to-real transfer for proprioceptive odometry in legged robots through tokenized attention and physics-inspired training; the approach generalizes across terrains and reduces drift.

Abstract: In this paper, we present TRACE (Tokenized Robust Attention for Contact-Aware Estimation), an end-to-end learned proprioceptive odometry estimator for legged robots under unreliable contact conditions. The proposed estimator directly predicts relative displacement, relative rotation, and body-frame velocity from a recent history of onboard inertial and joint measurements. To improve robustness under unreliable contact conditions, we introduce a foot-aware cross-attention module that adaptively weights IMU and leg-wise kinematic tokens without relying on manually defined contact or slip thresholds. The estimator is trained with direct supervision and two physics-inspired auxiliary losses that promote kinematic consistency and reliable use of leg information. To reduce policy-specific overfitting and consequently improve sim-to-real transfer, simulation training incorporates policy randomization, followed by partial real-world fine-tuning of the temporal encoder and prediction head. Experiments across diverse indoor and outdoor terrains demonstrate consistent reductions in position drift compared with classical filtering-based, hybrid, and purely learning-based baselines. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of the proposed training objectives, policy randomization, and real-world fine-tuning, particularly under unreliable contacts and sim-to-real mismatch.

</details>


### [307] [Beyond Flat Policies: Hierarchical Post-Training for Embodied Agents in Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05999)
*He Kong,Zengjue Chen,Qi Wang,Qianli Xing,Runliang Niu,Peidong Liu,Jiawei Li,Shiqi Wang,Yi Chang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HiRoC is a hierarchical post-training framework for robotic manipulation that separates high-level planning from low-level execution, using subgoal-guided reinforcement learning and a pre-RL alignment step to reduce planning-execution distribution shifts, yielding strong results on manipulation benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the limitations of flat post-trained VLA models that lack explicit task progression, and of offline hierarchical methods that rely on demonstrations and don't leverage online interaction for improvement.

Method: A two-module architecture: a planner that decomposes tasks into executable subgoals and an executor that learns subgoal-conditioned actions via reinforcement learning. An alignment step aligns executor subgoal-conditioned behaviors with planner subgoals before RL to reduce distribution misalignment between planning and execution.

Result: HiRoC consistently outperforms strong baselines across diverse robotic manipulation benchmarks; comprehensive analyses validate the efficacy of hierarchical post-training and the contribution of each component.

Conclusion: Hierarchical post-training with explicit task progression and subgoal-guided RL, coupled with a planner-executor alignment step, improves long-horizon manipulation and robustness.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robotic manipulation by leveraging pretrained vision-language models. However, existing post-training methods predominantly optimize VLA models as flat policies, making it difficult to explicitly model task progression and perform robust long-horizon manipulation. Although hierarchical approaches introduce task decomposition, they mainly rely on supervised learning from offline demonstrations and cannot effectively improve execution through online interaction. To address this limitation, we propose Hierarchical Robotic Control (HiRoC), a hierarchical post-training framework that decouples high-level task planning from low-level action execution. The planner decomposes complex tasks into executable subgoals to provide explicit semantic guidance, while the executor continuously improves subgoal-conditioned action generation through reinforcement learning. To enable effective collaboration between the two modules, we further align the executor with planner-generated subgoals before reinforcement learning, mitigating the distribution misalignment between planning and execution. Extensive experiments across diverse robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that HiRoC consistently outperforms strong baselines. Comprehensive analyses further validate the effectiveness of hierarchical post-training and the contribution of each key component.

</details>


### [308] [Adaptive-WAM: Quality-Guided Early-Exit Planning from Intermediate Video-Diffusion Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06008)
*Sining Ang,Yuguang Yang,Yan Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Adaptive-WAM introduces a quality-aware multi-exit planner for diffusion-based video world models in autonomous driving, enabling early exit from the DiT backbone based on trajectory quality to avoid full diffusion/VAE decoding, achieving state-of-the-art PDMS/EPDMS with low latency and good transfer without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large video diffusion models provide rich spatiotemporal priors for autonomous driving but are costly to run; deployment only requires an ego trajectory. The work investigates how much of the video diffusion model is necessary to produce reliable driving decisions, examining video-denoising timesteps and DiT depth, and seeks to reduce compute via adaptive depth.

Method: Attach trajectory diffusion heads to selected DiT blocks and use a lightweight trajectory-quality scorer to terminate inference once the best decoded trajectory meets a quality threshold; otherwise continue from cached hidden states to a deeper exit. Built on Wan2.2-5B backbone with trajectory heads and a multi-exit planner that avoids iterative classifier-free denoising and VAE decoding. Evaluates adaptive single-trajectory and fixed-exit variants with 64 proposals on NAVSIM and NAVSIM v2; tests cross-domain transfer to nuScenes; reports PDMS/EPDMS and L2 error with latency metrics on A100.

Result: Adaptive single-trajectory planner achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM; fixed-exit variant reaches 92.6 PDMS with 64 proposals. In NAVSIM v2, attains 89.9 EPDMS, the best among front-view video world-model planners. Zero-shot transfer to nuScenes yields 0.88 m average L2 error and 0.08% collision rate. On an A100, adaptive routing raises PDMS from 90.62 to 90.79 with end-to-end planning latency ~170 ms, about 10% faster than a fixed block-15 planner and ~47% faster than a fixed full-depth planner.

Conclusion: Adaptive-WAM demonstrates that reliable driving decisions can be produced with partial backbones by early exiting based on trajectory quality, avoiding heavy diffusion/VAE steps while maintaining state-of-the-art planning performance and transferability; code will be released.

Abstract: Large video diffusion models provide rich spatiotemporal priors for autonomous driving, but existing world-action models often inherit the cost of iterative future-video generation even though deployment only requires an ego trajectory. We ask a more basic question: how much of a video diffusion model must be executed to make a reliable driving decision? Through a controlled study of video denoising timesteps and Diffusion Transformer (DiT) depth, we find that planning performance is largely insensitive to the tested video-noise levels, whereas strong trajectories can already be decoded from intermediate layers. Based on this observation, we introduce Adaptive-WAM, a quality-aware multi-exit planner built on a Wan2.2-5B backbone. Trajectory diffusion heads are attached to selected DiT blocks, and a lightweight trajectory-quality scorer terminates inference once the best trajectory decoded so far satisfies a quality threshold; otherwise, computation continues from the cached hidden state to a deeper exit. The deployed planner therefore avoids the iterative classifier-free denoising loop and VAE decoding required for future-video synthesis, while dynamically allocating backbone depth according to trajectory quality. On NAVSIM, the adaptive single-trajectory planner achieves 90.8 PDMS; a separate fixed-exit variant reaches 92.6 PDMS with 64 proposals. It further obtains 89.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, yielding the best reported results among the compared front-view video world-model planners. Without target-domain fine-tuning, Adaptive-WAM transfers to nuScenes with 0.88 m average L2 error and a 0.08\% collision rate. On an A100, adaptive routing improves PDMS from 90.62 to 90.79 while averaging 170 ms end-to-end planning latency, approximately 10\% below the 190 ms fixed block-15 planner and 47\% below the 320 ms fixed full-depth planner. Code will be released.

</details>


### [309] [Topometric Autonomous Vehicle Localization by Combining Visual Embeddings and Feed-Forward 3D Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06021)
*Eulogio Quemada-Torres,Alberto Jaenal,Francisco-Angel Moreno,Javier Gonzalez-Jimenez*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Topometric sequential localization fusing probabilistic VPR with FF3D metric pose estimates via offline pose-appearance mapping and online particle filtering, yielding improved accuracy and robustness over appearance-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VL needs compact yet robust maps with metric precision. VPR offers compactness but lacks metric accuracy; FF3D provides accurate neural geometry. Integrating both aims to achieve scalable, metric-aware localization.

Method: An offline mapping tool models the topometric pose–appearance interaction across scene parts; an online particle filter combines odometry, place beliefs, and FF3D inference to estimate pose; modular design keeps descriptor extractor and FF3D model interchangeable; evaluated on three benchmarks with analysis showing resilience to perceptual aliasing.

Result: Substantial improvements over existing appearance-based methods demonstrated on three benchmarks; the framework’s modularity preserves interchangeability of descriptors and FF3D models; sequential belief helps mitigate severe failures due to perceptual aliasing.

Conclusion: The approach enables incorporating neural metric estimation into probabilistic appearance-based localization, with sequential belief improving robustness in appearance-driven localization tasks.

Abstract: Effective Visual Localization (VL) requires a map of the environment that combines compactness for efficient scalability with robustness against visual appearance changes and metric precision. Through low-dimensional image embeddings, Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is able to successfully meet the first two requirements, but its low metric accuracy makes it less suitable than standard VL approaches based on local features or neural representations. This limitation can be overcome by integrating VPR with the accurate local trajectory estimates produced by feed-forward neural 3D geometry (FF3D) models. In this paper, we address sequential appearance-based localization through a topometric framework that iteratively combines probabilistic VPR with FF3D metric pose estimation in controlled image sets. Our approach proposes an automatic offline mapping tool that models the topometric pose-appearance interaction in the different parts of the scene. This map is later employed by an online particle filter that estimates the pose from odometry and belief over places for FF3D inference, successfully incorporating neural metric estimation into probabilistic appearance-based localization. We extensively evaluate the framework on three known benchmarks, demonstrating substantial improvements over existing appearance-based methods. The modularity of our approach allows the descriptor extractor and FF3D model to remain interchangeable, and a focused analysis further shows that sequential belief can mitigate severe failures under perceptual aliasing.

</details>


### [310] [IcFuzz: Fuzzing Isaac Sim with Semantic Stage Guidance and Multi-level Mutation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06088)
*Zhixiang Chen,Zhuangbin Chen,Ruoxi Jia,Zeqin Liao,Wei Li,Jinyang Liu,Zibin Zheng*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: IcFuzz is the first fuzzing framework for NVIDIA Isaac Sim that uses an LLM-based semantic stage segmentation to decompose simulation programs into context-aware stages, applies multi-level mutation operators across hierarchical granularity, and uses a multi-armed bandit to adapt mutation scheduling. It achieves higher code coverage than baselines and uncovers more bugs, including multiple crashes and developer-confirmed fixes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure reliability and robustness of complex GPU-accelerated robotics simulators (Isaac Sim) by addressing reliability gaps due to bugs within its large, stateful, and semantically rich simulation programs; existing fuzzers struggle with context-aware semantics, hierarchical control, and vast state spaces.

Method: 1) LLM-based semantic stage segmentation to partition simulation programs into context-aware stages. 2) Design of multi-level mutation operators that operate at different hierarchical granularities guided by segmentation. 3) Multi-armed bandit algorithm to adaptively schedule mutation operators for efficient exploration of the simulation state space.

Result: IcFuzz achieved approximately 190%-205% code coverage compared with baselines. It detected an average of 3.7 unique crashes over three rounds of 12-hour tests, while baselines found no crashes. Across ~4 months, IcFuzz uncovered 11 bugs, with 9 confirmed or fixed by developers.

Conclusion: IcFuzz effectively enables fuzz testing for Isaac Sim by integrating semantic segmentation, hierarchical mutations, and adaptive operator scheduling, outperforming baselines in coverage and bug discovery and establishing a foundation for reliable simulation software development.

Abstract: Robotics simulators serve as a foundational infrastructure for embodied AI, facilitating safe and scalable robotic system development. NVIDIA Isaac Sim has emerged as one of the most popular simulators, distinguished by its GPU-accelerated physics engine and photorealistic rendering, which enable high-fidelity modeling of complex environments. However, its inherent complexity inevitably introduces software bugs that can compromise simulation reliability. Existing fuzzing approaches struggle to test Isaac Sim effectively due to challenges of context-aware object semantics, hierarchical simulation control, and a vast simulation state space.
  In this paper, we propose IcFuzz, the first fuzzing approach for Isaac Sim. IcFuzz first performs an LLM-based semantic stage segmentation, decomposing simulation programs into structured stages that capture context-aware object semantics. Guided by this information, IcFuzz designs multi-level mutation operators to systematically exercise the simulator across hierarchical granularities. To efficiently navigate the vast simulation state space, IcFuzz employs a multi-armed bandit algorithm to adaptively schedule mutation operators. Experimental results show that IcFuzz outperforms the baselines in terms of both code coverage and bug detection. Specifically, IcFuzz achieves approximately 190\%--205\% of the code coverage of the baselines and detects an average of 3.7 unique crashes over three rounds of 12-hour tests, while no crashes are detected by the baselines. Moreover, IcFuzz has uncovered 11 bugs over approximately four months, 9 of which have been confirmed or fixed by the developers.

</details>


### [311] [Visual Grounding in Zero-Shot Vision-Language Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06154)
*J. de Curtò,Dayani Plasencia,Diego Sánchez,I. de Zarzà*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VLMs largely fail to ground action decisions on visual input in direct-control tasks; findings show stimuli carry visual information (lead gap), but joint longitudinal and lateral grounding is not achieved; a symmetry-consensus guardian and an image-only perception show strong performance, suggesting VLMs are bounded hazard assistants rather than universal zero-shot controllers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether vision-language models used as zero-shot controllers actually ground decisions in visual input, or whether success stems from simulator dynamics or priors; quantify grounding through systematic input ablations and non-visual baselines across multiple models and simulators.

Method: Apply an input-ablation battery (blind-image controls, repeated identical inputs, lane-axis reflection, non-visual baselines, pipeline-integrity checks) to 9 direct-action models, 6 structured local VLMs, and an exploratory VLM-MPC; evaluate 32,874 scored calls across two embodiments and three simulators; assess joint longitudinal-lateral grounding; use post-hoc symmetry-consensus guardian to select models, then freeze a 2-of-4 hazard vote across original and reflected views; perform offline modular replay and nested cross-validation across held-out frames/episodes.

Result: Direct-control results largely negative: constant-SLOW policy outperforms a scripted geometric controller; several models are image-invariant or near-constant; models recognizing longitudinal hazards fail to translate LEFT/RIGHT under reflection; no local VLM meets joint grounding criteria. An image-only deterministic control estimates lead gap with 0.090 m MAE and exhibits exact mirror equivariance, indicating visuals carry sufficient information; failures are modular. A post-hoc guardian identifies two models from 16 calibration frames, achieving 0.954 balanced accuracy on 272 held-out frames (CI [0.895,0.990]); nested leave-one-episode-out recovers the same pair and threshold in all 12 folds; abstaining on ties increases balanced accuracy to 0.973 at 0.824 coverage. Offline modular replay with deterministic perception maintains lateral authority yields 0.934 action agreement and exact mirror equivariance.

Conclusion: VLMs in current form function as bounded, selective hazard-assist tools rather than universal zero-shot controllers. Grounding can be present under certain conditions (image-only perception), but reliable joint longitudinal-lateral grounding requires modular safeguards and gating; future work should emphasize interpretability, robust grounding tests, and safeguarded architecturals (guardians, calibrated ensembles) to harness VLMs for perception-enabled control.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as zero-shot controllers, but successful trajectories do not necessarily show that decisions are grounded in visual input: simulator dynamics and conservative action priors can produce favourable scores without meaningful perception. We investigate this with an input-ablation battery: blind-image controls, repeated identical inputs, lane-axis reflection, non-visual baselines, and pipeline-integrity checks. Across nine direct-action models, six structured local VLMs, and an exploratory VLM-MPC hierarchy, we analyse 32,874 scored calls over two embodiments and three simulators. The direct-control results are largely negative: a constant-SLOW policy outperforms a scripted geometric controller, several models are image-invariant or nearly constant, and models that recognize longitudinal hazards still fail to transform LEFT and RIGHT under reflection. No local VLM meets the joint longitudinal and lateral grounding criteria. However, an image-only deterministic positive control estimates the lead gap with 0.090 m MAE and exact mirror equivariance, confirming the stimuli carry sufficient visual information; the failures are modular, not universal. A post-hoc, leakage-controlled symmetry-consensus guardian selects two models from 16 calibration frames and freezes a 2-of-4 hazard vote across original and reflected views. On 272 held-out frames it reaches 0.954 balanced accuracy (episode-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [0.895,0.990]); nested leave-one-episode-out recovers the same pair and threshold in all 12 folds. Abstaining on ties raises committed balanced accuracy to 0.973 at 0.824 coverage. With deterministic perception retaining lateral authority, offline modular replay achieves 0.934 action agreement and exact mirror equivariance. These results support current VLMs as bounded, selective hazard assistants, not monolithic zero-shot controllers.

</details>


### [312] [Prior-SG: Task and Prior Driven Region Segmentation for Scene Graphs in Arbitrarily-Structured Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06170)
*Giorgio Tonetti,Laurent Kneip,Abel Gawel,Marco Hutter*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Prior-SG frames 3D scene understanding as probabilistic alignment, integrating priors and open-vocabulary cues to produce flexible, high-level scene graphs in open-plan environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome reliance on local clustering or rigid geometric rules that fail in open-plan or arbitrarily structured spaces; enable robust, task-driven semantic reasoning for autonomous platforms.

Method: Incremental fusion of RGB-D streams into a physically grounded Instance Graph; multi-scale open-vocabulary feature fusion; Prior Graph guided by a dynamically synthesized vocabulary from a Large Language Model; MAP inference with a Markov Random Field combining visual, geometric, and discrete-object cues to resolve perceptual ambiguities.

Result: Validated on diverse simulated residential datasets and large real-world open-plan environments; achieves state-of-the-art semantic region segmentation; robustly delineates distant functional boundaries without walls; enables zero-shot ontological flexibility to restructure spatial partitions according to high-level tasks.

Conclusion: Prior-SG delivers a robust, flexible, and scalable framework for task-driven 3D scene understanding, effectively fusing perception with topological priors and language-driven vocabularies to support adaptive spatial partitioning in complex environments.

Abstract: Hierarchical 3D scene graphs are a promising representation for high-level spatial reasoning in autonomous mobile platforms. However, existing extraction frameworks typically rely on purely local visual clustering or strict geometric heuristics, such as wall-separated rooms, which fail in open-plan or arbitrarily-structured environments. We propose Prior-SG, a task- and prior-driven framework that casts scene graph generation fundamentally as a probabilistic alignment problem. As the robot explores, it continuously aggregates an incoming RGB-D sensor stream into a physically grounded Instance Graph utilizing a multi-scale, open-vocabulary feature fusion strategy. The system then infers the high-level functional semantics of this map through a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate, guided by a Prior Graph-a logical expectation of the environment's structure and task-relevant vocabulary synthesized dynamically by a Large Language Model. By optimizing a Markov Random Field that fuses heterogeneous experts (visual, geometric, and discrete objects) with these topological priors, the system resolves local perceptual ambiguities. We validate this approach across diverse simulated residential datasets and large, open-plan real-world environments. Prior-SG achieves state-of-the-art semantic region segmentation accuracy compared to recent baselines, robustly delineates distant functional boundaries in the absence of physical walls, and uniquely provides zero-shot ontological flexibility, enabling the robot to entirely restructure its spatial partitioning based on a given high-level task.

</details>


### [313] [ErgoSurf: Ergodic Control for the Coverage of Unknown Surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06208)
*Stefan Schneyer,Timo Bachmann,Maged Iskandar,Korbinian Nottensteiner,Alin Albu-Schäffer,Freek Stulp,João Silvério*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An online ergodic control framework that learns unknown surface geometry online via GPIS using tactile sensing, using local tangent-plane point clouds as the sampling domain, and heat-diffusion potentials to drive ergodic exploration; validated in simulation and on a real robot with reconstruction errors near ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable systematic surface coverage for contact-centric tasks (inspection, cleaning, sanding, polishing) without prior surface geometry or vision-based scans, addressing dynamic/unknown environments.

Method: Integrate Gaussian Process Implicit Surfaces (GPIS) with tactile data to model the implicit surface online. At each contact, approximate the surface locally by tangent-plane point clouds, fit these samples with GPIS, and use this local GPIS as the sampling domain for both the target and ergodic coverage distributions. Employ a heat-diffusion analogy to convert coverage objectives into smooth potential fields guiding ergodic, energy-efficient trajectories.

Result: Demonstrated simultaneous ergodic coverage and online surface geometry learning in simulation and on real robots; reconstruction errors approach ground truth, indicating accurate surface learning without prior geometry.

Conclusion: The framework enables online, tactile-driven ergodic exploration over unknown surfaces, merging geometry learning with systematic coverage; suitable for real-time surface inspection/processing tasks, with potential extensions to dynamic or more complex surfaces.

Abstract: Contact-centric tasks on surfaces, ranging from inspection and cleaning to sanding and polishing, require robots to systematically cover the surface while maintaining stable contact. Ergodic control generates trajectories that spend time at a location proportional to a desired, task-specific spatial distribution, enabling efficient information gathering and coverage. However, traditional ergodic control methods rely on prior knowledge of surface geometry or require a vision sensory input to scan the geometry beforehand, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios with unknown or dynamic environments. This paper introduces a novel online ergodic control framework that achieves systematic surface coverage while simultaneously reconstructing unknown surface geometry. We employ a Gaussian Process Implicit Surface (GPIS) model that learns global surface geometry from intrinsic tactile sensing during execution. For efficient online planning, we approximate the surface locally using point clouds sampled from tangent planes at observed contact points and iteratively fit them to the Gaussian Process. This approximation simultaneously serves as the sampling domain for both the target and the coverage distributions. We employ a heat-diffusion analogy to compute potential fields that guide ergodic exploration, translating spatial coverage objectives into smooth robot trajectories. We demonstrate our framework through simulation and real-robot experiments, validating simultaneous ergodic coverage and online surface geometry learning with reconstruction errors approaching the ground truth.

</details>


### [314] [VIDP: Variable Impedance Diffusion Policy for Compliant Robot Manipulation from Diverse Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06210)
*Hisham Khalil,Neil Fernandes,Thomas M. Kwok,Hsiu-Chin Lin,Yue Hu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VIDP uses imitation learning with TP-DAMM to learn variable impedance control from demonstrations, mapping trajectory distributions to stiffness without force sensors, improving task success and reducing interaction forces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve robust contact-rich manipulation by endowing manipulators with task-consistent variable impedance learned from demonstrations, addressing the limitation that static compliance and naive trajectory variations may not reflect intentional compliance.

Method: Proposes Variable Impedance Diffusion Policy (VIDP) using Task-Parameterized Directionality-Aware Mixture Model (TP-DAMM) to extract physically consistent trajectory distributions from demonstrations, map to stiffness profiles, jointly predicting pose actions and task compliance without force sensors.

Result: Real-world experiments show VIDP outperforms fixed-impedance baselines in task success rate and reduces interaction forces compared to high stiffness controllers and tracking errors vs low stiffness baselines.

Conclusion: VIDP effectively learns compliant, variable impedance policies from demonstrations via TP-DAMM, enabling robust manipulation without force sensing in contact-rich tasks.

Abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires precise tracking and mechanical compliance, where variable impedance control can improve robustness in task success, whereas static compliance cannot adapt to varying contact constraints. Variable impedance skills can be learned from demonstrations, avoiding complex modeling, but compliance is a hidden variable in force-agnostic kinematic data. While existing methods infer compliance from trajectory variations, these variations may reflect geometric adaptation and not intentional compliance when subject to changing spatial layouts. Therefore, this letter introduces Variable Impedance Diffusion Policy (VIDP), an imitation learning-based variable impedance control framework leveraging a Task-Parameterized Directionality-Aware Mixture Model (TP-DAMM) to extract physically consistent trajectory distributions from diverse demonstrations. By mapping distributions to stiffness profiles, VIDP jointly predicts pose actions and task compliance without force sensors. Real-world experiments show that VIDP significantly outperforms fixed-impedance baselines in task success rate while reducing interaction forces with respect to high stiffness controllers and tracking errors with respect to low stiffness baselines.

</details>


### [315] [Design and Evaluation of a Touchscreen-Based Teleoperation Interface for Robotic Manipulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06219)
*Juan José García Cárdenas,Alperen Kenan,Hamidreza Raei,Paul Bremner,Manuel Giuliani,Arash Ajoudani,Adriana Tapus*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A touchscreen teleoperation interface mapping continuous finger movements to a Panda robot yields faster, more accurate surface manipulation with lower cognitive load than a joystick, and approaches autonomous mode in performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve teleoperation performance and operator cognitive load for delicate surface-contact tasks in challenging environments (e.g., nuclear industry) where conventional controllers hinder safety and efficiency.

Method: Design and evaluate a touchscreen interface that maps continuous finger motions to robot velocities, integrated visualization, and compare against a conventional joystick and a single-click autonomous mode. A 20-participant study used a Franka Emika Panda arm controlled remotely; tasks simulated surface manipulation; data collected included kinematic, physiological, and behavioral metrics, plus NASA-TLX for cognitive workload.

Result: Touchscreen outperformed the joystick: median completion time reduced by 53.5% (2.50 vs 5.38 min), in-area path coverage higher (90.7% vs 84.1%), and overshoot decreased. NASA-TLX dropped from 52 to 43 with touchscreen; autonomous mode achieved 31 (lowest). Overall, touchscreen provides improved performance with reduced cognitive load and latency-agnostic control.

Conclusion: A simple, easy-to-implement touchscreen interface can deliver more natural, precise teleoperation for surface tasks, reducing cognitive load versus traditional controllers; autonomous mode further minimizes workload, suggesting valuable integration in safety-critical remote manipulation.

Abstract: Intuitive teleoperation interfaces are crucial for the safe and effective operation of robotic manipulators in challenging environments. In the nuclear industry, surface contact tasks such as swab sampling require precise path and force tracking, obstacle avoidance, and sustained operator attention, which conventional joystick interfaces struggle to support effectively.
  This study designs and evaluates a novel touchscreen teleoperation interface that maps continuous finger movements directly to robotic manipulator motions, provides finer velocity control, and integrates control with visualization, enabling more natural, precise, and intuitive surface interaction than conventional controllers. A comparative user study with 20 participants evaluated task performance and workload using the proposed touchscreen, a conventional joystick, and a single-click autonomous mode. Tasks simulated realistic surface manipulation using a Franka Emika Panda arm, remotely controlled from another country. Kinematic, physiological, and behavioral data were recorded to comprehensively assess task performance, cognitive load, and operator trust across each control condition.
  Participants completed teleoperation tasks more efficiently and accurately with the touchscreen interface, achieving a 53.5% reduction in completion time (median: 2.50 vs. 5.38 min), higher in-area coverage on the sinusoidal path (90.7% vs. 84.1%), and lower overshoot on both path geometries compared with the joystick. Cognitive load, quantified via NASA-TLX (0-100), decreased from joystick to touchscreen (mean TLX 52 to 43; -9 points, -17.3%) and was lowest under the autonomous one-click mode (31; -21 points vs. joystick, -40.4%; -12 vs. touchscreen, -27.9%). This research presents an easy-to-implement touchscreen interface that improves performance in teleoperated surface tasks while reducing cognitive load.

</details>


### [316] [Robot Learning from Human Demonstrations: Handwritten Alphabet Trajectories and Human-Likeness Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06221)
*Alperen Kenan,Paul Bremner,Manuel Giuliani*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A comprehensive LfD framework for learning human-like robot motion using extended GMM/GMR, incorporating force and normalized time to handle multi-segment trajectories, evaluated via a perceptual study showing substantial human-likeness, with open-source data for benchmarking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable natural, trustworthy human-robot collaboration by generating human-like trajectories from demonstrations, generalizing to non-continuous, segmented motions with richer dynamic cues, and providing reproducible benchmarks.

Method: Extend Gaussian Mixture Model / Gaussian Mixture Regression for LfD by adding force and normalized time dimensions; collect a large handwriting dataset (3,142 demos from 22 participants across 52 Latin character-case combos) via touchscreen teleoperation; enable non-continuous, multi-segment trajectory generalization; evaluate with a perceptual user study using a 0–100 human-likeness scale; release data open-source.

Result: Mean human-likeness score 71.50 (SD=22.56); majority perceived as more human-like; participants identified geometric positioning and trajectory sequence as key perceptual factors; positive attitudes toward human-like robot behavior; datasets released for reproducible benchmarking.

Conclusion: The framework yields plausible, human-like motor trajectories and, with shared datasets, supports reproducible development of LfD-based methods for natural human-robot interaction.

Abstract: Learning from demonstration (LfD) provides a developmental framework through which robots can develop motor skills by observing and imitating human dynamics, reducing reliance on explicit programming to teach a skill to a robot. The resulting human-like robot motion is recognised as a key factor in building trust and enabling natural collaboration in human-robot interaction. This paper presents a framework for learning human-like robot motion from demonstration, including data collection, probabilistic trajectory learning, and perceptual user evaluation. A dataset of 3,142 handwriting demonstrations was collected from 22 participants across all 52 Latin alphabet character-case combinations via a touchscreen teleoperation interface, capturing planar position, contact force, and timing. Building on the widely used Gaussian Mixture Model and Gaussian Mixture Regression approach for learning from demonstration, the framework is extended in this work by incorporating force and normalised time dimensions to enable richer representation of human dynamics, and adapting it to handle non-continuous, multi-segment trajectories, enabling generalisation across demonstrations. A user study with 21 participants evaluated the perceived human-likeness of the generated trajectories using a continuous scale anchored between robotic and human-like motion, normalised to 0-100 where 50 represents the neutral midpoint. The generated trajectories achieved an overall human-likeness score of 71.50 (SD=22.56), indicating that the majority of trajectories were perceived as more human-like. Participants identified geometric positioning and trajectory sequence as the most influential perceptual factors, and reported positive attitudes toward human-like robot behaviour. The datasets are released as open-source, providing a reproducible benchmark for developing and evaluating human-like robot motion methods.

</details>


### [317] [GeniWorld: A Generalizable Interactive World Model for Robotic Manipulation via Visual Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06332)
*Chenghao Gu,Hanyang Yu,Jingbo Zhang,Haitao Lin,Wenyao Zhang,Jinghe Wang,Hanglei Jin,Shuzhao Xie,Jingyan Jiang,Zhi Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GeniWorld is an interactive, action-conditioned world model that decouples embodiment from dynamics to enable robust zero-shot generalization and data-efficient policy evaluation in robotics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalist robot policies struggle with robustness in unseen, real-world environments and action-conditioned world models often lack controllability and generalize poorly to out-of-distribution scenarios; scalable evaluation in diverse settings remains costly.

Method: Build on pretrained video generative models; apply URDF-based rendering to convert numerical actions into visual action representations; explicitly decouple embodiment kinematics from environmental dynamics; develop an autoregressive video predictor integrated with high-frequency robot kinematic control for closed-loop interaction with policies and teleoperators.

Result: Achieves superior in-domain performance and robust zero-shot generalization to highly randomized unseen environments even when trained on limited fixed-scene data; serves as a scalable policy evaluator under environmental perturbations; with limited demonstrations, generates diverse manipulation trajectories within the world model, improving downstream policy performance and robustness.

Conclusion: GeniWorld offers robust cross-scenario generalization, scalable policy Evaluation, and data-efficient trajectory generation by separating embodiment from dynamics and leveraging visual action representations with a high-frequency control loop.

Abstract: Generalist robot policies exhibit strong capabilities, but their robustness in complex and unseen environments remains limited. Scaling robot learning and evaluation in diverse real-world environments remains costly and challenging. Action-conditioned world models offer a promising alternative, but they often suffer from limited action controllability and poor generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. To this end, we present GeniWorld, an interactive world model for robots that generalizes robustly across unseen scenarios. Building on pretrained video generative models, we use URDF-based rendering to transform numerical actions into visual action representations, enabling spatially grounded action control. By explicitly decoupling embodiment kinematics from environmental dynamics, our model mitigates scene overfitting and facilitates modeling of robot-environment interactions. To achieve closed-loop control, we construct an autoregressive video prediction model integrated with high-frequency robot kinematic control, enabling interaction with both robot policies and human teleoperators. In our experiments, even when trained solely on limited fixed-scene data, our model achieves superior in-domain performance and robust zero-shot generalization to highly randomized, unseen environments. For downstream applications, GeniWorld serves as a scalable policy evaluator that remains reliable under environmental perturbations. Furthermore, even with limited real-world demonstrations, GeniWorld generates diverse manipulation trajectories within the world model, improving downstream policy performance and robustness in complex environments.

</details>


### [318] [A Master-Salve Robot Manipulator for Needle-Based Teleoperation in MRI Chamber](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06354)
*Omar Curiel,Jing-Yuan Huang,Po-Chih Chen,Ji Ma,Qing Dai,Wenqi Zhou,David Lu,Holden H. Wu,Tsu-Chin Tsao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MR-safe master-slave robot for MRI-guided abdominal interventions with 2+1 DoF controllers; uses remote fluid actuation and sub-mm precision; supports manual, digital, hybrid, and collaborative control; preliminary pig-in-vivo bedside results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable precise, real-time, MR-compatible robotic assistance for abdominal procedures inside the MRI bore, addressing safety, compatibility, and control flexibility challenges.

Method: A 2+1-DoF master manipulator drives a 2+1-DoF slave via fluid transmission. Elastomeric, high-input-impedance, low-leakage actuators handle remote angulation; graphite piston cylinders handle the needle insertion axis with sub-newton force transparency and sub-millimeter motion over bedside fluid piping. A digital master controller provides multimodal, collaborative control beyond split-axis or mode-switch hybrids. Real-time MRI integration supports manual, digital, hybrid, and collaborative modes; features include assisted tissue penetration, fault-driven virtual fixtures, and motion compensation via feedback. Preliminary results include an in-vivo pig experiment in bedside manual-control mode.

Result: Preliminary MRI scanner results show functional viability of the manipulator in a bedside setup, demonstrated in an in-vivo pig under manual control mode.

Conclusion: The system enables real-time MRI-guided interventions with multiple control modalities, achieving MR-compatibility and remote actuation for precise manipulation; initial feasibility is demonstrated, with future work needed on broader in-vivo validation, latency, safety, and control performance.

Abstract: We present a MR safe, master-slave robot manipulator for abdominal interventions in the MRI chamber. A human operated 2+1-DoF master controller manipulator transmits motion and force to a 2+1-DoF slave manipulator via fluid transmission. Jointly, a digital master controller provides multimodal control capability beyond common split axis or mode switchable hybrid human-digital controller configurations found in previous studies. High input impedance, low-leakage, elastomeric fluid actuators are delegated to remote angulation control. Low-friction graphite piston cylinders are delegated to needle insertion axis remote actuation given the sub-newton force transparency and sub-millimeter motion transmission over bedside fluid piping lengths. The device enables real-time MRI guided interventions allowing manual, digital, hybrid, and collaborative control modes. Collaborative tasks such as assisted tissue penetration, fault-driven virtual fixture, and motion compensation through feedback control are presented in this paper. Preliminary MR scanner results demonstrate manipulator functional viability for an in-vivo pig experiment in bedside, manual control mode configuration.

</details>


### [319] [DyPES-VLA: Learning Shared Dynamics Priors and Embodiment-Specific Control for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06374)
*Junfeng Li,Junjie He,Zhide Zhong,Yangyang Zheng,Pingyue Sheng,Jiayu Dong,Ruixin Li,Haodong Yan,Jiaguan Zhu,Tianran Zhang,Runze Yu,Wen Chen,Liuqing Yang,Yuxiang Gao,Haoang Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: DyPES-VLA is a cross-embodiment Vision-Language-Action model that learns shared dynamics priors via future prediction and uses an embodiment-specific Mixture-of-Experts head to map to each robot's native action space, achieving strong generalist policy performance across diverse embodiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome two limitations: (i) underutilization of dynamics priors across diverse visual/interaction data hindering cross-embodiment transfer, and (ii) reliance on manual preprocessing to align heterogeneous actions into a common format.

Method: 1) Train a Vision-Language Model with a future-prediction objective on cross-embodiment data to learn shared dynamics priors that capture object motion, contact, and scene changes. 2) Use an embodiment-specific Mixture-of-Experts action head that translates shared priors into executable controls in each embodiment's native action space, sharing attention layers and using embodiment-specific experts to handle kinematic constraints.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in both simulation and real-world tests: LIBERO 98.0%, RoboCasa-GR1 59.25%, RoboTwin 2.0 89.02%.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that cross-embodiment VLA is viable by decoupling dynamics priors from embodiment-specific control, enabling a generalist policy that transfers across robots with minimal manual alignment.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robot manipulation, but training a single generalist policy for heterogeneous robot embodiments remains an open problem. Existing methods have two main limitations. First, they underuse dynamics priors shared across diverse visual and interaction data, limiting cross-embodiment transfer.
