Second, they require extensive manual preprocessing to convert embodiment-specific actions into a common format. To overcome these limitations, we propose DyPES-VLA, a cross-embodiment VLA that learns shared Dynamics Priors and Embodiment-Specific control. First, we learn shared dynamics priors by training the vision-language model (VLM) with a future-prediction objective on cross-embodiment data, driving the shared query representation to capture object motion, contact, and interaction-induced scene changes. Second, an embodiment-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) action head translates these shared dynamics priors into executable controls directly in each embodiment's native action space, without manually pre-aligning heterogeneous actions into a common format. This head shares attention layers to capture common temporal action structures, while its embodiment-specific feed-forward experts resolve the unique kinematic constraints and control semantics of distinct embodiments. As a generalist policy, our \ourmethod achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-world evaluations, reaching 98.0% success on LIBERO, 59.25% on RoboCasa-GR1, and 89.02% on RoboTwin~2.0.

</details>


### [320] [$ω$-0: A Latent Predictive World Action Model for Concurrent Humanoid Loco-Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06375)
*Zhe Li,Zhenzhe Zhang,Yangyang Wei,Wenjie Zhang,Xichen Yuan,Peiyuan Zhi,Gen Li,Xinying Guo,Fengjie Gao,Jianfei Yang,Shanghang Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A latent predictive whole-body world-action model ω-0 enables real-world humanoid concurrent loco-manipulation by predicting controller-ready action latents from language, vision, and proprioception, using lightweight future observation embeddings and diffusion-based generation, trained on ω-HOME with 40+ hours of real data; outperforms baselines on 11 tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humanoid tasks demand simultaneous locomotion, posture control, balance, and manipulation. Current policies tend to decouple locomotion and manipulation, while world-action models are often arm-centric or video-centric. A unified, whole-body model conditioned on language and multi-view vision can enable seamless loco-manipulation in real robots.

Method: Train a latent predictive model ω-0 that maps language instruction, current egocentric/exocentric RGB and depth observations, and proprioceptive state to whole-body action latents suitable for a controller. Instead of video reconstruction, optimize a lightweight predictive objective of compact future observation embeddings and use diffusion-based generation to produce whole-body action latents. The model supports multiple input modalities and uses controller-based simulation replay to ground human/public visual priors into executable action latents. A new real-world dataset ω-HOME (>40 hours) with synchronized multi-view data, whole-body SMPL motions, robot states, and action latents.

Result: On 11 household tasks, a single ω-0 model generates smooth manipulate-while-moving behaviors and consistently outperforms representative imitation learning, VLA, humanoid, and WAM baselines.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of a latent, predictive whole-body world-action model for real-world humanoid loco-manipulation, highlighting benefits of solving prediction in latent observation space, leveraging diffusion-based action generation, and grounding priors with real-world data and simulation replay. The ω-HOME dataset provides a resource for future research.

Abstract: Humanoid household tasks often require concurrent loco-manipulation, where the robot must move, adjust posture, maintain balance, and manipulate objects as a single coordinated behavior. Yet existing humanoid policies typically decompose locomotion and manipulation, while recent world-action models remain either arm-centric or video-centered. We present $ω$-0, a latent predictive whole-body world-action model for real-world humanoid concurrent loco-manipulation. Given a language instruction, current visual observation, and robot proprioceptive state, $ω$-0 directly predicts controller-compatible whole-body action latents for real-robot execution. Rather than reconstructing future videos, $ω$-0 learns compact future observation embeddings as a lightweight predictive objective, coupling latent visual foresight with diffusion-based whole-body action generation. The model supports egocentric RGB, exocentric RGB, and exocentric depth inputs, and leverages controller-based simulation replay to ground human/public visual-motion priors into robot-executable action latents. We further collect $ω$-HOME, a 40+ hour real-world household humanoid dataset with synchronized multi-view observations, whole-body SMPL motions, robot states, and action latents. Real-world experiments on 11 household tasks demonstrate that a single $ω$-0 model can produce smooth manipulate-while-moving behaviors and consistently outperform representative imitation learning, VLA, humanoid, and WAM baselines.

</details>


<div id='cs.CG'></div>

# cs.CG [[Back]](#toc)

### [321] [NP-Hardness of Non-Crossing Hamiltonian Path and Cycle in Non-Planar Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06255)
*Randal Tuggle,Jack Snoeyink*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Direct 3-SAT to non-crossing Hamiltonian path/cycle reduction on non-planar graphs, separating hardness from planarity and avoiding planar gadgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hardness proofs for Hamiltonian path/cycle often rely on reducing to planar graphs, where non-crossing is automatic. This conflates two sources of difficulty. The work aims to isolate the hardness due to the non-crossing constraint.

Method: Provide a direct reduction from 3-SAT to the non-crossing Hamiltonian path and cycle problems on non-planar graphs, avoiding planar gadget constructions and ensuring the non-crossing constraint is the source of complexity.

Result: Shows NP-hardness of non-crossing Hamiltonian path/cycle on non-planar graphs by a direct reduction, disentangling the non-crossing constraint from planarity; yields a more transparent proof.

Conclusion: The approach clarifies the origin of difficulty, separating the non-crossing requirement from planarity, and offers a framework that may be easier to extend to related non-crossing problems.

Abstract: We seek to disentangle the hardness of finding a Hamiltonian path or cycle from the hardness of finding a non-crossing path or cycle by giving a direct reduction from 3-SAT to the non-crossing Hamiltonian path and cycle problems on non-planar graphs. Prior hardness proofs proceed by reduction to planar graphs, where every path is automatically non-crossing; this conflates the two sources of difficulty and leaves unclear why forbidding crossings on the path alone makes the problem hard. Our reduction places the difficulty squarely in the non-crossing constraint, avoids planar gadget constructions, and yields a more transparent proof that may be easier to extend to related problems.

</details>
